News.title: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
News.content:
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

News.title: Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military
News.content:
Similar contracts were signed by OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and the start-up Reflection, to allow AI technology to be deployed across a range of military settings such as transport, planning and battlefield operations.

As the tech quickly evolves, concerns are growing about the use of AI in theatres of war.

"AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment," said Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team.

"When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors."

Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticising the company.

"In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticising".

Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak."

A current employee at Google DeepMind, who declined to be named for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that "a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave â but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of the careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard."

Another Google DeepMind staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "A lot of people have left the company that feel strongly about this [how Google DeepMind has changed its ethics position]."

"Some people are putting up a fight, others are thinking: 'it's a big company. What do you expect to change?'", the employee said.

Google's agreements with Israel have also caused controversy. In 2024, the company was criticised by staff for a joint contract with Amazon worth $1.2bn (Â£960m) called Project Nimbus which provides Israel's government and military with AI technology and cloud computing infrastructure. At the time, Google said Project Nimbus "is not directed at highly sensitive, classified, or military workloads relevant to weapons or intelligence services".

Moreover, Israel's AI capabilities in warfare have been the focus of debate after they were featured in a recent documentary, Naza, which examines the role of AI-powered targeting systems to bombard the Gaza Strip, resulting in high civilian casualties. An Israeli government minister has said the claims presented in the film were false and distorted.

Former Google employee Andreas Kirsch believes AI technology in warfare is not ready for the battlefield. "Current AI models are not robust enough, and I don't think they have been trained for such tasks either," he said.

Additional reporting by Rosa Rahimi

News.title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
News.content:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.

The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.

Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.

The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.

Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.

The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X, external for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.

"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.

Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.

And in a post on X, external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.

"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.

That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.

Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.

They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.

News.title: Jailed former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson being investigated over alleged rape inside Parliament
News.content:
Jailed former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Jeffrey Donaldson is being investigated by London police about an alleged rape of a woman inside the Houses of Parliament, the BBC can reveal.

The disgraced former MP has been accused of raping the woman in Parliament in 2016, at the very heart of the political establishment.

Last week Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences against two victims, including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal against his convictions.

It is understood the woman has been interviewed by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officers.

The PSNI has now shared her claims with the Metropolitan Police, as the alleged incident happened in London.

While not naming the former DUP leader, the Met has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated.

It said: "On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report referred to us by the Police Service of Northern Ireland relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63.

"The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers.

"The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing."

In July, the Belfast Telegraph first reported that a woman from Northern Ireland alleged she had been sexually assaulted by Donaldson in the DUP offices at Parliament in 2016.

She claimed that he attempted to get her to drink vodka shots in his office, before trying to kiss her and put his hand up her skirt.

On Saturday, the newspaper further reported that the Met was set to investigate and interview Donaldson about these accusations.

But in response to BBC questions it has now emerged the same woman has also alleged Donaldson raped her.

Concerns about the ex-DUP MP's behaviour in London was raised in a BBC NI Spotlight film, earlier this year.

A former senior PSNI detective told the programme he had seen Donaldson drunk in the Houses of Parliament.

Two other former senior PSNI detectives also reported seeing him going into a gay sauna not far from Parliament in 2006, the same year in which Donaldson described homosexuality as "sinful".

News.title: Aberfan disaster 'most tragic of days imaginable' says King on 60th anniversary
News.content:
The King has described the Aberfan disaster which killed 116 children and 28 adults as the "most tragic of days imaginable" on its 60th anniversary.

Pantglas Junior School and a number of nearby houses in the village near Merthyr Tydfil, south Wales, were catastrophically engulfed in coal slurry after the colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966.

King Charles III, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales joined survivors and bereaved families on Wednesday and laid wreaths and a posy with the last surviving teacher in the Aberfan Memorial Garden, located on the site of the school.

The King also paid tribute to the community's strength, resilience and "unconquerable spirit".

Warning: This story contains upsetting details that some may find distressing

About half the children from the school died when excavated mining debris from the Merthyr Vale Colliery was dislodged, and 150,000 tonnes of coal waste came thundering down the hillside.

Emergency services, miners and people who rushed to the village began an around-the-clock battle to dig out those trapped by the debris.

News.title: 'I was only 8 but I realised my friend was dead' - Aberfan survivor recalls moment of disaster
News.content:
Four people who were children at the time of the Aberfan disaster recall the moment when a coal waste tip collapsed on schools and homes 60 years ago.

Gerald Kirwan told BBC Newsnight he thought it was an earthquake and found his classmate unresponsive, while his other classmate Gaynor Madgwick recalled waking up to finding herself buried up to her chest in the massive slurry.

Read more about this story here.

News.title: Don't Stop Believin'! - high school musical Glee set for reboot
News.content:
We never stopped believin'... now it's official: Glee, the Emmy-winning US high school musical comedy drama, is set to return.

Ryan Murphy's series, which chronicled the highs and lows of choir members from Ohio, premiered on Fox in 2009 and ran for six seasons until 2015.

The original cast included Lea Michele, Amber Riley, the late Cory Monteith, Jane Lynch and Matthew Morrison as Will Schuester, the optimistic teacher leading the fictional McKinley High's glee club.

The reboot was announced, external by Disney and Hulu via the show's social media team on Wednesday.

The show was a huge hit first time around, known for its big laughs and big heart, tackling topics such as sexuality, race, disability and mental health.

In the series, glee club New Directions helped misfit students find their voices through song and dance.

Lynch served as the club's main antagonist, the villainous cheerleading coach Sue Sylvester.

The choir's covers of Don't Stop Believin', River Deep, Mountain High and Smooth Criminal also brought older hit songs to the attention of younger audiences.

In 2010, the show was adapted for a concert tour in which was captured on film.

Around the same time, the cast overtook The Beatles as the non-solo act with the most Billboard Hot 100 appearances.

On Wednesday, the Wanted singer Max George told BBC Scotland that appearing in the show's sixth season was "an amazing experience", adding that he'd "love to do it again".

"I messaged the casting director from it, just with wide eyes from the announcement," he said.

Asked if it makes sense for the series to come back, he said: "I think soâ¦ It's been over 10 years, so I think that's a nice break.

"I think it was probably coming towards the end in terms of the storylines and everything, but 10 years has gone by, and Ryan Murphy will probably come up with something genius. So I'm expecting big things."

News.title: Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review
News.content:
The review into antisemitism in schools and colleges in England was led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell and presented to Parliament on Wednesday.

Powell told the BBC it marked a "generational moment" to re-educate young people, among whom she said the issue of antisemitism was "particularly prevalent".

She said: "It's definitely a crisis and I think it's actually got worse since Sir David began this review. This has become a real challenge for Jewish people in our country, but also Jewish students and Jewish teachers working in our schools and colleges.

"I do really feel it is a generational moment to educate this generation and the next â that is the job of education â to understand what antisemitism is in the modern world."

Speaking on Holocaust education, the education secretary said new lessons will "challenge" some of the concepts that young people have.

The review also calls for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers.

Powell told the House of Commons "teachers should not bring their own political views into the classroom" but they should not avoid discussing important topics.

The review was launched following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed.

Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws.

The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse.

It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters.

The review also recommends that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism.

Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.

He told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries."

Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.

Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role.

"When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said.

"We think about it a lot."

In response to the recommendations, the government will also encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.

The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.

However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".

In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."

Rabbi Charley Baginksy and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leads of the Movement for Progressive Judaism, said that the report "exposes serious failures in how schools recognise and respond to antisemitism".

They said: "Alongside that urgent question of how schools deal with hatred and educate about Jewish persecution, we also need to ensure they teach about Jewish creativity, music, literature, humour and the extraordinary pleasure of belonging to this diverse tradition."

Dan Green, Chief Executive of the Anne Frank Trust UK, said the review "confirms what we see in classrooms every day".

"Antisemitism in our schools is real, it is widespread, and too often it goes unrecognised and unchallenged."

"One-off assemblies are not enough, and neither is sitting pupils in front of a video. Young people need the space to ask difficult questions, challenge their own assumptions and understand that antisemitism did not start or end with the Holocaust."

The National Education Union raised concerns about creating a "hierarchy of racism" and adopting the IHRA definition.

It said the latter risked "blurring the line between antisemitism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government and the genocide in Gaza".

The union welcomed a "strengthened focus on antisemitism" while underlining that "no form of racism should be minimised".

Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.

It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year.

News.title: Lawyer caught offering to make illegal-worker fine go away
News.content:
A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a Â£45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine, if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

At least Â£150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures obtained by the BBC.

In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

In a statement, she said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

Many business owners do not take the fines seriously, a law enforcement official has told us anonymously.

She told us she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth Â£40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

When she had asked a member of staff if the business owners intended to pay, she said she had been told: "'It's got nothing to do with me.'"

News.title: Teenage boy guilty of trying to murder girl, 15, in school
News.content:
A teenage boy who had a hatred of women and an "obsessive interest" in killers has been found guilty of the attempted murder of a girl at his school.

The boy dressed in black and wore a face mask before stabbing the 15-year-old victim in the back at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, in March.

Armed police were called to the school, which went into lockdown, and the attack was caught on CCTV.

The boy, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, wrote notes about hating women and had an "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing", jurors at King's Lynn Crown Court were told. He will be sentenced on 18 December.

Jurors deliberated for just under four hours before delivering a majority verdict at the end of a trial which began two weeks ago.

The teenager "went to school not to learn, but to kill" while armed with a kitchen knife, the prosecution said.

The school went into lockdown after the attack and there was an armed police response, while the girl was taken to hospital with a minor injury.

News.title: Woman told Russell Brand he 'treated her like an animal', court hears
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

One of the women who claims Russell Brand raped her later told him he had "treated her like an animal", a court has heard.

The comedian's trial at Southwark Crown Court in London has been hearing recorded police interviews with a female complainant, who claims she did not consent to anal sex with him at his house in 2009.

Brand, 51, denies three charges of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one charge of indecent assault. He has said he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

On Wednesday, the jury heard an interview with a woman who says she first met Brand at one of his comedy shows at Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.

She said she had a boyfriend at the time but went to his dressing room, where she performed a sex act on him.

The woman said it was during their next meeting at his house when the sex was not consensual and she had only agreed to vaginal sex.

Asked by the detective in the interview whether there was ever a conversation about anal sex, she replied: "No."

She said she was surprised to receive a "random" text message from Brand six months later, saying he wanted to "push her further".

She said she replied asking: "Why are you even messaging me?"

"I remember his response, saying, 'Because you're dirty and I want to push you further'."

The jury heard that the woman did not respond straight away because she was upset, but then replied saying: "I think you've pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal."

The woman added: "I do remember his response was immediate. He said, 'I'm sorry'."

News.title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.

These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.

Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.

But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock Â£27 off a typical annual bill.

During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".

He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".

No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate, external, so people pay for what they use.

This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more.

For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.

Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.

News.title: MP harassed for 'being English' by man who took axe to pub
News.content:
A man who harassed a Labour MP for being "English", and claimed he knew where he lived, has been given a suspended jail sentence.

Michael Glover, 59, left a note on Mid and South Pembrokeshire MP Henry Tufnell's office door in Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, on 10 March, and carried an axe to the pub the following day.

In the letter, which he signed, he also wrote that he had taken "a look around" Tufnell's family home and had "left some presents".

The MP said he felt "uneasy" that the defendant said he knew where he lived with his family, including his newborn baby.

Swansea Crown Court heard Glover, who is a wheelchair user and has "complex mental health difficulties", was "frustrated" because of a delay in his application for a blue badge.

The court heard that CCTV captured the defendant taping a bag, which contained the letter, to the front door of Tufnell's office. He then made "gestures" to the camera before driving away.

On 11 March, he carried an axe in a plastic bag to a local pub, and picked it up in front of a member of the public.

Glover was arrested that day, and later pleaded guilty to both charges at the magistrates' court.

Regan Walters, prosecuting, read a victim personal statement by Tufnell, who said the incident made him feel "uncomfortable".

"Knowing that Glover knows where I live with my wife and young child has made me rethink things, such as the security of my address," the politician said.

He said he had to be mindful that his "panic alarms and CCTV cameras are working" and that, when he worked away, he felt "on edge, wondering if [his family] are safe".

Joseph Hocquard, representing Glover, said his client had been in custody for the past four months for breaching a probation order, which he said had been "incredibly challenging" because of his mental health and disabilities.

Glover appeared via video link with his barrister in the cells at Swansea Crown Court because of a "technical issue" with the lift in the building.

Judge Mark Powell KC told him "members of parliament are there to advocate for their constituents".

He said: "They are entitled to go about their business, without being subject to the sort of threats and harassment that you carried outâ¦ regardless of if they are English or not English."

He also said that brandishing an axe in public would have been "extremely frightening for those around" but that he "didn't intend to harm anyone".

The judge told the court that it was "frustration" and a "deterioration in his mental state" that led to Glover committing the offence.

He said he was satisfied the defendant had shown remorse for both offences, and that he needed support and medication for his "complex mental health" needs.

Judge Powell gave him a six-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, as well as a five-year restraining order.

He was also ordered to pay a victim surcharge of Â£154.

News.title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
News.content:
The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than Â£284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent".

Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood.

He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021.

The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs.

He told the court that staff and managers at the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had jobs elsewhere.

At the height of the alleged deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector.

In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.

Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid Â£11,000 for a single month's work in 2023.

Chowdhury said the jobs were a "lifeline" during a time his mother's health had declined.

Asked by defence barrister Pieter Briegel what extent stress in his life was due to the number of jobs, he replied: "The jobs at the time were my lifeline at the time, that was what I survived on at that particular moment.

"And they gave me a link to the outside, they were the only thing I had to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time," he told the court.

News.title: Tributes paid to 'bravest' woman who died of 'stab wounds' after crash
News.content:
Tributes have been paid to a woman who crashed a car into a wall after allegedly being stabbed.

Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to the crash in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision", which the BBC understands were sustained in a stabbing.

A 61-year-old man from Bridgend has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a "significant" police operation at a retirement housing complex, and remains in custody.

Eleanor, who worked for housing association Valleys to Coast which runs the complex, has been described by her family as the "kindest, most loving, bravest person in the world".

South Wales Police said Eleanor was taken to hospital after officers were called to the crash on Coity Road at about 12:40 BST on Monday, but later died.

Police were also called to nearby sheltered housing retirement complex, Ger-y-Nant, where the man was arrested.

Describing Eleanor, from North Cornelly, Bridgend, her family said: "She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock."

Jo Oak, chief executive of Valleys to Coast, added the organisation was "devastated by the tragic death of our colleague".

"Eleanor was a much-valued member of the Valleys to Coast team, and her loss has been deeply felt by everyone who knew and worked alongside her," she said.

"She made an important contribution to our organisation and to the communities we serve, and she will be remembered with great warmth and affection by her colleagues.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Eleanor's family and friends at this unimaginably difficult time."

Oak said the organisation would "continue to cooperate fully with South Wales Police".

Ch Supt Jason Rees said: "Our thoughts remain firmly with Eleanor's family. I want to assure the community that teams of detectives and specialist staff are investigating.

"We appreciate the patience and support of residents, especially those displaced following the incident. Local communities may notice an increased police presence as our investigation continues."

News.title: Crystal Palace urged to retire bald eagle mascot
News.content:
An animal rights group is urging Crystal Palace to retire their live bald eagle mascot with immediate effect, saying a "bright stadium filled with boisterous fans is no place for animals".

In a letter to Palace CEO Sharon Lacey, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) asked the Premier League club to stop using the eagle, named Phoenix, in pre-match displays at Selhurst Park and to never use live animal mascots again.

The London team, known as the Eagles since 1973, introduced a live eagle to matchdays in 2010. Kayla, who died in 2020, performed the role for 10 years and her replacement Phoenix made her debut against West Ham in August 2024.

Peta says birds can become "frightened, disoriented and panicked" in stadium environments, putting themselves and fans at risk.

Using them for displays and entertainment also denies the animals, who "would naturally avoid humans", the opportunity to engage with their natural instincts, leading to "frustration and stress", the group said.

The organisation has "detailed records" of incidents involving live mascots, including birds, being injured or killed in collisions with walls, windows and match balls, as well as a falcon embedding its talons in a spectator's scalp after landing on his head.

In 2017, a Charlton Athletic fan was found guilty of trying to punch Kayla the eagle at a League Cup fixture two years earlier.

"Many professional sports teams use only willing humans as mascots and the club already has Pete the Eagle to excite the crowd," said Dr Carys Bennett, Peta's senior corporate projects manager.

"Bald eagles are widely recognised as symbols of freedom. They deserve better than to be used as an entertainment prop to amuse the Eagles' fans."

BBC Sport has contacted Crystal Palace for comment.

News.title: Bayern Munich v Arsenal LIVE: Kane sets up superb Bayern equaliser after Saka injury blow
News.content:

Bayern Munich host Arsenal in a Champions League blockbuster and an early meeting of two sides who will be looking to go all the way in Europe this season.

The Gunners suffered heartbreak against Paris Saint-Germain in last season’s final but made a step further than the German champions, who were knocked out by the eventual winners in an epic semi-final.

Arsenal managed just one shot on target in their 1-0 win at Nottingham Forest on Sunday with the Premier League champions coming under some criticism for the style of their attack under Mikel Arteta this season.

But Arsenal are yet to concede a goal in the Champions League this term and will put their formidable defence up against Bayern’s free-scoring attack. Harry Kane will look to add to his 15 career goals against Arsenal, although Michael Olise is suspended.

News.title: California man claimed ICE snatched his wife. Cops now say he killed her
News.content:

A California man, who claimed ICE agents snatched his wife from their home, has been charged with murder after her burned remains were discovered, police say.

Gurinder Gill, 28, was arrested October 14 after investigators determined that human remains found in neighboring El Dorado County belonged to Jasmine Gill, 30, the Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office announced.

Jasmine Gill was last seen at the couple’s Sacramento home September 30. Her cousin reported her missing October 4, prompting an investigation into her disappearance.

During the initial inquiry, Gurinder allegedly told investigators that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents had taken his wife into custody while she was checking the mail at their home. Sacramento detectives subsequently contacted ICE which said no enforcement activity had taken place at the residence, authorities said.

Investigators then noticed several inconsistencies in Gurinder Gill’s statements and learned that the couple was in the middle of a divorce and child custody dispute, according to the sheriff’s office.

open image in gallery Jasmine Gill, 30, was missing for nearly two weeks before her burned remains were found ( GoFundMe )

At the beginning of October, burned human remains were discovered in El Dorado County, about 70 miles from the couple’s Sacramento home. Authorities later confirmed the remains belonged to Jasmine Gill.

Homicide detectives obtained an arrest warrant for her estranged husband, who was booked into Sacramento County Main Jail on murder charges. Authorities have not provided additional details about the alleged killing.

Jasmine Gill was a registered nurse and mother to an eight-month-old son. Her family described her in a GoFundMe campaign as “daughter, a sister, a nurse, and a mother who deserved so much more.”

“Jasmine lost her father at a young age. Jasmine's mother, a single mother worked full-time as a nurse in India, while raising Jasmine and her brother, making countless sacrifices to give her children a better future,” her family wrote on the fundraising page. “Inspired by her mother’s strength, Jasmine followed in her footsteps and became a registered nurse herself.”

open image in gallery Gurinder Gill has been charged with the murder of his wife Jasmine Gill in California ( Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office )

Her relatives said Jasmine had been seeking a divorce to secure a safe, fresh start for herself and her baby before her death.

Donations will help cover the cost of bringing Jasmine’s remains to her mother in India, funeral arrangements and expenses related to the baby’s care, future and any necessary legal proceedings.

“Jasmine's life mattered. Her dreams mattered. Her baby's future matters. Our goal is to help Jasmine’s family during this devastating period and ensure her baby’s future and welfare are protected,” her family wrote.

News.title: NFL chief speaks out on Eagles' handling of Jalen Hurts blood clots
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The NFL is open to an inquiry into the Philadelphia Eagles’ handling of Jalen Hurts’ blood clots after a request from the players’ union, Commissioner Roger Goodell stated Wednesday.

Speaking at a news conference marking the conclusion of the NFL's annual fall meeting, Goodell stated that Dr. Allen Sills, the league's chief medical officer, reviewed the procedures that took place, noting that the union was entirely within its rights to request a formal review.

"Obviously, there was a medical evaluation, and I think our protocols were incredibly good there," Goodell said. "The protocols were followed. Our process is to make sure that’s the case, and our chief medical officer has gone through that, so we’re comfortable that what we’ve seen in the protocols have happened."

On Tuesday, Sills mounted a firm defense of the Eagles’ medical team. The NFL confirmed that officials communicated with team doctors, trainers, and representatives from the Cleveland Clinic in London.

open image in gallery Roger Goodell has spoken out following Hurts' diagnosis ( AP )

League executive vice president Jeff Miller indicated that officials possessed a clear understanding of the timeline. Miller denied claims that Hurts had gone without sleep for over 30 hours prior to the October 11 game against Jacksonville, explaining that the quarterback went back to his hotel and slept for approximately seven to eight hours.

Hurts has been placed on injured reserve and is anticipated to miss the remainder of the season after a blood clot originating in his left calf reached his lungs. On Monday, the Eagles alongside agent Nicole Lynn confirmed that Hurts is being treated for deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary embolisms. His recovery plan requires blood thinners, prohibiting him from engaging in any football activities while on the medication.

Goodell minimized suggestions that international travel might have played a role in the situation.

"The most important thing here is Jalen’s health, ultimately, and the future of him," Goodell said. "He’s a wonderful young man: not just a great player, but he’s someone we all care deeply about. I’m more worried about his health, ultimately, but the protocols were followed."

Sills noted on Tuesday that clearance for air travel with a blood clot condition relies on multiple factors, such as the specific location of the clot and patient history.

"What I can tell you is expert people getting a lot of opinions," Sills said. "This isn’t just one doctor saying yay or nay. You’re going to poll a panel of experts both within the team and outside the team to get the best judgment and experience with a particular condition."

News.title: Roseanne Barr confesses to writing ‘extra make out scenes’ in hopes that new co-star will leave his wife for her
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Roseanne Barr is on the hunt for a showmance with her new co-star.

Eight years after the 73-year-old comedian was exiled from her hit ABC show Roseanne over a series of racist tweets, the Emmy-winning actor is returning to the TV world with a new self-financed sitcom, Meemaw: A Modern Day Fable.

The single-camera show, which has yet to be picked up by a network or distributor, follows Barr in the lead role as a “patriotic grandmother who is the matriarch of a mixed-race prepper family in Texas,” she told The Hollywood Reporter in an interview published Wednesday.

Barr’s sitcom co-stars Sopranos alum Drea de Matteo as her daughter, Omar Gooding as her son-in-law, and fellow Donald Trump supporter Randy Quaid as the local sheriff — who, spoiler alert, becomes her love interest.

“I’m in love with him and I wish he would leave his wife and marry me,” Barr told the magazine. She added: “I enjoyed making out with him so much that I wrote extra scenes where we would make out.”

open image in gallery Roseanne Barr and Randy Quaid play love interests on the comedian's new sitcom ( X/Randy Quaid )

Quaid, 76, has been married to his wife, Evi, for 37 years. Meanwhile, Barr has been with her boyfriend, Johnny Argent, since 2003.

In response to Barr’s praise, Quaid said in a statement to Entertainment Weekly: “Her show’s title should be changed to I LOVE ROSEANNE She’s luuuuscious...”

Barr described Meemaw as “the funniest s*** I’ve ever done,” telling THR, “I had a ball and I play a really wacky old lady this time.”

Roseanne was a smash hit during its original run from 1988 to 1997. The family comedy starred Barr, John Goodman, Laurie Metcalf, Sara Gilbert and Michael Fishman.

open image in gallery Roseanne Barr is starring in a new single-camera sitcom that is currently being shopped ( Getty )

The show was successfully rebooted in 2018, but spiraled into chaos when Barr was fired months after the premiere over her controversial tweets, one of which compared former President Barack Obama’s advisor, Valerie Jarrett, to an “ape.” She later apologized, claiming that she had been on Ambien while writing the post and that she did not know Jarrett was Black.

The reboot was brought back without Barr as The Conners, which aired its last episode in 2025.

Barr told THR that she is not in contact with any of her former co-stars, and that she was devastated when Fishman, who played her son on the original show, said earlier this year that Roseanne was “rightfully canceled.”

“Nobody is more brokenhearted than me,” she told the outlet. “I just choose to remember the fun and the good times. My son called Goodman and asked him to do a cameo on Meemaw and he declined.”

News.title: Bruno Fernandes unhappy with Michael Carrick’s tactics in dismal Man United defeat to Como
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes wasn’t impressed by the tactic of Michael Carrick during his side’s humiliating 4-1 defeat to Como in the Champions League.

United were outrun, outfought and outplayed by their Italian opponents, with Nico Paz in particular running the visitors ragged – notching two goals and an assist for Cesc Fabregas’s well-drilled side.

It was one of United’s worst performances in their long and storied European history and extends their winless run in all competitions to seven matches and ramp up the pressure on Carrick, who may well be on the brink of the sack.

open image in gallery Man United skipper Bruno Fernandes wasn’t happy with the tactics employed by the coaching staff ( Reuters )

Fernandes was largely ineffective once again as the Red Devils failed to gain a foothold before he was substituted off on 67 minutes, a rare move for the ever-present skipper, and his replacement Joshua Zirkzee scored an injury-time consolation.

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Fernandes criticised United’s tactics, specifically their lack of pressing which gave Como too much time and left them somewhat toothless.

“It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” said Fernandes.

When asked whether he was saying that Carrick got his tactics wrong, the Portuguese added: “That's on the manager and staff to see, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable.

“As you saw with them [Como], the centre-back was coming to mark me in my own half. We need to do that as a team but we were unable to.

“A team that plays through the middle with small connections, if you give them too much time and space then they can hurt you out wide.”

open image in gallery Fernandes was dejected after another defeat for Man United ( Reuters )

Midfielder Youri Tielemans admitted the performance wasn’t up to scratch, saying: “It was a very bad match from us. The fans come out here and we put out a non-performance like this, it's not good enough from us.”

The pressure is mounting on Carrick, with Sunday’s home match against Bournemouth now taking on even more importance.

And former United striker Dimitar Berbatov, speaking on TNT after the game, didn’t pull any punches when discussing the Red Devils’ display.

open image in gallery Dimitar Berbatov wasn’t impressed by United ( Getty )

“It was a terrible, terrible night,” said Berbatov. “A terrible game for United, nothing was happening and Como outplayed them in every way possible.

“From the goals, from the taking the ball, the possession, the confidence. Everything was there for Como. It was like they were playing a second team. Look at the first goal, the confidence on the ball, the time on the ball.

“Sometimes it’s not about the loss, it’s about how you lose, and today that was the point, how we lost that game of football.

“After a performance like this, probably, like every time, are these the right players to compete on the highest stage? Is that the right manager? Is this the right way? Of course after games like this, people will say we need more players, we need better players, we need this and that.

“What can you say after a performance like this? Today it didn’t look like everyone was giving their best on the pitch. Como looked like they were just having fun. It looked like men against kids.”

News.title: Trump weighs in after his envoy calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump on Wednesday seconded his roving peace envoy’s obsequious description of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” and praised the autocratic leader for having released an American his government had taken hostage after Trump waived bipartisan sanctions meant to hinder Moscow’s war against Ukraine.

Earlier in the day, Witkoff, a real estate developer with no experience in diplomacy who Trump has nonetheless tasked with international negotiations normally entrusted to the Secretary of State, praised Putin and credited him with saying nice things about Trump during a meeting that was recorded and released on Russian state media.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again,” Witkoff said.

Asked about the exchange and pressed on whether he agreed with Witkoff, Trump offered a qualified “yes” to the query.

“Well, I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out. But you know, I I wouldn't say anything one way or the other,” he said.

U.S. President Donald Trump (C) gestures as he departs with U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche (L) and U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin following a roundtable discussion on cybercrime in the East Room of the White House ( Getty )

The president then falsely claimed that Russia has “not gotten involved with Iran,” seemingly ignorant of the fact that Iran and Russia have a longstanding relationship that has seen both governments assist each other in their respective efforts to undermine Western-aligned governments — and the United States itself.

Trump’s comments came hours after Putin announced the release of imprisoned US citizen Stephen Hubbard following a plea for his release from his American counterpart, who had previously suggested his decision to allow Russia to continue to sell diesel fuel despite sanctions enacted by Congress was part of a gambit to secure Hubbard’s release.

Hubbard, 74, had been held in Russian custody since April 2022 and was serving a nearly seven-year prison sentence in a penal colony for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, charges he denies.

Putin told US special envoy Steve Witkoff that the former schoolteacher was at the St Petersburg Pulkovo airport and waiting to fly back to the US with him. Witkoff thanked him for the goodwill gesture.

The US envoy flew into Russia's second city on Wednesday morning to review new ideas on ending the war in Europe, with allies anxious that president Trump appears to be turning away from Kyiv while firming up relations with Moscow.

President Trump welcomed the news of Hubbard’s release on Wednesday, claiming the retired schoolteacher was released at his request in a telephone call with Putin last week.

“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia,” the president said.

“There was no “swap” necessary for this release. This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin.”

Following a closed trial, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary in October 2024 and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison.

James Reynolds and Liam Gilliver contributed reporting from London

News.title: Thinking of hitting the drive-thru? It may still be fast, but it’s no longer cheap
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A drive-thru used to be a quick way to get a cheap meal - they’re still quick, but recent inflation data indicates they aren’t cheap.

Fast-food prices went up 3.8 percent year on year in September, while groceries rose 1.8 percent, according to federal figures published in October.

Whether by cause or coincidence, 67 percent of consumers are spending less at restaurants this year compared to last year, according to a September report from restaurant consultancy Popmenu.

“Restaurants have pushed menu prices about as far as they can go,” Popmenu CEO Brendan Sweeney said. “Consumers are looking for value and incentives to come back.”

Indeed, the typical price range of a fast-food combo meal has risen from between $6 and $7.50 in 2020 to between $9.50 and $12.50 in 2026, according to price tracking site DriveThruPrices.

Fast food isn’t immune to inflation, and that’s causing consumers to rethink whether a quick stop at a burger-joint drive-thru is worth the cost ( AP2010 )

That has led some to swap fast food for items in their fridge as American consumers struggle with high prices on everyday essentials such as food and gas.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed the country’s affordability issues, saying at a Kentucky campaign stop this past Saturday that “we’re in the golden age of America” and that “our nation is doing better now than ever before.”

“We’re in the golden age of America,” Trump said Saturday at a Kentucky campaign stop. “So our nation is doing better now than ever before.”

Data from multiple sources tell a different story.

Inflation rose 3.7 percent in September after holding steady at 3.5 percent in July and August, according to a Bureau of Labor Statistics report released earlier this month. It was the second-highest inflation reading in the past three years, according to bureau data.

On October 14, U.S. gas prices broke an all-time record by averaging at least $4 a gallon nationally for 158 consecutive days, according to Patrick De Haan, head petroleum analyst at fuel-price tracking site GasBuddy.

Those looking to buy a home have watched mortgage rates soar from 6.66 percent in August to 7.4 percent this week, data from mortgage firm Freddie Mac shows.

As a result, consumers have been cutting back on non-essential spending, including restaurants, for at least six months.

In April, consumers planned to spend more on essentials such as groceries and automatic needs and less on non-necessary items, a report from accounting firm KPMG revealed.

“To offset these rising costs, planned discretionary spending is on track to continue its two-year decline, with reductions forecast across almost every non-essential category,” the April report said.

“This trade-off extends to the dinner table. Sixty-seven percent of consumers are eating at home more often than dining out.”

News.title: Josh Brolin shares the key to his 12 years of sobriety
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Josh Brolin has shared the secret to maintaining his 12 years of sobriety.

Speaking in a new interview touching on his career and sobriety journey, Brolin — currently starring in the new film Whalefall — shared the constant that keeps him on track.

“I do a meeting every morning at 6 a.m. on Zoom,” the 58-year-old told The Telegraph in an interview published Saturday.

“Drinking got boring in the end,” he continued. “I woke up on the sidewalk outside my house, yet again, and it felt like a fork in the road. Which way was I going to go for the rest of my life?”

Brolin added: “I love being sober. I’m having way more fun now than I ever did drinking, and I never end up in jail, which is a real bonus.”

open image in gallery Josh Brolin attends a meeting every morning to help maintain his sobriety ( Getty )

The No Country for Old Men star recalled his journey to sobriety, including an incident when he was 19 years old in which he assaulted six police officers.

“I was drunk and thought I was Bruce Lee,” he told the publication. “The court offered to reduce the sentence if I went to rehab and got sober, so that’s what I did. I ended up doing a few months in jail and then living in a halfway house with 15 other guys.”

Brolin told The Independent last year that he went into rehab and joined Alcoholics Anonymous after a particularly challenging 2013, which culminated with an incident that left him on the pavement outside his house.

“I shouldn’t have ended up where I ended up,” said Brolin. “And that doesn’t mean successful; it just means survived.”

open image in gallery Brolin is currently starring in the new film ‘Whalefall’ ( Getty )

Brolin got his start in the Steven Spielberg-produced 1985 film, The Goonies. He’s since appeared in dozens of films and television series including Milk, Sicario and the Dune films, as well as Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame, in which he played the villainous Thanos.

But he told The Independent that one experience required a transformation that left him full of panic.

The actor portrayed Cable, a cybernetic soldier from the future, in the 2018 superhero sequel Deadpool 2, for which he wore heavy prosthetic makeup to create the character’s distinctive facial scar, and he claimed the application was so intense that “most people can’t do it.”

“They do this thing – it’s a practical thing where they cover your head in clay and all that and then it hardens to get an impression of your head and your face,” he said.

“When they do it, it gets hot and it hardens and then slowly you start to lose your hearing. I remember I had a pad and I wrote at one point, ‘Mild panic.’ I remember hearing a voice – even though it was close, it sounded really far away, and it was like, ‘You’re gonna be fine,’ and they’re holding your hand and all that kind of stuff.”

News.title: Ebola case confirmed in Nigeria as outbreak spreads through Africa
News.content:
African ministers have been called to an urgent health summit after Nigeria confirmed its first case in the outbreak of the deadly Ebola fever tearing through eastern Congo.

Confirmation of a case in Africa’s most populous nation came days after a cluster was detected in Kenya and has heightened questions about border screening checks designed to stop the virus spreading from its epicentre in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

With cases now found in West Africa, Central Africa and East Africa, the epidemic “has already become the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in history,” said Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the continent’s main public health body.

DRC has recorded close to 10,000 cases since an outbreak began in mid-May, with around half of them dying of the haemorrhagic fever.

The Nigeria case meant “Ebola is now affecting three regions of Africa,” warned Dr Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

“The situation demands urgent action and political leadership at the highest level,” he said, convening an online summit for next week.

News.title: One billion children at risk from heatwaves, WHO warns
News.content:
More than one billion children are exposed to increasingly severe heat waves, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.

1.5 billion children under one experienced a fivefold increase in the number of heat wave days in 2024 compared with the 1986 to 2005 baseline period, jumping from roughly four days per year to a high of over 20, says the health agency. And these periods of high temperature are becoming longer, more frequent and more severe, the WHO warns.

According to the Met Office, this summer was the hottest on record in the UK, with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days where the temperature was above 30 degrees celsius. Europe also saw record-breaking temperatures, and Asia and Africa both experienced their warmest July on record, according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

Four UN agencies, including the WHO, the WMO, Unicef and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), have urged countries to monitor how extreme heat affects pregnant women, newborns and children.

The new framework tracks preterm birth, stillbirths, low birthweight, pregnancy hypertension, child deaths and health facility visits.

“Heat is already affecting our most vulnerable populations, including pregnant women, newborns and children. But what health systems do not count, they cannot respond to,” said Dr Pascale Allotey, director of WHO’s department of maternal and child health.

“By tracking outcomes such as preterm birth, child deaths and illnesses, and health-facility visits alongside heat exposure, countries can identify potential impacts and take action to protect women and children,” she said.

High temperatures are particularly dangerous for pregnant women because the body has to work much harder to cool both the mother and the baby.

Intense heat can cause surface-level blood vessels to dilate, which in pregnant women can restrict blood flow to the placenta and reduce the amount of oxygen and nutrients that reach the foetus. Heat can also put strain on the cardiovascular system, increasing the risk of gestational diabetes, dangerously high blood pressure, and pre-eclampsia.

The odds of a preterm birth also increase by 26 per cent during heatwaves: for every one degree rise in heat exposure, the likelihood of giving birth early rise by roughly 4 per cent, according to a systematic review published in Nature Medicine.

The WHO has also urged countries to develop and implement tailored heat-health action plans that account for the needs of pregnant women, newborns and children, as well as strengthening early-warning systems to ensure timely action to heat risks, such as alert systems and personalised public messaging.

“As our world continues to heat up, it creates new risks for health, and older people, pregnant women, newborns and children are among those least able to escape them,” said Bruce Gordon, director of environment and climate change at the WHO.

“Our health systems need the data to recognise this reality and take action – from protecting people during heatwaves to embedding climate risk consideration into everyday health services,” he said.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe
News.content:
Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he said, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas, who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

News.title: Inflation jumps in run-up to Healey’s maiden Budget
News.content:
Inflation has jumped to its highest level in almost a year, underlining the challenges facing John Healey, the Chancellor, ahead of his first Budget next week.

The consumer prices index climbed from 3.1pc in August to 3.5pc in September, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Inflation was ahead of the 3.4pc predicted by economists and is now at its highest level since October 2025.

The sharp rise was driven by soaring fuel costs as a result of the Iran war. The ONS said average petrol prices rose by 8.2p a litre in September and diesel by 10.7p. Both reached levels not seen since 2022, in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said: “Rising inflation is turning the Budget into a perilous high-wire act for the Chancellor, increasing pressure for cost-of-living support while pushing up government borrowing costs, which is shrinking fiscal headroom and narrowing his policy options.”

Britain spent more money on debt interest last month than in any September on record, official figures show.

The UK’s debt servicing costs rose to £10.9bn in September, the highest total for the month since at least 1997, according to the ONS.

This burden helped to push national debt above £3 trillion for the first time.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said the unhappy milestone and the rise in inflation “show Labour has lost control of the economy”.

Public sector net debt has soared by 50pc since it first exceeded £2tn in June 2020.

Mr Healey insisted the British economy still had “momentum” and pointed to Wednesday morning’s approval of new drilling for gas in the North Sea as evidence of this.

He said: “We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide. Last week, the IMF said our UK fiscal discipline stands out with the lowest forecast deficit in the G7 by 2029.

“And today we’ve given the green light to getting North Sea gas from the Jackdaw field, investing the revenues in our clean energy future and supporting British workers.

“In my Budget next week, I will keep up this momentum. Maintaining our fiscal discipline and drive for growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space.”

September’s inflation figure is used for the annual uprating of welfare payments, with the state pension now in line to rise by almost £500 next year.

The figure is also used to calculate increases in business rates in England, with pubs, shops, offices and other hospitality businesses now facing a £1.1bn increase in the collective bill from April, according to tax firm Ryan.

News.title: England dealt harsh lesson in Pakistan collapse
News.content:
Brendon McCullum wants his team to learn how to adapt as they prepare for the World Cup and this was a lesson in how not to master a run chase.

Failing to overhaul 302 is not an embarrassment, but the way England threw away a good start with some brittle batting gives McCullum plenty to ponder.

Spin exposed familiar failings as left-armer Arafat Minhas added six for 40 to his 59 from 58 with the bat, but it was also short balls from the seamers that hurt England. A two-paced pitch made the back-of-a-length delivery tricky, as it had in the match between Sri Lanka and Pakistan on the same ground at the weekend, but England failed to find a way to adjust their tempo.

Ben Duckett, Joe Root and Sam Curran were all dismissed by seamers hitting the pitch hard and forcing them to play square while Arafat exposed limitations against spin. He bowled Harry Brook for five with a beauty that dipped and straightened as he mixed up his arm ball with consistent accuracy to deadly effect.

News.title: Fried chicken and sugary drinks: Tanzania battles a growing obesity problem
News.content:
In early 2025, Said Shukuru, 31, was experiencing life-threatening health concerns. He weighed 150 kg (over 20 stone); his body mass index (BMI) was over 40 and he had a blood pressure of 190/100.

“It was very serious,” says Shukuru. In April last year, he underwent a successful mini gastric bypass operation at the Aga Khan Specialised Polyclinic in Masaki, Dar Es Salaam. His weight has since halved.

Shukuru’s case may be extreme, but his story serves as a warning. Overweight and obesity levels are increasing fast across East Africa, and particularly in Tanzania. Unless the government responds properly, the country faces a looming public health crisis.

Overweight and obesity in Tanzania have grown over the past 40 years because of economic development and liberalisation, urbanisation and increasingly sedentary lifestyles. Traditional diets, based on whole foods, are being replaced by refined and processed products. To make matters worse, chicken and chips, known as kuku chips, and sugary drinks are everywhere.

“When you live in an urban area like Dar (Es Salaam),” says Shukuru, “junk food is cheaper than groceries.”

The origins of these developments lie in Tanzania’s economic history. During the colonial period, fruits and legumes were exported while high-energy, starchy foods like maize were produced for domestic consumption, says Joyce Kinabo, professor of nutrition at Sokoine University.

“Food security was considered as having a lot of maize,” says Kinabo.

News.title: US warns over travel in Kenya as Ebola cases mount
News.content:
The United States has urged citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya, raising its travel alert level after the country reported an eighth case of Ebola.

The East African nation has recorded a rash of cases linked to a Kenyan businessman who died after travelling from Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

DRC is currently enduring the second worst Ebola outbreak on record with more than 4,000 deaths since May, though the true toll is thought to be far higher.

“The level was changed from Level 2 to Level 3 due to health risks,” the US embassy in Kenya said, a day after the State Department issued renewed travel advice for its citizens.

“Reconsider travel in Kenya due to risk of health, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and traffic safety. Some areas have increased risk,” it said.

The alert came as Kenyan doctors leaders demanded better protective equipment against the highly infectious virus.

Three of the confirmed Ebola cases are reported to be health staff who cared for the businessman and the others are thought to be relatives who visited him.

News.title: US records first human case of H5N1 this year
News.content:
A man in Washington has tested positive for H5N1, marking the first human case of bird flu in the US this year.

The patient, who works on a dairy farm, was reportedly infected after being exposed to two infected cows.

H5N1 has become endemic on US dairy farms after ‘spilling over’ from birds in 2024, and has since infected more than 1,000 herds across dozens of states.

The person is not seriously ill and is isolating at home, according to the Washington State Department of Health.

Scientists have long warned that if H5N1 mutates and gains the ability to spread person-to-person, it could trigger the next global pandemic – and each new infection gives the virus more opportunities to replicate and change.

Last week, a 50-year-old man in Taiwan was infected with a different strain of bird flu, H7N7, genetic analysis of which showed the virus had undergone adaptations to spread more effectively between mammals.

Of the more than 1,000 people who have contracted H5N1 since it was first detected in the late 1990s, almost half have died.

Its “extraordinarily high” mortality rate means that, were it to gain the ability to spread between people, it would be of “enormous concern”, the World Health Organization (WHO) previously warned.

However, the strain circulating among US dairy cattle, clade 2.3.4.4b, has proven less lethal to humans.

Sports.title: Billionaire ex-Arsenal ace Flamini gets engaged to partner he keeps very private after ‘a long time to align the stars’
Sports.content:
Next

MATHIEU FLAMINI has been raking in the cash since hanging up his boots – and now the Arsenal cult hero is set to tie the knot.

The Frenchman, 42, is worth an eye-watering £10BILLION after turning his back on football.



Flamini co-founded GF Biochemicals, alongside Italian entrepreneur Pasquale Granata, in 2008.

And the former midfielder is the chief executive of the hugely successful company.



But Flamini will now be spending time planning a wedding after announcing his engagement to his partner who he keeps very private.

The ex-Arsenal favourite proposed on the French island of Corsica and shared snaps of the memorable moment on Instagram.

Flamini also wrote an emotional caption which read: “It took the universe a long time to align the stars, but some things are worth waiting for. She said YES.”

And the happy couple had a host of famous faces racing into the comments section to send their well wishes.



Former England captain David Beckham, who played alongside Flamini at AC Milan, quickly sent a congratulatory message.

Ex-Arsenal team-mate Lukas Podolski and Gunners icon Ray Parlour were also quick to spot the stunning news.

Flamini made a whopping 246 appearances during his two spells in North London – notching 13 goals and 11 assists along the way.



He also got his hands on the FA Cup three times, as well as the Community Shield twice, with Arsenal.

But Flamini’s first move to the Gunners came after making his way through the ranks of boyhood club Marseille.

A five-year stint with Italian giants AC Milan bookended his two spells on Arsenal’s books.

Flamini then remained in the capital after joining Premier League rivals Crystal Palace.

The three-cap France international announced his retirement in 2019, following a move to Spanish side Getafe.

Sports.title: Man Utd ratings: Amad only one to show any positivity as Dalot and Mazraoui given runaround on dismal night in Como
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED suffered their heaviest Champions League defeat in 32 years to pile the pressure on Michael Carrick’s future.

Rising superstar Nico Paz scored two and set up another as the Serie A thumped the sorry Red Devils 4-1 on the rain soaked shores of Lake Como.



United became the first ever team to concede in the first two minutes of consecutive major European games as questions over Carrick’s job hang in the air.

Harry Maguire asked for more “bravery” on Sunday, but United chased shadows, failed in every area of the pitch and embarrassed themselves.



United, without nine senior players, are now winless in seven matches across all competitions—their longest run without a victory since December 2015.

Here’s how SunSport’s Katherine Walsh rated and slated the United players against Cesc Fabregas‘ side.



Senne Lammens – 5

Almost felt sorry for him. He shipped four but was vulnerable from the first minute and opponents love scoring stunners against the Belgian.

He doesn’t inspire the same confidence as last season, having parried the ball away three times when he should have held onto it. Cannot say he was really at fault for any of the goals. Stopped a fifth.

Diogo Dalot – 3

Can’t string two decent games together. Had to do better in the opposition box before Como broke away and went ahead inside 118 seconds.

Fumbled passes when United needed to take the sting out of the game and was left battered and bruised by Swiss winger Martin Baturina. Switched to left back in the second half, not that it matters.



Harry Maguire – 3

Dropped too deep to early and too slow to close down known threat Paz, before his stunner into the top corner inside two minutes.

The England defender was miles away from his man for the fourth goal, and was part of the problem for the other three. Awful night.

Matthijs de Ligt – 4

Unfortunately thrown into the deep end after 325 days out with a back injury as five senior defenders were missing.

His first competitive return in 11 months was marked with a thankless start against a young and hungry attack, that he could not get near.

His legs were long before 2-0 and Carrick was asking him for updates on fitness throughout.



Noussair Mazraoui – 3

Mazraoui does play left back for Morocco, but was wretched. Frequently skinned by Como’s silky right flank as Captain Lucas de Cunha and Maximo Perrone gave him the run around.

His disastrous press for the second goal put his side in a world of trouble. Another player who cannot guide United to where they want to go.

Andrey Santos – 3

A step behind the tempo and was eventually booked for his second late lunge before being hooked at half-time.

Can’t escape the feeling that Chelsea will have been delighted to get £50m for him this summer.

Mason Mount – 4

His pre-season partnership with Santos failed to resurrect. Rarely noticeable and almost a passenger in the first half.



Tried to step up the intensity straight after the restart but United’s midfield was wide open. A horrible ask on his second start of the season.

Youri Tielemans – 4

After two solid games in the main No10 role, Tielemans was sloppy and achieved next to nothing on the ball. His role is confusing to watch.

Bruno Fernandes – 3

Another checked out display. Looked bewildered in the false nine as kicked off at his teammates throughout and moaned when he was replaced on the hour. Just one goal involvement in his past nine games.

Could be seen furiously shouting at others to join him in pressing the Como backline to little avail. Looks like a man who knows it’s his last season at the club, he has given so much too.

Matheus Cunha – 4

On the receiving end of a Carrick tirade after 20 minutes and rowed with Fernandes after letting Paz jog past him for the opening goal.



Was a passenger after that and lacks the counter attacking threat of other United forwards. Struggled to get on the ball as Como dominated play and perhaps his 16 minutes in the last two games has hindered his rhythm. Rightly off at the break.

Bryan Mbeumo – 5

After two goals in three games, Mbeumo was incredibly wasteful in possession and his passing was wayward in an almost anonymous showing. Involved in a disjointed press.

SUBS

Carlos Baleba (for Santos, HT) – 3

Booked in quick fashion for a flailing hand into Paz. Then succumbed the ball to the Argentine in the lead up to 3-0 when United did not need to cause their own problems.

Amad (for Cunha, HT) – 6

At least showed some positive flashes. Had a shot tipped over on 60 minutes.

Joshua Zirkzee (Fernandes, 67) – 5

Consolation goal in stoppage time to try and restore some respect. First United goal since December 2025.



Harry Amass (for De Ligt, 79) -5

Have to feel for him coming in to this shambles at 4-0

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shea Lacey (Mbeumo, 84) – N/A

Booked straight away.

Subs not used: Darlow, Heaton, Kamason, Armer, J. Fletcher, T. Fletcher, Thompson
