World.title: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
World.content:
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.

Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.

Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that it is working to restore service.

“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”

Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between Moscow and the southern city of Krasnodar, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.

“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has 2 million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before.”

Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.

She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them. This came from the outside.”

Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, 30, a barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after she was unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.

She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay but that the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.

Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they could not see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He is originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.

World.title: A ‘Glee’ reboot is actually happening
World.content:
Rachel Berry is ready to collect another gold star.

“Glee,” the cult TV musical series from Ryan Murphy, is returning, Disney+ and Hulu announced in a social media post on Wednesday.

The series, which aired on Fox from 2009 to 2015, followed the fictional New Directions show choir at McKinley High School as they sang their way through love, heartbreak, bullying, coming out and other high school highs and lows.

It picked up 10 Golden Globe nominations and four wins during its run. The show’s soundtrack also garnered critical acclaim, with many of the covers performed by the cast making the Billboard Hot 100.

In recent years, a new fanbase has also gravitated toward the show, which streamed on Netflix after it aired on Fox. On TikTok, millions of “Gleeks” continue to share clips and

The news of its return comes just weeks after the showrunner teased the possibility of a reboot, telling Entertainment Tonight in September that he had “just finished” a script.

“Brad [Falchuk], Ian [Brennan] and I, who wrote all the first two seasons, have written something,” Murphy said. “I’ve been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members. It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.”

Online, fans couldn’t contain their enthusiasm, cracking jokes about what storylines Murphy should tackle in 2026 and brainstorming their dream covers and guest stars, including Olivia Rodrigo, Chappell Roan, Taylor Swift and Lin-Manuel Miranda.

While the show is beloved, its legacy has also been marred with a series of tragedies and controversies, both on and off screen.

Many fans, old and new, have pointed out on social media that some storylines on the show were “problematic” or “cringe.” They cited some of the performances, including those featuring the show choir’s teacher, Mr. Schuester, singing sexually suggestive songs to his students.

Additionally, three of the original core cast members have died since the show first aired in 2009.

Naya Rivera, who played cheerleader Santana Lopez, died after accidentally drowning while boating with her 4-year-old son on a California lake. She was 33.

Cory Monteith, who played Glee club co-captain and football team quarterback Finn Hudson, died at 31 in 2013 from a toxic mix of alcohol and heroin.

Mark Salling, who played Noah Puckerman, died in what appeared to be a suicide in 2018 at 35 after pleading guilty to child pornography charges.

Since the show came to an end, “Glee” actors Samantha Ware, Jeanté Godlock, Alex Newell and Dabier Snell accused lead Lea Michele (who played Glee co-captain Rachel Berry) of treating them poorly on the show. In 2020, she issued a lengthy statement on Instagram, where she apologized for her “behavior and any pain” she’s caused.

It’s unclear who from the original cast will return for the reboot.

Michele is reportedly reprising her role as Berry, according to Variety. A representative for Michele did not immediately respond to request for comment.

Former cast members Chord Overstreet, who played Sam Evans, and Heather Morris, who played cheerleader/Glee club member Brittany, hinted on social media that they’d likely be singing with the group once more.

“Reunited and it feels so good!” Overstreet wrote in a post on X on Wednesday.

Morris shared a photo of herself in her Cheerios cheerleader uniform from the series on Instagram.

“Yes ladies and gentle men of women, rumors are true. Brittany S Pierce was in fact lost in the sewers for all these years,” she wrote in the caption. “But I’m here to inform you that she is alive and well…And back for more.”

Many of the cast members have stayed friends.

Kevin McHale and Jenna Ushkowitz, whose characters Artie and Tina dated briefly on the show, hosted two “Glee” rewatch podcasts: “Showmance,” which ran from 2019–2020, and “That’s What You REALLY Missed,” which ran from 2022-2025.

McHale recently posted a reunion with co-star Amber Riley, who played Mercedes Jones, after she came to support him at his Broadway show.

Several cast members have also gone on to win Tonys. Darren Criss, who rose to mainstream fame playing Blaine Anderson on the show, has collected both a Tony and an Emmy in recent years.

On Sunday, Criss brought up co-star Chris Colfer onstage during his concert at London’s Royal Albert Hall to perform one of their popular “Glee” duets, a cover of “Baby It’s Cold Outside.”

And that’s what you missed ... on “Glee.”

World.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico in data privacy ruling
World.content:
Meta has been ordered by a judge in New Mexico to pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found that the social media company deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.

Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount, which New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez described as "one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history."

"This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," Torrez said in a news conference.

In September, jury members found that Facebook had made false or misleading statements by telling consumers that they controlled how their information was shared. The social media giant also misled consumers by claiming it didn't sell or share personal information with advertisers, the jury concluded.

The jury found that the company's "most senior leadership," including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg, made misrepresentations about the service's data privacy policies, the judge ruled.

"These communications were part of a coherent strategy designed to mislead the public," Mathew wrote.

The case stemmed from allegations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads.

In a statement on Wednesday, Torrez said that the case "has always been about more than one company or one scandal."

He added, "It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences."

Meta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Where the $25 billion could go

Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws are funneled toward state education spending.

"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," Torrez said, while noting that the money would be tied up if Meta appeals the decision, as expected.

Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own.

Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum large enough to affect its stock price.

Lawyers for Meta said the company should pay no more than $3.4 billion, arguing that a much larger award would violate due process, be unconstitutional and not hold up on appeal.

In 2019, the Federal Trade Commission hit Facebook, then called Meta, with a $5 billion fine over its role in allowing Cambridge Analytica to collect users' data without their consent.

Meta argued that New Mexico failed to prove that the tech giant's executives made misleading statements about privacy and that its content moderation practices harmed state residents.

Shares of Meta rose $13.56, or 2%, to $707.81 in Wednesday afternoon trading.

World.title: Armed federal agents knock on doors looking for noncitizen voters
World.content:
Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found.

The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S.

Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters.

"What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating."

Photos posted by HSI NorCal of Homeland Security agents knocking on doors in the San Francisco area. X/@HSINorCal

The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people, all of them green card holders, on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote.

As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections.

"HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders."

Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities.

"In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident of initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations.

In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering.

Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN, describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms, approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS."

One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand.

Homeland Security agents making an arrest in the Kansas City area. X/@HSIKansasCity

The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment.

For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters.

"It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University.

"And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that — because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth."

A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens… Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear."

"Target List"

In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, "Target List."

That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS.

In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject.

DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters.

"Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally," said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law ."

"There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden.

She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter.

World.title: Musk chose to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX network, sources say
World.content:
A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.

The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week.

Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine.

It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.

Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive.

"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X.

Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.

The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order.

The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.

Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown.

"I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service.

"We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office told CBS News on Wednesday that Ukraine's use of the system was still throttled.

What is Starshield?

Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink.

The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.

Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.

There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close.

What happened in Ukraine?

Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.

Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.

Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.

Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones.

The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things."

Zelenskyy has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored."

The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week.

"There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend.

Why have Trump and Zelenskyy clashed?

Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S., and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down.

A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."

Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.

The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.

Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.

In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.

"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.

World.title: Video shows moments leading up to police fatally shooting toddler
World.content:
Body camera and surveillance footage from the fatal police shooting of a 1-year-old boy show the moments several police officers rush out of a Mississippi Walmart and open fire as a driver accused of shoplifting tries to pull out of the parking lot.

Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced this week that no charges would be filed against the officer who opened fire on the car, striking and killing Kohen Wiley in the June 14 incident.

"Today, the Office of the Attorney General announced it has completed the review of a June 14, 2026 incident in Senatobia involving one officer with the Senatobia Police Department," Fitch said in a statement. "In this incident, the Attorney General's Office found the use of force was justified."

The video shows five law enforcement officers running out of the Walmart after being informed a shoplifter is attempting to drive away. When they reach the silver-colored sedan, they surround it and shout repeatedly to "stop the car." The woman driving the car, a friend of Wiley's mother, instead drives forward and nearly hits one of the officers. It is at this point that one of the officers opens fire on the car.

The video, which was posted online by Darkhorse Press, has been verified but not independently obtained by CBS News.

Wiley was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead, according to police.

Wiley's mother and her friend reject accusations they were shoplifting, according to their lawyer, Ben Crump. They have not been charged with any crime. The friend was driving the car, while his mother held Wiley in her lap in the vehicle, Crump said.

"I watched my baby take his first breath and I watched my baby take his last breath," the boy's mother, Vellesiya Wiley, said at a press conference alongside Crump in June. She alleges she held up Kohen to show they had a child in the car and stop them from shooting, according to Crump.

This undated photo provided by Veronica Roberson in June 2026 shows her grandson, Kohen Wiley, of Senatobia, Miss. Veronica Roberson via AP, File

The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation immediately launched an investigation into the incident, which then presented the findings to the attorney general.

"Before anything else, I want to acknowledge the tremendous pain our community is experiencing," Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves said in a statement after the shooting. "The child lost their life. That heartbreaking loss has touched every corner of our community. My thoughts and prayers remain with all those involved. We are committed to transparency throughout this investigation."

Crump and Wiley's family called for body camera to be released after the attorney general decided Monday the officer would not be charged.

"A 1-year-old baby was shot and killed by a police officer, and now the state of Mississippi says that use of force was justified. How can anyone accept that conclusion when Kohen's family and the public still have not been allowed to see the body-camera footage?" Crump said in a statement earlier this week, also noting the Senatobia police chief was recently fired for allegedly using racial slurs.

"If the footage supports the state's decision, release it," he added. "We will not stop fighting until this family gets the truth."

The Mississippi Department of Public Safety said it would officially release the video at the end of the week after the family views it.

CBS News reached out to the family's lawyer, Crump, about the video and whether the family has seen it, but he hasn't responded.

World.title: Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy
World.content:
Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that the Trump administration must continue providing gender-affirming care to transgender inmates in federal prisons.

The decision, in an emergency appeal, maintains a lower court's injunction on a federal Bureau of Prisons' policy that would terminate hormone therapy and other treatments for trans inmates.

The order offered no explanation behind the decision. It simply read, "The application for stay presented to The Chief Justice and by him referred to the Court is denied."

It also said Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would side with the Trump administration and would grant the application for stay.

Sponsor Message

A federal district judge barred the BOP from implementing its policy this summer.

A second court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, also rejected the administration's request to pause U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth's order.

That's when U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

As the federal judge's injunction remains in place, the legal battle over the policy continues.

Li Nowlin-Sohl, senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union and a lawyer involved in this case, said the organization believes there are more than 2,000 people in BOP custody who identify as transgender. (The BOP stopped publishing data reflecting transgender inmates after Trump took office in 2025. It only records male or female individuals incarcerated in the federal system.)

Kingdom v. Trump represents 1,000 inmates who have a gender dysphoria diagnosis, Nowlin-Sohl explained. Of those, the ACLU believes there are about 800 who have been prescribed hormone therapy and many who are also receiving social transition accommodations, Nowlin-Sohl said.

In its request for an emergency stay on the earlier rulings, the Trump administration argued that providing this care poses several risks, including for recipients of this specialized care, who it argued would become "targets for attacks." They also said that it raises "fairness concerns" as it would "breed resentment" with other inmates.

Sponsor Message

Access to gender-affirming care is considered medically necessary to treat gender dysphoria, a medical term used to describe the deep discomfort caused by a mismatch between a person's assigned sex at birth and their gender identity. Without it, individuals can struggle severely with mental health issues such as heightened anxiety and depression, with some turning to self-harm and suicide.

Gender-affirming care can include "...hormone therapy, and gender-affirming surgeries among others," according to the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. (In its filings, the Trump administration questioned WPATH's standards of care, which were developed by experts in transgender health and used by organizations across the world.)

Some people who are transgender may require hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries; others may not require any of these interventions.

The BOP has treated people diagnosed with gender dysphoria since at least 1992, the ACLU said in response to the government's filings to the Supreme Court.

"Had BOP's doctors found this treatment unhelpful or harmful to patients or had the agency found that the treatment compromised security, surely BOP would have mentioned it in the administrative record," the ACLU wrote.

This is a "glaring omission" and appears to indicate that the government's arguments now are simply "contrived," the ACLU continued.

NPR previously covered the impact of the loss of hormone treatments on people who are incarcerated. One woman said she experienced severe physical and mental anguish when she lost access to hormone treatments.

The Supreme Court's decision is at odds with other rulings that support the Trump administration's anti-trans policy agenda.

Last June, the court ruled that states can ban transgender girls from participating in sports at publicly funded schools. And in 2025, the court upheld state laws that make it illegal for doctors and other health professionals to provide gender-affirming care for minors.

World.title: New human data hints at psychedelics' potential to combat inflammation
World.content:
New human data hints at psychedelics' potential to combat inflammation

toggle caption i Cannabis-Pic/Getty Images

Efforts to understand how classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD summon powerful changes in consciousness tend to focus on what's happening inside our head.

That's because these compounds bind tightly to serotonin receptors that densely populate certain structures of the brain, and a growing number of studies demonstrate they can exert long-lasting changes in mental health and well-being for people with a range of psychiatric conditions.

Increasingly researchers have started to probe how these drugs elicit other physiological changes, given that many cells and tissues beyond the brain possess those same receptors, known as 5-HT2A.

Sponsor Message

Now, new research offers some of the first evidence in humans that psychedelics may also hold potential for treating diseases characterized by inflammation and immune dysregulation throughout the body.

The data, published Wednesday in the medical journal JAMA Psychiatry, draws from a small pool of patients with Parkinson's disease, but it reflects what's been observed in lab studies with animal and cell models for years. For certain diseases, psychedelics appear to combat inflammation and even help restore stressed mitochondria, the energy-producing factories of the cells.

The team at the University of California, San Francisco, who conducted the study, used blood tests to measure five different signaling molecules involved in inflammation in participants, both before and after two sessions with psilocybin.

The participants had significantly lower levels of inflammation following the treatments, compared to baseline, and those changes persisted a month after their final dose of psilocybin. The researchers also tracked a blood marker of mitochondrial stress. Here, too, there were substantial improvements immediately after participants were given psilocybin, though not during the longer-term follow up.

"This gives us an initial biological signal to investigate," says Dr. Ellen Bradley, an associate professor of psychiatry at UCSF who helped lead the analysis.

Sponsor Message

The findings were based on 12 participants in a pilot study to evaluate the feasibility and safety of giving psilocybin to people with Parkinson's disease. Patients with neurodegenerative conditions are typically excluded from trials on psychedelics and mental health for safety concerns.

The original study, which was published last year, assuaged researchers' concerns about the risks. Bradley says they found a "really promising safety profile" and that "symptoms even seemed to get a bit better."

The researchers emphasize that the study has limitations: they did not have a control group, and the participants knew they were receiving the drug. So the data on what was happening in their blood needs to be confirmed in follow-up studies before making definitive claims, says Aoife O'Donovan, a professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at UCSF and co-author of the paper.

Still, O'Donovan says the findings reflect "objective markers" that changed over time and that gives them confidence to pursue this line of research.

Parkinson's disease is characterized by dysregulated inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction. This data, Bradley notes, could help explain why the participants appeared to benefit from the drugs during the trial.

Beyond that, the results raise the proposition that psychedelics may help address others diseases that are characterized by troubles with inflammation, says D. Parker Kelley, a research scientist in the Mitochondrial PsychoBiology group at Columbia University who was a first author on the paper with Bradley.

"It's a potential jumping off point for a lot more research in this area," he says, "that may apply not only to Parkinson's, but also neuropsychiatric disorders like depression and anxiety, and even cardio-metabolic and inflammatory disorders."

While previous studies have looked at biomarkers of inflammation after psilocybin, those have generally included healthy volunteers – not people with real disease, says Charles Nichols, a professor of pharmacology, biochemistry and experimental therapeutics at LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans.

Sponsor Message

"I think it's really exciting," says Nichols, who didn't work on the study, but whose lab discovered that certain psychedelics could have powerful anti-inflammatory effects about fifteen years ago.

That insight came from studying lab-grown cell culture that simulated inflammation of blood vessels and hardening of arteries, also known as atherosclerosis.

In that experiment, they found a psychedelic acting on the 5-H2TA receptors functioned as a "potent anti-inflammatory," even at doses well below what would cause a psychoactive trip, he says.

Since then, Nichols' group has run numerous experiments in animal models of disease including asthma, arthritis, and cardiovascular disease, but the field has needed to test whether these protective effects hold up in humans.

He says this new study in Parkinson's patients is a proof of principle.

"We can only draw so much from those conclusions," he says. "But I do think it validates a lot of the pharmacology that we've been doing over the last 15 years on the anti-inflammatory, the mitochondrial protective effects."

World.title: Sentenced to death at 17, at 68, quilt artist receives solo museum exhibition
World.content:
Sentenced to death at 17, at 68, quilt artist receives solo museum exhibition

toggle caption i Sea Stachura for NPR

Imagine living all of your adult life behind bars for a murder you didn't commit and being released at 58. You're also a fabric artist, and the Smithsonian has acquired one of your quilts. That's the story of Gary Tyler, and now, the artist has his first solo exhibit.

At the Grand Rapids Art Museum in Michigan, Gary Tyler points to a black-and-white quilt that's based on a photo.

"That's a picture that was taken by my brother back in [19]74," he says.

He was a 16-year-old with a flair for fashion, living in Louisiana. One school morning, he dressed in a body shirt with a sweater overtop. Then he added fingerless gloves and a bandana.

Sponsor Message

"This body shirt was the shirt and bandana that I had the day of the incident," he said.

By dinnertime, Tyler was arrested. A white 13-year-old had been shot and killed during anti-school-integration violence. Tyler was put in a police car for "mouthing off." The next thing he knew, local police arrested and charged him with murder. He couldn't believe the charges would stick. He was still wearing the same clothes a month later, when his brother snapped the photo.

"You're looking at the innocence of a young, of a teenager, adolescent, you know, and who's who's at loss and and not knowing … what's definitely ahead of him," he says of the image.

toggle caption i Sea Stachura for NPR

A divorce lawyer incompetently represented him. Four friends testified against him, then recanted their testimony. The judge instructed an all-white jury to assume the 16-year-old meant to kill multiple people. It then convicted and sentenced him to death. Tyler maintained his innocence.

At the time, he was the youngest person on death row. He was sent to the Louisiana State Penitentiary, also known as Angola, and placed in a form of solitary confinement. His story isn't unique, says Wanda Bertram with the Prison Policy Initiative.

"There are a ton of people in prison who have shocking stories to tell about the defense they received, especially if they were indigent, the coercion they experienced from police and prosecutors," Bertram says.

Sponsor Message

Louisiana has the highest rate of incarceration in the U.S. Globally, it's second only to El Salvador. It also has one of the lowest parole rates.

The Louisiana Board of Pardons and Committee on Parole recommended Tyler be pardoned three times. Each time, the state's governor refused.

Eric Seiferth says sentences are often extremely long, especially at Angola. Seiferth is a senior curator at the Historic New Orleans Collection, in the French Quarter. He's also one of the authors of Captive State: Louisiana and the Making of Mass Incarceration.

"There are just more and more and more people than ever before in the history of the state who have received life sentences … that have no option to ever come home. They're convicted to die," he says.

Tyler was at Angola, watching other men die behind bars. In the late '80s, he and others created a hospice program.

"Men in prison, taking care [of] terminally ill men to, you know, end of life, it had the way of really transforming you, changing you," Tyler says.

The group raised money for coffins by making and selling quilts. That's how Tyler learned the craft. One of his quilts was raffled off at the Angola Prison Rodeo, a biannual public event, and raised $30,000 for the hospice program. Seiferth's museum has one of them, The Tree of Life.

"It has the names and people, you know, it's basically made of people. Essentially, of human forms," Seiferth says.

toggle caption i Sea Stachura for NPR

toggle caption i Sea Stachura for NPR

Tyler never received a pardon. A 2016 U.S. Supreme Court ruling required states to resentence all people who had been given life without parole as juveniles. As a result, the St. Charles Parish District Attorney proposed resentencing Tyler for manslaughter. Tyler was desperate to get out of Angola, so he agreed and was released soon after. The St. Charles Parish District Attorney declined to comment for this story.

Sponsor Message

For Tyler, the terms of his release were another injustice. "The [criminal justice] system is unfairly administered, especially to the people of color and poor people in the United States. There are better ways of being able to adjudicate, or punish a person in prison humanely," he says.

Now Tyler's art honors those still locked up. He points to portrait quilts featuring the incarcerated men and women he met behind bars.

"Because when you see Sandra Stall, Trinidad, Big Toe, Mary, and Bertha, that's my way of showing moral and spiritual support," Tyler says.

Only Mary and Bertha have been released.

At the opening reception of the exhibit, Caton Vance is admiring Tyler's work.

"I think it mostly has to do with dealing with consequences that are beyond imagining and somehow, despite the environment, finding hope," Vance says.

The exhibit, "Gary Tyler: Rebirth," runs through Jan. 3.

World.title: Israel detains dozens of Americans, including a congressional candidate, in West Bank
World.content:
Israel detains dozens of Americans, including a congressional candidate, in West Bank

toggle caption i Ruth Sherlock/NPR

NAHALIN, West Bank — U.S. Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was detained along with about 80 American and Israeli rabbis and activists by Israeli security forces, as the U.S. and Israeli delegation was helping Palestinians harvest olives from their grove close to a settlement in the occupied West Bank.

Lander, a House nominee and former New York City comptroller, later said he was released from Israeli military custody "with a warning," but several dozen others were still detained.

This is the largest mass detention of activists in the occupied West Bank in at least a decade, two Israeli lawyers who work on related cases told NPR. Rabbi Arik Ascherman, a longtime Israeli human rights proponent, called the detentions "unprecedented." This comes amid a spike in violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinian farmers in the West Bank.

Sponsor Message

The Israeli military said in a statement that harvesting in the area requires the farmers to submit requests to the authorities before the olive harvest season in order to coordinate "security of the area and maintain public order." The military said Palestinians in this area did not submit a request, so soldiers and police arrived and detained those present.

"Regarding reports of the detention of a congressional candidate, we note that he was released once the matter was brought to our attention," the Israeli military told NPR.

Lander, an ally of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, denounced the Israeli authorities' actions. He told his followers on social media, "Occupation is a crime under international law," but harvesting olives is not.

"We were on private Palestinian land. We were with the farmers whose land it is. There's no obligation to coordinate with the Israeli military," Lander told NPR and WBUR's Here & Now. "This was the IDF making it impossible for these poor Palestinian farmers to harvest their olive trees," he added, using the initials for the Israeli military.

Rabbis from the U.S. organization T'ruah, the Israeli group Rabbis for Human Rights and other activists had joined Palestinian families in picking olives at their grove in Nahalin, close to the Israeli settlement of Beitar Illit. They said they were participating in an action they called Protect the Harvest, bringing an international coalition of volunteers together to accompany Palestinian harvesters at a time when they and their farms and other property have come under attack from Israeli settlers.

toggle caption i Ruth Sherlock/NPR

Olive harvesting is an important time for Palestinians both culturally and economically. But it has become increasingly hard for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank to access their fields. Several Palestinians there told NPR they have been unable to harvest their olive trees there since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, saying it had become too dangerous in the face of rising settler attacks in the occupied West Bank.

Sponsor Message

The detentions come less than a week after American photojournalist Heidi Levine, working for The Washington Post was assaulted by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, the latest journalist to come under attack during the Palestinian olive harvest season. Democratic congressman Ro Khanna of California was also briefly detained by Israeli forces while visiting the West Bank in July.

On Wednesday, the group of Americans and Israelis joined the Palestinian farmers hoping their presence would help them harvest in peace.

After roughly two hours, drones began circling overhead and Israeli security forces arrived and declared the area a closed military zone. They detained the Israeli and American activists and took them to the police station for questioning. The rabbinical human rights group T'ruah said a Palestinian family was also detained.

"Let us be clear about what happened here: Rather than protecting Palestinian farmers and ensuring their right to work their own land, the Israeli military forcibly removed those who came to provide a protective presence," T'ruah CEO Rabbi Jill Jacobs said in a statement. "This is an outrageous abuse of power, and part of a systematic, state-backed campaign of ethnic cleansing aimed at driving Palestinians from their land," she said.

Lander, who won the Democratic primary for a New York House district in June, has been an outspoken critic of the Israeli government.

"What's going on here cries out for attention. I feel that profoundly as an American Jew, and as someone who's headed into the next Congress. My constituents don't want their tax dollars paying for this," Lander told NPR's team in the West Bank, before he was detained.

"When we say state-sanctioned ethnic cleansing, it's not just settler violence. It's the IDF's effort to prevent Palestinians from living their lives," Lander told Here & Now after his release.

Israeli authorities have rejected accusations of ethnic cleansing. Israel's Foreign Ministry accused Lander of a political "stunt," saying he was looking for a confrontation.

Sponsor Message

Amy Spitalnick, CEO of the Jewish Council for Public Affairs in New York, said 33 of those detained are U.S. citizens and she was in contact with some of them. She wrote on social media that some have been charged with "disturbing the peace."

The State Department told NPR it is aware of reports of Americans detained in the West Bank and is tracking the situation, but said it would not comment further due to privacy and other considerations.

Daniel Estrin reported from Tel Aviv, Israel, where Itay Stern also contributed reporting. Alex Leff, Michele Kelemen and Luke Garrett contributed to this story from Washington, D.C.

World.title: Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections
World.content:
Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections

toggle caption i Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

President Trump boasted this weekend of his growing power in his second term – and all the things he's doing now that he wouldn't dare in his first term, such as changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

"I don't think I could have done this in my first term," he told supporters in Northern Kentucky, "This is a much more powerful term. I can do stuff that's unbelievable."

He joked about how big companies wouldn't take his call in the first term, but "now they kiss my ass."

Less than two weeks before the election, Trump continues to crash through barriers that he wouldn't dare cross in his first term – and pointing to that power to make his case to midterm voters.

Sponsor Message

Trump's Justice Department is raiding a congresswoman's home. He's knocking down trees in Washington, D.C. against a judge's wishes. And he's making deals with Russia that fly in the face of congressionally passed sanctions.

Trump is hardly the first president to become frustrated and test the limits of executive authority.

George W. Bush issued controversial "signing statements" to challenge or reinterpret bills passed by Congress. Barack Obama famously said he had a pen and he planned to use it. Trump is part of that trend.

Trump inherited an increasingly powerful presidency, said Tevi Troy, is a presidential historian, who worked in the George W. Bush White House.

Congress has been basically giving away its own power for a quarter of a century. And Troy says Trump is using that power in a distinctive way - and not to just get around congressional gridlock.

Trump's using it to also go after political and cultural opponents.

"His goals include going after some of his opponents reigning in 'woke' or "DEI" stuff at universities, pushing back against the media," Troy said, adding. "He's what I call a unilateralist. He doesn't have an ideology, he has a methodology, and the methodology is unilateralism."

Sponsor Message

The targets are not entirely surprising. Trump has spent years attacking news organizations, criticizing regulators and confronting political opponents, including members of his own party.

Ryan Williams, a Republican strategist who helped lead Mitt Romney's presidential campaign, described Trump as a brawler who won't hesitate to use those extraordinary powers in all those fights.

"Trump has made it very clear that he wants to approach his second term in a way where he gets what he wants," Williams said. "He's the president, he's the boss, and he's not going to be restrained by traditions or aides that may say you should hold back."

The question is no longer how much Trump can accomplish through executive action. It's how far the president can go and what, if anything, will constrain him.

In another example, the Trump administration announced earlier this month investigations against nine universities, including Harvard and Yale, for allegedly bringing in international students in order to undercut American wages.

If the administration doesn't like a person or organizations point of view, Trump officials are "prepared to take the gloves off," said Frank Sesno, a former CNN Washington bureau chief who is now a media and public affairs professor at George Washington University.

Sesno said that could be waged in court or through contracts, revoking security clearances or launching investigations.

These are the extensions of power that can only be exercised in many ways by the executive branch of the federal government" Sesno said.

"And they are awesome weapons."

World.title: DOJ's noncitizen voter list is unreliable, officials say. And, U.S. pollution rises
World.content:
DOJ's noncitizen voter list is unreliable, officials say. And, U.S. pollution rises

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Los Angeles County election officials say that the Justice Department's list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote is "unreliable," based on their preliminary analysis. They also say some of the individuals on the list have indicated they were born in the U.S. and may be citizens. State and local officials disclosed these new details in court filings yesterday, in response to a federal lawsuit demanding that California investigate thousands of voters before their ballots are counted. The DOJ wants the state to segregate ballots associated with these individuals. California officials say the DOJ's request is unfeasible so close to the election and may violate federal and state election laws.

toggle caption i Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images

A new report from United Nations scientists says that countries are not doing enough to cut emissions that drive climate change, and the United States plays a significant role in climate pollution. The U.S. was the only major economy that saw an increase last year in planet-warming pollution. The report also found that, among G20 countries, the U.S. is tied with Russia for the highest per capita emissions. While China emits more total greenhouse gases annually than the U.S., China's population is more than four times that of the U.S. The rise in U.S. emissions was fueled by increased electricity demand and Trump administration policies that support burning fossil fuels.

Sponsor Message

Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, increased in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025, according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us. The report also highlighted a 188% increase in immigration violations. This comes as violent crime rates, including homicides, dropped to historic lows. The report examined publicly available FBI and immigration arrest data and does not include details about whether charges were dropped or if people served any time in jail or prison. This data covers the first full year of Trump's second term, during which his administration emphasized a tough-on-crime approach. Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us, told NPR ahead of the report's release that the rising trends signal a "really troubling return to some of the extreme law and order policies that defined the American criminal justice system during the '80s and '90s." Check out NPR's analysis.

President Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff is in St. Petersburg today to meet with Kremlin officials and explore potential solutions for ending Russia's war on Ukraine. Witkoff also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this week in Norway. Trump has accused Zelenskyy of obstructing a peace deal. The Ukrainian president says he is again seeking direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Norway and Finland's leaders believe a fair deal to end the war requires U.S. involvement, NPR's Joanna Kakissis tells Up First. They hope Witkoff's Russia leads to something constructive. But Ukrainians whom Kakissis has spoken to say they don't trust the White House and believe the U.S. is siding with Russia. Concerns grew among Ukrainians when President Trump announced he would lift sanctions on Russian diesel. Many argued that the move wouldn't lower fuel prices but instead help Russia continue its war against Ukraine.

On the ground

NPR

The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.

This week, Morning Edition's Steve Inskeep traveled to North Carolina and Georgia. Both states are among those Trump visited this week as he continues to campaign for Republicans vying to keep control of the Senate and House. Inskeep explored how the Trump administration's policies have affected public research in both states. Trump has eliminated hundreds of jobs from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which is headquartered in Atlanta. Universities and research firms in North Carolina's Research Triangle lost millions of dollars in federal grants last year. Inskeep spoke with people affected by these changes. Listen to what they had to say.

Hear more from voters in both states:

🎧 Inskeep got personal thoughts from random Georgia voters by knocking on some doors and meeting people along walking trails.

🎧 In North Carolina, he visited communities devastated by Hurricane Helene in 2024 to assess changes two years after the federal response became a campaign issue.

🎧 In Stokes County, N.C., Inskeep explores how AI data centers have divided the community. In 2024, 79% of voters in the county backed Trump. The president has supported these centers.

Sponsor Message

The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Follow the reporting: Ohio and Michigan coverage airs Oct. 27. You can follow along on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in this newsletter.

Introducing Machine Gods

by Tommy Evans , NPR's editor in chief

NPR

To cover a transformation as vast as AI, one that raises deep questions about work, culture, the environment, cybersecurity, education and so much more, we've teamed up with veteran tech journalists Casey Newton and Kevin Roose to bring their flagship AI podcast, Machine Gods, to NPR's audiences. Starting today, the video-first program will be offered twice a week across NPR's platforms and provide front-row access to the people and issues shaping this new AI era.

The show will look into things like the ways AI could be applied to the medical field, potentially helping us discover new drugs and improve healthcare overall, as well as the questions that keep Casey and Kevin both up at night, like what happens when AI eventually builds and improves upon itself beyond what humans understand. With each episode, we'll make sure you get the news you need to know about AI — both the technology's capabilities and its very real risks — without buying into the industry's hype or treating catastrophe as an inevitability.

Machine Gods is the culmination of years of Casey and Kevin's reporting from the front lines of Silicon Valley. While it represents an ambitious new format for public media, its core ethos fits seamlessly with NPR's mission: to bring audiences trusted, independent journalism that inspires, engages, and keeps you informed so you can navigate the world with confidence.

Sponsor Message

You can see the first episode here.

Follow and subscribe to Machine Gods on the NPR app, NPR.org, or wherever you get your podcasts.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Valerie Macon/AFP via Getty Images

Actress Christina Applegate has revealed that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis five years ago. The World Health Organization's new special envoy for health resilience, Dr. Vanessa Kerry, says building more-responsive healthcare systems is what her new job is all about. Utah is suing Kalshi, alleging that its yes/no event contracts resemble traditional sportsbook bets. The state says the prediction market website is operating illegally due to Utah's constitutional ban on gambling. (via KUER)

World.title: Alberta premier says UCP must be pro-Canada, separatists can 'join a different party'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Premier Danielle Smith says separatist UCP members should support the will of Albertans who voted to remain in Canada or leave the party.

That desire was clear in the results of Monday’s referendum, she told reporters at a news conference in Calgary Wednesday. She echoed the sentiment from her video message sent to UCP members earlier in the day.

“For those few who cannot reconcile this fact and remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement, I would respectfully invite them to join a different party,” Smith said in the video.

She said at Wednesday's news conference that she knows there are a lot of "hurt feelings," referencing those who voted to support the province holding a second, binding referendum on separation. But she said now is the time for them to recalibrate.

"You get to have your say, but you don’t always get to have your way.”

In the Wednesday video, Smith said she expects that, going forward, the UCP will be pro-Canada.

"The United Conservative Party is not an independence party," Smith said.

Smith said the party needs to be clear that "a strong Alberta within a united Canada is the position of our party and our government."

The premier said party members can hold whatever views they wish but candidates running under the UCP banner must be committed to the party's position.

Smith said the UCP also expects members of the provincial board and constituency boards to uphold the party's position on separatism. Smith said the party needs to focus its efforts on beating the NDP in the next election.

Referendum results

As of Wednesday morning, results are still trickling in on the 10-question referendum.

While CBC projected Monday night that Albertans strongly favour remaining in Canada, the results of other questions are too close to call.

Smith previously said that she would seek “majority rule,” meaning a 50 per cent-plus-one threshold, to act on the first nine questions, which deal with immigration and constitutional issues.

The five questions that focused on immigration seem to give the Alberta government a clear mandate to take greater control, she said, adding that other provinces share the sentiment and Prime Minister Mark Carney is “accepting the will of Albertans.”

"I think we're about to have a very honest discussion about returning to the kind of immigration system that worked and served us well for so many years, which is prioritizing economic migrants."

Cross Country Checkup is asking: A majority of Albertans voted in favour of non permanent Canadian residents paying an access fee for health care. What do you think? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for this Sunday's show.

Smith said her government will look to Quebec’s 1991 accord for inspiration on how to share responsibility for decisions about who gets to move to Alberta and how many — "to make sure we're matching newcomers with the jobs that are here."

New legislation could be introduced in the spring, she said.

Smith said that the results show a divide between urban and rural voters, and that the constitutional questions are less of a priority overall.

"There's a reason to be skeptical that some constitutional amendments would be worth the effort," she said. "What I'm seeing is that Albertans would rather we spend our time focusing on things where we can make meaningful change."

Full referendum results are expected by Wednesday night.

World.title: Canada's Russian envoy returns with advice on how to hit back against Putin
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's outgoing ambassador to Russia has returned with advice for crafting a response to Moscow's "cognitive warfare" campaign against the NATO alliance and why keeping sanctions on oil and gas can frustrate Vladimir Putin's struggle to finance his war machine.

Sarah Taylor's three-year tour of duty in Moscow, which ended Oct. 8, was defined by the Russian president's invasion of Ukraine from her first day in the country to her last, and that conflict, she says in a rare interview with CBC News, has all but returned the country to a Cold War mentality.

Taylor says that while many in NATO, particularly in Europe, worry about a conventional invasion of their territory by Russia, she doesn't see that happening "at least in the short to medium term."

"But I do think already we are effectively under attack in a form of cognitive warfare and we maybe don't really realize just how bad that is," she told CBC Radio's The Current, in an interview that aired on Wednesday.

LISTEN | Outgoing ambassador to Russia on life in Moscow: The Current 19:08 Outgoing ambassador to Russia on life in Moscow Longtime diplomat Sarah Taylor has just wrapped up nearly three years on the ground in Moscow as Canada's ambassador to Russia, her final posting before retirement. She speaks with Matt Galloway about her conversations with Russian citizens and officials as the war in Ukraine continues, and the cognitive warfare she warns is already underway.

Taylor says Russia's use of propaganda is widespread and effective because it uses its knowledge of how the West works and key language skills to ensure its campaigns will have maximum impact.

She says the large Russian dissident community, including independent journalists, that are now outside Russia could be an effective counteroffensive on the cognitive battlefield.

"I think part of Putin's power lies in an ability to sort of project inevitability and to say, 'Well, you know, it'll always be Putin and only Putin. And this is just the way it is,'" she told host Matt Galloway.

"To have an active, open discussion that's going on, particularly if some of it is in Russian and can filter back into Russia to say, 'No, Russia doesn't have to be like this. There are alternative futures.' That's really important."

Another vulnerability Taylor sees is Putin's ongoing struggle to fund Russia's war machine.

"One of their weaknesses in this war is financing it," Taylor said. "It's become a hugely expensive undertaking for them, lasting much longer than the Russians expected … and part of the way they are funding this is through their sales of oil and gas."

Frustrating Putin's war machine

She says that while some sanctions on Russia are more symbolic in nature, such as the ones targeting people who "visibly support the war," others have a deeper strategic impact — like those on oil and gas, which U.S. President Donald Trump has moved to lift with his recent diesel deal with Putin.

"I do believe, personally, that it's very important to try and maintain those as much as possible because the more you do that, the more you increase the dilemma for the Russian government about how they are going to fund this war going forward," she said.

While the cost of invading Ukraine has been steep for the Russian government, Taylor says the state has "made a huge effort to make life feel as normal as possible" in cities like Moscow and St. Petersburg.

That reality held largely true, she says, until the last six months when Ukraine began targeting oil refineries, the warehouses of Russian e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon that some call the "Russian Amazon" and more recently, large data centres.

Smoke billows into the sky following Ukrainian drone strikes on warehouses of Russia's online retailer Wildberries, in St. Petersburg, Russia, in July. (The Associated Press)

"Those are starting to have an impact, a bit more impact on daily life," she said. "It's obviously nothing like what, say, our colleagues in Kyiv are living every day … but it does feel like you're in the middle of a Cold War."

While admitting she did not mix with a "completely representative sample of Russians" while serving in Moscow, she says support for the war is paper thin.

"I have yet to meet a single ordinary Russian who was enthusiastic about the war. And most of them just want it to end, really," she said.

But wanting, and having the capacity to do something to feed that want, are very different, she says.

"The vast majority of people who have in any way either demonstrated against the war, or even … supported Ukraine by making donations or anything of that sort are now almost all in jail," she said.

"It's very telling that there are now as many, if not more … political prisoners in Russian jails than there were in the Khrushchev era of the Soviet Union. So we're really back to a Soviet-like feeling of repression, of dissent."

World.title: Carney, Ford announce nearly $9B partnership to support steel, auto, critical mineral sectors
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alongside Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced an $8.7-billion support package for steel, critical mineral and auto sectors on Wednesday.

The partnership with the Ontario government earmarks $2.5 billion over two years for the province's auto industry to build the "connected and electric vehicles of the future."

Ottawa is providing $1.5 billion of the auto funding with Ontario providing the remaining $1 billion.

The support for auto companies comes at a time of uncertainty caused by the trade war with the United States.

"An integrated North American auto sector will be stronger, more competitive and provide better jobs for our workers," Carney said. "But we recognize these are not the objectives of the current U.S. administration. Their approach has changed, and so must ours."

WATCH | Carney announces plan with Ford: Carney and Ford announce $9B plan to 'protect' Ontario jobs | Duration closed caption 1:10 Standing with Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Wednesday that new investments in Ontario's Ring of Fire critical minerals projects, the steel sector and the auto sector will protect up to 290,000 jobs across the province.

The federal-provincial partnership also launches a $5-billion Joint Steel Action Fund — $3.55 billion from Ottawa and $1.67 billion from Ontario, both over five years.

Carney said the investment will allow steel mills to upgrade their machinery, manufacture more products that Canada needs and expand to meet demand from markets other than the U.S.

"When Canadian projects need specialized steel, they can increasingly count on Canadian mills, and Canadian steelworkers, to supply it," Carney said.

Ottawa is also setting out $1 billion over three years to match Ontario's investment toward building a road to reach the mineral-rich Ring of Fire region.

Ontario has been trying to get the federal government to help pay for and speed up development of the Ring of Fire.

Ford has called mining critical minerals in this area an "ace in the hole" that could help give Canada leverage against American tariffs.

Carney said Ottawa and Ontario are creating a co-ordinated process for federal and provincial permitting to open mines. Carney said the process for opening a mine in Ontario has historically taken over 15 years.
