Angola Politics at a Glance

Angola politics runs through a presidential republic of 21 provinces. Its 2024 census counted about 36.6 million people, and roughly two in three live in towns and cities.

The MPLA, the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola, has governed since independence from Portugal in 1975. Its main rival is UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola.

In Angola politics the constitution does not let voters choose the president directly. The person who heads the winning party’s national list becomes president, and that same ballot fills the 220-seat National Assembly.

The president also picks a vice-president from his own list. Executive power sits with the president, who is helped by the vice-president, ministers of state and ministers.

The new National Assembly building in Luanda, where the 220 members of parliament sit, during construction. File photo, 2013. (Photo: Fabio Vanin, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The President and His Government

João Lourenço took office as president in 2017 and was sworn in for a second term on 26 September 2022. The constitution allows two five-year terms, so he must step down in 2027.

On 15 October 2026 he gave his tenth and last State of the Nation speech to parliament. He said the economy grew 3% in 2025 and 5.3% in early 2026.

Inflation, he said, fell to 10.8% by June 2026. Public debt, he said, dropped to 51.2% of output in 2026.

Those figures are the government’s own, as reported by Portugal’s public broadcaster RTP. The opposition disputes the picture, as the section on UNITA explains below.

Esperança da Costa has been vice-president since 2022 and was still carrying out official duties in October 2026. She is the formal number two in the executive.

José de Lima Massano, Minister of State for Economic Coordination, steers economic policy and investment talks.

Vera Daves de Sousa, Finance Minister, issued new orders on 1 October 2026 dividing work among her secretaries of state.

Téte António, Foreign Minister, was attending a southern African ministers’ meeting on 21 October 2026.

Lúcio Amaral, Minister of National Defence, led the armed forces’ 35th anniversary event in Huambo on 9 October 2026.

Manuel Homem, Interior Minister, oversees the police, migration and criminal investigation services.

Officials greet one another at an arrival ceremony outside the Presidential Palace in Luanda. File photo, August 2023. (Photo: Lula Oficial, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The MPLA and the Race to Succeed Lourenço

The MPLA has governed since 1975, and in Angola politics its leader steers the country. Lourenço is its current president and is seeking another term as party leader.

Its IX Ordinary Congress is set for 9 and 10 December 2026. The winner of the party leadership is expected to shape who becomes the MPLA candidate for the 2027 presidential race.

The party’s vice-president is Mara Quiosa, who led a meeting of the congress preparatory commission in June 2026. Lourenço himself chaired the commission in September 2026.

The sharpest clash is over retired general Higino Carneiro, who wanted to challenge Lourenço for the party leadership. His team said it handed in 19,158 membership signatures on 25 June 2026, against a minimum of 5,000.

On 21 July the party’s candidacy sub-commission rejected the bid, citing allegedly forged signatures. Carneiro went to the Constitutional Court, Angola’s top court on constitutional questions, to try to suspend that ruling.

On 21 October 2026 the MPLA Central Committee upheld its finding that his bid was void and opened a disciplinary process, state radio RNA reported. Angola’s Attorney General’s office has also accused him of embezzlement and money laundering, and he has invoked the presumption of innocence.

Lourenço’s own candidacy for party leader was formalised in May 2026 with about 11,000 signatures. If he wins in December, he would be well placed to influence who runs for president in 2027.

UNITA and the Opposition

UNITA is the main opposition force in Angola politics and is led by Adalberto Costa Júnior. It holds the second-largest group in the National Assembly.

In the August 2022 election UNITA took 43.95% of the vote and 90 seats, its best result since multiparty politics began. Turnout was 44.82%, and abstention was the highest in the country’s history.

On 14 October 2026 Costa Júnior called Lourenço’s rule a lost decade with few results for ordinary Angolans. He said oil still makes up more than 90% of exports and that unemployment is near 30%.

He cited a market trader who earned 42,000 kwanzas (about US$45) in a month, at about 927 kwanzas to the US dollar. Those are UNITA’s figures, not official ones.

On 19 October 2026 he told a UNITA seminar that the constitution is not democratic because voters cannot elect the president directly. He added that UNITA will not back any constitutional revision that extends presidential terms.

Tension has also reached the streets. On 8 August 2026 UNITA said police surrounded its office in Uíge, in the north.

Officers fired tear gas during an event honouring its late founder, Jonas Savimbi, according to the party.

UNITA wants to revive a coalition called the United Patriotic Front (FPU) in a new form. Abel Chivukuvuku’s party PRA-JA Servir Angola, which ran with UNITA in 2022, is preparing to stand alone.

Smaller parties hold few seats. The 2022 result gave two each to the PRS, the FNLA and the PHA, all minor parties.

Parliament, Courts and Prosecutors

Adão de Almeida has led the National Assembly since November 2025, when he replaced Carolina Cerqueira. The assembly has 220 members, and the MPLA holds a majority of 124 seats.

Lourenço’s October 2026 address opened the last parliamentary year of the fifth legislature.

The Constitutional Court is led by Judge President Laurinda Prazeres, according to the court’s own website in October 2026. It rules on election disputes, party rules and constitutional questions.

In 2022 this court validated the MPLA’s win and rejected UNITA’s appeal. The constitution lets the president appoint its presiding judge.

The Supreme Court is the top court for ordinary cases. Its president, Norberto Sodré João, was appointed in November 2025 after Joel Leonardo left.

Sodré João was visiting provincial courts in October 2026.

Pedro Mendes de Carvalho was appointed Attorney General in March 2026, replacing Hélder Pitta Gróz. The office has accused Carneiro of embezzlement and money laundering.

A solemn session in the chamber of Angola’s National Assembly in Luanda. File photo, October 2011. (Photo: Dilma Rousseff from Brasil, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Army, the Police and the Security Chiefs

In Angola politics the army answers to the president, who is commander in chief of the Angolan Armed Forces (FAA). The force marked its 35th anniversary in October 2026, and Defence Minister Lúcio Amaral presided at the central ceremony.

Lourenço called the National Security Council to review the retirement of senior generals in August 2026. Later in 2026 he replaced dozens of commanders in the FAA and the National Police, according to the state daily Jornal de Angola.

The police fall under Interior Minister Manuel Homem. The force says it is preparing to secure the 2027 general elections.

On 29 June 2026 the FAA signed a partnership with the Ohio National Guard under the US State Partnership Program. It covers public health, cybersecurity, disaster response and leadership training.

A US diplomat at the signing called Angola a strategic partner in sub-Saharan Africa, according to the Angolan outlet Imparcial Press.

Provinces, Governors and Local Elections

Angola has 21 provinces, each run by a governor, and the capital province of Luanda is the political and economic heart. Its governor, Luís Nunes, was defending himself in October 2026 against claims of a conflict of interest in public contracts.

Nunes told the press he does not do business with himself.

Angola’s municipal elections, known as autarquias, have been delayed for years, although the president promised them in his first term. Election observer Luís Jimbo has urged the president to explain the delay and to hold them together with the 2027 vote.

Costa Júnior said in October 2026 that Angola cannot be governed as the property of one party.

What It Means for US Readers

Angola sells oil to the world, and the president has named the Lobito Corridor as a main focus for foreign investment. A smooth handover in 2027 would protect that agenda.

The Ohio National Guard link is a new channel between the two militaries. US companies can also read the succession fight as a gauge of policy stability.

Watch three dates for Angola politics. They are the MPLA congress on 9 and 10 December 2026, the formal calling of the election and the vote, expected in August 2027.

For more, see the Rio Times guides to Angola’s economy and Angola’s geopolitics, the ruling party congress report and the Angola country page.

What Is Not Known

It is not yet known who will be the MPLA candidate for president. The party has not named one, and the December congress could reshape the field.

The election date has not been set. Under the law the president calls it after consulting the electoral commission and the Council of the Republic, an advisory body.

It is also unclear whether UNITA and smaller parties in Angola politics will agree on one coalition. Their talks continue, and the lists are not yet filed.

Figures on growth, debt and jobs differ between the government and the opposition, and no independent audit settles the argument.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the president of Angola in 2026?

João Lourenço of the MPLA has been president since 2017. He was sworn in for a second term on 26 September 2022 and cannot run again in 2027.

Does Angola have a prime minister?

No. The president is both head of state and head of government, and Vice-President Esperança da Costa serves under him.

When is the next general election in Angola?

The vote is expected in August 2027, though the president has not yet set the date. It will choose the president and the 220-seat National Assembly.

Who leads the opposition in Angola politics?

Adalberto Costa Júnior, the president of UNITA, leads the main opposition party. UNITA won 90 of 220 seats in 2022.

Who could succeed Lourenço as MPLA leader?

The party chooses its leader at the IX Congress on 9 and 10 December 2026. Lourenço is seeking another term as party president, while his rival Higino Carneiro’s bid was ruled void.

Can Angolans vote directly for the president?

No. The head of the winning party’s national list becomes president, so one ballot decides both the presidency and parliament.

Sources: Constitution of Angola (text of 2010, as revised in 2021), provisions on the president, the executive and terms, consulted 21 October 2026; INE Angola, Census 2024 results, 2024 census, consulted 21 October 2026; Tribunal Constitucional de Angola, official website, 12 October 2026; RNA (Rádio Nacional de Angola), Defence Minister at the FAA 35th anniversary, 9 October 2026; RNA, MPLA preparatory commission and Higino Carneiro, 1 June 2026; RNA, José de Lima Massano at the Africa CEO Forum, 16 May 2026; RTP, Lourenço’s last State of the Nation address, 15 October 2026; Observador (Lusa), UNITA on a lost decade, 15 October 2026; Observador, Higino Carneiro and the MPLA candidacy, 30 July 2026; Notícias Lusófonas (Lusa), UNITA on the constitution, 19 October 2026; Ver Angola, Higino Carneiro submits his candidacy, June 2026; Novo Jornal, UNITA accuses police in Uíge, 8 August 2026; Expansão, experts on the last State of the Nation, 14 October 2026; Imparcial Press, Finance Minister reallocates duties, 8 October 2026; Imparcial Press, Angola and the US formalise military cooperation, 29 June 2026; Imparcial Press, new Attorney General, 7 May 2026; ANGOP, Constitutional Court validates the 2022 results, 8 September 2022; Plataforma Media, Angola heads to elections in 2027, 24 August 2026; Brasil 247, interview with the president of the National Assembly, 20 September 2026.

World.title: Who Runs Algeria’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026
World.content:
ALGERIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Algeria is North Africa’s largest country, with about 47.9 million people in 2026 (IMF estimate). Its economy is run mainly by the state, and oil and gas pay most of the bills.

— Size The IMF puts output at about US$331.9 billion in 2026, or about US$6,700 per person. Real growth is projected at 3.8% in 2026.

— The big player Sonatrach, the state oil and gas company, has more than 200,000 staff. It earned 812 billion dinars (about US$6.0 billion) in net profit in 2024.

— Money from exports Hydrocarbon exports earned US$37.5 billion from January to September 2026, Hydrocarbons Minister Mohamed Arkab said. Agence Ecofin reported US$31 billion a year earlier.

— The banks The Bank of Algeria licenses 20 banks, 7 of them state-owned. Governor Mohand Bourai took office on 3 September 2026.

— Decision-makers President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb, Finance Minister Mohammed Lamine Lebbou and Sonatrach chief Noureddine Daoudi all hold office in October 2026.

— Weak points The IMF says reserves fell from US$68.9 billion in 2024 to US$51.0 billion in 2025, and annual price rises hit 8.3% in August 2026.

The Algeria economy matters to Americans because Algeria sells gas to Europe and buys US goods.

A few state bodies, private families and foreign partners hold the levers. This guide names them as of October 2026.

The port and city of Oran, western Algeria’s main harbour and industrial hub. File photo, 2015. (Photo: YACINE K, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Algeria Economy in Numbers

The Algeria economy serves about 47.9 million people in 2026, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Output is projected at about US$331.9 billion this year, which works out to roughly US$6,700 per person.

The IMF estimates real growth at 3.9% in 2025 and projects 3.8% in 2026. Growth outside oil and gas is projected at 3.3% in 2026, while the hydrocarbon sector grows 2.7%.

This guide converts dinars at about 134.5 to the US dollar, the October 2026 rate. The Bank of Algeria’s own quotation was 133.64 dinars on 2 October 2026.

Public money drives the Algeria economy. The IMF says large deficits have used up fiscal savings, with the central government running a deficit of 10.5% of output in 2025.

Public debt stood at 52.1% of output in 2025 and is projected to reach 60.4% in 2027. Almost none of it is foreign: gross external debt is below 1% of output.

Prices and the Dinar

Prices are rising faster. The national statistics office reported that consumer prices in August 2026 were 8.3% higher than a year earlier, while the annual average rate was 3.9%.

TSA reported on 19 October 2026 that the Council of Ministers ordered an inquiry into meat importers and price ceilings on vegetables, pasta and meat. Our guide to the price measures explains the seven steps.

The dinar trades at two prices. The official rate was 133.64 to the US dollar on 2 October 2026, while the street market in Algiers quoted 239.5, about 79% higher.

The IMF wants the central bank to stop financing the Treasury and to let the dinar move more freely. It also warns that the gap with the street market has widened.

Sonatrach, the State Energy Giant

Sonatrach is the state-owned oil and gas company, created in 1963. Its website lists more than 200,000 employees and more than 150 subsidiaries.

Noureddine Daoudi has led it since 26 October 2025, when President Tebboune dismissed Rachid Hachichi. Daoudi was still running the company in mid-October 2026, when he met US energy companies.

Sonatrach’s 2024 annual report, as reported by the news site TSA, shows revenue of 6,523 billion dinars (about US$48.5 billion). Net profit rose 20% to 812 billion dinars (about US$6.0 billion).

It paid 3,872 billion dinars (about US$28.8 billion) in oil taxes to the state in 2024. That single payment explains why the Treasury watches Sonatrach’s every move.

Primary output was 193.7 million tonnes of oil equivalent in 2024, of which 127.9 million was natural gas. The company made 18 discoveries that year, all on its own.

A Sonatrach office building in Béjaïa, a Mediterranean oil port east of Algiers. File photo, 2008. (Photo: Zil, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Ministers and Officials Who Set the Rules

President Abdelmadjid Tebboune holds the last word on economic policy. Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb chairs the government meetings, including the one held on 21 October 2026 on industry and public works.

Mohamed Arkab is Minister of State in charge of Hydrocarbons. He told parliament’s finance committee on 17 October 2026 that hydrocarbon export revenue reached US$37.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026.

Mourad Adjal is Minister of Energy and Renewable Energies, and oversees the electricity side. On 13 October 2026 he said the state utility Sonelgaz should help Algerian firms enter regional energy markets.

Mohammed Lamine Lebbou became Finance Minister on 1 September 2026, when Tebboune replaced four ministers. He had been governor of the Bank of Algeria, the central bank.

Farid Kourtel is Minister of Industry. He presented the 2027 industry budget to parliament on 19 October 2026.

Head of state: Abdelmadjid Tebboune, president.

Government: Sifi Ghrieb, prime minister.

Hydrocarbons: Mohamed Arkab, Minister of State.

Energy and renewables: Mourad Adjal.

Finance: Mohammed Lamine Lebbou, since 1 September 2026.

Industry: Farid Kourtel.

Central bank: Mohand Bourai, governor since 3 September 2026.

Gas, Oil and Who Buys Them

Hydrocarbons earned US$37.5 billion between January and September 2026, Arkab said, against US$31 billion a year earlier, Agence Ecofin reported. The IMF sees the rise as a chance to rebuild reserves.

Europe is the main gas customer. According to Spain’s grid operator Enagás, Algeria supplied nearly 35% of Spain’s gas in the 12 months to July 2026, mostly through the Medgaz pipeline.

From January to July 2026, pipeline exports rose 13% to Spain and 5% to Italy, the Gas Exporting Countries Forum says, as cited by Afrik. Our gas and Europe explainer covers the pipelines.

In mid-October 2026 Sonatrach met ExxonMobil, Halliburton and Devon Energy, then Baker Hughes, KBR and Occidental Petroleum (Oxy). It also joined the Algeria Energy Day in Louisiana.

Arkab wants more of the gas and oil processed at home. About 32% is processed locally now, and the target is more than 50%.

The investment programme runs to US$71.6 billion through 2030, with about US$13 billion for refining, Agence Ecofin reported from his testimony.

Aerial view of a company housing compound and industrial yards at Hassi Messaoud, the centre of Algeria’s oil fields in the Sahara. File photo, 2015. (Photo: Youceflabed, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Public Banks, the Central Bank and the Stock Exchange

Mohand Bourai took over the Bank of Algeria on 3 September 2026. He previously headed the state farm bank BADR and the banks’ association ABEF.

As of January 2025, Algeria licensed 20 banks: seven public and thirteen private. The public group includes BEA, BNA, CPA, BADR, BDL, CNEP and BNH.

The private banks include subsidiaries of Société Générale, BNP Paribas and Natixis, plus Gulf and Arab lenders such as Al Baraka and Trust Bank. Citibank and HSBC operate as branches.

The IMF warns of tight links between the state, state banks and state companies. It urges tighter supervision and better governance of the public banks, and calls non-performing loans high.

The Algiers stock exchange is tiny. Its main market lists seven names, including the state-owned lenders CPA and BDL, the drugmaker Saidal and Alliance Assurances.

In October 2026 the exchange showed free-float value of 97.9 billion dinars (about US$727 million) for CPA. For BDL it was 61.8 billion dinars (about US$459 million).

The Treasury also borrows from Algerians directly. Its first sovereign sukuk, an Islamic bond, targeted 296.65 billion dinars (about US$2.2 billion) over seven years from January 2026.

State Utilities, Telecoms and Holding Companies

Sonelgaz is the state electricity and gas utility. In 2025 it served 12.6 million electricity customers and 8.5 million gas customers, with 26,706 megawatts of installed capacity.

Madar Holding is a state holding company that took over firms seized from former oligarchs. Its board confirmed Adel Khemane as chief executive on 8 January 2026.

Mobilis had 23.47 million subscribers and Djezzy 17.75 million. Agence Ecofin calls both state-owned, while Qatar’s Ooredoo had 14.7 million, according to regulator data cited in May 2026.

Ooredoo told the telecoms minister in May 2026 that it was ready to invest more in 5G and data centres. No amounts were given.

Private Families and Foreign Investors

Cevital, headed by Malik Rebrab, is described by the news site TSA as the largest private group in Algeria. Its website lists food, cars and services, and about US$4 billion in revenue.

In May 2026 it began a US$600 million sugar beet project on 1,200 hectares in Ghardaïa province. The refinery is due in 2028.

Condor is the family company of the Benhamadi family, known for TVs, appliances and phones. In July 2026 it signed a deal with Germany’s Maincor during Tebboune’s visit to Berlin, according to Agence Ecofin.

Tosyali Algérie runs the steel complex at Bethioua, near Oran. It said its 2025 export income was US$1.2 billion and targets US$2 billion to US$2.5 billion in 2026.

Stellantis builds Fiat cars at Oran, in the only car plant then running, and had about 2,000 staff in January 2026. Rules require 40% local content within five years of a plant opening.

See our Algeria country hub for more. Our guide to the Algerian car push explains Tebboune’s target of a fully national vehicle.

A port crane at the harbour of Béjaïa, the Mediterranean port town where the private group Cevital is based. File photo, 2008. (Photo: Zil, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Iron Ore, Exports and the Push to Diversify

Non-hydrocarbon exports reached about US$4 billion from January to August 2026, up around 10%, an official of the Ministry of Foreign Trade said. The 2026 target is US$5 billion.

Chocolate, olive oil, biscuits and cheese lead the food list, which earned US$213 million in the same months. Our report on non-oil exports has more.

The Gara Djebilet iron ore mine near Tindouf holds more than 3.5 billion tonnes, according to the Jeune Indépendant daily.

A primary processing unit was over 95% complete in June 2026, the same daily reported.

The draft 2027 finance bill assumes growth of 4.2% and an oil price of US$60 a barrel, economist Brahim Guendouzi wrote in TSA. It would also add value-added tax on e-commerce platforms.

What It Means for US Readers

The United States bought US$2.24 billion of Algerian goods in 2025 and sold Algeria US$1.28 billion, according to the US Census Bureau. From January to August 2026 the United States bought US$1.93 billion and sold US$1.00 billion.

US oil service firms are the clearest opening. Sonatrach’s talks with ExxonMobil, Devon, Halliburton, Baker Hughes, KBR and Oxy in October 2026 show where the state wants partners.

Buyers and investors in the Algeria economy should expect the state at the table, since Sonatrach, state banks and ministries approve most large deals. Dinar access is tight.

Readers of Europe’s gas story should note that Spain and Italy depend on Algeria’s pipelines. Read our Algeria geopolitics guide for the diplomatic side.

What Is Not Known

Little is public about the wealth or accounts of Algeria’s private families. Ownership of the biggest private groups is held within the families.

It is not clear how fast reserves will fall. The IMF projects US$46.5 billion at the end of 2026 and US$19.8 billion in 2030, but oil prices could change that path.

Nor is it clear whether the October 2026 price controls will curb inflation. The 2027 finance bill is also still before parliament.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who runs the Algeria economy?

The state does. President Abdelmadjid Tebboune sets the line, and Sonatrach, the state banks and ministries such as Hydrocarbons and Finance carry it out. A few private families, including Cevital and Condor, sit beside them.

What is the biggest company in Algeria?

Sonatrach, the state oil and gas company, is the largest. It reported revenue of 6,523 billion dinars (about US$48.5 billion) for 2024 and employs more than 200,000 people.

How big is the Algeria economy?

The IMF puts output at about US$331.9 billion in 2026, with real growth projected at 3.8%. That is about US$6,700 per person.

What does Algeria export?

Mostly oil and gas, worth US$37.5 billion from January to September 2026. Non-oil exports such as steel, cement and food reached about US$4 billion from January to August 2026.

Who controls Algeria’s banks?

The state controls the biggest ones. Seven of the 20 licensed banks were public as of January 2025, and Mohand Bourai has led the central bank since 3 September 2026.

Is Algeria’s dinar stable?

The official rate has stayed near 133 dinars to the US dollar since March 2026. The street market in Algiers quoted about 239.5 on 3 October 2026.

World.title: Who Runs Cameroon’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026
World.content:
CAMEROON · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Cameroon is a Central African nation of more than 28 million people on the Gulf of Guinea. It shares its currency with five neighbours.

— Money The Central African CFA franc, pegged to the euro. All conversions here use about 584 CFA francs to the US dollar in October 2026.

— Top exports Cocoa beans earned about US$1.4 billion in 2025, 26.3% of export earnings. Crude oil came second at about US$1.2 billion, or 22.9%.

— Who holds the levers The state runs oil, power, ports, telecoms and a growing share of banking. Private giants include Orange, MTN, the brewer SABC and Castel.

— Public debt The state debt agency counted CFA15,607 billion (about US$26.7 billion) at the end of June 2026, equal to 44.2% of output.

— Why it matters to the US US firms were shown about US$7 billion of possible projects in August 2026. US goods exports to Cameroon were only US$169.3 million in 2025.

— Still open Cameroon has no active IMF programme in October 2026, and a new one is not yet agreed.

The Cameroon economy, one of Central Africa’s largest, is run by a handful of state companies, foreign-owned giants and a few family fortunes. It matters to US readers because Washington is courting Yaoundé for minerals, energy and ports, while the country carries a high risk of debt distress.

This guide names the main players, shows who controls them and explains what that means for American readers.

Douala, Cameroon’s largest city, main port and business centre. File photo, 2014. (Photo: Guaka, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

How the Cameroon Economy Is Built

The Cameroon economy grew 3.4% in 2025, according to the World Bank. It expects growth to average 3.7% a year from 2026 to 2028, while the IMF projects 3.3% for 2026.

Services have driven growth since the 1993 currency devaluation. Agriculture employs nearly 60% of the population, the World Bank says.

Cameroon sells raw goods and buys finished ones. In 2025 exports earned CFA3,084 billion (about US$5.3 billion), while imports cost CFA5,229 billion (about US$8.9 billion), according to the national statistics institute.

The trade deficit reached CFA2,145 billion (about US$3.7 billion), up 22.8% on 2024. Exports covered only 59% of imports.

Cameroon shares its currency with five neighbours through the CEMAC union. The regional central bank, the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), cut its main rate from 4.75% to 4.50% on 29 June 2026.

Many of the biggest actors are state-owned, and the IMF calls their weak governance a brake on growth. The Cameroon economy is best read sector by sector, following the money.

Oil and Gas Under State Control

The National Hydrocarbons Corporation, known as SNH, is the state oil company. It was created on 12 March 1980 and, in its own words, manages the state’s interests in oil and gas.

SNH also sells the state’s share of Cameroon’s crude through contracts. Foreign companies pump the oil and share output with the state.

Perenco, a Franco-British group, calls itself the leading operator. In September 2026 it put its operated output at about 75,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day.

It says it has invested over US$1.5 billion alongside SNH since 2012.

Addax Petroleum, a subsidiary of China’s Sinopec, produced about 30% of Cameroon’s crude in 2025, or close to 5.8 million barrels. Finance ministry data put national output at 19.8 million barrels that year, down from 21.3 million in 2024.

Old fields are running down. Crude earned CFA705.6 billion (about US$1.2 billion) in 2025, 29.6% less than in 2024, as volumes and prices both fell.

Gas took a hit in 2026. The floating gas plant Hilli Episeyo, owned by Golar LNG, left Cameroon after its contract with SNH ended in July 2026.

It had sold gas abroad as liquefied natural gas since 2018. That trade earned CFA350.2 billion (about US$600 million) in 2025, or 11.4% of export earnings.

The national economic and financial committee expects the oil sector to shrink 16.1% in 2026. The hoped-for replacement is Yoyo-Yolanda, a gas field shared with Equatorial Guinea, which the two countries agreed to develop jointly on 3 February 2026.

SNH puts that field at about 2.5 trillion cubic feet of gas and nearly US$4 billion of investment. First gas is unlikely before about 2029.

The Refinery and Fuel Prices

Sonara, the national refinery, is now almost wholly state-owned. A notarised notice dated 14 October 2026 shows the government holding 98.09%, up from 81.95%, after it converted claims into new shares.

TotalEnergies Marketing Afrique’s stake fell to 0.42%. Sonara also owed CFA191.3 billion (about US$327 million) in domestic debt at the end of June 2026.

The state keeps pump prices steady by paying the difference. Finance Minister Louis Paul Motaze said that cost CFA57 billion (about US$98 million) in September 2026 alone.

Cocoa, the Top Export

Cocoa beans overtook crude oil as Cameroon’s biggest export in 2025. They earned CFA810.2 billion (about US$1.4 billion), or 26.3% of export earnings.

Cocoa paste and butter added 12.2%, so cocoa products together made up 38.5% of export revenue, the statistics institute reports.

The 2025 boom came from prices. Volumes fell 9% that year, but the price per kilo rose enough to lift revenue 18.7%.

The 2025-26 season, which ended on 15 July 2026, reversed that. The national cocoa and coffee board says marketed output fell 19.9% to 247,914 tonnes, and bean exports fell 34.7% to 125,469 tonnes.

Export revenue dropped from about CFA1.07 trillion to CFA400.9 billion (about US$690 million), a fall of about 63%. Lower world prices did most of the damage.

Three exporters shipped 70.3% of the beans: Telcar Cocoa with 32.4%, Ofi Cam with 19.4% and SBET with 18.5%. Europe took 84.6% of exports, led by the Netherlands.

Millions of small farmers sit below these traders. They bear the swings in world prices, and the 2025-26 fall could cost cocoa its top spot in the 2026 export tables.

Cocoa pods on a tree in Cameroon, the country’s top export crop in 2025. File photo, 2012. (Photo: Barada-nikto, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Plantations, Sugar and Cotton

The Cameroon economy on the farm is split between state estates, listed groups and French-owned sugar. The state-owned Cameroon Development Corporation, known as CDC, grows bananas and rubber in the English-speaking North-West and South-West.

Palm oil and rubber estates sit on the regional stock exchange, BVMAC. It lists Socapalm, a palm oil company, and Safacam, a rubber estate.

Safacam’s controlling group, Socfinaf, expects its 2026 profit to fall 58.3% to CFA1.34 billion (about US$2.3 million). Sales are forecast at CFA29.37 billion (about US$50 million).

Sosucam is the country’s main sugar maker. Its French parent, Somdiaa, holds 82% and told the government in June 2026 that it intends to sell all of it.

A Kenyan bidder is reported to have offered about US$350 million. Local output of 120,000 to 160,000 tonnes covers only part of demand.

Cameroon imported 208,443 tonnes of refined sugar in 2025, costing CFA69.3 billion (about US$119 million).

Cotton is the north’s cash crop. The company Sodecoton works with 150,000 to 200,000 growers and aimed for a record 440,000 tonnes in 2025-26, after 286,000 tonnes the season before.

Cotton earned CFA124.4 billion (about US$213 million) in 2025, down 29.8%, and timber earned CFA217.6 billion (about US$372 million), down 12.8%.

An oil palm plantation run by Socapalm at Souza, Cameroon. File photo. (Photo: Minette Lontsie, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Power, Water and Ports

Electricity is the state’s biggest recent takeover. A presidential decree of 4 May 2026 turned the power distributor Eneo into Socadel, a state-owned company.

The government paid CFA78 billion (about US$134 million) to Actis, a British investment fund, for its 51% stake. Socadel’s capital is CFA43.903 billion (about US$75 million), and the state holds 95%, with 5% reserved for staff.

Its debts are still being counted. The state debt agency’s early estimate is about CFA800 billion (about US$1.4 billion).

Socadel plans to spend CFA52.6 billion (about US$90 million) on fuel for 33 power plants. Its board includes the heads of Sonatrel, the state grid company, and EDC, the state power developer.

The 420-megawatt Nachtigal dam, fully commissioned in 2025, supplies close to 30% of the country’s generating capacity, the plant’s operator says. The Edéa dam on the Sanaga River is among the country’s oldest hydro plants.

Ports are the second state lifeline. Cameroon’s ports handled 23.7 million tonnes in 2025, the transport minister says, and the port of Douala carries about 85% of foreign trade.

The Kribi deep-water port earned CFA38.97 billion (about US$67 million) in 2025 and made a profit of CFA4.02 billion (about US$6.9 million). Its second container terminal opened on 9 May 2025.

Camtel, the state telecom firm, shows a stronger side of the public sector.

It made a net profit above CFA13 billion (about US$22 million) in 2025.

The State Companies’ Debt Problem

The state debt agency counted CFA319.6 billion (about US$547 million) of direct domestic debt owed by public enterprises at the end of June 2026. Three firms owed 93% of it.

Sonara owed CFA191.3 billion (about US$327 million), Camair-Co CFA62.4 billion (about US$107 million) and Camtel CFA43.6 billion (about US$75 million).

The Edéa hydroelectric dam on the Sanaga River, one of Cameroon’s oldest power plants. File photo. (Photo: Simbanematick, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The Banks That Hold the Money

Cameroon has 18 operating banks. Their combined balance sheets stood at CFA13.593 trillion (about US$23.3 billion) at the end of November 2025.

In a press tally of 2025 results, Afriland First Bank reported the largest profit: CFA38.75 billion (about US$66 million). Ecobank Cameroun followed with CFA27.29 billion (about US$47 million), and CCA Bank and AFG Bank each made about CFA21.5 billion (about US$37 million).

Not every bank had published its results when the tally was compiled in October 2026.

The state is moving into banking. On 12 May 2026 it closed the purchase of a 58.08% stake in Société Générale Cameroun.

The price was CFA129 billion (about US$221 million), lifting its holding to 83.68%.

The bank is now called General Bank of Cameroon. Officials say the state’s control will be temporary, and that other investors will be invited in later.

Foreign names are also changing. Access Bank, from Nigeria, completed its purchase of Standard Chartered’s Cameroon unit on 5 December 2025, for about US$29 million.

BGFI Holding, the parent of BGFIBank, listed on the regional stock exchange on 7 May 2026. The BEAC and the regional banking regulator, known as COBAC, set the rules for all banks in the union.

Mobile money is a new financial layer. Orange Money and MTN MoMo handled CFA32.667 trillion (about US$56 billion) of transactions in 2025, the national economic and financial committee says.

They kept CFA473 billion (about US$810 million) in bank accounts for customers.

Telecoms, Beer and Cement: The Private Giants

Orange and MTN dominate mobile phones. In 2024 Orange Cameroun took 50.08% of telecom revenue and MTN Cameroon 47.26%, the telecoms regulator ART reports, the first time Orange had led.

Orange had 15.67 million active customers and MTN 13.71 million. The state-owned Camtel had 2.08 million and 2.67% of revenue.

MTN Cameroon earned a 2025 profit of 2.091 billion rand (about CFA67.9 billion, or US$116 million). Revenue was 13.452 billion rand (about US$748 million), and minority holders own 20% of the company.

Nexttel, a fourth operator, belongs to Viettel of Vietnam, with a minority stake held by the businessman Baba Danpullo.

The brewer SABC is the Cameroon arm of France’s Castel group. Its 2025 revenue was CFA483.2 billion (about US$827 million), and it is set to merge with Guinness Cameroon.

Cement shows how a downturn bites. Cimencam and Dangote Cement Cameroon, the two largest producers, sold 677,392 tonnes in the first quarter of 2026, down 12.1% on a year earlier.

Dangote Cement Cameroon’s sales fell about 15.8% in the same period, the company reported on 29 April 2026.

Business Families, Tycoons and Who Sets the Rules

Cameroon’s richest man is Baba Ahmadou Danpullo, according to Forbes Afrique, which puts his fortune at about CFA547 billion (about US$936 million). His group, based in Douala, has interests in tea estates, commercial property, telecoms and road transport.

On 3 July 2026 he confirmed plans for a private airline, Danpullo Air Line, with about CFA500 billion (about US$856 million) to be invested. Work on a private Yaoundé airport was due to begin in September 2026, with flights targeted for 2030.

In banking, Afriland First Bank reported the largest 2025 profit in a press tally of results.

Foreign groups hold much of the rest. Castel owns the brewer, Orange and MTN run phones, Perenco and Addax pump oil, and Somdiaa runs sugar.

President Paul Biya holds ultimate power. On 12 October 2026 he signed the circular that sets the 2027 budget deficit at 2.7% of output.

Prime Minister Joseph Dion Ngute coordinates the government, and Alamine Ousmane Mey is economy and planning minister. Louis Paul Motaze, the finance minister, speaks for Cameroon at the IMF and World Bank.

The IMF reportedly wants each CEMAC member to hold its 2027 deficit to 1.5% of output as a condition of new programmes. Cameroon’s last IMF reviews were completed in July 2025.

About CFA300 billion (about US$513 million) of budget support planned for 2027 assumes a new programme, the finance ministry’s planning paper says. An IMF mission in September 2026 kept its high-risk rating for debt.

Public debt, as counted by the state debt agency, was CFA15,607 billion (about US$26.7 billion) at the end of June 2026, or 44.2% of output. Of the central government’s debt, 64.5% is external.

The World Bank approved US$5.01 billion for 21 Cameroon projects, the planning ministry said on 15 October 2026. Agreements worth US$4.129 billion are signed for 18 of them.

What It Means for US Readers

US business with Cameroon is small but growing in interest. US goods exports were US$169.3 million in 2025, and imports were US$287.3 million, according to the US Trade Representative.

At the first US-Cameroon economic dialogue on 27 August 2026, the US Embassy listed about US$7 billion of possible projects. They include a US$500 million rutile mine by Tronox and Lion Rock.

Others are a US$3.5 billion Sanaga River dam proposed by Hydromine and a US$2 billion airport near Douala.

These are opportunities at various stages, not signed money. Many depend on power supply, state-owned partners and financing from a government that carries a high risk of debt distress.

US investors should also watch cocoa, which feeds chocolate makers, and the 2026 fall in oil and gas output. The geopolitics explainer covers Cameroon’s foreign partners.

For wider context, see the Rio Times Cameroon country guide and the guide to Cameroon’s role in Africa. The explainer on who takes over if Biya goes covers politics.

Regional banking is covered in the report on the BDEAC bond. More coverage sits on the Rio Times Cameroon page.

What Is Not Known

SNH does not publish a full breakdown of what it earns from selling the state’s crude. The company’s own site lists its units and managers but no production totals.

The size of Socadel’s debts is still an early estimate of about CFA800 billion (about US$1.4 billion). The price and buyer for Somdiaa’s 82% of Sosucam are not public.

Bank profits for 2025 come from a press tally that did not cover every bank. No official ranking of the biggest companies by revenue is published.

The IMF has not set a date for a new programme. Whether Cameroon’s 2027 budget will meet the regional deficit limit is not yet known.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big is the Cameroon economy?

The World Bank says it grew 3.4% in 2025 and projects average growth of 3.7% a year for 2026 to 2028. The IMF projects 3.3% for 2026.

What are Cameroon’s main exports?

Cocoa beans were first in 2025, earning CFA810.2 billion (about US$1.4 billion). Crude oil followed with CFA705.6 billion (about US$1.2 billion), then cocoa paste and butter, gas, timber and cotton.

Which state companies matter most?

The oil company SNH, the refinery Sonara, the power company Socadel, the telecom firm Camtel, the airline Camair-Co and the ports of Douala and Kribi. The estates CDC and Sodecoton also matter.

Who owns the biggest private companies?

The brewer SABC belongs to France’s Castel group. MTN Cameroon reports through South Africa’s MTN Group, and minority holders own 20% of it.

Is Cameroon’s government now a bank owner?

Yes. Since 12 May 2026 it holds 83.68% of General Bank of Cameroon, formerly Société Générale Cameroun. Officials call the control temporary.

Does Cameroon have an IMF programme?

No. Its last reviews under the previous programme were completed in July 2025, and talks on a new one continued after an IMF mission in September 2026.

Which currency does Cameroon use?

The Central African CFA franc, pegged to the euro and shared with five neighbours. In October 2026 it traded at about 584 to the US dollar.

Sources: National Institute of Statistics, foreign trade in 2025 (provisional), 2026-04-01; World Bank, Cameroon country overview, 2026-10-05; IMF, Cameroon country page and 2026 Article IV consultation, 2026-04-03; SNH, National Hydrocarbons Corporation, 2026-10-21; BVMAC, listed companies, 2026-10-21; US Trade Representative, Cameroon, 2026-10-21; Business in Cameroon, Sonara ownership, 2026-10-16; Business in Cameroon, 2027 budget and IMF, 2026-10-20; Business in Cameroon, Socadel, 2026-05-07; Business in Cameroon, state company debt, 2026-07-31; Investir au Cameroun, Société Générale Cameroun takeover, 2026-05-13; Business in Cameroon, cocoa exports 2025-26, 2026-08-26; Sika Finance, public debt end-June 2026, 2026-07-28; EcoMatin, bank profits 2025, 2026-10-16; EcoMatin, telecom market shares (ART data), 2025-12-10; Business in Cameroon, Perenco, 2026-09-19; Business in Cameroon, Addax and national oil output, 2026-01-31.

World.title: Who Runs Zambia’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026
World.content:
ZAMBIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Zambia is a landlocked southern African republic of about 20.1 million people. Copper drives its economy.

— Size and direction Output grew 5.4% in 2025, according to the Zambia Statistics Agency. Inflation was 6.1% in September 2026.

— The copper Zambia mined 890,346 tonnes of copper in 2025. The State Department says copper brings more than 75% of export earnings and 25% of government revenue.

— Who holds the keys First Quantum, Barrick, Vedanta, Abu Dhabi’s IRH and Chinese groups run the big mines. The state holds stakes through ZCCM-IH.

— Banks and markets The three largest banks hold half of banking assets, about US$7.9 billion of US$15.9 billion in April 2026. Four companies on the Lusaka exchange are worth over US$1 billion each.

— Decision-makers President Hakainde Hichilema, Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane and Central Bank Governor Denny Kalyalya all hold office in October 2026.

— Still open IMF staff agreed a new US$1.47 billion programme on 9 October 2026 that awaits board approval, and a dispute over the Mopani mine is unsettled.

The Zambia economy matters to Americans because Africa’s second-largest copper producer supplies metal for power grids, electric cars and data centres.

A short list of mining groups, state companies, banks and power suppliers decides how the money flows. This guide names them and says who controls what.

Cairo Road, the main business street of Lusaka, Zambia’s capital. File photo, 2010. (Photo: Shaun Metcalfe, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The Zambia Economy in Numbers

Zambia had about 20.1 million people in 2024, according to the Labour Force Survey cited by the US State Department. The Zambia Statistics Agency says real output grew 5.4% in 2025, up from 3.8% in 2024.

Annual inflation fell to 6.1% in September 2026 from 6.2% in August, the same agency reports. The Bank of Zambia cut its policy rate to 13.25% in May 2026.

The State Department lists 2025’s largest sectors as trade (14.2% of output), information and communications (12.6%) and construction (9.6%). Mining took 9.6%, manufacturing 9.4% and agriculture 6.4%.

Mining looks small in that list, but it earns most of Zambia’s foreign currency. The State Department says copper brings more than 75% of export earnings.

This guide converts at about 20.2 kwacha to the US dollar, the rate on 21 October 2026. The kwacha gained about 30% against the dollar between May 2025 and May 2026, according to the same State Department report.

Budget and Debt

Press reports of the finance ministry’s budget hearings on 5 October 2026 say the 2027 budget would spend 271.9 billion kwacha (about US$13.5 billion). It expects revenue of 218.6 billion kwacha (about US$10.8 billion).

Planned borrowing is 44.9 billion kwacha (about US$2.2 billion). The ministry is reported to expect growth of 5.3% in 2026, below the 6.4% it projected a year earlier.

Since its 2020 default Zambia has restructured US$12.4 billion of external debt, the State Department says. The country finished a three-year IMF programme worth US$1.9 billion in January 2026.

On 9 October 2026 IMF staff reached a staff-level agreement with Zambia on a new 36-month Extended Credit Facility worth US$1.47 billion. It still needs approval from the IMF’s executive board.

Who Holds Economic Power in Lusaka

Hakainde Hichilema, a former businessman, won a second five-year term on 13 August 2026. He took 60.7% of the vote, according to the State Department, and was sworn in in early September.

Situmbeko Musokotwane was reappointed Minister of Finance and National Planning on 14 September 2026. He has held the post since 2021 and was also named acting Minister of Energy by October.

Denny Kalyalya governs the Bank of Zambia, the central bank. In mid-October 2026 he said Zambia plans to settle some copper sales to China in renminbi from 2027.

In the Zambia economy the Zambia Revenue Authority collects taxes, and the Zambia Development Agency licenses foreign investors. The Minerals Regulation Commission, created by a 2024 law, now issues mining licences.

For the wider picture, see the Rio Times Zambia explainer and the Zambia hub.

Finance Ministry: writes the budget and runs debt talks.

Bank of Zambia: sets the policy rate and supervises banks.

ZCCM-IH: the state’s mining investment arm, listed on the Lusaka exchange.

Industrial Development Corporation: oversees 44 state companies, according to the State Department.

Copper Miners and the State

Zambia produced 890,346 tonnes of copper in 2025, up 7.8% from about 826,000 tonnes in 2024, according to press reports of figures given to Parliament. The government wants three million tonnes a year by 2031.

Related coverage: ZCCM-IH on the Mopani deal and Zambia’s mining local content rules.

First Quantum and Barrick

First Quantum Minerals, a Canadian company, runs the Kansanshi and Sentinel mines. Kansanshi produced 181,183 tonnes in 2025 after a US$1.2 billion expansion began operating in August 2025.

The two mines together produced 184,929 tonnes in the first half of 2026, according to company data. Zambia made up about 93% of First Quantum’s group copper output in 2025.

Barrick Mining, a Canadian gold and copper miner, owns the Lumwana mine.

It is spending about US$2 billion to double Lumwana to around 240,000 tonnes a year. First copper from the expansion is due at the end of March 2028.

Vedanta, IRH and the Chinese Groups

Konkola Copper Mines, controlled by India’s Vedanta, produced 80,215 tonnes in 2025, according to the Ministry of Mines. ZCCM-IH holds 20.6% of the company.

Konkola restarted its Nchanga smelter on 21 September 2026 after a 106-day overhaul that cost about US$40 million. It also signed a US$498 million contract with China Nerin Engineering on 17 September for a tailings leach plant.

Mopani Copper Mines is 51% owned by International Resources Holding (IRH), an Abu Dhabi group, and 49% by ZCCM-IH. ZCCM-IH wrote to IRH on 18 September 2026 alleging breaches of the takeover deal and threatening arbitration.

On 14 October 2026 the two issued a joint statement saying they remain aligned on the mine’s next phase. Both keep a target of 300,000 tonnes of finished copper a year by 2029.

New Entrants

Chinese state-linked groups run the Chambishi and Luanshya mines, and China-owned Nkana Mining and Minerals Processing also operates on the Copperbelt. Chinese miners have paid some taxes and royalties in renminbi since October 2025.

KoBold Metals, a US-backed exploration company, began work on its US$2.3 billion Mingomba copper mine in April 2026. The US Embassy in Lusaka held a groundbreaking ceremony on 29 April.

Headgear at the Nkana copper mine in Kitwe, on the Copperbelt. File photo, 2007. (Photo: Per Arne Wilson, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

State Companies and Public Finances

Zambia has 48 state-owned enterprises, with the government holding a majority in 35 and a minority in 13, the State Department reports. Combined accounts for 36 of them showed assets of US$4.5 billion and a net loss of US$797.9 million for fiscal 2024.

ZCCM-IH holds stakes in most large mines, including Konkola, Mopani, Kansanshi, Lubambe and Chambishi Metals. It also holds Copperbelt Energy Corporation, Maamba Energy and Investrust Bank, according to its website.

Its board chairman is Phesto Musonda.

The government also holds Zamtel, the state telecom company, and the Tanzania-Zambia Mafuta pipeline jointly with Tanzania. Zambia has no sovereign wealth fund, the State Department says.

The government owed companies more than US$890 million in overdue VAT refunds in December 2025, and mining firms held 87% of that backlog. The figure was down from a peak of US$2 billion in December 2021.

Power, Water and the Grid

ZESCO, the state utility, runs hydropower stations with a combined capacity of more than 2,900 megawatts, according to its website. Up to 85% of Zambia’s electricity comes from water, the State Department says.

A drought in 2024 emptied Lake Kariba and caused nationwide power cuts. By late June 2026 the lake held 48% of its usable storage, against 23% a year earlier, the Zambezi River Authority says.

See also Zambia’s solar capacity surge and Zambia and the region.

Solar and Independent Producers

Installed generating capacity stood at 4,722 megawatts in October 2026, the Ministry of Energy says. Solar capacity reached 1,027 megawatts in early October, up from 178 megawatts in 2024.

The government wants 10,000 megawatts by 2031. Private producers can now sell power directly under an open-access market, and Copperbelt Energy Corporation is one of the larger private names.

Industrial plant on the outskirts of Kitwe, the main Copperbelt city. File photo, 2007. (Photo: Per Arne Wilson, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Banks, Markets and Telecoms

In April 2026 the three largest banks held about US$7.89 billion of the sector’s US$15.9 billion in assets, the State Department says. Most banks are regional groups headquartered outside Zambia.

The government holds minority stakes in Zanaco, Indo Zambia Bank and Zambia Industrial and Commercial Bank. Bad loans were 2.7% of the total in April 2026, the lowest in decades.

Lending is costly. Average loan rates were about 28% in May 2026, because banks earn high yields buying government securities.

The Lusaka Securities Exchange had a market value above US$17 billion, according to chief executive Nicholas Kabaso in September 2026. Four companies each passed US$1 billion: Copperbelt Energy, ZCCM-IH, Zambia Sugar and Airtel Zambia.

Kabaso said the first gold exchange-traded fund is due in October 2026. Five listings worth about US$1 billion in total are in the pipeline.

Farming, Food and Business Groups

ZamStats forecast a maize crop of 4.9 million tonnes for the 2025/26 season, up 27.8% on the season before. Small and medium farmers grew 94% of it, according to Statistician General Sheila Mudenda in May 2026.

Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa warned that below-average rain is more likely in 2026/27. That would hit crops and hydropower together.

Food Producers and Manufacturers

Zambia Sugar is listed in Lusaka and crossed US$1 billion in market value in 2026. Zambeef Products, listed in Lusaka and on London’s AIM market, produces beef, poultry, dairy, flour and bread.

The State Department notes that several of Zambia’s multi-facility economic zones are occupied almost entirely by Chinese companies. The Lusaka South zone is government-owned and hosts a mix of multinationals.

A man carries a sack of maize by bicycle. Maize is Zambia’s staple crop. File photo, 2020. (Photo: Collins Musonda, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Rules That Shape Business

Since 1 January 2026 mining firms must buy all designated non-core goods and 20% of designated core goods from Zambian citizen-owned companies. The core share rises to 25% in 2027, 35% in 2028 and at least 40% by 2031.

Insurers must be at least 30% Zambian-owned, and insurance brokers at least 51%. Foreign insurers have until December 2026 to comply.

A 10% export duty on copper concentrate was waived from August 2025 for six producers while smelters were repaired. The waiver was due to expire on 30 September 2026.

The State Department also lists slow permits, delayed VAT refunds and weak asset-seizure law among business obstacles. Companies say the government treats Chinese-linked firms more gently than others.

What Prediction Markets Say

No prediction market on the Zambian economy, its banks or its mines passed the US$10,000 volume threshold in October 2026. The only Zambia contracts found were cricket matches.

What It Means for US Readers

Copper from Zambia feeds the grids and electric vehicles that US buyers want. The State Department says Zambia holds 6% of the world’s known copper reserves.

The United States has no investment treaty or income tax treaty with Zambia, according to the State Department. American firms should expect slow permits and rely on contracts with local partners.

KoBold Metals, a US-backed company, is building a mine on the Copperbelt. American money is already in the Zambia economy.

Buyers of copper should also watch the renminbi settlement plan, which would route more sales through Chinese banks.

What Is Not Known

The IMF executive board has not yet approved the new programme, and its final terms will follow board approval. Zambia has no public ranking of private fortunes, so the owners of many family groups are not on record.

The outcome of the Mopani dispute between ZCCM-IH and IRH is open. Several ministers beyond finance, health, foreign affairs and green economy had not been named in published reports by 21 October 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the biggest part of the Zambia economy?

Copper earns most of Zambia’s export income. The State Department says copper brings more than 75% of export earnings and 25% of government revenue, although trade and ICT are larger parts of output.

How much copper does Zambia produce?

Zambia produced 890,346 tonnes of copper in 2025. The government targets three million tonnes a year by 2031.

Who owns Zambia’s biggest copper mines?

First Quantum runs Kansanshi and Sentinel, Barrick owns Lumwana, and Vedanta controls Konkola Copper Mines. Mopani is 51% owned by IRH of Abu Dhabi and 49% by the state’s ZCCM-IH.

Who runs Zambia’s finances in October 2026?

Situmbeko Musokotwane was reappointed finance minister on 14 September 2026. Denny Kalyalya leads the central bank.

Is Zambia still in debt trouble?

Zambia restructured US$12.4 billion of external debt after its 2020 default and finished an IMF programme in January 2026. IMF staff and the government reached a staff-level agreement on a new US$1.47 billion programme on 9 October 2026.

What is ZCCM-IH?

ZCCM-IH is the state’s mining investment company, listed on the Lusaka exchange. It holds stakes in most large mines, including 49% of Mopani and 20.6% of Konkola.

Why does the weather matter for the Zambia economy?

Up to 85% of Zambia’s power comes from hydro, and most maize comes from small farms. A drought in 2024 caused power cuts and cut the maize crop by about half.

Sources: US Department of State, 2026 Investment Climate Statements: Zambia, 29 September 2026; Zambia Statistics Agency (ZamStats), October 2026; ZCCM Investments Holdings, October 2026; ZESCO Limited, October 2026; Lusaka Securities Exchange, 21 October 2026; International Monetary Fund, press release 26/331: staff-level agreement with Zambia, 9 October 2026; Lusaka Times, cabinet appointments, 14 September 2026; US Embassy in Zambia, KoBold groundbreaking, 29 April 2026; Forbes Africa, interview with LuSE chief executive, 22 September 2026; News Diggers, Airtel Zambia market value, 10 June 2026; News Diggers, ZamStats maize forecast, 27 May 2026; Zambia Monitor, Bank of Zambia rate decision, 13 May 2026.

World.title: Zimbabwe Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
ZIMBABWE · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Zimbabwe is a landlocked southern African country. The ruling Zanu-PF party has governed it since independence from Britain in 1980.

— The big change A constitutional amendment signed in July 2026 stretches presidential and parliamentary terms from five to seven years. It also hands the choice of president to Parliament.

— Who rules President Emmerson Mnangagwa leads the state and Zanu-PF. Vice-Presidents Constantino Chiwenga and Kembo Mohadi sit beside him.

— The rivalry Chiwenga, the former army chief who helped remove Robert Mugabe in 2017, used a party conference in October 2026 to question the president’s record.

— The numbers The amendment passed the 280-seat National Assembly by 216 votes to 42 in June 2026. The Senate backed it 75 to 4.

— Opposition The main opposition coalition is split and weak. Its former leader Nelson Chamisa had no party as of August 2026.

— Still open The Constitutional Court has yet to rule on challenges, and Zanu-PF has not said who follows Mnangagwa.

Zimbabwe politics in October 2026 revolves around one question: how long President Emmerson Mnangagwa stays, and who takes over when he leaves.

A new amendment lengthens presidential terms, which Zimbabwean outlets read as keeping him in office until 2030. Americans who invest in, trade with or send aid to Zimbabwe deal with a government shaped by these decisions.

The new Parliament of Zimbabwe building at Mount Hampden. File photo, August 2024. (Photo: Mangwanani, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Zimbabwe Politics in Brief: One Party, One Dominant Presidency

Zimbabwe politics has been dominated by Zanu-PF, short for the Zimbabwe African National Union, Patriotic Front, since 1980. The party grew out of the liberation war against white-minority rule in what was then Rhodesia.

Robert Mugabe led the country for 37 years. In November 2017 the army moved against him, and Mnangagwa, his former right-hand man, took over, a period Zanu-PF calls the Second Republic.

In the 2023 vote Mnangagwa won a second term with 52.6% of the vote, or 2,350,711 votes, according to the results reported by Daily Maverick. His rival Nelson Chamisa took 44%, and the opposition rejected the result.

Under the 2013 constitution the president can serve two five-year terms. The July 2026 amendment changes that arithmetic, as the Rio Times report on the amendment explains.

More background sits in the Zimbabwe hub of The Rio Times.

The President and the Vice-Presidents

In Zimbabwe politics the president is both head of state and head of government. Under section 88 of the constitution, executive power sits with the president and runs through the Cabinet.

He also leads Zanu-PF as its First Secretary. His term as president began in September 2023 and, under the new amendment, now runs for seven years.

Constantino Chiwenga, the Rival Deputy

Chiwenga is a Vice-President and a former commander of the army. ZimLive describes him as central to the November 2017 coup that ended Mugabe’s rule.

On 16 October 2026, at the party’s annual conference in Chinhoyi, he called for a brutal and honest self-appraisal of the party. He asked whether Zimbabwe was repeating the mistakes that led to 2017.

He did not name the president or the term extension. ZimLive reported that his questions appeared to challenge both.

Mnangagwa answered by defending his record. He said the economy grew 8.3% in 2025 and that annual inflation had fallen to 2.8%, figures that the government supplies.

Kembo Mohadi, the Second Vice-President

Kembo Mohadi, a veteran Zanu-PF figure, is the other Vice-President. He turns 77 in November 2026.

He fell ill at the Chinhoyi conference on 16 October and was flown to a Harare hospital. The presidency’s spokesman said he was stable.

Zanu-PF: The Ruling Party and Its Factions

In Zimbabwe politics, Zanu-PF decides most things before Parliament or the Cabinet do. Its top bodies are the politburo, the central committee and the annual national people’s conference.

At the October 2026 conference in Chinhoyi, Legal Affairs Secretary Ziyambi Ziyambi read out the resolutions.

The party will move its next congress from 2027 to 2029, and Mnangagwa stays leader and candidate. That is according to the Herald, a state-controlled daily.

Newsday, an independent daily, reported that the resolutions were widely seen as aimed at Chiwenga and his allies. Oppah Muchinguri-Kashiri, the party’s national chairperson, steered the debate.

Ziyambi also said the party would discipline its MPs who missed votes on the amendment, according to the Daily News. That shows how closely the party watches its members.

The Mnangagwa camp: the president, ministers close to him, and business allies such as Kudakwashe Tagwirei.

The Chiwenga camp: the vice-president and former officers who say the party should reflect on 2017. ZimLive reported that his dismissal or departure cannot be ruled out.

The retired generals: Philip Valerio Sibanda, the former head of the defence forces, was named to the politburo in May 2026, according to the Herald.

Parliament, the New Amendment and the Opposition

Parliament is the second arena of Zimbabwe politics, with two houses. The National Assembly has 280 seats, and the Senate had 80 before the amendment.

Zanu-PF held 190 of the 280 Assembly seats as of February 2024, according to the Herald. That is above the 187 needed for a two-thirds majority.

The Constitution Amendment (No. 3) Act, or Act No. 6 of 2026, was signed on or about 7 July 2026. Veritas, a Zimbabwean legal-information group, published it.

What the Act Changes

Parliament, not the voters, will now elect the president, in a joint sitting of both houses, under the new section 92 of the constitution. A candidate needs more than half of the valid votes of members of Parliament.

The terms of the president, MPs and senators rise from five to seven years, and the Act applies this to the officeholders now in place. Zimbabwean outlets read that as carrying Mnangagwa’s term from 2028 to 2030.

Other Changes in the Act

The Senate grows from 80 to 90 members. Ten new senators are chosen by the president after consulting the National Assembly.

The Registrar-General, a civil servant, now registers voters, a job that belonged to the electoral commission. A new Delimitation Commission, appointed by the president, draws constituency boundaries.

The National Peace and Reconciliation Commission, set up to deal with past political violence, is abolished.

The Vote and the Dispute

The National Assembly passed the bill 216 to 42 on 18 June 2026, according to NewZimbabwe. The Senate followed 75 to 4 on 24 June, according to ZimLive.

Critics, including Veritas, say a change to term limits that benefits sitting officeholders needs a national referendum under section 328. The Attorney General has called the demand for a referendum unconstitutional, according to ZimLive in May 2026.

The Opposition

The Citizens Coalition for Change, known as the CCC, won 73 elected Assembly seats in 2023, according to Daily Maverick. It then fractured when Sengezo Tshabangu claimed its leadership and recalled dozens of its lawmakers.

The Speaker named Tshabangu Leader of the Opposition in May 2024, according to ZimLive. Chamisa left the CCC in 2024 and, as of August 2026, had promised a new Citizens’ Movement but not launched it, according to NewZimbabwe.

Tendai Biti, a former finance minister, convenes the Constitution Defenders’ Forum and has called the amendment a coup against the 2013 constitution. A separate group of war veterans is also in court against it, which keeps Zimbabwe politics tense.

Ministers and the Men Around the President

Ministers are the third arena of Zimbabwe politics, and Mnangagwa appoints them under section 104 of the constitution. On 8 October 2026 Chief Secretary Martin Rushwaya announced a split of the finance ministry.

Professor Mthuli Ncube stays Minister of Finance. Tagwirei, a businessman, became Minister of Economic Development and Investment Promotion, according to the Herald and ZimLive.

Tagwirei runs the fuel and trading group Sakunda Holdings, and the US Treasury sanctioned him and the company in 2020. They stayed on its Global Magnitsky list after Washington ended its Zimbabwe sanctions programme in March 2024.

For the business side, read the Rio Times guide to who runs Zimbabwe’s economy and the geopolitics pillar.

Foreign Affairs and International Trade: Amon Murwira, who dealt with China and Serbia in August 2026.

Justice, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs: Ziyambi Ziyambi, who defends the Act in court.

Defence: Oppah Muchinguri-Kashiri, who is also the party’s national chairperson.

The Military, Police and Security Forces

The army has shaped Zimbabwe politics since 2017.

In November 2025 Mnangagwa named new commanders for the defence forces and the army. General Philip Valerio Sibanda retired, according to the Herald.

The US Treasury added several senior officers to its Global Magnitsky sanctions list in March 2024.

The Act rewrites the defence forces’ constitutional duty. It now reads that they protect Zimbabwe, its people, its national security and its interests, and uphold the constitution.

A soldier on an armoured vehicle in central Harare during the army takeover of November 2017. File photo, 2017. (Photo: Public Domain Pictures, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Courts and Commissions

Justice Elizabeth Gwaunza became Chief Justice on 15 May 2026, the first woman in the post, after Luke Malaba retired, according to NewZimbabwe. Paddington Garwe is her deputy.

The Act gives the president the power to appoint all senior judges after consulting the Judicial Service Commission.

The Zimbabwe Electoral Commission runs elections, according to the Herald in July 2026. Its work on voter rolls and boundaries has been handed to the Registrar-General and the Delimitation Commission.

The Constitutional Court heard six war veterans’ challenge on 22 September 2026 and reserved judgment, according to the Herald. Four other challenges were removed from the roll, and one remains pending, according to The Zimbabwean.

The National Assembly chamber in Parliament House, Harare. File photo, 2022. (Photo: Mangwanani, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Rising Figures to Watch

Tagwirei is the fastest riser. He moved from party donor to presidential adviser, central committee member, senator in September 2026 and minister in October, according to ZimLive.

Chiwenga’s own future is the main unknown in Zimbabwe politics. His allies could accept the outcome, keep contesting it, or face further marginalisation, according to ZimLive.

Biti and Chamisa are the best-known opposition voices.

Neither holds an official post. The war veteran Blessed Geza, once a loud critic of Mnangagwa, died in February 2026, according to News24 and NewZimbabwe.

The liberation-war relief at Heroes’ Acre, the national monument in Harare where Zanu-PF figures are buried. File photo, 2003. (Photo: Gary Bembridge, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What It Means for US Readers

The United States ended its broad Zimbabwe sanctions programme in March 2024. It kept targeted Global Magnitsky sanctions on officials and companies, including Mnangagwa, Chiwenga, Tagwirei and Muchinguri-Kashiri, according to the Treasury’s sanctions office.

US companies and banks dealing with Zimbabwe need to screen their partners. Tagwirei’s new ministry will handle state enterprises and investment approvals, according to ZimLive, which makes that check more pressing.

Political risk in Zimbabwe politics is mostly about timing. The longer terms postpone the next national election to about 2030, according to Zimbabwean outlets, so a vote is not a near-term trigger for change.

The likelier surprise is the rivalry inside the ruling party. The Zimbabwe explainer and the guide to Zimbabwe in Southern Africa add background.

What Is Not Known

Zimbabwe politics has a gap at its centre: nobody outside the inner circle knows who Zanu-PF will pick to follow Mnangagwa. The party has endorsed him as its candidate, and it has not named a successor.

The Constitutional Court has not ruled on the direct-access application or the pending case. The outcome of any ruling is open.

It is not known whether the new ten appointed senators and the new Delimitation Commission are in place. Nor is it known how Chiwenga will respond to the October resolutions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who runs Zimbabwe in October 2026?

President Emmerson Mnangagwa heads the state, the government and the ruling Zanu-PF party. His two vice-presidents are Constantino Chiwenga and Kembo Mohadi.

How long can Mnangagwa stay in office?

Under the July 2026 amendment, presidential terms last seven years instead of five. Zimbabwean outlets read this as keeping him in office until about 2030, and Zanu-PF has backed him as its candidate.

Will Zimbabweans still vote for their president?

Not directly in Zimbabwe politics after the amendment. The amendment says Parliament elects the president in a joint sitting of the Senate and the National Assembly. Voters still elect members of Parliament.

Who leads the opposition in Zimbabwe politics?

Sengezo Tshabangu was named Leader of the Opposition in Parliament in May 2024. Nelson Chamisa, the former main challenger, had no party as of August 2026.

Is the constitutional amendment being challenged in court?

Yes. The Constitutional Court reserved judgment on a war veterans’ application on 22 September 2026. Four other challenges were removed from the roll and one remains.

Are there US sanctions on Zimbabwe’s leaders?

The US ended its Zimbabwe sanctions programme in March 2024. It kept targeted Global Magnitsky sanctions on people including Mnangagwa, Chiwenga and Tagwirei.

Sources: Constitution of Zimbabwe Amendment (No. 3) Act, Act No. 6 of 2026 (text, via Veritas), July 2026; Veritas, Constitution Watch posts 2026, October 2026; US Treasury Office of Foreign Assets Control, recent actions, 4 March 2024; Parliament of Zimbabwe, 2026; The Herald, President splits Finance and Economic Development portfolios, 8 October 2026; The Herald, Zanu-PF shifts Congress to 2029, 18 October 2026; ZimLive, Chiwenga questions Mnangagwa’s record, 17 October 2026; NewZimbabwe, Constitution Amendment Bill 3 passes National Assembly, 18 June 2026; NewZimbabwe, Gwaunza appointed Chief Justice, 14 May 2026; The Herald, Court reserves judgment in CAA3 challenge, 23 September 2026.

World.title: Guyana Geopolitics Explained 2026
World.content:
GUYANA · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts — The country Guyana is an English-speaking South American country of 878,674 people (2022 census). President Irfaan Ali, re-elected in September 2025, runs a foreign policy built around oil, security and the border.

— The oil The Stabroek Block, run by ExxonMobil, produced about 902,000 barrels a day in the first half of 2026. Crude exports earned US$15.05 billion in those six months, says the Finance Ministry.

— Venezuela Caracas claims the Essequibo region, about 160,000 square kilometres. The World Court ended its hearings on 11 May 2026 and has announced no date for its judgment.

— United States Washington is the closest partner. Guyana signed a new security memorandum with the US on 11 August 2026, and the US imposed a 12.5% tariff on most Guyanese exports on 24 July 2026.

— China China’s state oil company CNOOC holds 25% of the Stabroek Block. Chinese firms built the Demerara River Bridge for US$260.8 million, and Guyana’s statistics bureau counted US$1.79 billion in two-way trade for 2025.

— Others The EU, Qatar, India and Turkey each have a stake. Guyana is not a BRICS member.

— Still open When the World Court rules, whether Caracas will obey, and how far Washington’s tariffs, security push and mineral deals reshape the balance.

Guyana geopolitics matters to Americans because a US-run oil field off its coast pumps about 900,000 barrels a day. Venezuela claims much of the country, China holds a quarter of that oil block, and Washington is the main security partner.

This guide explains what each power wants from Guyana, with dates and figures as of October 2026.

The USS Normandy passes floating oil production vessels in the Stabroek Block off Guyana, 27 March 2025. (Photo: US Navy, Petty Officer 2nd Class Dylan Kinee, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)
