Guyana Geopolitics in Brief

Guyana is a small country on the north coast of South America, with 878,674 people at its 2022 census. It is the only English-speaking nation on the continent and a founding member of CARICOM, the Caribbean Community.

President Irfaan Ali was re-elected in September 2025. In October 2026 Bharrat Jagdeo was Vice President and Mark Phillips Prime Minister, and Hugh Todd was Foreign Minister as of September 2026.

Oil explains why great powers now pay attention. The Ministry of Finance’s mid-year report of September 2026 says the economy grew 33.3% in the first half of 2026.

Three facts shape Guyana geopolitics. A US company runs the oil, Venezuela disputes the border, and Guyana leans on Washington for security.

More background sits in the Rio Times Guyana section and in Guyana in Latin America. The neighbours are covered in Guyana and its neighbours in the Guianas, and the oil boom in Guyana Explained.

The Oil Block at the Centre

The Stabroek Block lies offshore in the Atlantic. ExxonMobil operates it with a 45% stake, Chevron holds 30% after taking over Hess in July 2025, and CNOOC holds 25%.

The Finance Ministry reports 163.3 million barrels produced in the first half of 2026, from four floating production vessels. Production averaged about 902,000 barrels a day, up from about 639,000 a year earlier.

Guyana’s state earns money mainly through a share of the oil, called profit oil. It received US$1,778.6 million from this in the first half of 2026.

The money goes into the Natural Resource Fund, a sovereign savings account. Its balance stood at US$4,294.2 million at the end of June 2026, after withdrawals of US$1,020 million.

This one block is why Guyana geopolitics draws Washington, Beijing and Caracas. Each wants either the oil, the revenue or the security of the sea lanes around it.

Venezuela and the Essequibo Claim

Venezuela claims Essequibo, the region west of the Essequibo River. It covers about 160,000 square kilometres, and 313,175 people lived there at the 2022 census.

A tribunal in Paris fixed the border on 3 October 1899, and Guyana says that award settled the matter. Venezuela first challenged it in a letter to the United Nations in February 1962.

Guyana took the dispute to the International Court of Justice, the UN’s top court in The Hague, on 29 March 2018. The court ruled on its jurisdiction on 18 December 2020 and rejected a Venezuelan objection on 6 April 2023.

On 1 December 2023 the court told Venezuela to refrain from changing the situation in the disputed land. On 1 May 2025 it ordered Venezuela not to hold or prepare elections there.

Public hearings on the merits ran from 4 to 11 May 2026. The court’s website shows no date for the judgment.

Ali said in September 2026 that he expects a ruling early in the new year. He added that Venezuela’s leaders do not intend to accept it, and that Guyana is prepared for any reaction.

Venezuela’s politics changed on 3 January 2026, when a US operation removed President Nicolás Maduro. Delcy Rodríguez is now interim president, and on 11 May 2026 she said Venezuela would reject a ruling upholding the 1899 award.

Ali said in September 2026 that Venezuelan rhetoric has “reduced substantially” since Maduro’s arrest.

Ali and Maduro had pledged in the Argyle Declaration of December 2023 not to escalate the dispute. Brazil and CARICOM observed that meeting.

The Peace Palace in The Hague, seat of the International Court of Justice, which is hearing Guyana’s border case with Venezuela (file photo, 2006). (Photo: International Court of Justice, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

The United States as Security Partner

Washington is Guyana’s closest ally. On 24 September 2025 the US State Department said Secretary of State Marco Rubio reaffirmed US support for Guyana’s territorial integrity.

On 11 August 2026 Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and Foreign Minister Todd signed a security and counter-narcotics memorandum in Georgetown. It builds on a March 2025 agreement, and the US will provide US$2 million for air-domain awareness and drone capabilities.

Military ties are close.

On 23 May 2026 Ali and his security chiefs visited the US carrier USS Nimitz. The ship was exercising with the Guyana Defence Force.

Under a shiprider agreement, Guyanese officers ride on US ships on anti-drug patrols. As of October 2026 no public agreement for a US base in Guyana has been found.

On 22 September 2026 Ali signed a memorandum of the Shield of the Americas, a US-led security grouping that lists 15 countries. It focuses on economic resilience, security and joint action against drug-trafficking groups.

Guyana’s alignment has a price in the Caribbean.

In May 2026 Guyana and Trinidad and Tobago reserved their positions on a CARICOM statement. It warned against US military action in Cuba.

Guyana has also ended its Cuban medical brigade programme, after US concerns about trafficking and visa threats against officials.

Then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken and President Irfaan Ali at a joint press event in Georgetown, 6 July 2023. (Photo: US Department of State, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Trade, Loans and Minerals With Washington

The US is Guyana’s largest source of foreign investment and a leading trading partner, according to Senior Minister Ashni Singh in July 2026. He said trade between the two exceeded US$25 billion over the past decade.

US trade policy has also bitten.

On 24 July 2026 a 12.5% tariff took effect on most Guyanese goods. It was part of US action against 60 countries over forced-labour import rules.

Permanent Secretary Sharon Roopchand-Edwards of the Foreign Ministry told a US hearing in July 2026 that Guyana knew of no forced-labour goods. She said Guyana was negotiating a reciprocal trade agreement with Washington.

The US Export-Import Bank has approved a US$526 million loan for the Wales gas-to-energy project, meant to bring cheaper power to Guyana. The Finance Ministry’s debt table shows US$240.8 million owed to US lenders at the end of June 2026.

Minerals are the newest front.

On 7 August 2026 the US Department of War announced US$85.5 million for a bauxite mine in Guyana. Private investors would add US$64.5 million.

The stated aim is to cut US reliance on China for the refractory bauxite used in heat-resistant materials. The State Department said Landau’s August visit would cover energy and critical minerals.

China, Between Contractor and Rival

China arrived in Guyana as a builder and lender before oil mattered. Its state company CNOOC now holds 25% of the Stabroek Block, as a minority partner of ExxonMobil.

A Chinese consortium led by China Railway Construction built the Demerara River Bridge, which opened in October 2025.

Minister Juan Edghill put the cost at US$260.8 million. A €160.8 million loan from the Bank of China (about US$172 million at signing) helped pay for it.

The Finance Ministry’s debt table shows US$443.0 million owed to China Eximbank, CAMCE and China Road and Bridge at the end of June 2026. That is about 13% of Guyana’s US$3,306.4 million external debt, and Bank of China is listed separately at US$109.6 million.

Trade is growing fast. Guyana’s statistics bureau estimated US$1.79 billion in two-way trade in 2025, while the Chinese embassy cites US$2.89 billion.

Chinese ambassador Yang Yang wrote in May 2026 that Chinese firms had invested about US$13 billion by the end of 2025. He said six regional hospitals built by Chinese companies are now operating.

Washington reads this presence as a risk, and the bauxite deal shows its answer. Georgetown, for its part, says it wants to diversify beyond oil and keep Chinese cooperation in renewable energy and infrastructure.

One more bridge is in play.

In December 2024 Public Works Minister Juan Edghill said China Road and Bridge Corporation was chosen to build a Corentyne River bridge. It would link Guyana and Suriname.

The older Demerara Harbour Bridge across the Demerara River near Georgetown, photographed in November 2019. A Chinese-built bridge opened in 2025. (Photo: Dan Lundberg, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Europe, the Gulf, India, Russia and Turkey

The European Union is represented in Georgetown by Ambassador Luca Pierantoni. The EU and Guyana trade under the EU-CARIFORUM Economic Partnership Agreement.

A Guyana Chronicle report of October 2025 says 66% of Guyana’s crude oil went to Europe in 2024. In early October 2026 Ali called the EU’s Schengen visa process for Guyanese “backward”, because applicants must travel to Suriname or Trinidad for biometrics.

Qatar is the Gulf partner in the news. Ali made a state visit to Qatar from 6 to 10 September 2026, and Todd signed an agricultural-technology memorandum with Qatar’s municipality minister.

The Finance Ministry’s debt table also lists small loans at the end of June 2026. They came from Kuwait (US$16.0 million), the United Arab Emirates (US$9.1 million) and Saudi Arabia (US$1.2 million).

India wants Guyanese crude. Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited in November 2024, and a memorandum on hydrocarbons followed.

India’s new High Commissioner, Chinmoy Naik, presented his credentials to Ali in October 2026. India is owed US$82.2 million by Guyana at the end of June 2026.

Russia plays a minor role. Its foreign ministry spokeswoman, Maria Zakharova, called in December 2023 for both sides to refrain from actions that could unbalance the situation.

On 24 February 2025 Guyana voted for the General Assembly’s Ukraine resolution, which passed 93 to 18 with 65 abstentions. Turkey appears mainly through Karpowership, whose floating power ships supply about 96 megawatts to the grid.

Guyana is not a member of BRICS, the grouping founded by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. It is on neither the member list nor the partner list on the official BRICS Brazil website in October 2026.

CARICOM, Brazil and the United Nations

CARICOM has backed Guyana in the border dispute. The bloc’s secretariat is based in Georgetown, which gives Guyana a diplomatic voice beyond its size.

Guyana sat on the UN Security Council in 2024 and 2025. Its ambassador to the UN, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, is a candidate for UN Secretary-General, endorsed by CARICOM on 11 July 2026.

Brazil observed the Argyle talks of December 2023 and shares a long border with Guyana. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva visited Georgetown in February 2024.

Suriname, to the east, says it plans to finance the Corentyne bridge itself. Ali said in July 2026 that this was news to him, and Guyana says it wants a joint venture.

What It Means for US Readers

US companies sit at the centre. ExxonMobil operates the Stabroek Block and Chevron holds 30%, so Guyana’s output matters to American oil earnings.

Guyana geopolitics now links trade and security. A 12.5% US tariff on most Guyanese exports sits beside new US funding for bauxite.

Washington treats Georgetown as a partner in its contest with Beijing.

The border is the main risk for investors. A court ruling in Guyana’s favour would settle the law, but Caracas has said it will not accept it.

For travellers, the State Department’s own travel advisory is the guide to current conditions. Policy shifts between Washington and Georgetown can change visa and investment rules quickly.

What Is Not Known

No date has been announced for the World Court judgment. Guyana’s government expects it early in 2027.

Whether Venezuela‘s interim government will obey a ruling is unclear. So is whether Washington would act if Caracas ignored it.

Guyana and the United States were negotiating a reciprocal trade agreement in July 2026, and its terms are not public.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Venezuela claim in Guyana?

Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, about 160,000 square kilometres west of the Essequibo River. Guyana says a Paris tribunal settled the border on 3 October 1899.

Who owns Guyana’s oil?

ExxonMobil operates the Stabroek Block with 45%, Chevron holds 30% and China’s CNOOC holds 25%. Guyana’s government takes a share of the oil and pays it into a savings fund.

Does the United States have a military base in Guyana?

As of October 2026 no public agreement for a US base in Guyana has been found. The two countries signed a security memorandum on 11 August 2026, and US ships and troops train with Guyana’s army.

How big is China’s role in Guyana?

In Guyana geopolitics, China holds 25% of the main oil block through CNOOC, built the Demerara River Bridge and is owed US$443.0 million by Guyana through three Chinese state lenders and contractors at the end of June 2026.

Is Guyana a member of BRICS?

No. Guyana appears on neither the member list nor the partner list on the official BRICS Brazil website in October 2026.

What is the Shield of the Americas?

It is a US-led security grouping of countries in the Western Hemisphere. On 22 September 2026 leaders including Ali signed a memorandum at the UN in New York.

Sources: Guyana Ministry of Finance, Mid-Year Report 2026, 14 September 2026; International Court of Justice, case 171, Guyana v. Venezuela, 11 May 2026; US State Department, readout of Rubio meeting with President Ali, 24 September 2025; Guyana Bureau of Statistics, October 2026; International Court of Justice, Order of 1 May 2025 (Guyana v. Venezuela), 1 May 2025; BRICS Brazil, official member and partner lists, October 2026.

World.title: Ministry of Public Service says driver lost control following blowout, totaling Government ride
World.content:
Ministry of Public Service says driver lost control following blowout, totaling Government ride

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of the Public Service, Disaster Risk Management and Enterprise issued a statement confirming a road traffic incident involving a government vehicle assigned to the Minister.

The accident reportedly occurred on October 2.

The Ministry says that Minister Usher and his driver were returning from official duties in San Ignacio Town in the Ford F-150 pickup truck when the incident occurred.

“After dropping the Minister at his residence, the driver was on his way home when the vehicle experienced a blowout near the roundabout at Mile 2 on the Philip Goldson Highway, causing it to flip and suffer extensive damage. Fortunately, the driver did not sustain any injuries,” the Ministry explained.

The Ministry says that police responded to the scene and commenced an investigation into the matter.

“Following the incident, and in accordance with government procedures, the Ministry reported the matter to the Assets and Utilities Management Unit (A.U.M.U.),” it added.

In addition, the ministry urged drivers of government vehicles to exercise caution when driving particularly during periods of heavy rain.

World.title: Ministry of E-Governance strengthens digital skills among public officers
World.content:
Ministry of E-Governance strengthens digital skills among public officers

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of E-Governance continued its efforts to strengthen digital skills across the public service with its Digital Confidence and Foundational Workplace Skills Training program on October 20, 2026.

The training, delivered through the E-Governance Academy, brought together public officers from the Southern Regional Hospital, Immigration Department and Western Regional Hospital for Cohorts 3 and 4.

Held in the Ministry’s Training Room, the sessions featured practical exercises and interactive learning activities designed to help participants become more confident in using digital tools. The training also focused on essential workplace skills to improve productivity, communication and the delivery of public services.

The program forms part of the Ministry’s broader public sector modernization agenda and its ongoing efforts to build the capacity of government employees. By equipping public officers with relevant digital knowledge and workplace competencies, the initiative aims to help them adapt to an increasingly digital working environment and contribute to greater operational efficiency.

The Ministry of E-Governance says it remains committed to providing continuous learning opportunities to support a digitally empowered and future-ready public service.

World.title: Jamaica’s Gang violence: Belize has a different story
World.content:
Jamaica’s Gang violence: Belize has a different story

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Nuri Muhammad: I read with considerable interest the October 21, 2026, New York Carib News editorial, “Violence in Jamaica Frightening,” following a deadly confrontation that left two police officers and three civilians dead. The editorial calls for a national initiative of reconciliation, redemption and community renewal, recognizing that Jamaica cannot arrest or imprison its way out of a deeply entrenched culture of violence.

I agree with much of that argument. In fact, we have been making similar arguments in Belize for more than thirty years. However, while Jamaica and Belize share many of the social conditions that produce gang violence, there are important differences in the development and character of our gang problems.

Jamaica’s modern gang phenomenon stretches back some sixty years, with roots in political garrison communities and criminal organizations that eventually acquired considerable wealth, weapons and influence. Belize’s modern gang culture is approximately thirty-five years old. Our gangs are generally smaller, less wealthy and less institutionally organized. We have experienced serious gang-related murders, but not the same established pattern of organized gangs engaging in deadly armed confrontations with the police.

These differences matter. Belize still has an opportunity to prevent the emergence of the kind of entrenched criminal organizations that have made Jamaica’s problem so difficult to resolve. Neither should we be tempted to imitate El Salvador’s model of mass incarceration, which raises serious questions about due process, human rights and the long-term consequences of relying overwhelmingly on imprisonment.

But Belize has something else: a history of intervention that has produced encouraging results.

In February 1995, representatives of fourteen Belize City gangs participated in the historic Bird’s Isle Declaration. The truce, which held for approximately one year with relatively minor breaches, gave rise to the Conscious Youth Development Program (CYDP), providing opportunities for education, employment, counselling and rehabilitation. A subsequent independent evaluation commissioned by the Caribbean Development Bank reported encouraging results, demonstrating that intervention could achieve what enforcement alone could not.

In 1997, the Youth Enhancement Academy provided another important lesson. Of the 73 young men released from the program, nine were subsequently identified as having reoffended, according to our program records. That is approximately 12 percent, although the figure must be understood within the program’s particular follow-up period and definition of reoffending.

In 2020, a training initiative conducted by my consultancy, Innadynamics, at Feinstein’s Stake Bank involved forty still gang-affiliated young men. Eighteen months later, approximately 80 percent were reportedly employed. These are results worth examining, learning from and building upon.

More recently, during the 2024 state of emergency, approximately 200 detained young men participated in intervention and counselling activities. Our subsequent After-Care proposal, called Surviving Soldiers, recognized that releasing a young man from detention without addressing his circumstances is often simply returning him to the conditions that helped produce the problem.

These experiences reinforce something I have consistently argued: crime and violence are symptoms of deeper social conditions. The gang often provides identity, belonging, protection and recognition where families, schools, communities and other institutions have failed to meet those needs.

This does not excuse criminal behavior. Those who commit crimes must be held accountable. But punishment alone cannot transform the circumstances that continually produce another generation of young men attracted to gang life.

Belize has made progress through policing, intelligence gathering, community engagement and targeted interventions. We should recognize those achievements without pretending that our problems have disappeared. Our challenge remains sustaining successful programs, providing meaningful opportunities for young men who want to change, and preventing political changes from interrupting effective interventions.

The Jamaican editorial proposes a National Commission for Reconciliation, Redemption and Community Renewal. Belize may not need to copy that particular model. We already have considerable experience, institutional knowledge and individuals who have demonstrated that intervention and rehabilitation can produce positive results.

What we need is the political will to bring those experiences together into a sustained national strategy.

I have spent more than thirty years working with young men involved in gang culture. I have witnessed the violence, the tragedies and the disappointments. But I have also witnessed remarkable personal transformations.

Jamaica’s experience should serve as a warning, not a prediction of Belize’s future. We do not need to become another Jamaica, nor should we believe that El Salvador’s methods offer the only alternative.

We do not have to begin again. We need to build upon what we have already learned.

World.title: Orange Walk Town Council condemns bullying and intimidation against traffic wardens
World.content:
Orange Walk Town Council condemns bullying and intimidation against traffic wardens

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Orange Walk Town Council issued a statement expressing concern over the continued bullying, verbal abuse, intimidation, and physical violence directed at Traffic Wardens by some motorists and members of the public.

“The increasing hostility and dangerous confrontations faced by our Wardens while carrying out their duties are unacceptable and pose a serious threat to their safety and well-being,” the council said.

The council says that on Friday, October 16, 2026, a male Traffic Warden was physically assaulted by a motorcyclist who had entered a one-way street against the direction of traffic.

“When the motorcyclist was stopped by the Warden, the individual reportedly dismounted his motorcycle and confronted the officer before punching him in the face. As a result of the assault, our Warden sustained a broken tooth and a fracture to a second tooth. The Council strongly condemns this act of violence against an employee who was simply carrying out his assigned duties to help maintain traffic order and public safety,” the council said.

In another incident, on Monday, the council says that a female Traffic Warden was subjected to verbal aggression and disrespectful treatment by a male business owner on Park Street. This incident occurred amid temporary traffic restrictions being implemented to facilitate ongoing rehabilitation works along Main Street.

The council says that they are concerned as these confrontations appear to become more hostile when temporary street closures and barricades are in place.

“Our Traffic Wardens deserve respect, dignity, and a safe working environment, while carrying out responsibilities assigned to them by the Council. Their role is not to inconvenience the public, but to help maintain order, enforce traffic regulations, and protect the safety of all road users, including our most vulnerable citizens,” the council said.

The council says that they know construction works may cause temporary inconvenience, but these measures are necessary to improve the town’s infrastructure and ensure public safety.

The council calls on the public to exercise patience, understanding, and courtesy when encountering traffic restrictions.

World.title: Work from home in Belize: Halo BPO hiring full time sales agents
World.content:
Work from home in Belize: Halo BPO hiring full time sales agents

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Imagine starting your workday without leaving the house, and getting paid every Friday.

That is what Halo BPO is offering Belizeans as it hires full time outbound sales agents.

The role pays $8.50 an hour from day one, with raises to $9.00 after two weeks and $10.00 after 30 days. Pay is weekly.

The shift runs from 8:00am to 5:00pm Belize time, so agents can keep their evenings free.

Halo BPO is especially interested in candidates with experience in appointment setting or home improvement sales.

Because the job is fully remote, applicants need the right setup before applying. That includes a wired ethernet connection with at least 40 Mbps upload and download, a webcam, a clear USB headset, a capable computer with at least 8GB of RAM and a quad core processor, and a quiet space free from distractions. Chromebooks will not be accepted.

To apply, email [email protected] and include your full name in the subject line.

World.title: Belize highlights Blue Bonds success at regional Blue Economy workshop
World.content:
Belize highlights Blue Bonds success at regional Blue Economy workshop

By Zoila Palma: Belize is highlighting its progress in innovative financing for marine conservation and sustainable economic development at a regional workshop in Grenada.

Beverly Wade, Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry of Blue Economy and Marine Conservation, participated virtually in the Blue Economy and Partnership Building for Marine Protected Area (MPA) Managers Regional Peer-to-Peer Workshop, being held from October 21 to 23, 2026, in St. George’s, Grenada.

During her presentation, titled “Belize Blue Bonds – The Story of Pursuing an Innovative Financing Mechanism,” Wade outlined key achievements of Belize’s Blue Bonds initiative, including conservation milestones, the expansion of Biodiversity Protection Zones, and advances in marine spatial planning and management.

Wade noted that the initiative has strengthened Belize’s conservation commitments while enhancing the country’s international reputation for protecting nature, promoting responsible blue economic growth, and meeting its financial obligations to investors.

She also highlighted Resilient Bold Belize, a permanent financing project intended to expand conservation efforts, improve climate resilience, support sustainable livelihoods, and advance Belize’s blue economy goals by mobilizing additional resources for long-term protection of coastal and marine resources.

The workshop brings together marine protected area managers and practitioners from across the Caribbean to exchange knowledge, strengthen partnerships, and explore sustainable financing opportunities.

World.title: Shyne says UDP was “stolen” 2 years ago
World.content:
Shyne says UDP was “stolen” 2 years ago

By Zoila Palma: Today, former Leader of the Opposition Shyne Barrow says that 2 years ago on October 20, the UDP was stolen.

“What Tracy Panton, Patrick Faber, John Saldivar and others did on October 20th, 2024 was one of the worst moments in our Democracy.

The Belize Constitution and the UDP Constitution trumps all. Personalities don’t matter. No matter how much you loathe the duly elected Leader of the UDP you don’t attempt an overthrow,” Barrow said.

Barrow alleges that “Tracy, Faber, Saldivar et al decided to lie, connive, and defraud to seize power they set in motion a train of events that are irreversible. The same people that thief Budna watched Tracy and her alliance of corruption steal the UDP on October 20, 2024.”

In addition, Barrow says that if they hadn’t done that, the UDP would have increased their seats in the House of Representatives by at least double in 2025 General Elections.

“There has been no remorse, no amends, just continued hubris and disregard for the UDP Constitution and the laws of Belize,” he said.

He further said that there has still been no reform of the UDP Constitution, zero reform to the public policy agenda of the UDP.

World.title: International News: Italy to deploy 500 troops in Milan following violent protests
World.content:
International News: Italy to deploy 500 troops in Milan following violent protests

By Zoila Palma: Italy is preparing to deploy 500 military personnel to Milan following a weekend of violent protests that saw demonstrators clash with police, damage property and attempt to occupy public spaces.

The move comes as authorities in Italy and France strengthen security measures amid continued unrest and concerns about further demonstrations, Fox reports.

Violence erupted in Milan on Saturday, October 17, as hundreds of demonstrators reportedly threw firecrackers, glass bottles and metal barriers at police near the city’s historic cathedral. Officers attempting to contain the clashes were forced to retreat.

In Paris, police also faced large crowds during demonstrations, with officers using crowd-control equipment as they attempted to prevent advancing protesters from overwhelming security lines.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced the planned deployment of 500 troops to Milan, while the country’s deputy prime minister indicated that personnel would be granted expanded police powers.

The unrest comes as demonstrations in both countries have been linked to grievances over the cost of living, low wages, high rents and public services.

World.title: NWC seeks 51% hike
World.content:
Acting president of National Water Commission Kevin Kerr (left) speaks during Tuesday’s sitting of the Public Accounts Committee as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Water, Environment and Climate Change Wayne Robertson listens. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

The Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) will decide within 10 days whether to accept a National Water Commission (NWC) application for a tariff review which could pave the way for higher water and sewerage rates.

The OUR confirmed Tuesday in a release that it received the application on Friday, October 16, covering the five-year period from 2026/27 to 2030/31.

The regulator said it would first assess whether the application meets its requirements and may request additional information from the NWC before deciding whether to formally accept it for review.

The development comes as the NWC seeks a 51 per cent increase in water and sewerage rates amid worsening revenue collection and rising expenses.

The utility wants to raise its annual revenue from about $40 billion to $60 billion to cover operating costs and critical investments over the next five years, while noting it owes the Government approximately $21 billion in General Consumption Tax (GCT).

The disclosures were made by NWC officials on Tuesday during a sitting of the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), where the utility’s unpaid bills and financial difficulties came under scrutiny.

Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr told the committee that the proposed increase was included in a tariff application submitted to the OUR last Friday and noted that the commission is awaiting approval from the regulator.

“So what our submission includes is a 51 per cent increase, and there are some scenarios involved if that is not provided; we will have to revise our investment plan, adjust with the determination made at the end of the process and, as usual, the public will be required to participate in a more consultative process by the OUR over the review period,” Kerr said.

Chief financial officer at the NWC Fabian Christie told the committee that the request reflected the utility’s financial challenges.

“The fact is that our revenues have worsened in terms of paying from our customers, and also the fact that we would require a tariff increase, because our expenses have been increasing dramatically,” Christie told the committee.

He also pointed to the impact of natural disasters and worsening droughts on the commission’s finances. Christie said these events could reduce the utility’s revenue by between 10 and 15 per cent in a given year, depending on their severity.

The proposed increase comes against the background of a sharp rise in the NWC’s unpaid bills.

PAC Chairman Julian Robinson, referring to the Auditor General’s findings, said the commission’s payables rose from $10.6 billion in the 2016/17 financial year to $33.2 billion in 2025/26.

The report also found that the NWC’s net receivables — money owed to the utility — stood at $4.6 billion as at March 2026.

Christie told the committee that the $21-billion owed in GCT accounted for the largest share of the NWC’s $33.2 billion in payables. He explained that the commission withholds GCT when it is billed by suppliers and is expected to pass that tax on to the Government.

Christie also confirmed that the money was being used to support the utility’s day-to-day cash needs.

He revealed that the remaining approximately $12 billion in payables includes approximately $6 billion owed to Central Wastewater Treatment Company, which treats much of the sewage from Kingston and parts of St Catherine at the Soapberry facility. The other roughly $6 billion is owed to contractors and suppliers.

Christie acknowledged that the outstanding payments were affecting the commission’s ability to carry out work.

He gave an approximate breakdown of some payments owed to contractors and suppliers, saying about $1.3 billion was between zero and 30 days overdue, $400 million between 30 and 60 days, $500 million between 60 and 90 days, and $1.6 billion outstanding for more than 90 days.

The proposed tariff increase is not the only measure being pursued to improve the NWC’s finances. Kerr said reducing non-revenue water was a priority.

He said the commission had previously undertaken reduction projects in Kingston, St Andrew and Portmore, and was in the final stage of procurement for an islandwide programme, adding that the NWC hopes to select a bidder or bidders by the end of the current financial period.

The planned programme would be rolled out in stages, beginning in areas including Spanish Town, Old Harbour, May Pen, Mandeville, Montego Bay, Negril, Lucea, Ocho Rios, and Port Antonio, before further work in Kingston and Portmore.

Kerr said the long-term target was to reduce non-revenue water to 30 per cent islandwide within 11 years as the current level averages between 70 and 73 per cent.

The NWC’s financial position was also a concern for Robinson, who questioned how the utility would improve its cash flow beyond seeking higher tariffs. He pointed to the growth in payables and the amount owed to suppliers, while raising the need to reduce losses and improve the collection of money owed to the commission.

Christie said the NWC was working on a plan to improve its working capital management, which he expects to submit to the board at the start of next year. He said the effort would need to improve the amount of cash available to meet the utility’s obligations.

Furthermore, Kerr said, the tariff application was tied to an investment plan designed to ensure that financing could be secured for priority projects. He noted that the NWC received an interim tariff in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 eroded its cash flow.

World.title: $2b reasons for flexi-work
World.content:
A screen shot of a section of the Ministry of National Security and Peace submission to Parliament’s Economy amd Production Committee last Wednesday.

JAMAICA’S approximately 114,000 public servants could save nearly $2 billion annually in transportation costs if more of them are allowed to work remotely under flexi-work arrangements.

This point was emphasised by representatives of the Ministry of National Security and Peace during their appearance last Wednesday before Parliament’s Economy and Production Committee to discuss the progress of flex-work arrangements in Jamaica.

A PowerPoint presentation from the ministry’s team, which was shared with the media afterwards, painted what it called the “big picture” involving public sector workers and the costs associated with their daily commute.

It shows that it costs between $12,000 and $24,000 weekly for each public servant to get to and from work.

With vacation and other days off, it is estimated that each public servant spends between $456,000 and $912,000 annually to get to work.

For all public servants combined, the annual figure is between $1.3 billion and $2.7 billion.

The document argued that if public sector employees were allowed to work from home two days each week, they would each save between $4,800 and $9,600.

Across the entire public service, workers would collectively keep between $547 million and $1.9 billion in their pockets annually.

In terms of the impact at the ministry level, the document showed that 196 or 52 per cent of its 374 employees reside in St Catherine; 160 or 43 per cent live in Kingston and rural St Andrew; and 18 or five per cent live in rural parishes.

It emphasised that each of these workers is spending between $12,000 and $24,000 every week to get to and from work.

The ministry said its embrace of flexi-work arrangements is in response to fuel-price pressures and is aimed at modernising work and strengthening public sector resilience.

The security ministry’s team underscored that more people working from home meant an overall smaller fuel bill.

The document referenced a study which shows that 10 minutes of creeping or idling in traffic burns between 300 and 500 millilitres or more than one to two cups of petrol.

Hourly idling while stuck in gridlock sees an average car wasting 0.5 litres to 1.3 litres of fuel per hour, while larger vehicles burn between 1.5 litres and 2.5 litres.

The ministry team cited the negative effects of gridlock on the economy, climate change, productivity, and mental wellness.

It referenced a 1965 World Bank appraisal which described the Kingston–Spanish Town corridor as “the most heavily travelled highway in Jamaica”.

The ministry noted that in 2008 then Minister of Transport Mike Henry indicated that motorists were taking eight times longer on typical journeys as he pointed to the economic cost of congestion

In 2023, Jamaicans were reportedly spending 90 minutes or 40 per cent of working hours daily in traffic.

This is according to a United Nations Jamaica/UWI Department of Economics panel discussion titled ‘The Economics of Congestion’.

It described the time lost as a massive cost for a small island developing state with enormous economic implications that could affect people’s psychological and physiological well-being.

The ministry said it was making the case for action now on flexi-work arrangement having considered the mental wellness of employees, national cost pressures, workforce realities, and public sector modernisation which together strengthen the case for a Government of Jamaica-wide approach.

In terms of the mental health toll, the document cited an international study of January 2025 published in the Makara Journal of Health Research which stated that a significant proportion of workers experienced stress from their commuting routines.

The study found that approximately 74.5 per cent of workers reported that commuting had a detrimental effect on their mental health, while 82.1 per cent experienced mental fatigue which directly impacted their ability to concentrate and perform effectively at work.

The security ministry said the overall approach is for a structured, phased and monitored Government-led flexible work arrangement framework, informed by its experience.

It said eligibility should be transparent, role-based and subject to operational requirements, not a universal entitlement, and argued that the roll-out should be phased in.

The security ministry pointed to positives such as reduced commuting stress and greater autonomy which, it said, can support productive time and work-life balance.

Additionally, it said flexible work can support talent retention, inclusion and recruitment in a changing workforce.

The ministry said it also maintains operating capacity during fuel shortages, natural disasters, and transport disruptions.

Potential savings include transport, toll, fuel, maintenance, and in-office support resources, alongside reduced absenteeism.

World.title: Twinkle Brothers honoured on home turf
World.content:
Councillor for the Falmouth Division Garth Wilkinson (left) shares a light moment with Twinkle Brothers band member Ralston Grant and his wife Della following the Trelawny Municipal Corporation, in collaboration with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission, National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony in Falmouth on Monday.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — There was a flood of emotions as reggae musicians Ralston and Norman Grant, of the Twinkle Brothers, Falmouth natives, were recognised for their contribution to Jamaican music at a National Heroes’ Day awards ceremony in historic Water Square in the parish.

Norman is currently on tour, but for Ralston, the occasion held special significance, as decades ago the siblings operated a record shop almost on the exact spot where the awards ceremony was held, long before their music took them to audiences around the globe.

The recognition came through the Trelawny Municipal Corporation, in collaboration with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC), during its 2026 National Heroes’ Day Civic and Awards Ceremony.

Reflecting on the moment, Ralston said the honour was particularly meaningful because it was his first award in their native Trelawny, despite receiving international recognition for the band’s musical achievements since they started out in 1962.

“It means everything, you know, because I’ve never got one from Trelawny before,” he said.

The musician recalled the brothers’ early accomplishments in the Jamaica Festival Song Competition in 1970, where they placed third behind winner Hopeton Lewis and the Jamaicans.

Their musical journey also includes performances before former Governor General Sir Clifford Campbell during an era when their talent was gaining recognition at home.

The citation accompanying the award praised Norman and Ralston for their outstanding contribution to Jamaican music, cultural heritage, and the country’s representation on the international stage.

It also traced their beginnings on how they fashioned their own musical instruments, demonstrating the ingenuity and determination that would underpin their careers that have spanned more than six decades, with an extensive catalogue of albums and singles.

Through their commitment to independent music production, conscious reggae and roots culture, the brothers helped preserve the tradition of live-band reggae while introducing Jamaican sounds to audiences beyond the island.

Their collaboration with Polish group Trebunie-Tutki was also highlighted as an example of their ability to bridge cultural divides through music.

Despite spending more than four decades living largely overseas, Ralston maintains ties to Jamaica, travelling between the island and California, with his wife Della.

The Twinkle Brothers boast an extensive catalogue of songs which include

Faith Can Move Mountains, Never Get Burn, Jahoviah, Since I Threw the Comb Away, Give Rasta Praise, Rasta Pon Top, Enter Zion, among many others.

World.title: Jamaica braces for cyber stress test
World.content:
JAMAICA’s ability to withstand and recover from major cyberattacks will be put to the test later this month when the Jamaica Cyber Incident Response Team (JaCIRT) stages a national exercise — CyberXJM26 — aimed at identifying weaknesses in the country’s cybersecurity defences and strengthening its response capabilities.

Scheduled for October 28 and 29, the exercise seeks to provide the first full test of the country’s ability to coordinate its response to a major cyber incident.

“CyberXjm26 puts national readiness to a public test, showing how well agencies, security forces, and the private sector can coordinate during an incident, identifying gaps that can be fixed before a real one,” JaCIRT director Lieutenant Colonel Godphey Sterling told the Jamaica Observer during a recent interview.

“The aim is to cut the number of attacks that succeed and to recover quickly when one does,” he added.

Dubbed Operation Sargasso Surge, the exercise seeks to simulate a single, escalating cyber incident, starting with minor activity before progressing through serious disruptions to a multi-sector national crisis.

During the exercise participants will investigate incidents, solve challenges, and make decisions under pressure. The initiative is designed to test existing procedures, strengthen communication and collaboration, and identify weaknesses that need to be addressed before an actual emergency.

It will bring together representatives from government ministries, departments and agencies, private-sector organisations, critical infrastructure operators, financial institutions, telecommunications providers, academic institutions, and other stakeholders. Activities will also extend to schools, universities, cybersecurity enthusiasts and professional incident-response teams.

The initiative forms part of activities planned for National Cybersecurity Awareness Month, observed this October under the theme ‘One Nation, Cyber Strong’. The month-long programme of events includes lectures, webinars, in-person sessions, a social media awareness campaign, and a cyber careers symposium. A national cyber exposé, scheduled for October 29, will also feature demonstrations and exhibits as it recognises contributors and volunteers who have helped to build Jamaica’s national incident-response capabilities for more than a decade.

“The 2026 campaign seeks to change behaviour as it brings more awareness so that the public and organisations can begin to adopt habits that close off the easiest routes for attackers,” he said.

“The cyber careers symposium, the competition tracks, and the Cyber Reserve also strengthen the talent pipeline, giving students and professionals a route into the field while giving the division a pool of skilled people it can call on before seeking outside help,” the lieutenant colonel added.

Providing an update on Jamaica’s cybersecurity posture, Sterling said progress had been made, although significant gaps remain.

“Key foundations are now in place — the Cybercrimes Act was amended in February and the national cybersecurity standards framework and incident response plan are finalised. A national coordinating council is proceeding to Cabinet and a Cyber Reserve is being established to draw on students, professionals, and members of the security forces during national incidents. However, some gaps are remaining,” Sterling said, as he pointed to the more than 35,000 instances of cyberattacks that originated from Jamaica since the start of this year, in addition to approximately 12 million vulnerability instances that have affected local systems and services.

“These continue to be monitored and prioritised for mitigation by the CIRT Division. The principal active threats are ransomware, phishing, and AI-assisted attacks,” he added, while noting that opportunistic fraud, including fraudulent donation websites that emerged following Hurricane Melissa, remains a concern.

Going forward, Sterling said that improving the country’s defences will require greater investment in modern detection and automation tools, stronger vulnerability management, and closer information-sharing arrangements with banks, telecommunications providers, and other critical sectors.

He also underscored the need for stronger legislative authority to empower JaCIRT to require organisations to meet cybersecurity standards and report incidents in a timely manner.

To build long-term capacity, Sterling said the entity is relying on the Strengthening Cybersecurity in Jamaica (SCIJ) Project, supported by the Inter-American Development Bank and implemented through the Office of the Prime Minister. The project, which runs from September 2025 to March 2031, aims to bolster cybersecurity protection across public institutions as it expands the pool of specialised professionals available locally.

“JaCIRT’s work is about shifting from reacting to incidents towards preventing them, building a deeper pool of skilled people and ensuring that the country can withstand and recover from an attack. The SCIJ Project is the long-term engine behind much of this as it aims to turn the completed standards framework and incident response plan into practical protection and a stronger workforce across the public sector,” he said.

Beyond testing national readiness, JaCIRT is stepping up its monitoring of cyberspace as it urges individuals and businesses to remain vigilant ahead of the busy Black Friday and Christmas shopping periods, when financially motivated cybercrimes are expected to intensify.

“The outlook for the rest of 2026 is for high, seasonal threat activity, with the main risk shifting to fraud and financially motivated attacks,” Sterling said.

“Phishing and WhatsApp account takeovers remain the most common routes to harm individuals, while ransomware and credential theft remain the main risks for organisations, especially over the holidays when staffing is reduced and detection is slower,” he further said.

World.title: A CLASS ABOVE
World.content:
Calabar’s Christopher Taylor, seen here competing in the Class 2 boys’ 400m at the ISSA Boys’ and Girls’ Athletics Championships in 2016, is one of several athletes, who started their Champs careers in Class 3 despite being young enough to compete in Class 4 at regional championships. ISSA is reportedly contemplating adding a Class 4 age category for next year’s staging of the championships.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Inter-secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) Boys’ Championships-winning Coach Neil Harrison has thrown his support behind reported plans for the high school sports administrative body to introduce Class 4 boys’ competition at the annual track and field championships, although questions remain about the potential long-term developmental implications for younger athletes.

There have been persistent whispers that ISSA plans to introduce Class 4 boys at next year’s staging of the five-day championships, along with other changes.

Presently, there are three age classes for boys — Classes 1, 2 and 3 — unlike the girls, who compete across four age groups: Classes 1, 2, 3, and 4. For years, ISSA has resisted requests to add an age group for younger boys. The lowest class currently for boys, Class 3, includes athletes under the age of 13.

Earlier this week, ISSA President Keith Wellington said the organisation had discussed a number of changes but was awaiting feedback from principals and coaches.

Two proposals he mentioned were allowing first-year Class 3 boys to compete in more than one individual event and adding the 400m to the Class 4 girls’ events.

While David Riley, head coach at Excelsior High and a member of the coaching staff when Wolmer’s Boys’ won Champs in 2010, declined to comment, saying, “I cannot comment at this time until the details are released for us as coaches to digest.” Harrison is among those who are leaning towards the change.

Harrison, who is currently the head boys’ coach at St Elizabeth Technical (STETHS), having previously held the position at Jamaica College, Kingston College and Munro College, said that, given Class 4 boys have been competing at regional championships, the proposed inclusion at the national high school championships would not be that big of a jump.

“Yes, I think so,” Harrison told the Jamaica Observer. “Class 4 boys compete in our regional championship, so why not the ultimate? It’s a good motivation for them because when they are not allowed to compete, not only the interest in the sport is lost, but sometimes they get lost in the school system as well.”

Meanwhile, Machel Woolery, head coach at Petersfield High, pointed out that Class 4-aged boys have in fact been competing at Champs, but against generally older boys.

“It is just that they will now be separating them and having them run independently and in their own class,” said Woolery before weighing up the pros and cons of their potential inclusion at Champs.

“It can be a plus as well as can be a negative.”

Woolery noted that Class 4 girls have been competing at Champs for a long time, but raised concerns that younger boys, who are good enough to qualify for the championships and compete in an age group above their own, may already be facing excessive demands on their developing bodies.

From a physiological perspective, the doubts linger.

Supporters of the potential move have argued that the introduction of a separate Class 4 boys’ category could provide younger athletes with a more appropriate competitive environment, reducing the need for some to compete against older and potentially more physically developed opponents.

However, such a move would not come without some opposition.

Detractors have raised questions about training loads, recovery, injury risk and the demands placed on boys who are still undergoing significant physical growth and maturation.

There is also a broader question about whether introducing another competitive category would improve long-term athlete development or place additional pressure on schools and young competitors to achieve results at an earlier age.

The challenge for ISSA, the coaches note, would be to ensure that any new category serves as a developmental pathway rather than simply creating another level at which young athletes are expected to produce results.

Woolery suggested that ISSA introduce restrictions for Class 4 boys, similar to those already in place for the girls.

“Maybe they can be limited to one event and a relay,” he added.

World.title: Still sold on 90
World.content:
Petrojam says motorists whose vehicles are designed for 87 octane generally gain no improvement in power, mileage or engine protection by choosing 90. (Photos: Garfield Robinson)

MONTHS after Petrojam urged motorists to stop paying for higher-octane petrol their vehicles may not need, some taxi operators remain convinced that 90 is cleaner, gives more power, or lasts longer in the tank.

Drivers who depend on their cars to earn a living may see the extra cost as money well spent if they believe it protects the engine or takes them further. But Petrojam says those using 90 in vehicles designed for 87 are generally spending more without getting those benefits.

“The general view is that 90 is cleaner. The 87 kinda dirtier and heavier than the 90. That’s why most people use the 90, because they feel it cleaner. But the 87 burns better to me,” said one operator who gave his name as David during a Jamaica Observer vox pop.

With world oil prices climbing again, that extra spending deserves another look. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose 4.9 per cent last week to close at US$109.86 a barrel on October 16,

Reuters reported. While that does not mean an immediate increase at Jamaican pumps, it puts the possible savings from choosing the correct grade back in focus.

Another operator, identified as “Bigga”, associated 90 with greater power and newer vehicles.

“The 90 burns better to me. The newer type vehicles work with 90 better. The older type vehicles you have to work with the 87. The 90 puts a stronger power on the system and a stronger revv.”

The interviews offer a glimpse of beliefs surrounding fuel purchases rather than a measure of how all taxi operators choose. They also do not establish whether participants had heard Petrojam’s earlier advice.

In May, the refinery encouraged motorists to check their manufacturers’ requirements, explaining that using 90 in a vehicle designed for 87 usually offered no benefit.

Yet Petrojam told the Business Observer that its sales still reflect a stronger preference for 90, even though most vehicles on Jamaica’s roads are designed to operate on 87.

“It is a misconception that 90-octane gasoline is inherently ‘stronger’ than 87. Both 87 and 90 contain 10 per cent ethanol (E-10) and have broadly similar energy content per litre. A higher octane rating means greater resistance to engine knocking, not more energy or power,” the company said in written responses.

“For years we’ve been advising the motoring public that 90-octane fuel is only required for high-compression, turbocharged, or spotrs car engine. However, because the premium grade is really for those types of vehicles, people are often mistaken in their belief that adding 90-octane gas to a non-high-performance vehicle will make it run faster,” Petrojam said.

The refinery, which is the only internationally rated fuel testing facility in Jamaica, also dismissed claims that 90-octane gas “burns” slower or stronger than 87-octane.

“Both grades operate at the same rate…For vehicles designed to operate on 87-octane gasoline, the additional octane generally provides no meaningful benefit.”

Petrojam attributes some of the preference to the instinctive belief that a higher number means a better product, alongside established buying habits and perceived performance benefits.

“The 90 lasts longer in the car. They say 90 is for certain cars and 87 is for the older cars. 90 is for the higher end vehicles,” motorist Renea told the Business Observer.

Meanhile, Kema Neil follows her mechanic’s advice.

“My mechanic always tells me to use 87, so I just work with the 87. He said that depending on the vehicle, it can take 90, but the older vehicles take 87 and they run much better.”

However, a vehicle’s age alone does not determine the correct grade, according to Petrojam. The octane number measures resistance to knocking — abnormal combustion inside the engine — rather than cleanliness or how much energy the petrol contains.

Petrojam says servicing, tyre pressure, and driving habits have a far greater influence on fuel efficiency than switching to 90 in an engine designed for 87.

For a taxi operator buying fuel regularly, the price difference can add up. At an illustrative pump-price gap of $30 per litre, purchasing 40 litres of 87 instead of 90 would save $1,200. Repeated weekly, that would amount to $62,400 over a year, assuming purchases and the price gap remained unchanged.

Actual savings depend on prices at the station, and apply only where 87 meets the vehicle’s requirements.

Understanding the octane numbers

Even motorists who check their manuals can become confused if the number printed there differs from those displayed at Jamaican pumps.

Petrojam explained that Jamaica uses the Anti-Knock Index, or AKI, while many vehicle manuals use the Research Octane Number, or RON. AKI is calculated by averaging RON and another measure, the Motor Octane Number.

The different scales mean a manual specifying 91 RON does not automatically rule out Jamaica’s 87-octane petrol.

“As a general guide, 87 AKI is approximately equivalent to 91 RON, while 90 AKI is approximately equivalent to 95 RON. Motorists should therefore compare their vehicle manufacturer’s minimum octane requirement with the corresponding local grade,” Petrojam said.

Under that guide, local 87 is generally suitable where the manual specifies a minimum of 91 RON or lower. Local 90 is generally appropriate for a 95 RON requirement. The refinery added that motorists whose manuals specify above 95 RON should check the manufacturer’s requirements against the available fuel specifications.

The wording in the manual also matters. A higher grade being “required” establishes a minimum the fuel must meet. A recommendation can allow more flexibility.

“Where a higher grade is recommended but regular gasoline is permitted, the lower grade may be used, although some reduction in performance or fuel economy may occur,” Petrojam explained.

Meanwhile, the refinery acknowledged that it sees an opportunity for vehicle dealers to clear up these questions before customers establish their buying habits.

“We think that it is important for motor vehicle dealers to advise owners that, where applicable, 87-octane should be the recommended fuel type,” it said.

In response to queries from the Business Observer on what more can the industry do to explain fuel requirements clearly, Petrojam reasoned that dealers could explain at the point of sale that Jamaica’s 87 is approximately equivalent to 91 RON, helping buyers match the instructions in their manuals to the grades available locally.

The refinery said it also supports making that information easier to find when motorists pull up to refuel.

“In this regard, Petrojam would also support clearer fuel grade labelling at service stations, including a simple RON-to-AKI conversion guide at the pump, to help motorists make informed purchasing decisions.” That would give drivers a reference when deciding what to buy, alongside advice from mechanics and fellow motorists.

—Additional reporting by Jason Cross

World.title: Former CMU worker details university’s accounting, banking systems
World.content:
Campus of Caribbean Maritime University in Kingston (Photo: CMU)

A former senior member of staff of the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) is expected to continue testimony regarding the school’s finances on Wednesday, with information on the now-defunct CAP-YES programme, in the fraud trial of former CMU boss Fritz Pinnock along with former education minister Ruel Reid and their co-accused.

The witness, appearing before Senior Parish Judge Sanchia Burrell at the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court on Tuesday, testified how money came into and left certain bank accounts controlled by the university between 2016 and 2019, including accounts for payroll, CAP (Career Advancement Programme) and CAPYES (Career Advancement Programme – Youth Empowerment Services) programme, among others.

The department in which they worked was guided by the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit Act) and PBMA ( The Public Bodies Management and Accountability Act), the witness said, adding that it oversaw payroll, including salary deductions for CMU employees; accounts receivable, which dealt with collecting money owed to the school; and accounts payable, which dealt with any money the school owed to vendors or debt obligations.

While testifying, the witness indicated that the weekly accounts payable process included the submission of documentation verifying the debt obligation, which would be entered on CMUs system and included in an aged payables report. Any vendors to be paid by the school would then be selected from that report.

When pressed on what type of vendors this included, the witness listed utility entities, suppliers of goods to the school’s tuck shop and others undertaking special projects.

The witness also told the court that the school received a monthly subvention from the Ministry of Finance through the Ministry of Education that was deposited to a specific bank account.

When asked where that subvention was funded from, to their understanding, the witness said “from taxes”.

That account, the witness said, was used as a flow-through to other bank accounts, including payroll accounts.

The witness also touched on the operations of the school’s canteen or tuck shop, which had multiple accounts associated with it. The witness testified that cash proceeds would be deposited into the accounts and canteen vendors paid from it, adding that when enough cash was not in the account to pay vendors, the canteen would be provided with an advance by CMU, which would also go to the account.

The school also received money from the government for the operation of the CAP and CAP-YES programmes, deposited directly into accounts set up by CMU, the witness told the court. The witness said accounts were used for expenses associated with CAP and CAP-YES, including paying some salaries as well as stipends for students in need and other initiatives.

CAP, which is carried out at institutions across the island, was intended to provide technical, vocational, and academic training to youth, and CAP-YES was a programme offshoot attached specifically to the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU).

CAP and CAPYES were shuttered at the Caribbean Maritime University in 2020 with instructions to complete the course for those already in training and take in no further applicants.

During testimony, the witness identified Pinnock as the former head of the university, pointing out his striped shirt and orange tie. Pinnock, who has sought leave to take notes during the trial, did not react visibly at being identified. He was represented by a junior of his attorney in the matter, Hugh Wildman.

Pinnock, Reid and their co-accused, Reid’s daughter Sharelle Reid and wife Sharen Reid and Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence’s are before the court on a 35-count indictment, accused of participating in a scheme with others unknown that siphoned off more than $25 million from the Ministry of Education and CMU.

They have pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Issues with disclosure were also put before Burrell in the courtroom on Tuesday with defence attorney Linda Wright, who represents Reid, Carolyn Chuck, who represents Sharelle and Kevon Johnson, who holds for Brown Lawrence’s attorney Oswest Senior Smith, all rising to express concern.

Wright maintained that more documents relating to certain witnesses, including the witness scheduled to be called that day, had been shared by the prosecution at a late hour, thus creating challenges for the defence to go through the documents and take instructions from their clients.

Wright maintained that this was not a “trial by ambush”, describing the disclosure as untidy.

The prosecution maintained that the documents in relation to Tuesday’s witness were not new and that any late disclosure of new documents was not a deliberate effort on its part.

Burrell, who reminded counsel to exercise care around disclosure, is expected to grant a brief adjournment in relation to the issue.

World.title: NWC seeks 51 per cent tariff increase
World.content:
Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The National Water Commission (NWC) has applied to the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) for a 51 per cent tariff increase, a move that could affect its approximately 500,000 customers.

Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr told the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) on Tuesday that the application was submitted to the OUR last Friday, adding that the regulator is expected to make an announcement shortly.

Kerr said the proposed increase is tied to an investment plan designed to secure funding for the company’s priority projects.

He warned that if the OUR does not approve the full 51 per cent increase, the NWC would have to revise its investment plan.

Kerr also noted that members of the public would have an opportunity to provide feedback through a consultation process before the OUR makes a determination on the application.

The NWC has argued that the increase is necessary to bring its revenues in line with its expenses. The commission last received a tariff increase in 2019.

NWC Chief Financial Officer Fabian Christie told the committee that the company’s revenue position had deteriorated over time, particularly in relation to customer payments.

He said the proposed increase was needed to keep pace with rising operating costs, including energy expenses.

World.title: Russia ready for 3-way talks on Ukraine war, Kremlin says
World.content:
Witkoff confirmed on X that discussions “will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level.”

His visit was the latest in a new round of U.S. attempts to bring Moscow to the negotiating table to end its war against Ukraine. The special envoy also met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, subsequently announcing a proposal for a three-way leaders’ negotiation.

There have been several rounds of talks between the U.S. and Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The most recent discussions stalled in February when the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran.

Previous negotiations were largely political theater and failed to yield any broader breakthrough on halting hostilities, prisoner-of-war exchanges or a truce regarding strikes on energy infrastructure.

Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported Moscow proposed a potential high-level summit with China and the U.S. to negotiate a deal on ending the war in Ukraine.

On Wednesday, footage emerged of Witkoff praising Putin during their face-to-face talks in St. Petersburg, after the Russians released a U.S. prisoner from captivity.

World.title: Ex-DUP chief faces new allegation of raping woman inside Westminster
World.content:
A woman visiting the House of Commons in 2016 alleges that Jeffrey Donaldson tried to sexually assault her inside the Democratic Unionist Party’s Westminster offices.

The jailed former leader of Northern Ireland’s Democratic Unionist Party, Jeffrey Donaldson, is facing a new allegation that he raped a woman inside the DUP’s Westminster offices in 2016.

Donaldson, who last week received a 15-year prison sentence for sexually assaulting two girls, is serving his punishment in an isolated wing for sex offenders in Northern Ireland’s Maghaberry Prison. Donaldson — who is tentatively scheduled for release by 2033 after serving half of his sentence — is appealing his conviction on 18 counts, including one of rape.

The Metropolitan Police in London said Wednesday it has opened its own investigation after receiving an evidence file from Police Service of Northern Ireland detectives, who interviewed the woman on October 13.

World.title: Perquisitions au Parlement européen dans une enquête visant l’ancien groupe du RN
World.content:
Les perquisitions ont eu lieu dans les bureaux du secrétariat général du groupe, selon deux responsables qui ont souhaité garder l’anonymat pour s’exprimer au sujet de l’enquête en cours.

Lorsqu’ID a été dissous en 2024, bon nombre de ses membres ont rejoint les Patriotes, notamment des élus du Rassemblement national, du Parti de la liberté d’Autriche (FPÖ), du Fidesz hongrois, du Vlaams Belang (Intérêt flamand) belge, de l’ANO 2011 tchèque et du parti espagnol Vox.

Dans un communiqué, les Patriotes insistent sur le fait qu’il n’existe “aucune continuité juridique” avec le groupe ID, et qu’ils “ne sont pas visés” par les perquisitions.

Les soupçons portent sur l’utilisation du budget alloué chaque année par le Parlement européen aux groupes politiques pour couvrir leurs frais administratifs et opérationnels. Le Parquet européen enquête pour déterminer si le groupe ID a versé des dons irréguliers à des organisations régionales dans plusieurs pays de l’Union européenne, et s’il a enfreint les règles relatives aux appels d’offres dans le cadre de contrats attribués à des entreprises proches du groupe.

En 2025, le service financier a ordonné aux Patriotes de restituer 276 967 euros de fonds européens qui, selon lui, auraient été indûment dépensés au cours du second semestre 2024, dans le cadre de procédures d’appel d’offres irrégulières similaires.

“Comme toujours lorsqu’on le lui demande, le Parlement coopère avec les autorités compétentes. Nous n’avons pas d’autres commentaires à faire”, a déclaré un porte-parole du Parlement européen dans un SMS.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

World.title: Water sector to wait until 2027 for full details of Burnham’s overhaul
World.content:
Water UK Chief Executive David Henderson urged the government to move ahead with reforms suggested last year by former Bank of England Deputy Governor Jon Cunliffe, before ministers decide the overall path of how the sector is owned.

The Cunliffe report “was given to the government 15 months ago and the credit rating agencies are watching,” Henderson told POLITICO. “If the government doesn’t pretty soon decide what it wants to do with that report, then we risk a downgrade, as Moody’s has indicated. And if there’s a downgrade, that would sadly see £40 being added to every single water bill across England and Wales. That’s the last thing anybody wants.”

He added: “We still have no idea how [a proposed] new regulator will look, what status it will have, what its duties will be, which parts of the Environment Agency will stay in the Environment Agency, and which parts will go into the new regulator. That is causing uncertainty … an important consideration for any investor.”

One government official insisted the 10-year plan would contain some finer details of plans to overhaul the water industry, though they accepted that fiscal implications were always dealt with in fiscal events such as the spending review.

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle is also due to bring a water bill to parliament before Christmas with separate policy, such as closing what Burnham has called “loopholes used to pay excessive bonuses” to water company executives. It will also contain scrutiny powers for regional mayors.

Burnham announced last month that the bill would lift a ban on the government owning more than 3% of shares in any English water firm. But he has also long made clear that he would not fully nationalize the industry, a move the government previously estimated would cost £100 billion for England and Wales together.

First Secretary of State Louise Haigh, one of Burnham’s most powerful allies in government, is leading three task forces including one on public control of water alongside housing, energy and transport.

Officials have been working through a “spectrum of options” for how public control in the water sector will look, a second government official said. They added that ministers are due to begin deciding which option — or combination of options — will be taken forward before the 10-year plan.

World.title: Prosecutor searches far-right group offices in EU Parliament
World.content:
The EPPO confirmed it carried out searches in the Parliament’s buildings in France and Belgium “as part of an ongoing investigation into the use of European funds by a former political group in the European Parliament.”

The searches took place at the group’s secretariat offices, according to two officials, granted anonymity to speak about the ongoing investigation.

When ID dissolved in 2024, many of its staff moved to the Patriots, including lawmakers from France’s National Rally, Austria’s Freedom Party, Hungary’s Fidesz, Spain’s Vox, Belgium’s Flemish Interest and Czechia’s ANO 2011.

In their statement, the group insisted “there is no legal continuity with the ID Group” and that “it is not involved in the ongoing investigations.”

The allegations of mismanagement of funds relate to the budget allocated annually by the Parliament for political groups to spend on administrative and operative costs. EPPO is probing whether ID made irregular donations to regional organizations in several EU countries, and whether the group breached tender rules in contracts awarded to companies friendly to the group.

In 2025, the finance department ordered the Patriots to give back €276,967 in EU funds it says the group misused during the second half of 2024, related to similar irregular tender procedures.

World.title: Publishers want Brussels and London to stop Meta’s new AI terms
World.content:
“The Commission remains committed to ensure that Meta’s practices fully comply with all applicable obligations under EU law, including competition rules and the Digital Markets Act,” Commission spokesperson Ricardo Cardoso told POLITICO, referring to the EU’s rulebook for Big Tech. He said Brussels was aware of both Meta’s changes and publishers’ concerns.

The U.K. competition watchdog has moved as well. British publishers have complained to the Competition and Markets Authority that Meta is so dominant they are compelled to accept its terms.

The watchdog’s chief, Sarah Cardell, told British lawmakers on Tuesday that it had asked Meta to explain the changes and would meet the company on Wednesday. She named Meta as a possible candidate for Britain’s new rules for tech giants.

Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), speaks in a panel discussion during the Annual CBI Conference, at Queen Elizabeth II Centre on November 25, 2024 in London. | Leon Neal/Getty Images

The terms cover businesses that use Meta’s tools to run Facebook pages, Instagram accounts or ads, which includes almost every newsroom.

The fight began in the U.S. last week, when Nieman Lab, a journalism research outlet at Harvard, reported on the terms after receiving a tip from a small business owner.

As first written, they let Meta send automated programs to copy websites linked to those accounts and use the material to “train” its products, Nieman Lab concluded. There is no opt-out, and a business that continues to use Meta’s tools after Oct. 30 will be deemed to have consented.

World.title: Die AfD-Leaks
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Ein massiver Datenklau erschüttert die AfD: Über 400.000 interne E-Mails, darunter von Alice Weidel und Alexander Gauland, sind an die Öffentlichkeit gelangt. Die geleakten Papiere offenbaren nicht nur eklatante Sicherheitslücken, sondern bergen teilweise politische Sprengkraft.

In Nordrhein-Westfalen eskaliert derweil erneut der Machtkampf zwischen Landeschef Martin Vincentz und dem Lager um den Bundestagsabgeordneten Matthias Helferich. Der Konflikt wird mittlerweile sogar mit scharfen Klingen bei einer burschenschaftlichen Mensur ausgetragen. Gleichzeitig greift der Bundesvorstand mit harten Ordnungsmaßnahmen ein und droht, die internen Mehrheitsverhältnisse zu kippen.

Auch in der Bundestagsfraktion zeigt sich Uneinigkeit: Bei Abstimmungen über Auslandseinsätze der Bundeswehr stimmt die Partei zersplittert ab, Fraktionschef Tino Chrupalla enthält sich. Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler analysieren den Spagat zwischen Sicherheitspolitik und der Inszenierung als Friedenspartei.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.
