World.title: Witkoff to Putin: ‘You are a humanitarian … I salute that’
World.content:
The American envoy met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, and is expected to propose trilateral talks between the two leaders and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Russia’s strikes on Kyiv and Kharkiv continued overnight, killing three people, local mayors reported.

Putin’s assault on Ukraine killed 328 civilians in September alone, according to the United Nations, while Kremlin forces bombard energy infrastructure across the country heading into winter.

The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023 over the forced transfer of children to Russia after the Kremlin’s invasion of Ukraine began.

World.title: Colombia seizes 7.6 tonnes of Netherlands-bound cocaine at Cartagena port
World.content:
Colombian police have seized 7.6 tonnes of cocaine bound for the Netherlands at the port of Cartagena, President Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Tuesday.

 

"The National Police has just achieved the largest cocaine seizure in the port of Cartagena in the last 10 years," he wrote on X.

According to Colombia's National Police, the drugs were hidden in powdered panela, an unrefined cane sugar, and were found by its anti-narcotics directorate in an operation coordinated with the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).

De la Espriella said security forces had seized 132 tonnes of cocaine, worth around $6.1 billion, in his government's first 75 days.

"There is no truce against narco-terrorism! Every dose we prevent from reaching the streets saves lives, and every dollar we take from them weakens their criminal structures," he added.

Separately, the Dutch Public Prosecution Service (OM) confirmed to the Dutch newspaper AD that two Dutch nationals had been arrested in Colombia at its request.

Colombian prosecutors named them as Ronny and Ulrich. Neither authority has linked the arrests to the seizure. According to the EU Drugs Agency, 330 tonnes of cocaine were seized in the EU in 2024, down from 419 tonnes in 2023.

World.title: Thélyson Orélien row: publisher says AI used to write 'C'était ça ou mourir'
World.content:
The case has been shaking the French-language publishing world for weeks. On Wednesday 21 October, the Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal announced via a press release (source in French) that Thélyson Orélien had indeed used artificial intelligence (AI) to write his novel "C'était ça ou mourir", contrary to what he had previously claimed.

 

"New information, confirmed in recent days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process (of the novel), even though the author had assured us, on several occasions, that he had never resorted to it in creating his book", the publisher said in a statement on Wednesday.

"As a result, Boréal will not reprint the novel and will not publish any further books by Thélyson Orélien."

This announcement comes just a week after the publisher had said it was backing the author, insisting it had no evidence that would make it possible to establish with certainty that AI had been used.

In the face of mounting doubts, and after Thélyson Orélien "announced that he would not provide any further material", the publisher says it has "commissioned an in-depth external analysis" of "all the working versions of the novel".

"We still do not know to what extent AI was used in the creation of "C'était ça ou mourir", and we will probably never have a definitive answer on that point" but "for us, the fundamental issue is the relationship of trust between authors and publishers", the publishing house added.

The controversy was sparked by accusations from the X account "Balance ton Claude", which claimed to have identified extensive use of AI in the novel. The affair has since shaken the sector and, for weeks, fuelled questions about the future of the writing profession.

World.title: Riots in France: tourism sector fears drop in foreign visitors
World.content:
Images of the riots in France, broadcast around the world, are alarming tourism professionals. The first consequences are already being felt in hotel bookings, and those in the sector fear the situation will worsen if the violence continues.

 

"This surge in violence in city centres, in Nice, Paris and Lyon, is catastrophic", laments Christelle Cassagne, head of ADN Tourisme, a federation that brings together France's institutional tourism bodies.

"When you book a hotel for a week, it is not to stay shut away in your room", she adds.

Tourists hesitant to go ahead with their stay

In Paris, the closure of the Louvre museum on Monday because of a student gathering at its entrance also frustrated many tourists who had come to discover the famous museum.

In this tense climate, some travellers are reconsidering their stay in the capital.

Charred bicycles the day after a quiet night under curfew in Paris, Tuesday 20 October 2026. (Photo AP/Christophe Ena)

According to MKG Consulting, the first effects are already visible, with Parisian hotels reporting a slowdown in bookings for the next six weeks.

In the space of just 24 hours, between 19 and 20 October, their lead over the same period in 2025 narrowed significantly, dropping from 1 to 0.2 percentage points for stays scheduled from 20 to 29 October, and from 3.5 to 1.9 points for those from 20 to 25 October.

Fear of fresh riots weighs on tourism

According to Didier Arino, director of the consultancy Protourisme, the scale of the repercussions will depend mainly on whether the unrest continues. A single day of riots in Paris is thought to have triggered the cancellation of around 1% of bookings for the month, still a relatively limited impact.

"The further customers travel, the more sensitive they are to security risks, and the greater the consequences", he points out.

The United States, China and Germany are among the countries that have issued warnings to their nationals planning to travel to France.

These advisories could particularly weigh on arrivals of American and Asian tourists, whose spending is generally higher than that of European visitors.

"If this lasts for two weeks, it is not very serious. But if it continues for several months, it will be catastrophic", warns Laurent Abitbol, chairman of the management board of the Selectour travel agency network.

World.title: Dussehra: Giant effigies of demons go up in flames in India
World.content:
Crowds in New Delhi watched giant effigies of demons go up in flames on Tuesday, as India marked Dussehra, the Hindu festival of good over evil.

 

Fireworks lit the sky as the figures of Ravana, his son Meghnad and his brother Kumbhakarna burned.

In Hindu tradition, the ritual recalls the defeat of Ravana by the god Rama. Actors dressed as Rama and his brother staged the final moments of the battle.

The prime minister joined the spectators at a ground in the city and shot an arrow from a bow.

Hindus observe nine days of ceremonies, rituals and fasts, which end on the tenth day. The festival is also called Vijayadashmi, from ‘Vijay’, meaning ‘victory’, and ‘Dashmi’, meaning ‘tenth day’.

World.title: EU journalism prize awards investigation into human rights abuse at Italy’s migrant centres in Albania
World.content:
An investigation highlighting human rights violations at the controversial migrant centres Italy established in Albania won the European Parliament’s Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize for journalism on Wednesday.

 

The investigation, published by Dutch outlet De Correspondent in January 2026, explored two centres in Shëngjin and Gjadër built to accommodate asylum seekers rescued at sea while Italian authorities reviewed their applications.

The report is titled "Cuffed, caged, cast away: this is Europe’s ‘innovative solution’ for unwanted migrants". It puts into question the legality of the centres, opened in 2024, which have become a model for European migration policy, as several countries seek to establish return hubs for migrants outside the EU.

Following repeated legal setbacks, Giorgia Meloni’s government repurposed the centres in March 2025 to detain irregular migrants already in Italy ahead of their deportation to their countries of origin.

The report documented violations of fundamental rights and European law in the treatment of migrants and their transfer to the centres, issuing a warning on the new EU policy on migration.

Access denied, FOI requests ignored

Five EU countries seek to establish similar return hubs in Africa by 2027, following the adoption of a controversial EU law that provides a legal framework for such arrangements, legalizing the transfer of irregular migrants to countries they have no connection to.

“The deal is a blueprint for how to erode human rights, undermine the European rule of law, and normalize far-right views on migration,” reads the prize-winning report.

Maite Vermeulen and Giacomo Zandonini, the authors of the report published in January 2026, also estimate that around €259 million was spent on the facilities over their first two years of operation, during which 256 people were detained — equivalent to approximately €1 million per person.

“It is a big PR operation, more than a policy that would actually expedite returns [of migrants],” Vermeulen told Euronews, considering that the Italian approach is neither cheaper nor more effective, and does not deter irregular arrivals.

She argued that other EU countries could not follow the Italian model without breaching human rights. “That is a story we tell ourselves to make [return hubs] acceptable or palatable,” she told Euronews.

The investigation also denounces the “smokescreen” put in place by the Italian authorities to hide the details of the deal. Journalists were denied access, freedom of information requests often went unanswered, staff at the centres signed strict non-disclosure agreements, and contracts were not made public.

The jury for the prize is composed of journalists from all EU member states.

World.title: Zelenskyy backs freezing front line as first step towards Ukraine ceasefire
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that halting the fighting along the current front line is the most realistic route to ending the war with Russia, opening the way to ceasefire talks.

 

"Right now we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire... freeze and stop," Zelenskyy told US broadcaster Fox News's "Fox and Friends" programme on Wednesday. He was asked whether he would accept a deal that fixed the front along its current lines.

His comments came as US special envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was willing to negotiate in any format, but insisted that Kyiv must be directly involved.

"I always said that we are open to negotiate in any format, any topics. But don't speak about us without us, please."

He also stressed that any agreement must come with security guarantees from Ukraine's partners, including the United States and European allies. Such guarantees, he said, would mean Ukrainians are not "afraid... that occupation will come back, aggression will come back, killings will come back."

Satellite row

The interview came days after Kyiv accused Washington of deliberately slowing Starshield, the SpaceX-operated military communications system that Ukrainian forces depend on at the front. Ukraine also uses Starlink, SpaceX's civilian satellite network.

Zelenskyy said both services remained "still limited", but added: "Secretary (of State Marco Rubio) told me that he will work with his team on this to unblock this."

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that SpaceX owner Elon Musk had personally ordered the cut in Starshield services. Musk had previously suggested that any restrictions would have come from Trump, a claim the US president has denied.

World.title: Nine Emperor Gods Festival: Devotees walk across burning embers for good luck
World.content:
Barefoot worshippers crossed a bed of smouldering embers at Si Thian Kong Temple in Kuala Pilah, Malaysia, on Saturday night.

 

It took place during the Nine Emperor Gods Festival. Fireworks and firecrackers filled the sky, and performers staged a lion dance.

Before the ceremony, the group levelled the fire pit and scattered salt over the coals. The temple chairman said crossing the fire is meant to bring good luck, health and business success for the year ahead.

Others lit candles, made offerings and were blessed with red paint.

The nine-day Taoist festival is observed by Chinese communities across Southeast Asia. Followers keep a strict vegetarian diet for its full length.

World.title: What China wants from a Trump-Putin summit on Ukraine
World.content:
Moscow is pushing for a summit with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, without Kyiv or the EU. What does Russia hope to gain, and why might China be willing to take part?

The administration of US President Donald Trump has stepped up diplomatic efforts this autumn to revive stalled negotiations aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine.

Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv and its European partners while seeking to draw Moscow back to the negotiating table through a series of concessions, including a deal involving Russian diesel exports to the US and the temporary easing of some sanctions.

Yet the Kremlin appears in no hurry to resume meaningful peace talks. Moscow is ready to hold negotiations with Ukraine at a technical level next month, the Kremlin said after the meeting between US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on November 21.

Putin agreed to resume the peace talks mediated by Washington after November 10, his aide Yury Ushakov said after the meeting. He added that the next round of negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi and would focus on "building the security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the war."

US special envoy Steve Witkoff at and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands during a meeting in St. Petersburg on October 21 Image: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/REUTERS

According to his aide, Putin also shared some thoughts with Witkoff on the possible trilateral summit involving US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Ushakov pointed out that Beijing is already preparing the meeting.

Trilateral summit in China without Ukraine

Moscow proposed to hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen, China, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week. According to WSJ sources, Putin hopes to reach an agreement with Trump and Xi on ending the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Russia.

Moscow's proposal for the three-way summit involving Russia, the United States and China — but excluding Ukraine and the European Union — offers a glimpse of the negotiating format the Kremlin would prefer. Russia insists that Ukraine must be prepared to make territorial concessions before negotiations can move forward. Putin has also repeatedly stressed that he is willing to negotiate only if Russian interests are taken into account.

According to the WSJ, Putin views the proposed gathering in Shenzhen as a potential new Yalta Conference, referring to the 1945 meeting of the leaders of the United States, Great Britain and the Soviet Union to discuss the defeat of Nazi Germany and the postwar order in Europe.

The newspaper reported that Chinese officials had indicated through diplomatic channels that Beijing would not object to the three-way format if Trump agreed to participate. Trump, whose relations with Kyiv have deteriorated significantly in recent weeks, has also expressed openness to such talks.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pointed out during his visit in Oslo on October 20 that talks concerning the future of his country will be acceptable only if Ukraine gets a seat at the negotiating table.

What does China stand to gain from the talks?

Temur Umarov, a researcher at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin who specializes in China-Russia relations, is not surprised by the Kremlin's proposal. He told DW that Moscow wants to feel respected by Washington and treated as a major international power.

The previous US administration was unwilling to discuss questions affecting Ukraine's sovereignty with Russia without Kyiv's participation. Now, Umarov said, the Kremlin believes such negotiations may have become possible.

Moscow apparently hopes that any agreement reached at the proposed meeting would prompt the White House to pressure Ukraine and the EU into accepting its terms. But what role would China actually play?

Umarov believes Beijing would participate largely as a symbolic partner, rather than as an active mediator responsible for the outcome. "Beijing has no intention of taking responsibility for Ukraine's future," he said.

China's leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump agreed to hold a trilateral summit with Russia in Shenzhen Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

Simply attending the summit would not impose any additional obligations on China. "It is hardly surprising that the Kremlin insists on this format," Umarov explained. "Russia wants to demonstrate that it is on an equal footing not only with the United States, but also with China. Yet, objectively speaking, Moscow is not the senior partner in that relationship."

Umarov believes China has little direct interest in such negotiations. Even if the leaders issued a joint statement, Beijing would seek language that was as vague and noncommittal as possible, he said. That would allow China to present almost any subsequent development in the war as consistent with the understanding reached at the summit. For Umarov, such flexibility would be essential to Beijing's participation.

However, Yurii Poita, a senior associate researcher at the Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), offers a different assessment. He believes China and Russia have overlapping strategic interests, particularly in their efforts to promote an alternative security architecture across Eurasia.

Both countries, he argues, would benefit from a reduction in Western military presence in Europe and Asia and from a weakening of NATO's influence. "If Russia and China manage to convince the United States to reduce its military presence in Europe and military assistance to Ukraine, Russia would gain additional advantages on the battlefield," Poita told DW.

He added that such a development would further undermine the EU's confidence in the United States as a NATO ally. Poita believes Moscow and Beijing would seek precisely these outcomes in any negotiations with Washington.

Is Putin's political survival crucial for China?

Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, also doubts that Beijing is preparing to take a more active diplomatic role in ending the war.

Speaking to DW, Kimmage said China may see the conflict as destabilizing and would prefer to maintain trade relations with Ukraine and other countries in the region. But he believes another priority outweighs those concerns. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin," he said.

President Zelenskyy said deciding on Ukraine's future without Ukraine was unacceptable Image: Dan Bashakov/AP Photo/picture alliance

According to Kimmage, Russia provides China with several geopolitical advantages, including low-cost energy and a foreign policy partner that rarely stands in Beijing's way.

He believes China will continue indirectly supporting Russia's military efforts to prevent a Russian defeat. An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said, but ensuring Putin does not lose is crucial. For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.

Does excluding Europe reveal the EU's weakness?

Neither Ukraine nor the European Union would be part of the proposed talks in China.

Kateryna Krasina, a junior researcher at the Kyiv-based New Geopolitics Network, believes their exclusion could reveal how Beijing actually views their international influence.

In her assessment, China's approach suggests that it does not regard Ukraine as an independent player in the negotiations and considers Europe relatively weak.

Kimmage, however, argues that excluding Europe from the summit would not necessarily diminish its influence over the course of the negotiations.

He acknowledged that European governments may have little power to prevent a meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi. But he pointed to European efforts surrounding the 2025 Alaska summit between Trump and Putin, which he believes helped prevent outcomes that would have been unfavorable to Europe.

Kimmage said Europe's influence has grown through financial assistance to Ukraine and extensive defense industry cooperation, particularly involving Germany and other European countries.

He argued that European support has played an important role in Ukraine's ability to resist Russian advances. "And that support equals leverage," Kimmage said.

He believes Russia, China and the United States may all be interested in portraying Europe as a secondary power, but that such a portrayal would overlook Europe's actual influence.

"The optics and the reality are not quite the same," he said, drawing a distinction between the appearance of great-power diplomacy resembling the Yalta Conference and Europe's role in supporting Ukraine.

Umarov offers another perspective.

He believes that any diplomatic agreement between the US, Russia and China would face the reality on the ground.

"China understands that whatever the outcome of negotiations with the United States and Russia, the reality on the ground will be very different and will depend above all on Ukraine," he said.

"Whether the Kremlin likes it or not, Ukraine has agency of its own. Neither the United States nor Western countries can fully determine what happens on the battlefield through diplomatic pressure alone."

This article was originally published in Russian.

World.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in Cambridge Analytica case
World.content:
A New Mexico judge ordered Facebook's parent company, Meta, to pay $25 billion for misleading users over the Cambridge Analytica breach, which took place during Donald Trump's first presidential campaign.

US tech giant Meta, owner of Facebook, was ordered to pay $25 billion (around €22.5 billion) to the US state of New Mexico after a jury found Facebook deceived its users over privacy and content moderation.

"Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false," Judge ⁠Francis ⁠Mathew wrote in his order following the Wednesday verdict.

The case links back to the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal, when a third-party quiz harvested the data of some 87 million Facebook profiles and sold it to the UK-based political consulting firm. The firm used the data for targeted ads, including campaign ads for Donald Trump's first presidential run.

New Mexico rejects deal with Meta

Nearly all US states agreed to settle with Facebook over a myriad of legal issues for an overall payment of $18 billion in August. This included releasing the company from future liability for the Cambridge Analytica breach.

Meta settles for $18B. What it means for you. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New Mexico refused to settle and filed a lawsuit against the platform. Prosecutors claimed that the social network deceived the state's entire population of some 2.1 million people by its public statements on privacy. The US state also argued that Facebook allowed the spread of misinformation and violent content.

In turn, the company's lawyers said the state failed to prove people were actually harmed by Facebook's statements, and claimed the platform had robust content moderation.

In September, a jury found Facebook liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws. Meta pledged to "continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record."

Meta's billions could go to New Mexico's education system

Following the jury's decision last month, it was up to the court to determine how much Meta would pay the state. While the $25 billion fine is lower than the $35 billion to $40 billion demanded by the New Mexico prosecutors, it far exceeds the cap of $3.45 billion suggested by Meta's lawyers.

US jury fines Meta in landmark child‑safety case To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is ​money, and the value of its stock price," New Mexico attorney Randi McGinn said during the trial.

On Wednesday, New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said the outcome should be "an unambiguous message" to Silicon Valley.

While noting that the money will likely be tied up due to appeals, Torrez also noted that the fine is legally due to be paid into New Mexico's education fund.

"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," he said.

The case is the latest in the string of legal challenges large social media companies face in the US and other parts of the world, including the separate August verdict in New Mexico ordering Facebook to pay $567 million over harm to children.

World.title: PHP developers say key patches available after global scare
World.content:
Newly discovered vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language have put millions of websites at risk, with government agencies sounding alarms and taking down sites. Developers say updating systems is "imperative."

The updates patching the recently leaked PHP security issues are now online , developers of the open-source programming language said on Wednesday afternoon.

"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the team said in an online statement.

Millions of websites worldwide, including critical infrastructure and government portals, as well as news sites and online shops, rely on PHP. The software is free.

The new patches aim to fix two "critical vulnerabilities" hackers could exploit to remotely take control of websites and servers, bypassing usual obstacles such as password-protected accounts. The gaps were labeled CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

How did hackers trick Berlin's city government? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

By exploiting them, malicious actors could gain access to government databases and customer data, deface websites, or compromise entire businesses or other online services.

"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation said in a blog post.

Cloudflare reports 'early attacks'

The weaknesses were flagged by two separate security companies, Calif and Wiz, this August. Both of the firms used AI tools to detect the PHP issues.

PHP developers kept the flaws confidential while working on the fix. News of the security issues, however, leaked on Tuesday, a day before the scheduled update.

Hours before the PHP update, Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of security firm Cloudflare, said hackers were already trying to exploit these weaknesses.

"We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up," he said in an online post.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.

"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.

Is AI the new weapon of mass data theft? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

NSA urges taking websites offline if update not feasible

Authorities in multiple countries, including Australia, Japan, and several European nations, issued warnings and took down government websites in an effort to preempt potential attacks.

In France, the website of the Paris Police Prefecture was taken offline due to "detection of a critical security vulnerability," along with local government pages. Germany's government IT service took down some sites that used PHP. Belgium's Foreign Ministry temporarily blocked its own online presence, while the Dutch cybersecurity agency took itself online as a precaution.

The US National Security Agency (NSA) warned that vulnerabilities "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database."

"If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommend that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," they said on X.

Meanwhile, the White House said it was informed of the issue last week and that US federal agencies were assessing the potential impact to government systems and infrastructure.

World.title: Raids at far-right group's offices at European Parliament
World.content:
Authorities searched the Patriots for Europe's European Parliament offices in a long-running funding inquiry. The group says the charges pertain to its predecessor and there is "no legal continuity" between the two.

The third-largest alliance of parties in the European Parliament, the right-wing nationalist Patriots for Europe (PfE) group, on Wednesday said searches had been carried out at "administrative offices" at the European Parliament buildings in Brussels and Strasbourg.

PfE said the searches appeared to be tied to the long-running probe into alleged misuse of funds by members of the now-disbanded Identity and Democracy (ID) Group.

PfE formed out of the ashes of ID, losing and gaining some members along the way, after the last European Parliament elections in 2024.

What did the investigative body say about the searches?

The European Public Prosecutor's Office — the independent body that investigates and prosecutes crimes against the EU budget, such as corruption or misuse of EU funds — said it searched premises in France and Belgium.

It said this was part of an ongoing investigation into the use of European Union funds by a former European Parliament group.

EPPO did not say which group was involved and said it would not publish further details for now for fear of compromising the investigation.

What did the PfE say about the searches?

PfE, meanwhile, confirmed the activity around its offices but also tried to stress its distance from the case since its rebrand and reformation — even though its constituent political parties are largely the same with the notable exception of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) now being excluded.

"Since this morning, the European Public Prosecutor's Office has been carrying out searches in administrative offices at the European Parliament in Brussels and Strasbourg. It would appear that these searches are linked to the complaint lodged against the Identity and Democracy Group (ID) dissolved in 2024," it wrote in a statement.

"The Patriots for Europe Group emphasizes that there is no legal continuity with the ID Group and that it is not involved in the ongoing investigations," it said.

A French member of the European Parliament for the Rassemblement National or National Rally (RN) party, Jean-Paul Garraud, said that "the offices of staff members of the former Identity and Democracy group" were targeted.

What were the details of the ID misuse of funds probe?

European Parliament auditors concluded last year that ID members had misused at least €4.3 million (roughly $4.8 million) in EU funds during the previous legislative term from 2019 to 2024.

According to their report, the money flowed to companies close to the group and to associations supporting anti-abortion campaigners.

The case was reminiscent of, but separate from, the conviction against RN leader Marine Le Pen, herself a former MEP, that for a time looked set to stifle her bid for the French presidency.

Appeals court clears way for Le Pen's presidential bid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ID group existed for one term in the European Parliament, from 2019 to 2024. It included France's RN, Germany's AfD, Austria's Freedom Party (FPÖ) and Italy's Lega, among other members.

It fell apart after major internal friction during the 2024 European election campaign, not least because of dissatisfaction within the group with their lead candidate Maximilian Krah of the AfD over a number of issues — from controversial remarks about Nazi Germany through to allegations of his close allies being Russian and Chinese influence, with one of Krah's aides since convicted of spying for China.

RN, FPÖ and Lega are part of the new PfE group, which claims "no legal continuity" to the dissolved ID alliance, but the AfD was not invited to join the PfE.

PfE has 85 seats in the 719-seat European Parliament, making it the third-largest group in the chamber, but a rather distant third behind the center-right European People's Party (184) and the center-left Socialists and Democrats (135).

The European Parliament relies heavily on such groupings, which try to unite political parties from various member states with broadly comparable policy positions and political alignment.

The AfD set up a much smaller splinter far-right grouping called Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN), with just 27 seats, 15 of them held by the AfD.

World.title: Russia arrests German man, calls him a Ukraine 'mercenary'
World.content:
Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national and accused him of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine's military. They claim he deserted over unpaid wages and say he was a sniper who once served in the Bundeswehr.

Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) domestic intelligence agency said on Wednesday that it had arrested a German national on allegations of mercenary activity, calling him an "active member of the Ukrainian armed forces."

The news came on the same day that Russia released a retired teacher from the US, Stephen Hubbard, after years in detention on similar mercenary charges, which he denied.

Russia has detained a number of foreign nationals since its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, accusing them of assisting Kyiv in some way or another.

There was no immediate comment from Germany's government, besides acknowledging that it had seen the reports and was pursuing them.

What did the FSB say about the arrest?

The FSB said in a statement carried widely by Russian media that the man was a former Bundeswehr soldier and trained sniper. It did not issue his name but published a short video in which he could be heard speaking German.

The FSB also published footage that it said showed the man holding a sniper rifle with Ukrainian Armed Forces Image: Russian Federal Security Service/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

According to the FSB, the man was a Bundeswehr soldier from 1996 to 2010, who served in Afghanistan and Somalia between 2004 and 2010.

They alleged that he later operated as a mercenary fighter in Syria's civil war.

From 2016 to 2018, according to the Russian spy agency, he fought in Ukraine against the Russian-backed rebels in eastern states, prior to Moscow's full-scale invasion in 2022.

The FSB claimed that he returned to Ukraine as a "mercenary" in 2025 and was fighting in the contested region of Donetsk, but then deserted over non-payment of wages.

They did not comment on why or how the man, whom they said was born in 1976, had come to be in Russia. Nor did they say where or under what circumstances they arrested him.

How did German authorities respond?

A spokesperson at the German Foreign Ministry only initially responded by saying that Berlin was aware of the reports from Russia.

The spokesperson said the ministry would not comment on the individual case or specifics for the time being.

German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Similar Swedish arrest last week, US prisoner freed

Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals on charges like espionage, sabotage and treason amid its invasion of neighboring Ukraine. The charges can carry lengthy prison sentences.

A smaller number have also been accused of mercenary activity.

The FSB last week arrested a Swedish national, again accusing him of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.

In his case, they said he was operating as the commander of a drone unit and that he was detained attempting to illegally cross the border in the western Pskov region.

A Japanese journalist was also arrested last week, accused of espionage, prompting sharp criticism from Tokyo.

Also on Wednesday, Russia released a retired US teacher, Stephen Hubbard, who had been arrested in 2024 on comparable allegations.

This took place as US negotiator Steve Witkoff was visiting St. Petersburg and after a series of recent concessions to Russia and criticisms of Ukraine from US President Donald Trump.

Trump claimed there was no quid pro quo involved in the release, but later said Hubbard would not be free if he had not eased sanctions on Russian diesel shipments.

World.title: Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard during Witkoff talks
World.content:
During talks between Vladimir Putin and Steve Witkoff, Putin announced that jailed American Stephen Hubbard had been released. The Kremlin also said Russia was "in principle" ready to resume trilateral talks next month.

Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of US captive Stephen Hubbard during talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.

Hubbard had been taken captive by Russian forces on charges of being a mercenary, which he denies. He was sentenced to seven years in prison at a closed trial in 2024.

Putin said Hubbard was at the airport and Witkoff said he was now "going home to his family."

US President Donald Trump later said he had made the request directly to Putin during a phone call last week.

"The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia," Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform. "There was no 'swap' necessary for this release."

Putin and Witkoff met in St. Petersburg for their ninth in-person talks Image: Kristina Solovyova/TASS/picture alliance

However, in a follow-up post, Trump also claimed that "numerous people" had called him to apologize after they criticized him for suspending a new round of sanctions, which he said was a necessary concession.

"If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt," Trump's post said.

Russia agrees to trilateral talks with Ukraine, US

The release of Hubbard was seen as a goodwill gesture to the Trump administration as the two sides discuss a deal for peace between Russia and Ukraine.

"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff told Putin.

After the talks, the Kremlin said Witkoff's proposals "lacked substance" and would not be of real use for a potential peace settlement.

However, Putin agreed "in principle" to resume peace talks with Russian, Ukrainian and US delegates after November 10.

Such talks should focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends," Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said.

Putin also proposed that Witkoff discuss the restoration of bilateral ties between Washington and Moscow.

Meanwhile, Putin appeared open to a potential trilateral meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

"A possible first-ever meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the United States... is being prepared," Ushakov said.

The meeting — the ninth such talks between Witkoff and Putin — came a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway.



How Trump is helping Putin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European leaders hope for productive negotiations

Zelenskyy on Wednesday called for freezing the front line as a first step toward ceasefire talks.

"Right now we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire... freeze and stop," Zelenskyy said in an interview with "Fox & Friends."

The European Union, which was represented by delegates from several member states at the Oslo talks on Tuesday, said it expected to be debriefed by Washington after Wednesday's talks.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also said on Wednesday that Berlin was supporting Ukraine to end the war as quickly as possible, adding that any capitulation by Ukraine would be "a capitulation by all of us."

Witkoff to return to Oslo

The Ukrainian leader remained in Oslo on Wednesday where met with lawmakers in the Norwegian parliament.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said that Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for further consultations after his trip to St. Petersburg.

"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," he told Norway's public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.

World.title: Germany news: Nvidia CEO optimistic about EU's AI economy
World.content:
Alice Weidel (center) said the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more Image: Ann-Krisitn Wenzel/dpa/picture alliance

Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.

"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."

On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."

"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."

This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.

She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."

Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.

Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."

"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.

She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."

While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.

World.title: Pakistan-Taliban conflict: How India could benefit from shifting regional dynamics
World.content:
As Pakistan's influence in Afghanistan comes under strain, India is rebuilding ties with the Taliban in Kabul. Can New Delhi turn this diplomatic opening into lasting strategic gains?

Pakistan and Afghanistan right now are locked in a cycle of escalating tension. Repeated border clashes have strained ties between the two nations.

The current round of tensions began in February 2026, when Pakistan launched strikes into Afghanistan targeting Taliban militants. At one point in March, Pakistan's defense minister said the country was at "open war" with Afghanistan. Periodic bouts of violence have continued since then, with the latest Pakistani strikes targeting the Afghan Taliban's "terrorist hubs" reported earlier in October.

At the heart of the dispute is Pakistan's accusation that the Taliban authorities in Kabul allow the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group, to target Pakistan from Afghan territory. Kabul denies providing the group with sanctuary.

Militants kill dozens of security officers in Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Where does India come into play?

As the two neighbors trade strikes, the escalating conflict "presents a significant diplomatic and strategic opportunity for India," Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, an Afghanistan expert and founder of the India-based Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.

D'Souza argues the confrontation has weakened Pakistan's traditional influence in Afghanistan and encouraged the Taliban to broaden its external relations.

"India can respond by expanding diplomatic engagement, humanitarian assistance, development projects and trade, while seeking assurances that Afghan territory will not be used by anti-India militant groups," she said.

However, D'Souza cautioned against interpreting the opening as a fundamental realignment.

"There is no ideological alignment between India and the Taliban," she said. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is likely to pursue a diversified foreign policy rather than align exclusively with New Delhi.

India also lacks the geographical advantages, economic leverage and security presence needed to replace Pakistan's influence, she notes. "The scenario of the Taliban becoming a strategic ally remains far-fetched."

Former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan Amar Sinha warned against viewing the conflict simply as an opportunity for New Delhi to gain at Pakistan's expense.

"The issues have very little to do with India," Sinha told DW, arguing that India was not seeking strategic advantage from the fighting. He also pointed to the consequences of Pakistan's military actions for Afghan civilians.

"Yet the rupture has made Kabul's search for alternative partners more pressing," he added.

For India, that creates an opening, but not necessarily a strategic alignment, Sinha notes. The Taliban can seek Indian assistance while maintaining relations with China, Russia, Iran and Gulf states, preserving its autonomy rather than exchanging dependence on Pakistan for dependence on India.

The cost of closer ties

Gautam Mukhopadhyaya, another former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan, sees the deterioration in relations between Pakistan and the Taliban as an opportunity for India to recover some of the strategic ground it lost when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

"The crisis has allowed strategic openings for India," Mukhopadhyaya told DW. He warned, however, that New Delhi's own treatment of Afghans could undermine its efforts to build a durable relationship.

He pointed to restrictions affecting Afghans seeking Indian visas for education, scholarships, work and medical treatment.

"For all practical purposes, India's security establishment treats Afghans as proxy Pakistanis and 'terrorists' by default," he said.

Former Afghan partners had been left "disappointed, even bitter," Mukhopadhyaya added. "A strategic relationship built on the sands of oppression is not a sound foundation."

'Don't send us back': Afghan women in India fear deportation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trade cannot overcome geography

India has restored air freight links between Kabul and Delhi and between Kabul and Amritsar in northwestern India in December 2025.

Bilateral trade between India and Afghanistan stood at about $908 million (€807 million) in the 2025-26 fiscal year, while trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan fell sharply amid repeated border closures.

On October 14, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi stressed the importance of relations with India during talks with Indian charge d'affaires Yatin Patel, signaling Kabul's interest in expanding economic cooperation.

But air freight is expensive, and India cannot easily replace Pakistan as a transit route.

New Delhi has sought to use Iran's Chabahar port to improve access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, but regional instability and complications surrounding Iran have constrained those ambitions.

D'Souza cautioned that "the ongoing conflict in Iran" limits India's ability to use Chabahar as a crucial trade and connectivity hub.

Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University specializing in Afghanistan and Eurasian connectivity, highlighted similar obstacles.

"In the last few decades, Islamabad has obstructed Kabul's efforts to gain access to the vast Indian market. However, political instability in Afghanistan and sanctions on Iran have undermined these efforts," Sachdeva told DW.

"Afghanistan's potential as a connector between regional markets remains considerable, but the infrastructure and political conditions needed to realize it are far from assured," he added.

Sachdeva also sees Russia and China as better positioned to shape Afghanistan's wider economic integration. Alternative routes may become more attractive to India, but they are not commercially viable overnight.

Islamabad's security fears

Pakistan has portrayed arch-rival India's growing engagement with the Taliban as a security threat. On October 7, Pakistani diplomat Muhammad Jawad Ajmal accused India at the United Nations of providing the Taliban with material and logistical support.

"Under the guise of humanitarian aid, they have been actively supporting the Taliban regime with material and logistical support for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan," Ajmal said.

The allegation reflects Islamabad's position and has not been established as fact.

Pakistan has accused India of supporting the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army, a militant organization.

India rejects accusations of backing militant activity, while the Taliban denies allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, offered a more nuanced assessment of Pakistan's position.

"India has stepped into a space and is trying to exert its influence and feed anti-Pakistan groups intelligence," she told DW.

Siddiqa added that Pakistan's establishment continues to view the crisis through "a singular security lens."

"Islamabad feels physically squeezed from both sides," she said, adding that closer Kabul-New Delhi ties could create "a dangerous two-front security trap" for Pakistan.

India may gain more room to operate in Afghanistan as ties between Kabul and Islamabad deteriorate. But the Taliban is unlikely to put all its eggs in New Delhi's basket.
