World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019142/Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.title: Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019142/Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.content:
In wildlife conservation, there are three steps to helping an injured or orphaned animal: rescue, rehabilitate, and release. “Returning” isn’t part of the plan, but try telling that to China’s celebrity seal Nana.

This 2-year-old wild spotted seal, a Class I protected species in China, was a must-see attraction this summer for visitors to Dachangshan Island, part of Dalian’s Changshan Archipelago in the northeastern Liaoning province.

Nana has been released twice far out into the Yellow Sea, with the hope he’d join a migrating colony. Both times he’s made his way back alone, once covering more than 200 kilometers in just six days.

When he first showed up on the island in June, he was wary of humans and swam away when approached. But over time, he grew braver. Tourists tempted him near with tasty fish, though this sometimes resulted in him receiving a prod or a kick, and often a startling camera flash.

Concerned for Nana’s welfare, the local government put up warning signs telling people not to feed him and to keep a safe distance, and vowed “not to use him to promote tourism.” Yet within months, a “Nana Line” shuttle service had opened, running directly from the island’s Yuanyang Port to its “best seal-watching spot,” while the local tourism bureau began working with a private business to make and sell seal-related merchandise.

For many locals, Nana’s presence has been bittersweet: he’s a cute addition to the neighborhood, but the risks to his safety outweigh the benefits, they say.

Despite the falling temperature, authorities have ruled out moving him again, much to the delight of those who feel the seal has “made his choice.” But as the tourist season ends and his steady, fan-fueled food supply dries up, others worry that Nana could face a harsh winter alone.

Hello, new neighbor

Nana was just a pup in the summer of 2024, when fishermen first spotted him resting on a buoy in waters off Beihai, in the southern Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Noticing he was thin and had wounds on his body, likely caused by boat propellers, they alerted the authorities, who transported him to the Beihai Aquatic Rescue and Rehabilitation Center.

The spot where Nana was discovered lies just off a migration route for spotted seals between the western Pacific Ocean and Dalian’s Liaodong Bay. Experts suspect he drifted from his colony and was stranded alone.

In November 2025, after being nursed back to health, Nana was transferred to a wild species rehabilitation center in Dalian operated by the Liaoning Ocean and Fisheries Science and Research Institute. There, he quickly went from 50 to 70 kilograms and grew a new coat of glossy fur. “You could see him looking better every day,” says Chai Yuqiao, a researcher at the base.

By this spring, Nana was deemed well enough to return to the wild. On April 16, the institute released him and two other rescued seals roughly 10 kilometers from shore in the Yellow Sea, thinking they would naturally head for the migration route and find a new colony.

Nana’s two companions did exactly that, but data from his satellite tag shows he never left the Yellow Sea. Two months later, he popped up at Dachangshan Island.

Locals first spotted the seal relaxing in a rocky tide pool on June 19.

“Back then he was wary and rarely came close,” recalls Feng Zhi, who runs a guesthouse on the island. “He’d just hang around, and if someone walked over, he’d swim away.”

But that changed the more he interacted with tourists. “Wherever the crowd was thickest, that’s where he’d be,” says Li Ai, who also works in the hospitality industry. “But he can be picky about people,” she adds, explaining that Nana appeared especially fond of a wetsuit-wearing livestreamer known as “Man in Black,” who has 24,000 followers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. Nana often chased him and snuggled up to him.

Zhou Long, another guesthouse manager, says Nana once squeezed in between him and several friends as they stood in the shallows. The seal was warm, slippery, and plump, “like a balloon that’s about to pop,” he says.

People soon began feeding Nana fish and petting him when he got close. A local boat captain says he often tried stopping tourists from doing this, but few listened. He worried Nana might accidentally be fed a fish containing a fishhook, “the consequences of which don’t bear thinking about.”

Some people were even captured on surveillance cameras throwing Nana barbecued meat, bread, and potato chips, foods that could seriously upset his digestive system, while others kicked him, and thoughtless children threw stones at him.

“I couldn’t bear to watch and couldn’t do anything about it. I could only turn around and walk away,” says Li.

Many locals breathed a sigh of relief on Sept. 7 when the authorities finally arrived to take Nana away.

Gone, but not forgotten

To protect and “re-wild” Nana, the Changhai County government, which administers Dachangshan Island, decided to again transport the seal out to the Yellow Sea, this time to a spot about 140 kilometers away by boat.

Nana was back on the island just six days later. His tracking tag had fallen off a month earlier, but Tian Jiashen, director of marine rare animal conservation research at the Liaoning institute, estimates the seal’s return journey must have covered at least 200 kilometers.

Zhou had an inkling he’d not seen the last of Nana. Social media users had been eagerly sharing news of sightings, and the seal was getting closer all the time. On the evening of Sept. 13, Zhou went to the shore, opened a livestream, and lay in wait, with nearly 200 followers logging on to watch.

As night fell, Zhou heard a splash, like “a huge creature leaping into the water.” When he ran over, Nana was beside the blue pontoon bridge that he’d frequented all summer.

Within hours, Lin Gao, an employee at a beachside water sports center, had reinstalled the giant inflatable yellow duck Nana had liked to sleep on. “We couldn’t let him come back and find it gone,” he says, adding that work had felt “hollow” without Nana around.

Tian admits he never expected the seal to return but now believes Nana’s interactions with tourists might have reawakened his memories of being rescued and fed by humans.

Staff at the Liaoning institute recall that Nana was initially more curious than cautious. Marine researcher Chen Yanyu says he was once scrubbing the rearing pool when Nana surprisingly pushed a long-handled brush toward his hand. He badly wanted to pat the seal’s head, but that would be against the rules of “rehab and release.”

In wildlife conservation, keeping a safe distance is paramount. Rescued seals are fed by pouring live fish into the pool, while researchers deliberately approach the animals with nets to condition them to avoid people. By the time of his release, Nana had begun watching the staff from afar.

On that first release day, Chen watched Nana slide down the boat’s ramp into the sea with tears in his eyes.

However, when the seal became a celebrity, the institute came under attack from netizens who felt it had failed in its responsibilities to rehabilitate Nana.

Tian, who has worked there since 2010, believes the criticism was unfair. He explained that the institute is manned year-round by researchers who volunteer their time for free, and that in the past two decades it has helped rescue 244 spotted seals, releasing 223.

“The sea is his home, and he should go home,” he adds, talking about Nana. “Keeping him here, in a human environment — that would be cruelty.”

The risks human behaviors pose to wildlife are obvious. Ah Nong, a spotted seal rescued late last year after spending 15 months in waters off Wenchang, in the southern island province of Hainan, was found to have diarrhea, elevated liver function, and ultraviolet skin burns from being fed, touched, and photographed by tourists.

When Nana returned a second time, Chai and some colleagues wanted to go see him, “to find out whether he still remembered us.” Others, like researcher Shi Hongyue, held another wish: that one day they would come across Nana naturally during a survey of a wild colony.

Sealing his fate?

Nana became even more famous after returning to Dachangshan Island last month. By 7 a.m., at least 10 livestreamers would already be set up on shore, waiting for the seal to wake up. These channels quickly became a key marketing tool for guesthouses and other local businesses.

In August, Chinese media quoted an unnamed local official as saying that authorities “would not use (Nana) for cultural tourism promotions.” However, that attitude appeared to shift after the seal’s return in September.

The Changhai Culture and Tourism Bureau opened the “Nana Line” on Sept. 25, and beachside stalls hawking Nana-themed merch began popping up this month.

More warning signs and loudspeakers have been placed along the beach, reminding tourists that feeding protected species is forbidden, while enforcement officers and volunteers now regularly patrol the area. The local government has announced it will not attempt to move Nana again and is planning to build him a shelter on the pontoon bridge, away from the crowds.

Residents say the feeding and touching has declined, but it still happens.

This will naturally trail off as the tourist and fishing seasons wind down ahead of the coldest months, leading some to worry that Nana could starve. Despite the rules, in October, Sun Zongjun, the owner of the water sports center, pledged on a livestream that “we’ll definitely keep feeding him when it gets cold.” The county government has yet to confirm whether live fish stocks will be provided for the seal over winter.

Tian says it’s hard to predict whether Nana will ever leave and fully return to nature; it depends on diverse factors like water temperature, his physiological state, and whether he meets any companions and joins a new colony.

Scientific studies using tracking data show that spotted seals tend to rest or breed in the same place, year after year. Tian believes this behavior, and his memories of human interaction, could be what led Nana back to Dachangshan Island.

While most locals were happy to welcome Nana “home,” his presence has also brought pressure. “Our island lives off tourism. If anything happens to him, the criticism of millions of people could crash down on us in an instant,” says Lin, who regularly volunteers to patrol the pontoon bridge in the early hours.

On most nights, Nana can be found sleeping soundly on his giant yellow duck as it rocks gently in the waves. Soon, he will be joined in these waters by other spotted seals. No one knows what will come next.

“It’s fine if Nana stays,” says Liu Yi, a guesthouse owner on the island. “But I still hope he leaves.”

(Due to privacy concerns, Lin Gao, Feng Zhi, Li Ai, Zhou Long, and Liu Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Qin Bing and Feng Haoni.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Beijing News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: PaperBuddy; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Nana comes ashore at Dachangshan Island, Liaoning, Sept. 27, 2026. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019137/Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.title: Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019137/Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.content:
More than 150 Chinese apps have forbidden ByteDance’s mobile AI assistant Doubao from operating them on smartphone manufacturer Nubia Technology’s newly released agentic AI smartphone.

In a list published Oct. 14 on Doubao’s official account on messaging app WeChat, its developers identified dozens of apps that prohibit its graphical user interface (GUI) automation. The technology interprets a user’s spoken command, reads what is displayed on their smartphone’s screen, and navigates across and operates apps to complete the task.

Doubao had released its Smart Assistant Execution Protocol on Sept. 14, giving developers one month to decide whether to let the assistant operate their apps.

Apps owned by ByteDance’s rival technology companies Tencent and Alibaba make up nearly 60% of the list, including WeChat from the former and digital payment system Alipay from the latter, according to domestic media outlet Cailian Press. Others include those from e-commerce giant Meituan, ride-hailing platform Didi, lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, e-commerce platform Pinduoduo, China’s three state-run telecommunications carriers, several banks, and rival AI apps DeepSeek and Kimi. The listed apps can still be installed and used manually.

Absent from the list are e-commerce giant JD.com and most apps from internet service company Baidu, with the exception of Baidu Maps. A Baidu employee told domestic media outlet Caijing magazine that the phone’s shipment volume remains too small to pose a meaningful concern for the company.

Nubia bills the NaviX Ultra as “the world’s first AI-powered smartphone,” bringing agentic AI to consumers. The company, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, said that within seconds of the smartphone’s Sept. 16 launch, it generated 100 million yuan ($15 million) in sales. The phone’s price starts at 5,999 yuan.

Nubia released a prototype of the current AI phone, the M153, for 3,499 yuan in December last year. Though it quickly sold out, users soon reported that whenever the assistant attempted to operate WeChat, they were automatically logged out of the app. Doubao’s developers later disabled the assistant’s ability to operate the super app.

On the same day Doubao published the list of restricted apps, Nubia announced a software update — including improved localized data search, call-recording summaries, and call screening functions — and offered users six months of free Doubao membership, worth roughly 400 yuan.

As of Monday, none of the included app developers have commented publicly on the news.

Liu Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University’s Institute for National Strategic Studies, told Cailian Press that China has no regulations relating to how AI agents operate third-party applications.

Given the lack of oversight, Liu said, it is understandable that developers would deny such access over data security and user privacy concerns. He added that their resistance may also reflect a desire to protect their own AI ecosystems, particularly given Doubao’s already vast user base.

In its post, Doubao’s developers stated that other apps can opt out of its GUI technology at any time, and its list of cooperating companies would be updated every Wednesday.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.title: Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.content:
SHANGHAI – Popular language-learning app Duolingo has released a Shanghainese course featuring lessons on modern culture and life in old Shanghai as well as offline activities in the city.

The course, launched Thursday, features roughly 50 lessons drawn from everyday life in Shanghai, from ordering street food and taking public transit to exchanging greetings and navigating the city’s landmarks. To access the Shanghainese course, users must first set Chinese as their display language.

Founded in the U.S. in 2011, Duolingo offers courses in over 40 languages. The launch of the company’s Shanghainese course marks its second Chinese dialect offering, following Cantonese released in 2022. China is the company’s fastest-growing and second-largest market.

The course revolves around aspects of modern life in Shanghai like workplace dynamics and coffee culture, while also featuring old Shanghai themes, such as life in the city’s longtang lane houses and local phrases for traditional games, Tan Xiuting, a senior course designer of Duolingo, told Sixth Tone at the launch event in Shanghai on Friday.

Lessons also extend beyond the screen, with offline check-in spots around Shanghai, as well as themed activities on buses and in subway stations. Duolingo has also partnered with local shops; for example, if a user orders a coffee in Shanghainese at a partner café, they will receive a gift.

Wang Chen, an official with Duolingo, said that the course underscores the company’s “long-term commitment” to the Chinese market and its linguistic diversity.

“We want to make dialects cool and help local language and culture stay alive in contemporary life through products that are digital, engaging, and easy to access,” Wang said.

Shanghainese, or the Hu dialect, is a Wu Chinese variety spoken by roughly 10 million people, primarily in Shanghai and the surrounding Yangtze River Delta region. Difficult for native Mandarin speakers to understand, it features more tones and numerous English and French loanwords due to the city’s opening as a treaty port in the mid-19th century. It also preserves many classical Chinese words and structures.

The dialect has declined in recent decades, as national policies have pushed Mandarin use in schools, workplaces, and the media. In the last decade, Shanghai has reintroduced Shanghainese in some kindergartens and on public transportation, and has held speech competitions to inspire younger generations to learn it. TV programs, films, music, and standup comedy shows in Shanghainese have also emerged in recent years.

Zhou Yuwen, a 30-year-old branding manager born and raised in Shanghai, told Sixth Tone that her generation was expected to speak Mandarin both inside and outside the classroom, but over time, Shanghainese-speaking environments decreased.

“I can understand Shanghainese, but when I try to speak it, it comes out so ‘Yangjingbang’ that I feel too embarrassed to keep going,” she said, referencing the colloquial name for the pidgin English used between European and local merchants in Shanghai in the 19th century.

Zhou said she felt “excited” by the release of Duolingo’s Shanghainese course, and shared news of the course’s launch on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, hoping to encourage others to learn. “It’s a pity that someone like me, who was born, grew up, and worked my whole life in Shanghai, can’t speak proper Shanghainese,” she said. “I absolutely love the dialect, and I hope to see it not just preserved, but truly flourish.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.title: In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.content:
“I’m pregnant. After much consideration and thorough discussions with the company and my bandmates, I have decided to temporarily leave the group to focus on rest and recovery,” reads a statement signed by Mity, one of five members of the new girl group BABYQUEEN, alongside a selfie of her wearing pink pajamas in bed.

At first glance, nothing seems out of the ordinary, except that she and the entire BABYQUEEN pop group are AI-generated.

The announcement, published Tuesday on the group’s official Xiaohongshu account, also known as RedNote, has drawn criticism for turning women’s reproductive health into entertainment, as well as jokes and incredulity about the situation’s perceived absurdity.

AI girl group accounts have proliferated on Chinese social media in recent months, with virtual idols often maintaining social media accounts where they share glimpses of their daily lives and even secure and promote brand endorsements.

BABYQUEEN, styled as a South Korean girl group, launched its Xiaohongshu account on Sept. 7. As of Friday, the account, whose IP address is located in China’s northeastern Liaoning province, has roughly 1,000 followers.

Mity’s pregnancy was initially announced on the group’s account the day before, reading, “To prioritize her health during pregnancy and prepare for childbirth, she will temporarily suspend all group and individual variety show appearances and stage performances after thorough discussions with the team.” It also urged followers not to “over-speculate about her private life.”

Since it went viral on social media, the topic has attracted more than 6 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Friday.

Many users have expressed astonishment. “AI group members can get pregnant now? I don’t understand the virtual world anymore,” one highly upvoted comment reads. Others joked that the group’s creators might be running short on tokens, implying they had to let one member go because they lacked the computing power.

Users also accused the band’s makers of using the story for views while showing little respect for women. “Using ‘pregnant and preparing for childbirth’ as a marketing hook and a sensationalized narrative trivializes real women’s reproductive experiences by turning them into entertainment,” one comment reads.

The day of the announcement, the account also released a teaser post for a new song performed by the group’s four remaining members.

In a since-deleted Tuesday post on the BABYQUEEN account, the group’s creators cited pressures of running the group as the reason for the pregnancy announcement.

“We’re just a few girls who like K-Pop, and we’re still students,” they wrote, adding that they had “not earned a single cent” from the endeavor. They also said they had experienced personal attacks and online harassment.

On the group’s official parent account, BABYPVSSY Entertainment, the creators said Mity might next “explore two possible career paths: acting or becoming a maternity and infant content creator.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.title: The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.content:
In 2016, two groups of Chinese livestreamers began feuding on Kuaishou, a short-video platform popular in China’s countryside and lower-tier cities. Their leaders, Brother Hu and Captain Shamate, were both grassroots streamers from Northeast China, or Dongbei. Video after video, they traded insults, accusations, and challenges. These gang-style exchanges were loud, theatrical, and unmistakably regional, full of Northeastern Chinese dialects, bravado, and the kind of chaos that early Chinese livestreaming platforms thrived on.

The feud was widely believed to be staged, a scripted collaboration designed for dramatic effect. But that did little to diminish its appeal. Audiences couldn’t stop watching, and clips of the confrontations soon took on a life of their own. Over time, they spawned an influential body of memes that spread across various media, even video games, one of which has now become an unlikely hit on Steam.

The phenomenon emerged against the backdrop of Dongbei’s changing cultural identity. Once the heartland of China’s heavy industry, the region is often referred to as the country’s Rust Belt after decades of industrial decline. Locals have turned that history into both tragedy and comedy. TV dramas such as “The Long Season” have tapped into nostalgia for the region’s industrial heyday, helping make the “Dongbei Renaissance” a cultural buzzword. Northeasterners have long played an outsized role in Chinese comedy. On television, Zhao Benshan’s sketches made the Northeastern accent familiar to audiences nationwide; on Kuaishou, Northeastern dialects and slang became a rich source of humor and memes.

It was in this context that the feud between Brother Hu and Captain Shamate gained traction. Fans recorded and reposted clips to streaming site Bilibili, where they were remixed, quoted, and jokingly treated as “classics.” The saga became known as “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.”

Seven years later, those memes were turned into a video game. A Summer in Northeast China (DongBeiZhiXia), released for free on Steam on Jan. 9, 2023, was developed and published by Zhuangbuchun Studio, led by Zhuangbuchun, a Bilibili content creator with over 2 million followers. Up till today, the game has since accumulated more than 12,000 positive reviews on Steam, earning an “Overwhelmingly Positive” rating despite being available only in Simplified and Traditional Chinese. Its success shows just how far a regional internet joke can travel when platform dynamics, an existing fan community, and a developer’s instincts align at the right moment.

A Summer in Northeast China is a “gal game,” a genre typically centered on interactions with female characters. Set years after the original Kuaishou incidents, the game follows Xiaoliang, who must recover her memories with the help of a cast of female companions, each loosely inspired by figures from the “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” phenomenon. The game’s most conspicuous adaptation is its gender-swapping: the male roles at the center of the original memes are reimagined as women, retaining their names, signature visual traits, and personalities while being reshaped to fit the conventions of the gal game and ACGN (anime, comics, games, and novels) aesthetics.

In effect, the game translates its source material across cultural registers. “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” ran on masculine confrontation, local bravado, and the rough-edged authenticity of Kuaishou livestreaming. A Summer in Northeast China recasts that material through the softer, character-driven lens of the gal game, while keeping enough recognizable references to reward those who remember the source. Events from the original memes return as callbacks for longtime fans, while the first-person linear narrative gives newcomers an accessible way into Xiaoliang’s story.

The game also draws on subcultures Zhuangbuchun knows well, including shamate — a Chinese youth subculture known for its flamboyant hairstyles and fashion — and otaku — intense fandom of anime, manga, games, and related media, originating in Japan — while its use of Northeastern dialect keeps it rooted in Dongbei. Together, these influences reflect the game’s broader approach: combining distinctly Northeastern humor and internet culture with the appeal of manga and anime.

Zhuangbuchun made the game the way many Chinese indie developers do: on a limited budget and in public. The project was self-funded, with a crowdfunding campaign on domestic creator-sponsorship platform Afdian covering part of the cost. He handled much of the design and direction himself, outsourced some work, and recruited voice actors for the female cast.

But developing the game in public was not simply a funding strategy. It also became central to how Zhuangbuchun built an audience around the project. Nearly a year before the game’s launch, in April 2022, he posted a video announcing his gender-swapped take on “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” The video received over 1.5 million views, 71,000 likes, 23,000 saves, and 11,000 reposts.

From there, Zhuangbuchun kept followers closely involved in development. He posted early character designs, solicited feedback on voice acting, and explained delays. When viewers complained about an accent or suggested a different look, he listened and sometimes changed the game accordingly. In that sense, the project was not simply marketed to its eventual players. It was partly shaped by them.

Zhuangbuchun also visited Shenyang, the capital of the northeastern Liaoning province, several times to document where the original Kuaishou events took place. On one return trip after the game’s release, he even ran into some of its fans. These travel vlogs reinforced the sense that the game was being made by someone invested not only in the memes but also in the places and culture from which they emerged.

The steady updates kept the project visible on Bilibili and positioned Zhuangbuchun as part of the internet culture that turned the original Kuaishou videos into “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” His existing followers helped attract attention, while the project’s local roots kept audiences engaged. The original Kuaishou streamers added another layer to this relationship, posting reaction videos and engaging with Zhuangbuchun’s posts, further blurring the line between the game and the people who inspired it.

A Summer in Northeast China is neither the first game to adapt internet memes nor the first to blend Chinese regional culture with global subcultural aesthetics. What makes it unusual is the particular combination: a free gal game with a gender-swapped cast, a distinctly Northeastern setting, a developer who was already a prominent Bilibili creator, and source material rooted in the unruly world of early Kuaishou livestreaming.

For indie developers working with limited resources, A Summer in Northeast China offers a distinctive example of how online culture can move across platforms and media. The same platforms that provided the game with its source material also supplied an audience, feedback, publicity, and a community willing to participate in its development. Rather than simply adapting an existing meme, Zhuangbuchun used the participatory culture surrounding it to carry the material far beyond its origins.

That process creates tensions between local authenticity and internet marketability, and between the crude energy of the original memes and the game’s polished presentation. Yet, A Summer in Northeast China never loses sight of its regional origins. Zhuangbuchun, who has told me he loves Dongbei despite not being from the region, is part of that story: an outsider drawn into its culture who now helps reshape it for new audiences. The game has traveled from Kuaishou to Bilibili to Steam, changing along the way. But for all the distance it has traveled, it has never really left Northeast China.

Zhu Siheng, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Rochester, and Han Yisong, a postdoctoral researcher at the City University of Hong Kong, also made contributions to this research.

(Header image: Promotional art for the video game “A Summer in Northeast China” on Steam.)

World.title: Where in the world is Atong Ang? Is he in the Philippines or not?
World.content:
But whether or not Ang has already left the country, one thing remains unchanged: the police have failed and continue to fail to locate and arrest the fugitive

After months of dead silence, the Philippine government again mentioned the name of fugitive and gaming tycoon Charlie “Atong” Ang.

But this time around, it’s because the tycoon might have already left the country.

Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) chief Juanito Victor “Jonvic” Remulla refused to provide more details regarding Ang’s supposed exit.

“Wala na (Nothing). I have nothing to add,” said Remulla on Tuesday, October 20.

“He has used the backdoor [exit]. Yes, the backdoor,” the DILG chief later confirmed.

Ang has a pending warrant of arrest from Santa Cruz, Laguna Regional Trial Court Branch 26 due to his kidnapping with homicide cases related to the missing sabungeros (cockfighting enthusiasts) controversy. He has yet to be arrested since his warrant’s issuance in January.

But there seems to be confusion within the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in so far as Ang’s case is concerned. Apparently, the Department of Justice (DOJ) believes — at least based on available records — that the fugitive is still in the country.

“I’m not aware kung ano ‘yung intel report or the source of information ni Secretary Jonvic but from our sources, which we verified with the BI (Bureau of Immigration), wala kasi kaming records,” acting DOJ secretary Fredderick Vida told reporters on Wednesday, October 21.

(I’m not aware what is the intel report or the source of information of Secretary Jonvic but from our sources, which we verified with the BI, we don’t have any records.)

“So I cannot confirm that he is already out of the country kasi (because) we will rely based on what we have in immigration records, and based on immigration records, wala kaming record that he left (we don’t have records that he left),” Vida added.

This is possible, actually. If Ang indeed used backdoor exit points, then the immigration bureau would not have a record of his flight. There are alleged backdoor points in Palawan and in Mindanao, according to several reports.

Besides, Ang would and could not have used proper exit channels because it would have alerted authorities.

But whether or not Ang has already left the country, one thing remains unchanged: the police have failed and continue to fail to locate and arrest him.

The police, earlier this year, attempted to arrest him in Pasig City and in Zambales, but failed because he was not there. As of February, the DILG also raised the bounty for Ang’s arrest to P20 million, but to no avail.

Play Video

So who’s answerable for these failures? Who will be held accountable by the Marcos government?

“Tingnan po natin at sa ngayon ay dapat malaman natin, maimbestigahan kung talagang may lapses. So, may mga tao talaga na mabibilis tumakbo at hindi naman ito ang unang pagkakataon na tumakas itong si Atong Ang. Noong unang nakasuhan din ito, nakaalpas din ito agad-agad,” said Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro on Wednesday.

(We’ll see and for now, we should find out, investigate if there are lapses. There are people who are good at escaping and this is not the first time that Atong Ang has escaped. When he was charged, he immediately fled.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Lacson calls out Cayetanos for hijacking DENR budget hearing
World.content:
PING LACSON. Senator Ping Lacson at the briefing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of National Defense on October 19, 2026.

Senators Alan Peter and Pia Cayetano take turns grilling LLDA Acting General Manager Leopoldo Parumog over his supposed 'special interest' in reclamation projects in Taguig

The subject of the ongoing spat between senators Alan Peter Cayetano and Panfilo “Ping” Lacson — Taguig’s “ghost projects” — found its way to the Senate hearing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), where the Cayetano senator-siblings subjected the Laguna Lake Development Authority (LLDA) representative to intense questioning.

During the budget hearing of the DENR, which oversees the LLDA, Alan and his sister, Senator Pia Cayetano, took turns grilling LLDA Acting General Manager Leopoldo Parumog over what they alleged to be his “special interest” in Taguig City, the Cayetanos’ baliwick.

At the October 19 budget hearing, the Cayetanos questioned Parumog over the LLDA’s inspection of projects along Laguna de Bay, accusing him of singling out Taguig City by publicly disclosing their investigations into the reclamation projects. Taguig Mayor Lani Cayetano is Alan’s wife.

“Why do you make it appear in public that a lot of bad things are happening in Taguig? And if you don’t — if that is not the intention, then why publicize for Taguig and you don’t publicize your work in other places?” asked Pia.

According to Alan, while the LLDA issued cease-and-desist orders against projects in Angono, Rizal, and Muntinlupa City these were not publicized.

Parumog denied that the LLDA’s actions on Taguig projects were politically motivated.

“There is no politics involved. We are not selective and we act on everything,” Parumog said in Filipino.

The Cayetano siblings’ questioning did not sit well with Lacson, who called them out for turning the budget deliberations into a “full-blown” Senate investigation.

“They took turns interrogating the hapless LLDA general manager with questions totally unrelated to the agency’s proposed 2027 budget as if it were a full-blown Senate inquiry in aid of legislation,” Lacson said in a statement on Tuesday, October 20.

The latest clash adds another layer to the feud between Lacson and Alan, which began in July when Lacson questioned the increase in the minority leader’s declared net worth in 2025.

The dispute has since intersected with allegations of irregularities in flood control projects in Taguig, with Lacson — former Senate blue Ribbon committee chairperson — turning over to the Ombudsman the evidence the panel had gathered on the alleged anomalies.

This is not the first time an individual was caught in the crossfire between the two senators.

In September, Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon found himself in a similar situation after he denied in a Senate budget hearing that there were ghost projects in Taguig City.

Lacson had previously said his team identified at least 32 allegedly anomalous flood control projects in Taguig, two of which were considered as ghost projects.

After his denial, Lacson said Dizon apologized for his remarks. – Rappler.com

World.title: El Niño ‘wrecking ball’ could cause record Pacific temperature rise, UN says
World.content:
EL NIÑO. Tropical Storm Rachel and El Niño fueled Kelvin waves pound the boardwalk in Long Beach, California, US, on October 10, 2026.

In Southeast Asia, warmer conditions and a lack of rainfall could impact agriculture and water supplies, while Latin America could see increased rainfall, according to the World Meteorological Organization

GENEVA, Switzerland – The El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels around the globe like a “wrecking ball,” causing floods and droughts, UN officials said on Wednesday, October 21.

The new World Meteorological Organization (WMO) seasonal outlook predicted the El Niño event would become extremely strong, with temperatures in the central Pacific rising about 3.8 degrees Celsius above normal between November and January, peaking around December.

“We have not seen in our records 3.8. We have seen around 3 in some record El Niños before, with very substantive impacts across the world. So we are beyond that limit,” WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said.

El Niño is the warm phase of the naturally occurring El Niño-Southern Oscillation cycle — a climate pattern that influences weather around the world.

It tends to cause higher global temperatures and disrupt rainfall patterns across large regions, meaning drought in some areas and heavy rains in others.

It is a natural climate pattern and is not caused by climate change. However, global warming can make El Niños more intense.

El Niño-linked weather extremes could worsen pressure on housing, water, sanitation and health services, with flooding risks rising in southern Africa from November, the WMO said.

In Southeast Asia, warmer conditions and a lack of rainfall could impact agriculture and water supplies, while Latin America could see increased rainfall, according to the WMO.

The WMO and the UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, called for urgent action to get ready.

“This El Niño is the behemoth; it is a wrecking ball. It will tear through Latin America, Eastern and Southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific with extreme heat, droughts, and floods,” Fletcher said, warning of massive humanitarian consequences.

Some 50 million people could face increased hunger, he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Super Typhoon Rosal begins to weaken but warnings still in effect
World.content:
ROSAL. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) as of October 21, 2026, 4 pm.

Batanes, Cagayan, and Apayao face moderate to heavy rain from Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) in the next 24 hours, says PAGASA on Wednesday afternoon, October 21

MANILA, Philippines – Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) started to weaken on Wednesday afternoon, October 21, with its maximum sustained winds slightly easing to 205 kilometers per hour from a peak of 215 km/h.

The super typhoon’s gustiness also eased from 265 km/h to 250 km/h, said the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) in its 5 pm bulletin on Wednesday.

PAGASA expects Rosal to be downgraded to a typhoon by Friday, October 23. Under the weather bureau’s classification, a typhoon has maximum sustained winds of 118 to 184 km/h.

Rosal was last spotted 725 kilometers east of Aparri, Cagayan, at 4 pm on Wednesday. It is still moving west northwest at 25 km/h and will continue to stay offshore.

However, Rosal will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday afternoon, October 22, and Friday morning. Although landfall is not expected, it is still affecting portions of the country.

The following provinces face significant rainfall due to Rosal in the next 48 hours:

Wednesday afternoon, October 21, to Thursday afternoon, October 22

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Batanes, Cagayan, Apayao

Thursday afternoon, October 22, to Friday afternoon, October 23

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Batanes

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Cagayan

Aside from the provinces mentioned above, Ilocos Norte, Isabela, and Catanduanes are also likely to have rain with gusty winds from Rosal on Wednesday evening.

The rest of Cagayan Valley, the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, the rest of Bicol, Aurora, Northern Samar, and Eastern Samar may have scattered rain and thunderstorms as well, still due to the super typhoon.

PAGASA added that Rosal’s trough or extension might cause scattered rain and thunderstorms in the Negros Island Region, Antique, Iloilo, Guimaras, and Palawan.

Meanwhile, the same areas remain under tropical cyclone wind signals as of 5 pm on Wednesday:

Signal No. 2

Gale-force winds (62 to 88 km/h), minor to moderate threat to life and property

Batanes

Signal No. 1

Strong winds (39 to 61 km/h), minimal to minor threat to life and property

Cagayan including Babuyan Islands

eastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan, Santa Maria, Cabagan, Delfin Albano, Santo Tomas, Tumauini, San Pablo, Ilagan City, San Mariano, Dinapigue)

Ilocos Norte

Apayao

northeastern part of Catanduanes (Pandan, Bagamanoc, Panganiban, Viga, Gigmoto)

There is a possibility of Signal No. 3 being raised, depending on Rosal’s track.

The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the super typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to the following areas:

Wednesday, October 21

Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley, Bicol, Romblon, Aurora, Quezon, Eastern Visayas, Siquijor, Bohol, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Davao Region, Sarangani

Thursday, October 22

most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Northern Mindanao, Agusan del Norte, Surigao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Sarangani, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Friday, October 23

most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Conditions in many seaboards across the country remain dangerous, especially in Batanes, where waves can now go as high as 10 meters or nearly 33 feet.

Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Northern and eastern seaboards of Batanes – waves up to 10 meters high

Remaining seaboard of Batanes; eastern seaboard of Babuyan Islands – waves up to 9 meters high

Northern seaboard of Babuyan Islands; northeastern seaboard of mainland Cagayan – waves up to 8 meters high

Remaining seaboard of mainland Cagayan; remaining seaboard of Babuyan Islands; northeastern seaboard of Isabela – waves up to 7 meters high

Northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte; remaining seaboard of Isabela – waves up to 6 meters high

Northern and eastern seaboards of Catanduanes; northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte; northern seaboard of northern Aurora – waves up to 5 meters high

Northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte and Camarines Sur; remaining seaboard of Aurora; northern seaboard of Northern Samar; eastern seaboards of Albay and Sorsogon – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Eastern seaboards of northern Quezon and Eastern Samar; remaining seaboards of Northern Samar and Ilocos Norte – waves up to 4 meters high

Remaining seaboard of Eastern Samar; northern seaboard of Ilocos Sur – waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboard of La Union; eastern seaboards of Dinagat Islands and Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group; remaining seaboards of Catanduanes and Ilocos Sur; northern and eastern seaboards of Davao Oriental; northwestern seaboard of Pangasinan – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Seaboards of Surigao del Sur and Surigao del Norte; southern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining eastern seaboard of Quezon; remaining seaboards of Ilocos Sur, Dinagat Islands, and Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group; remaining seaboard of Pangasinan; northwestern seaboard of Zambales – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Eastern seaboard of Davao Occidental; remaining seaboard of Zambales; western seaboards of Bataan, Batangas, and Cavite; northwestern seaboard of Occidental Mindoro including Lubang Islands – waves up to 2 meters high

ALSO ON RAPPLER

Rosal could leave the Philippine Area of Responsibility by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24. It entered PAR on Tuesday, October 20.

Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: Ombudsman suspends DICT Usec Almirol over alleged eGov conflicts of interest
World.content:
The complaints stem from a June 2025 report by the DICT Internal Audit Unit, which flagged possible conflicts of interest involving the hiring of former Multisys personnel as well as the awarding of contracts to other related companies

MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered the preventive suspension of Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Undersecretary for e-Government David Almirol Jr. for alleged conflicts of interest involving government contracts worth approximately P1.55 billion.

The Ombudsman said on Wednesday, October 21, that it “found sufficient grounds to place Almirol under preventive suspension for six months without pay pending the resolution of administrative complaints of Grave Misconduct, Conduct Prejudicial to the Best Interest of the Service, and violation of Republic Act No. 6713 or the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees.”

A preventive suspension is a cautionary measure undertaken to help ensure impartial and unimpeded investigation proceedings.

In this case, the complaints stem from a June 2025 report by the DICT Internal Audit Unit, which flagged possible conflicts of interest involving the hiring of former Multisys personnel as well as the awarding of contracts to other related companies.

Rappler reported on this issue in December 2025, citing the internal audit report of the DICT dated June 5, 2025, and our own review of Multisys’ Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings.

“It is a known fact that Undersecretary David Almirol is the founder and former Chief Executive Officer of Multisys Technologies Corporation, a privately held software engineering and digital solutions firm,” the audit report said.

The audit report also said “a conflict of interest may arise” in the following circumstances: in hiring ex-Multisys personnel and in awarding contracts to ePLDT.

According to the Ombudsman, the investigation revealed “at least 8 DICT contracts were awarded to companies with financial relationships with Multisys,” which totaled about P1.55 billion and ranged from ICT consultancies, e-government application deployment, web-based messaging services, cloud infrastructure, and data center colocation to software subscriptions.

Multisys’ audited financial statements showed revenues from the related companies “for managed services of P110.8 million in 2023 and P514.6 million in 2024.”

At the time of Rappler’s report, Almirol disputed the audit’s findings, claiming other service providers of equal or similar size such as Globe and Converge had also received contracts comparable to PLDT’s.

Conflicting SEC filings also pointed to Almirol not divesting from his Multisys business interests immediately or within the 60-day period from assuming office following his appointment to the DICT.

“Multisys’ General Information Sheet (GIS) notarized on 27 October 2022 and received by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on 2 November 2022 showed that respondent was still listed as a stockholder of Multisys holding 49.21% of the stocks,” the order said.

The Ombudsman, in its preventive suspension order, noted that Almirol’s continued stay in office “could prejudice the investigation, particularly given his control and custody of documents and evidence relevant to the case.”

The Ombudsman’s order is immediately executory. The suspension will stay in effect until the administrative adjudication is completed. – Rappler.com

World.title: Buying Gas or Buying Surveillance? Gas-Rich Myanmar’s Deal With Russia
World.content:
Anyone who still thinks Russia is simply bankrolling Myanmar has the direction of money backwards. In this arrangement, Myanmar is the customer. It is preparing to buy Russian gas and, in doing so, send money into a Russian economy still financing the war in Ukraine. Russia, meanwhile, is offering technology in return: satellite navigation, communications, Earth observation and aerospace cooperation. In other words, Myanmar is not being paid to stand with Russia. Myanmar is paying Russia, while Russia trades technology for access to a new market.

In August 2026, Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing traveled to Moscow for an official visit and met Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin. The visit produced 12 agreements and memoranda covering everything from energy and culture to competition policy and space technology. Four of them are particularly interesting because the technologies involved have obvious civilian applications, but equally obvious military ones.

The four were:

Memorandum Memorandum on information and communication technologies; Memorandum satellite navigation, human spaceflight Memorandum between the Myanmar Space Agency and Bauman Moscow State Technical University on technological and aerospace cooperation.

At roughly the same time, Russia and Myanmar were also negotiating something much less futuristic: liquefied natural gas.

The interesting part is that Myanmar was not discussed only as the final customer. According to the Myanmar President’s Office, the talks also covered onward supplies of Russian LNG to China and Thailand. That changes the scale of the arrangement considerably. Russia is not simply looking for another buyer. Myanmar is being considered as a possible regional distribution point for Russian LNG into Southeast Asia.

That is where the arrangement starts to look slightly extravagant.

Myanmar already has substantial natural-gas reserves and remains a major gas exporter. Recent estimates put its proven reserves at around 22.5 trillion cubic feet, while a large share of its production is exported. It certainly does not suffer from a geological shortage of natural gas.

So why import Russian LNG?

Part of the answer may simply be infrastructure, contracts and energy shortages. Having gas underground is not the same thing as having sufficient gas available in the right place, at the right time and in the right form. But the Russian side has another obvious problem: it needs markets.

Western sanctions and the war in Ukraine have placed sustained pressure on Russia’s traditional energy relationships. Russia’s finances are under considerably more pressure than before the war. The liquid part of the National Wealth Fund on September 1, 2026, was lower than ever, at 13,194.88 billion rubles (US$159.94 billion). Russia therefore has every reason to find new buyers for what it still has in abundance. And what Russia has in abundance is natural resources.

Myanmar offers access to the Southeast Asian market. Russia offers LNG. So far, fairly conventional.

The LNG story did not begin in August. In April, Russian Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilev and Myanmar Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin were already discussing supplies of Russian LNG, petroleum products and crude oil. Myanmar’s Ministry of Electricity and Energy was quite specific about what it wanted: favorable prices, quality guarantees, secure transportation and long-term supply. The same visit produced a Memorandum of Cooperation between the Ministry of Electricity and Energy and RC-Investments. The framework was designed with Russia identifying suppliers and partners and Myanmar facilitating Russian hydrocarbon and petrochemical deliveries.

Myanmar’s LNG import system already exists. Imports resumed in late 2025 after a four-year break, with LNG loaded at the Bintulu LNG complex in Malaysia and delivered to the Thilawa floating storage unit near Yangon. So, Russia is effectively trying to insert itself into an existing supply chain. Kpler expected Myanmar to import around 0.4 million tonnes of LNG in 2026, mainly to supply the Thanlyin and Thaketa power plants. Myanmar’s own Ministry of Information confirms that LNG imports are now feeding around 500 MW of generation in Yangon.

What Russia appears prepared to provide alongside it is considerably more interesting.

The Roscosmos agreement includes satellite-navigation measurement stations, access to navigation data, a COSPAS-SARSAT ground station and an ASPOS opto-electronic telescope station. Russia will also help select and train Myanmar astronauts. According to the Myanmar Space Agency (which already took the announcement down from their website), the stated purposes include economic development, search and rescue, scientific research and monitoring hazardous objects in space. All very peaceful.

Then the cooperation expanded further. On August 19, Min Aung Hlaing met Roscosmos Director General Dmitry Bakanov. Their discussions included Earth-observation satellite imagery, a satellite-navigation measuring station, the Rassvet low-orbit communications system, nano-satellites and continued Russian assistance in developing Myanmar’s space capabilities.

None of these technologies is inherently military. That is precisely the point. They do not need to be. Remember the Chinese balloon incident in 2023? A Chinese high-altitude balloon crossed the United States before being shot down by an F-22 off the coast of South Carolina on February 4. Beijing insisted that it was a civilian airship used mainly for meteorological research which had simply been blown off course. The U.S. State Department had a rather different interpretation. A U-2 surveillance aircraft examined the balloon while it was still in the air and confirmed that it carried intelligence-collection capabilities. The U.S. government later described it as part of a broader Chinese military-linked aerial surveillance program.

Earth-observation technology works on exactly the same uncomfortable boundary between civilian and military use. The same satellite imagery that monitors forests, floods, agriculture or climate can also show roads, buildings, camps, vehicles and changes on the ground. Optical satellites provide detailed imagery; synthetic-aperture radar can observe through cloud and at night; repeated passes over the same area show what has moved, appeared or disappeared. Communications systems can connect remote communities. They can also support command and control. Radio-electronic technology can support industry. It can also support surveillance and electronic warfare. Calling the technology civilian therefore tells us very little about what it can actually be used for. A satellite looking for deforestation can look at a military base just as easily.

Below is the kind of imagery Russia can produce. These are examples from Russian Resurs-P and Canopus-V satellites:

Resurs-P4 and P5 can produce panchromatic imagery at about 1 m resolution and multispectral imagery at roughly 3-4 m. As for the Canopus-V imagery, you can clearly distinguish agricultural plots, settlements, roads and terrain. Russian Space Systems explicitly lists infrastructure monitoring among the applications of these Earth-observation systems.

And what about Rassvet? It is essentially Russia’s answer to Starlink, a low-Earth-orbit broadband communications network being built by Bureau 1440, part of Russia’s X Holding. Bureau 1440 describes the satellites themselves as “5G base stations in orbit”. The target orbit is around 800 km, with advertised speeds of up to 1 Gbit/s and latency below 70 milliseconds. The satellites communicate with each other through laser links, while user terminals can be installed on fixed sites as well as cars, ships, aircraft and trains.

Militarily, the potential is obvious. What it can potentially do is provide broadband communications in places where terrestrial networks are absent or unreliable. That could support communication between command posts, mobile units, aircraft or unmanned systems. It could also transmit satellite imagery and other intelligence quickly from one location to another.

Myanmar is an unusually important place to make that distinction.

Myanmar’s civil war is nearly as old as the country itself. Armed conflict between the central state and ethnic organizations began almost immediately after independence in 1948. The Karen conflict started in 1949, while other ethnic insurgencies developed across Kachin, Shan and other border regions. These were not temporary rebellions. They became long-running territorial conflicts over autonomy, federalism, political control and, in some cases, independence.

The Myanmar military has never been particularly effective in many of these areas. Geography is one reason. Ethnic armed organizations operate in mountains, jungles and forests along the borders with Thailand, China and India. They know the terrain, move in small units, use ambushes and landmines and often operate among populations with which they have close local connections. The Myanmar military has traditionally been much stronger in towns, on major roads and around fixed military positions.

The military is therefore not acquiring these capabilities in an abstract security environment. It is fighting an actual war.

Better Earth observation means better information about what is happening on the ground. Better satellite navigation means better positioning. Better communications mean better coordination. Better mapping means a clearer picture of roads, settlements, bases and infrastructure in territories that the military has historically struggled to control.

Russia does not need to sign a memorandum saying that it will help Myanmar locate ethnic armed organizations. No government writes agreements like that. It only needs to provide the infrastructure that makes locating them easier.

Ana Brown is a nuclear lawyer, academic and intelligence analyst specialising in defence economics, and an ALM candidate at Harvard University.

World.title: ‘They’re Definitely Afraid of Her’: Aung San Suu Kyi’s Son Speaks Out
World.content:
Kim Aris would much rather stay out of the spotlight. But when his mother Aung San Suu Kyi was once again imprisoned after Myanmar’s military coup in 2021, he realised he could no longer remain silent. As a part of his mission to draw attention to his mother’s plight and the continuing struggle of the people of Myanmar, he came to Prague last week.

There he attended the democratic Forum 2000 Conference to remind the world that wars raging closer to home have not brought an end to those that have been devastating countries thousands of miles away for years.

His mother is now 81 and her family do not know exactly where she is being held or in what conditions. In an interview with Chechia’s Seznam Zpravy daily, he asks: if he, as her own son, does not stand up for his mother, how can he expect anyone else to do so?

When you look at Myanmar today, more than five years after the coup, what kind of country do you see?

I see a country torn apart by civil war, with people on the ground facing a very, very desperate situation. The military continues to bomb civilians regularly and refuses to stop its brutality against the population despite international pressure.

And yet, despite all this, I don’t think the situation is quite as straightforward as the rest of the world tends to portray it.

The people of Burma have shown incredible strength over the past five years, and the military is nowhere near as strong as it would like the rest of the world to believe. In fact, I would say the country is more united today than it has been for decades. It’s just very difficult for the outside world to see that at the moment.

We are witnessing something of a diplomatic rehabilitation of regime leader Min Aung Hlaing. He was warmly received in Malaysia, and the United States has begun direct talks with his government. What do you think of these developments?

I think those who are now trying to negotiate with the military are going to be very disappointed when they realise that the military is making promises it simply cannot keep.

Are you referring, for example, to American efforts to gain access to Myanmar’s rare earth mineral deposits?

Yes. But those minerals are not being mined in areas controlled by the military. Many of the promises the military is making concern things it simply cannot deliver. And even if it could deliver them, we’ve known for decades that the military frequently breaks its promises.

When was the last time you heard from your mother directly?

I’ve received just one letter from her in the past five years. That must have been about three years ago now.

This summer, photographs finally emerged showing her meeting representatives of the Red Cross. When you first saw those pictures, did they reassure you, or did they raise even more questions?

At first, I wasn’t even sure whether to believe that the meeting had actually taken place. After all, over the past five years, the military has put out a great deal of false information about my mother’s health and whereabouts.

For example, they claimed she had been transferred to house arrest, and we know that isn’t true. But when I found out that the photograph was genuine—or at least that one of them was—it gave me some hope that she was, at least, still alive.

Do you think the military is afraid of Aung San Suu Kyi herself or of what she continues to represent?

They’re definitely afraid of her. Why else would they keep her locked up?

And she really is a symbol for the people. People in Burma recognise how much she has sacrificed for them over the past 30 or 40 years. They know that she has been willing to stay in Burma, to remain with them and go through the same hardships they’ve had to endure.

Your mother remains a symbol of democracy for many people. But is there anything from her time in government that you personally disagree with? I’m thinking, for example, of the Rohingya crisis.

No, I’ve never had a problem with any of her decisions. She was in an extremely difficult position, and the international community failed to understand just how delicate that situation was.

I think it’s much clearer now that she simply wasn’t able to do everything she might have wanted to do. But I believe she did more for the Rohingya than anyone else, and people don’t realise that.

They say she remained silent on the issue, even though what she actually said about it would fill entire volumes. They say she went to The Hague to defend the military. But they say that without ever having properly listened to what she actually said there. So my advice to people is this: go and listen to what she said. Find out exactly what she did to help the Rohingya.

She initiated the establishment of the Kofi Annan Commission the day after she came to power. That was before the issue had even become a major concern for the international community. She was taking steps to help the Rohingya, and representatives of the Rohingya community I’ve spoken to have told me that she did everything she could for them.

Most people associate Aung San Suu Kyi with politics or the Nobel Peace Prize. Was it difficult growing up with someone who was both a parent and such a prominent public figure?

I grew up with it, and I think that, when you’re a child, everything just seems normal. You don’t know any other way of life, so you don’t really know what’s normal and what isn’t. From a very early age, I was aware of what she represented, but I don’t think those two things are mutually exclusive. She can be my mother and, at the same time, a very prominent political figure.

You’ve said before that you never wanted to become involved in politics, and that your mother didn’t want that for you either. Yet here you are, travelling, campaigning and speaking publicly about Myanmar. When did you realise that staying out of the spotlight was no longer an option?

When they put her in prison five years ago, I realised I had to speak out. After all, I’m her son. And if I don’t do anything, how can I expect anyone else to stand up for her?

How much of what you’re doing today is about your mother personally, and how much is about Myanmar itself? If your mother were released tomorrow, would you continue campaigning for democracy in Myanmar?

I think my mother would do a pretty good job of that herself. If I manage to secure her release, then I can feel that I’ve done my job well too.

For much of her life, Aung San Suu Kyi was seen as the daughter of Aung San, the general who played a key role in Burma’s struggle for independence from British colonial rule. Do you sometimes feel that you, too, are defined by your mother’s name?

I suppose I do, to some extent. After all, it’s very difficult not to have that image hanging over you. But at the same time, I’m doing this because I want to. I think it’s important that we all try to do whatever we can. People often don’t realise that they’re capable of doing much more than they think.

As a child, did you understand why your mother chose to stay in Myanmar rather than live a safe life with her family in Britain?

Yes, I did. I was actually with her when she was first placed under house arrest, so I saw what was happening with my own eyes. In some ways, it felt like a natural continuation of what had been happening before, because we’d been watching the situation in Burma gradually deteriorate.

I can’t say it was easy, but I think that, because I was a child at the time, I was somehow able to accept it. It’s difficult to explain. I think adults often find it harder to deal with change. And if she’d been imprisoned five years ago without my having already spent decades living with our separation, I think it would have been much harder.

What was it actually like when your mother was first placed under house arrest? Can you describe what happened?

When they first came to arrest her, they arrived with several trucks to take away the student revolutionaries who were staying in the house as well. I remember watching them being taken away. Then they put barbed wire around the entire compound, set up guard posts, cut the telephone lines and stopped us from leaving the house.

But at least we were still in her own home, and her own doctor was allowed to visit her. Even after I returned to England, I could send her parcels, and sometimes we were able to communicate. The past five years have been completely different.

You mentioned the student movement earlier. Is the revolution still visible on the streets of Myanmar today?

Yes, it is. It may not be as visible as it once was, but there is still an enormous amount of resistance across the country. In some places, like Yangon, things might appear quite normal. Other journalists I’ve spoken to who have been there have told me that everything looks remarkably normal. But it certainly isn’t. There are still huge numbers of people doing everything they can to change the situation. They’ve simply gone underground, so they’re not as visible as they used to be.

Do you ever feel that the junta has forced you into a role you would never have chosen for yourself?

Yes. I wouldn’t be doing this otherwise.

And what would you be doing?

Spending time with my children and working. I’m a trained carpenter.

How do you explain to your children what’s happening to their grandmother, and what’s happening in Myanmar more generally?

We’ve been talking about it for years, and they’ve had to come to terms with it too. They understand what’s happening in Burma. I still try to protect them as much as I can. Being in the public eye isn’t easy, and I want to keep them as far away from all that as possible.

Do you believe you’ll ever see your mother again?

Yes, I do. She’s been released before, and the situation in Burma could change at any moment. Even if the resistance doesn’t achieve victory in the near future, I think there’s still a chance that she could be released.

The interview first appeared in Czech at Seznam Zpravy. Daniela Kucerova is the new outlet’s foreign news department editor. Her main area of focus is Asia, particularly China and neighboring regions.

World.title: China Moves to Cement Myanmar Influence After U.S. Talks With Regime
World.content:
As Washington resumes direct engagement with Myanmar’s military regime, Beijing moved to cement its overarching influence last week by meeting with nine political parties in Yangon to gauge public sentiment.

The Chinese delegation was led by Peng Xiubin, director‑general of the Chinese Communist Party’s International Liaison Department. Present at the meeting were representatives of the military’s proxy Union Solidarity and Development Party, the National Unity Party, People’s Party, People’s Pioneer Party, Shan and Nationalities Democratic Party, Arakan Front Party, Kayin People’s Party, Unity and Development Party, and New Chinland Congress Party.

Participants said the Chinese side raised five key points, including Myanmar public attitudes toward China and challenges in bilateral relations.

“The Chinese side asked how the Myanmar people view them,” one participant told The Irrawaddy. “Some parties noted that sections of the public hold negative or skeptical views. They urged China to do more to show how it is helping Myanmar so that people understand.”

Anti-China sentiment in Myanmar has surged since the 2021 coup, triggered by Beijing’s support for successive military regimes, supplying them with battlefield hardware, technology and diplomatic cover. China is a key arms supplier and the biggest investor in post-coup Myanmar, propping up an embattled regime shunned by much of the international community and sanctioned by the West.

Most of the parties present at the meeting took part in Jan.-Feb. regime elections that were widely dismissed as a fraud to cement military rule.

However, leaders of the National Democratic Force (NDF) and the Shan Nationalities League for Democracy (SNLD)—Htet Aung Kyaw and Sai Kyaw Nyunt—joined the talks despite their parties being dissolved for defying the regime’s electoral roadmap. One party leader said the duo attended in a personal capacity after being invited individually, rather than as representatives of their banned organizations.

The CCP delegation also asked about priority areas for cooperation, and parties’ views on peace, the economy, and domestic issues.

The meeting came as coup leader Min Aung Hlaing made progress in securing formal engagement with Washington. U.S. officials held their second round of talks with regime representatives in Tokyo earlier this month after Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance flew to Naypyitaw for talks with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in September.

“The Chinese side made no mention of the recent U.S.-Myanmar talks, focusing instead on gauging our views,” said one participant. “Some parties stressed that they prefer engagement with China, a neighbor.”

Party leaders said they also discussed trade policy and technical support for agriculture while urging China to help reopen the Muse–Mandalay highway, a vital trade corridor. After losing control of major trade routes with China in northern Shan, the regime has imposed a near total blockade on Chinese imports to starve ethnic armed organizations of tax revenue.

Saw Han Aye, chair of the People’s Pioneer Party, said: “We asked the Chinese to increase investment and reopen trade routes as soon as possible, and Beijing affirmed it wants more frequent exchanges.”

While Beijing rejects accusations of interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs, the belief that its investments prop up a military regime waging war on its own people is widespread within the country. Anti-China sentiment soared to new levels in 2024, when Beijing pressured ethnic armies to halt northern Shan offensives that were threatening the regime’s grip on power.

When China’s Asia envoy Deng Xijun called for ethnic autonomy during a Naypyitaw ceremony marking the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement’s anniversary last week, critics pointed out that northern Shan State is already controlled by ethnic armies under Beijing’s thumb.

World.title: Migrants Urge Thai Gov’t to Let Them Work Free of Myanmar Regime Extortion
World.content:
Myanmar migrants are urging the Thai government to let them work legally without so-called Certificates of Identity (CI), which they say the military regime back home is weaponizing to extort money from them.

CI, issued by the regime under a quota system for overseas laborers hired in Myanmar, allow workers to register for work permits and renew their visas in Thailand.

Starved of hard currency, the regime has recently moved to harness CI issuance to grab the hard-earned money of migrant workers, saying it will not renew the papers unless workers remit a portion of their earnings back home through official channels and pay two percent income tax.

Under remittance rule introduced in late 2023, workers must send at least 25 percent of their monthly salaries home through regime-controlled banks, which means a fixed, artificially inflated exchange rate. Traditionally workers rely on the informal “hundi” system, which offers better exchange rates.

In response, the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT) has launched a campaign calling on Thai authorities to abolish the CI requirement for visas and work permits and instead allow employment solely based on the Pink Cards issued by the Thai government to regularize the status of migrants and refugees

Since Oct. 18, workers have staged an online photo campaign to press their demands.

Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government (NUG) has expressed support for the campaign.

Workers say they are not willing to pay any form of tax to the regime which does little to protect and promote their rights.

“The regime does not even provide proper passport services, so why should we pay them any money?” said a Myanmar worker in Chonburi.

The campaign began after the regime opened new CI issuing centers on Oct. 14 in Samut Sakhon, Samut Prakan, Surat Thani, Chiang Mai and Chonburi in order to prey on migrant workers whose permit cycle expires in December. There they must show evidence that they have remitted their due share of their earnings through the regime’s banking channels.

Pouring oil on the flames, Labor Minister Maung Myint earlier this month told migrant workers in Thailand to “think of the money as a donation.”

“We are campaigning to live and work with Pink Cards only,” said Khaing Gyi of the Aid Alliance Committee. “The regime’s demand for 25 percent remittance and tax payments can only be stopped by the workers themselves.”

He insisted this is not a protest against Thailand, but “simply a request to be allowed to work legally with Pink Cards.”

Workers complain that the CI centers are expensive, Byzantine and riddled with corruption in the form of demands for unofficial fees. Many laborers, who may be barely literate and speak little official Burmese, have to reply on brokers, which makes them prone to overcharging and fraud.

Campaigners have petitioned both houses of the Thai Parliament to abolish the CI requirement and crack down on brokers profiting from migrants.

MP Sia Jampatong of the House of Representatives committee said the government “must seriously review the CI center system, because the labor registration process must exist to certify status and protect rights, not be left to become a channel for officials to make a living, or provide an opportunity for the military government to exercise power over the lives of working people,” according to news outlet The Reporters.

And Senator Thewarit Maneechai pledged to bring the demand to the consideration of the Senate Labor Committee “to consider further relevant actions,” it added.

Thai activists also expressed solidarity. The Thailand Migration Reform group warned that allowing Myanmar’s regime to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the Pink Card framework used before 2009.

Until then, migrants lived and worked legally in Thailand with Pink Cards alone. “If workers could survive with Pink Cards before, why not improve that system and use it again?” said one migrant who has lived in the country for over 30 years.

According to Thailand’s Labor Ministry, there were nearly 3.5 million registered Myanmar workers with work permits in the country as of August this year, of whom only about 430,000 hold CI cards. The regime recently admitted that remittance has become a major source of foreign currency income for Myanmar.

World.title: Thousands Flee as Regime Troops Push Into Myanmar’s Oil Hub
World.content:
Regime troops backed by airstrikes are pouring into Magwe Region’s Myaing Township as the battle for Myanmar’s oilfields escalates, forcing thousands of residents to flee.

Reinforcements from the Light Infantry Division in Pakokku, an hour to the south, are bolstering the offensive to seize territory — nicknamed “Anyar Dubai” for its oil wealth — from resistance groups.
