World.title: Georgia’s party ban: Court to begin hearing government case against opposition on 21 October
World.content:
At noon on 21 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court will begin hearing on the merits a case brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party, which is seeking to ban five opposition parties and political groups. The hearings will take place in Batumi and continue on 22 and 23 October.

Four of the five parties intend to defend their positions in court, while the fifth will boycott the proceedings. Some opposition groups also plan to hold protests in Batumi and Tbilisi alongside the hearings.

The Constitutional Court’s full bench will hear the case, meaning all its sitting judges. The court has nine seats, but only seven judges currently serve on it, with two vacancies. On 13 October, Manana Kobakhidze, one of the founders of Georgian Dream, left the court. She had previously asked to recuse herself from the case, but the court rejected her request. Kobakhidze said she had made the decision to leave the court independently and for personal reasons.

Georgian Dream MPs Archil Gorduladze, Giorgi Kakhiani, Tengiz Sharmanashvili and Tornike Cheishvili will represent the party in court.

Under the law, the court must deliver its ruling by 24 June 2027.

Why is Georgian Dream seeking to ban the parties?

The claimants — 88 Georgian Dream MPs — argue that all five parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties that aim to overthrow or forcibly change the constitutional order.

According to information released by the court, the claimants cite alleged human rights violations between 2004 and 2012, when one of the parties, the United National Movement (UNM), was in power. They also point to the parties’ current refusal to recognise Georgian Dream’s legitimacy. The claimants say the parties have rejected the government’s legitimacy since 2016 and are pursuing a common goal.

The claimants also accuse the parties of attempting to overthrow the government. In the case of the United National Movement, they further allege that it undermined the country’s independence and territorial integrity, citing the August 2008 war.

The opposition parties reject all these accusations.

What do the parties facing a ban plan to do?

United National Movement

The party will attend the court hearings, said Irakli Pavlenishvili, chair of its governing council. He called on members of the public to gather outside the courthouse in Batumi on the days of the hearings.

The UNM’s jailed founder and Georgia’s third president, Mikheil Saakashvili, has also demanded that he attend the proceedings. In a statement released on 17 October, he said he wanted the authorities to bring him to Batumi so he could “fully expose this so-called court and its master for their historic betrayal”. Much of the case against the parties concerns Saakashvili’s time in power, from 2004 to 2012.

The party’s leader, Levan Khabeishvili, who is also in prison, has likewise demanded permission to attend the hearings.

The UNM belongs to the opposition alliance and takes part in its protests.

What is the Opposition Alliance? The Opposition Alliance “Unity for Victory” was formed by nine pro-Western Georgian parties on 2 March 2026, following months of negotiations. Its members are the United National Movement, Ahali, Girchi – More Freedom, Droa, the Federalists, European Georgia, Strategy Aghmashenebeli, Freedom Square and the National Democratic Party. The alliance says its goals are to end the rule of Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of Georgian Dream, restore Georgia’s Euro-Atlantic course, release political prisoners and form a coalition government after Georgian Dream loses a free election. The parties retain their ideological independence but have agreed on a joint strategy for protests and communications. The alliance’s largest rally to date took place in Tbilisi on 26 May 2026, Georgia’s Independence Day. Two other major opposition parties, Lelo and For Georgia, led by Giorgi Gakharia, have not joined the alliance. Lelo chose to operate independently, while For Georgia rejected an alliance with the United National Movement and parties that split from it.

Coalition for Change

The coalition will also take part in the hearings. Its member parties — Ahali, Girchi – More Freedom and Droa — also belong to the Opposition Alliance. On 15 October, Nika Gvaramia, leader of Ahali, announced the launch of a joint campaign by the alliance.

Gvaramia said their struggle would not be confined to the courtroom. “We will be everywhere, including on the streets of Tbilisi,” he promised.

Strong Georgia – Lelo

Lelo will attend the hearings and has asked the Public Defender (ombudsman) to submit a legal opinion on the case. As of 19 October, the ombudsman’s office had not responded.

Lelo is not a member of the alliance. The party’s political council says it has several scenarios and an action plan ready in case the court approves the ban.

For Georgia

The party announced in a statement on 20 October that it would take part in the proceedings. However, it insists that the court consider the case against it separately, rather than together with the other parties.

The party of former Georgian prime minister Giorgi Gakharia does not belong to the Opposition Alliance. It was the only one of the five parties that refused to surrender its parliamentary mandate in protest and nevertheless entered parliament.

The Federalists

The party has decided not to attend the hearings, saying it does not want to lend the proceedings a veneer of legal legitimacy.

According to party leader Tamara Chergoleishvili, the Federalists will travel to Batumi but protest against the court proceedings outside the courthouse rather than in the courtroom.

Why does it matter whether the parties attend the hearings?

The parties’ attendance could affect their chances of appealing the verdict to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg.

Sandro Baramidze, a lawyer with Transparency International Georgia, explains that the ECHR requires applicants to raise and document their arguments through domestic legal proceedings first. If a party does not attend the hearing, its application to the court in Strasbourg could therefore be declared inadmissible.

Who is organising the protests?

As Georgian Dream seeks to ban the parties listed above, the Opposition Alliance has announced a protest campaign.

The first demonstration will take place at 11:00 on 21 October in Batumi, outside the Constitutional Court. Freedom Square, a member of the alliance, is organising the protest.

At 19:00 on 25 October in Tbilisi, outside the first building of Tbilisi State University, the Opposition Alliance will launch a joint campaign aimed at organising a large demonstration in Tbilisi on 28 November.

As of 20 October, Lelo and For Georgia had not said whether they would join the protests.

What is the rest of the opposition doing?

In addition to the parties facing a ban, the Opposition Alliance includes European Georgia, Strategy Aghmashenebeli, Freedom Square and the National Democratic Party. These parties are not named in the lawsuit but take part in all the alliance’s protests.

Levan Tsutskiridze, leader of Freedom Square, believes that banning the parties would create a bigger problem for Georgian Dream itself.

He says a ban will not make the country’s problems disappear. Instead, it will “close off the political path to solving these problems and guarantee an even worse end for Georgian Dream”.

Viktor Kipiani, leader of the party For Georgia First, points to the same risk:

Banning opposition parties through the courts effectively brings the political process to a standstill, while making change through elections virtually impossible.

He believes this will accelerate radicalisation in the country.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association has now issued its independent legal assessment of the case for the third time, arguing that the lawsuit aims to eliminate political competition.

What is the European Union saying?

EU institutions have reacted strongly to the Georgian authorities’ attempt to ban opposition parties:

The European Parliament adopted another critical resolution, calling for the immediate withdrawal of the lawsuit and saying it was considering personal sanctions against those who initiated the proceedings.

Christian Wigand, a European Commission spokesman, said Brussels was closely monitoring developments. He said the attempt to abolish leading political forces, alongside the Georgian authorities’ earlier statements and legislative changes, pointed to a worrying instrumentalisation of the justice system. This directly threatens democratic pluralism and fundamental freedoms.

On 20 October, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded that questioning the legitimacy of the proceedings before the court had even examined the case amounted to an attempt to pressure the court and interfere in the country’s internal affairs. The ministry urged EU representatives to refrain from statements that prejudge the proceedings.

What happens if the court upholds the lawsuit?

If the court upholds the lawsuit, the five parties will legally cease to exist. According to official figures from the Central Election Commission, a total of 784,820 voters backed the five parties in the 2024 parliamentary election.

Under current legislation, the court may also, at the claimant’s request, ban people associated with the dissolved parties from engaging in political activity. The law also provides a 14-day procedure for banning a successor party.

The hearings scheduled for 21–23 October mark the first stage in the proceedings. It remains unclear how long the case will take or when the court will deliver its ruling.

World.title: Families of missing Azerbaijanis hold rally in Brussels (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 21. On October 21, 2026, families of missing Azerbaijanis held a rally organized by the public association "Karabakh Families of Missing Persons" Public Unionin Brussels’ central Schuman Square—home to the main institutions of the European Union. This event followed a demonstration held the previous day in the square in front of the European Parliament in Brussels.

This was reported by the Agency for State Support to Non-Governmental Organizations of Azerbaijan.

During the event, it was emphasized that Armenia has still not provided information regarding the fate of 4,010 missing Azerbaijanis and continues to withhold information about them. Particular attention was paid to the importance of providing information about missing persons as part of advancing the peace agenda.

Families of missing Azerbaijanis have stated that the European Parliament—which consistently advocates for Armenia and is viewed in international relations as an example of anachronism and atavism—has never once raised the issue of the missing Azerbaijanis.

Konul Behbudova, chair of the "Karabakh Families of Missing Persons" Public Union, stated that actions dedicated to the missing persons will continue.

As part of the event, a special installation was presented, featuring photographs of missing Azerbaijani citizens, along with their clothing and envelopes containing letters. The poignant messages, written on behalf of those who have gone missing, left a deep impression on visitors. Attendees expressed their solidarity with the families of the missing by leaving words of support, tying commemorative ribbons, and laying flowers.

The "Families of the Missing in Karabakh" Public Union has emerged as a winner in the 2026 grant competition held by the Agency for State Support to Non-Governmental Organizations of Azerbaijan, with its project titled "Echo of Absence."

World.title: Families of missing Azerbaijanis meet with EU representatives in Brussels (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 21. A meeting with members of the “Karabakh Families of Missing Persons” public association was held on October 21 at the European External Action Service (EEAS) of the European Union in Brussels.

The families of missing Azerbaijanis met with Okke Bouwman, Political Adviser to the EU Special Representative for the South Caucasus and the crisis in Georgia, and Marco Cardinali, Coordinator for Relations with Azerbaijan.

During the meeting, which lasted about an hour, the families of missing Azerbaijanis stated that Armenia had provided no information about their loved ones, even after the end of the conflict.

Konul Behbudova, chairperson of the public association, noted that on October 20, the previous day, families of missing Azerbaijanis had held a protest at Place du Luxembourg in front of the European Parliament in Brussels and adopted a statement.

She stressed that Armenia bears direct responsibility for the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and is obliged to share information with Azerbaijan about the locations of mass graves. Behbudova noted that 32 mass graves have been discovered to date in Azerbaijan’s territories liberated from occupation.

The meeting also addressed another protest held by families of missing Azerbaijanis in Brussels that day, at the central Schuman Square. It was emphasized that the families would not remain silent until they received information about their loved ones and would continue to hold regular protests.

World.title: Vanuatu minister contradicts own government on Chinese police drawdown
World.content:
Vanuatu's Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat says he has no plans to cut China's police presence in his country, despite his own government issuing a joint statement with Australia saying its policing cooperation program with Beijing was set to be reduced.

The joint statement, which was given a green light by both governments in the wake of a high-level meeting on the implementation of the Nakamal Agreement, stresses that China's police assistance program with Vanuatu is "time-limited and expected to reduce over time".

It also contrasted China's policing program with Australia's police assistance arrangements under the Nakamal pact, which it stresses is "legally binding" with "no expiry date".

Andrew Napuat says Vanuatu is not in a position to "phase out" any policing partner. (ABC News: Lillyrose Welwel)

But Andrew Napuat, who travelled to Beijing just last month to renew Vanuatu's police cooperation agreement with China, appeared to take aim at that clause, saying there was "no need to talk about a third party in any agreements".

"Our prime minister, Jotham Napat, after signing the Nakamal Agreement, already announced that Vanuatu will not take sides when it comes to its relationships, highlighting the long-standing position Vanuatu has always taken of being a friend to all and an enemy to none," he said in a statement.

"Therefore, such statements targeting one partner do not reflect our country's position on its relationships with its partners."

Jotham Napat and Anthony Albanese signed the Nakamal Agreement earlier this year. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Mr Napuat also criticised the ABC's report on the statement, saying it suggested that Vanuatu was "targeting" China, and stressing Vanuatu still needed policing assistance from Beijing, as well as other international partners.

"At the moment, we are still building our [police] force," he said.

" That is why we are grateful to all our partners for their help. We are not in a position to phase out any partner as reported. "

The minister said that in the long term, Vanuatu hoped to "slowly phase out all advisers and be able to run its own force", suggesting that Australian Federal Police (AFP) officers, as well as Chinese police, would then be asked to leave.

But he said Vanuatu had not yet decided to take this step.

"We will make that decision when we decide as a nation. We will not phase out any partner due to the conditions in any agreement," he said.

Minister's 'different' message on police

Mr Napuat's intervention is unlikely to be welcomed by the Australian government, which sees the internal affairs minister as one of the most pro-China voices in Mr Napat's cabinet.

Last year, Mr Napuat took aim at Pat Conroy after the Australian government Pacific Island affairs minister made public comments about Vanuatu's move to renew policing agreements with Beijing.

Johnny Koanapo meets Penny Wong and Pat Conroy in Canberra last week. (Facebook: Senator Penny Wong)

One federal government source said Mr Napuat's message on policing was "very different" to the one conveyed by the Deputy Prime Minister Johnny Koanapo in Canberra last week.

Mr Napuat's statement about Vanuatu eventually phasing out "all advisers" also sits uncomfortably with the public statements Australia has made on policing cooperation, particularly as the federal government has never suggested the AFP's commitment to Vanuatu is time-limited.

Vanuatu expects fall in China police presence Vanuatu has signalled it expects a change in Beijing's police presence after the Pacific nation signed the landmark Nakamal Agreement with Australia.

Under the Nakamal Agreement, Australia has agreed to "elevate assistance to the Vanuatu Police Force in police training and equipment, policing, maritime security, cyber security, intelligence cooperation, and infrastructure".

And last week a senior AFP officer, David McLean, told a parliamentary committee he expected the AFP contingent in Vanuatu could "nearly double in size over the coming years" in order to implement the pact, although Vanuatu's prime minister subsequently said his country would need to sign off on any increase.

The ABC contacted Prime Minister Jotham Napat for a response.

The ABC also sent questions to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT); however, it declined to comment.

China's Embassy in Vanuatu has not responded to the ABC's questions on Australia and Vanuatu's joint statement.

World.title: How do we actually turn down the temperature in political debate?
World.content:
Only two months ago, a group called Compassion in Politics Australia gained the first signatory to its "Civility Pledge".

Helen Haines.

The organisation, based on a similar foundation in the United Kingdom, aims to turn the tide of toxic debate and build a better politics.

As a start, it's asking elected officials to sign a simple pledge. "In my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect, and compassion," is all it states.

This week the independent MP was the victim of an attack widely described as shocking but unsurprising. Sadly predictable, was the common reaction amongst MPs who have been at the receiving end of increasing threats and harassment.

Flowers and cards from well-wishers pile up outside Helen Haines's Wangaratta electoral office. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

Yesterday, security agencies briefed MPs on the risks to their safety. Security will no doubt be improved as much as is practicable, without sacrificing the critical ability of MPs to interact in their communities.

The more difficult question is what, if anything, can be done about the increasingly hostile political environment. What can be done to restore the "civility" that Haines, at least, pledged to pursue?

Civility was the word emphasised by the Governor-General late yesterday, who stood alongside the husband of Helen Haines in an effort to calm a worried nation.

"We don't have to all agree, but we can wrestle with the issue not the person," Sam Mostyn said from Melbourne's Alfred Hospital. Her message echoed the call to turn the temperature down.

"Words matter, whether spoken or in written form or increasingly in the virtual world."

This call for civility is something ASIO boss Mike Burgess has been going on about now for years.

"I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint," he said after the attack on Haines.

Burgess draws a line between words and actions: "ASIO has seen direct correlations between inflamed language, inflamed tensions and acts of violence."

The intelligence chief must feel at times he's talking to a brick wall. He warned against "inflamed language" and called for a return to civility after the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel in 2023, again after lifting the terrorism threat level to "probable" in 2024, and again after the Bondi terrorist attack in 2025.

Will anyone listen this time? Will an attack on one of their own force politicians to re-think their part in setting the tone of political discourse?

For some, the answer is clearly yes. There is a degree of self-reflection this week.

"We should all, every single one of us, me included, find ways to minimise the temperature of these debates," said shadow minister Jono Duniam, who will soon depart the Senate.

"We could all do better. I don't exclude myself or any political party," acknowledged the prime minister who, like Burgess, has repeatedly called for a more civil debate.

"By all means disagree but consider how you disagree. By all means protest but consider how you protest. By all means criticise elected officials but consider how you criticise elected officials," urged ASIO director-general Mike Burgess. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, by contrast, is worried about limiting robust argument. While condemning anything that intimidates or incites violence, he defended the role of vigorous debate.

"We have, like so few other countries in the world, avoided political violence. This is part of the great Australian achievement, and we've done that by having vigorous and rigorous debate and choice at the ballot box," he said.

"This is what's worked for us. We need to make sure it stays there."

It's certainly true — Australia has long enjoyed robust political debate while largely avoiding political violence.

But this misses the point being made by the ASIO boss. Times have changed.

We're now in an environment, according to Burgess, where "politically motivated violence is more likely than previous years".

Angus Taylor's own colleagues can recognise the deterioration, too.

"It's clear that the political environment has become more heated in recent years," said shadow minister James Paterson.

"In the last few years things have gotten much worse," said independent MP Monique Ryan, adding that "the 2025 election was completely different to 2022", with more aggression and anger. It's a common view, particularly among female politicians.

MPs are worried. For themselves, for their families, and for the fate of Australia's democracy.

So, what does it take to turn the temperature down?

Threats against MPs rising The attack on Helen Haines comes amid a rise in threats of political violence.

"Gosh, if only I could say what the answer to that is," One Nation's Barnaby Joyce admitted on Radio National yesterday. "I don't know," he said.

It's rare to hear Barnaby Joyce stumped for an answer on anything. He's certainly not accepting any blame on the part of One Nation for raising the temperature.

Many might agree with Joyce that there are no easy solutions to counter the powerful domestic and global forces driving voter frustration, political polarisation, toxic online discourse and hate.

Politicians are certainly limited in what they can control. But they're not entirely powerless.

As Burgess says, language matters: "By all means, disagree. But consider how you disagree."

Signing a "Civility Pledge" might seem like a mere symbolic gesture, but it's something. If it's good enough for Helen Haines, why not others?

Compassion in Politics Australia issued a statement after the horrific attack on Monday, calling it "a stark reminder that compassion and civility in public life are not abstract ideals. They matter profoundly".

The attack on Helen Haines may prove to be just another brief interruption before regular political mud-slinging resumes. Or it could see all sides of politics try to course correct.

David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or can be streamed anytime on ABC iview.

World.title: Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day
World.content:
Steve Smith doesn't return after reaching a major milestone and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve as Australia is sent barrelling towards a chastening defeat in Gqeberha.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Fiery Marco tears through the Aussies

Fresh from his swashbuckling 85 on day three, the towering Marco Jansen continued to terrorise the Australians on day four.

The left-arm seamer was at his fiery, probing best, with his aggression and accuracy proving all too much for the tourists in their first innings.

Jansen dismissed both Scott Boland and Travis Head early in the day, before a few tense exchanges with Marnus Labuschagne appeared to light a fuse somewhere deep in the big man.

Labuschagne and Jansen had a few tense exchanges on day four. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

He proceeded to treat Matt Renshaw to a send-off — seemingly in Afrikaans — upon having the Yorkshire-born Queenslander caught at short leg, before sending Alex Carey packing in a double breakthrough in the shadows of lunch.

Unfortunately for the Aussies, Jansen wasn't done there, with the South African having Beau Webster caught in the cordon to claim his fifth wicket and continue Australia's horror day.

2. Sore Smith reaches 11,000 and doesn't return

Amid the carnage up the other end, Steve Smith was just about hanging in there.

Struggling with a neck issue, the Australian received running repairs at multiple points during his innings and never quite looked his usual self.

Smith received multiple rounds of treatment for a stiff neck. (AP Photos)

Even so, Smith was at the crease long enough to become just the 12th batter to score 11,000 Test match runs, joining Ricky Ponting and Allan Border as the only Australians in that rare air.

But the Australia vice-captain was in serious discomfort throughout his innings, and departed promptly after joining that exclusive club.

The stiff-necked Smith was bowled through the gate by Wiaan Mulder for 28 as Australia was asked to follow on after being skittled for just 99, their fourth-lowest Test total against the Proteas.

And in a massive blow for his team, the Australia vice-captain did not recover in time to return to the crease as wickets started falling in the tourists' second dig, remaining in training gear in the dugout as Australia limped towards stumps.

3. Two remarkable grabs, two very different reactions

We have been treated to some seriously sensational slip catching in Gqeberha.

Following in the footsteps of Renshaw — who made a stunning low catch late on day two — Simon Harmer produced his own moment of magic early on day four.

With Australia 3-45 in its first innings and already beginning to teeter, the desperately out-of-touch Labuschagne drove unconvincingly, sending his thick edge flying low and hard towards the cordon.

Harmer dived dramatically to his left, using his sizeable left hand to pluck the quickly dropping ball from the air in front of second slip.

It was a stunning reflex grab from Harmer. (Fox Cricket)

And the off-spinner was absolutely pumped with his effort, throwing his head back and roaring as he got to his feet.

It provided quite some contrast to Renshaw's bewilderment after pouching his similarly excellent catch earlier in the Test.

Harmer and Renshaw had very different reactions to their similarly excellent catches. (Fox Cricket)

4. Marnus throws it away after enormous reprieve

With Australia beginning its second innings needing 326 runs to just make South Africa bat again, Labuschagne had a golden opportunity to revive his sputtering Test career and make up for his rash dismissal earlier in the day.

Coming in after the early departure of Nic Maddinson, the signs were good for the Queenslander, who knuckled down with Head to push Australia towards 100.

And it was beginning to feel like Labuschagne might have finally been on for a score when he was the beneficiary of a huge reprieve in the 28th over.

Given out LBW to a Harmer off break, Labuschagne reviewed the decision in a blink and it was high drama as both camps waited for ball tracking to take an unusually long time to build.

Eventually, the technology projected the ball to be missing leg stump by what surely wasn't much more than a coat of paint.

Labuschagne survived by the skin of his teeth. (Fox Cricket)

Helmet off and head back, Labuschagne was making no secret of his relief.

But only moments later, he threw it all away, mistiming his slog and holing out to long-on for 39.

Labuschagne's relief was short-lived. (Fox Cricket)

It was an ugly, ugly dismissal and one that left Australia once again on the rack with shadows lengthening in St George's.

5. Consecutive night shifts for Boland

With Australia proceeding to lose both Renshaw and Webster late on, Boland once again found himself batting in the dying embers of a day.

It was the second consecutive evening the Victorian had been called on as nightwatchman, and for the second consecutive evening, he made his way through to stumps.

Again, he betrayed no hint of annoyance with his sacrificial role, instead digging in and bravely finding his way through a couple of overs of twilight finger spin.

It was another committed shift from Boland — but boy, it's some reward for taking a five-wicket haul on his return to the team.

He'll begin day five alongside Head (87*) with Australia 4-156 and still 170 runs away from making South Africa bat again.

World.title: NSW reveals opening date of long-awaited Southwest Metro line
World.content:
An opening date for the long-awaited Southwest Metro extension has been revealed.

NSW Premier Chris Minns says it will officially open with the first service departing at 4:31am on Friday, October 30.

On the new metro service, commuters will be able to cut down on travel time, connecting the south-western suburbs to the Sydney CBD, north-Sydney and the north-western suburbs.

The T3 Bankstown Line between Sydenham and Bankstown ceased operations in September 2024 to convert the 130-year-old heavy rail line to a metro line.

During that time commuters were forced to take replacement buses, known as the Southwest Link, making travel time twice as long.

The conversion deadline was pushed back due to industrial action and complexity issues. It was initially meant to take 12 months.

It is the final stage of Sydney's M1 Metro North West and Bankstown Line, which will connect Bankstown to Tullawong along a 66-kilometre stretch.

World.title: 'We're unbreakable': Ex-Israeli hostage's message to Bondi attack survivors
World.content:
Former Israeli hostage Daniella Gilboa wants those affected by the Bondi Beach terror attack to know "we're unbreakable", as the shooting's first anniversary approaches.

Ms Gilboa, an Israel Defense Forces (IDF) soldier, was stationed at the Nahal Oz observation post on the edge of the Gaza Strip when she was abducted by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023.

Fifteen female spotters were killed at the base during the attacks and seven were taken into Gaza. One of the seven women was killed in captivity, with her body retrieved, and one was rescued during an IDF raid.

Music has been a source of peace for Ms Gilboa throughout her life, including her time in captivity.

"There [in Gaza], it was mine and my friend's comfort. We used to sing quietly some songs, Jewish songs too, to remind ourselves of our community.

" Sometimes a song or a prayer can help when it's hard to find words. "

Ms Gilboa was held hostage for 477 days.

Ms Gilboa was released in January 2025. (Supplied: IDF)

As part of the second hostage and prisoner exchange, in January 2025, Hamas militants handed Ms Gilboa, along with Liri Albag, 19, and 20-year-olds Karina Ariev and Naama Levy, to the Red Cross, which transported them to the Israel-Gaza border and handed them over to the IDF.

In exchange, Israel freed about 200 Palestinian prisoners from its jails.

"I waited so long for this freedom, for this feeling — to control my own thoughts, my own actions," Ms Gilboa, now 22, said.

After finding freedom, Ms Gilboa is now pursuing her dreams. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

'We're unbreakable'

Sydney's Bondi Beach terror attack on December 14 last year, where 15 people were killed and dozens more were injured while celebrating Hanukkah, was a triggering event for Ms Gilboa and countless other Jewish people across the globe.

Ms Gilboa, who is currently in Australia to perform as part of the SHIR Australian Jewish Music Festival in Sydney and Melbourne, said she was grateful to have visited Bondi and seen the temporary menorah memorial at the scene of the attack at Archer Park.

"I was so sad. I wanted to send the families that were affected a big, big hug … we're unbreakable," she said, noting she felt a connection with the survivors and victims' loved ones.

Pinned to her shirt was a bee brooch in honour of 10-year-old victim Matilda.

The bee motif is an enduring symbol of remembrance for Matilda, who was the youngest victim of the Bondi Beach attack. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

Upon being released as a hostage, Ms Gilboa said it dawned on her how many people from across the world, including Australia, had been praying and hoping for their safe return.

"It really touches me to know that people who didn't know me were thinking about me and praying for me. Now that I'm here in Australia, I can meet them and say thank you in person.

"Through the stories, the messages and meeting people I felt so much love and support. I want to tell the [Sydney Jewish] community that I'm thinking of them."

Ms Gilboa sent her love and support to Sydney's Jewish and Bondi communities. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

New classified hearing for antisemitism inquiry

After 62 days of public hearings, the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion closed in August.

On October 12, the royal commission confirmed it would hold a classified hearing this month to take additional evidence related to hearing block two, which focused on the circumstances surrounding the Bondi Beach attack.

The inquiry said the sensitivity of the evidence meant the hearing would be closed to the public to avoid prejudice to national security and the ongoing criminal proceedings relating to the attack.

The evidence from closed hearings will be covered in a confidential volume of Commissioner Virginia Bell's final report.

Virgina Bell will deliver her report in December. (ABC News)

But the commissioner said "substantial parts" of confidential sections of her interim and final reports should be made public after the conclusion of criminal proceedings related to the shooting.

It is expected the report will be delivered on December 18, four days after the first anniversary of the terror attack.

Ms Gilboa she had noticed a rise in antisemitism, especially in online spaces.

"On social media, the hatred, it makes me cry sometimes," she said.

"I really think we're all one; it's not just a slogan for me. We're all human beings and we all have the right to live."

Ms Gilboa has been supported by her loved ones, including mother Orly. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

She hoped that being a former hostage would not define her in the future, and that her passions, her love of singing and her desire to connect with people would instead triumph over the darkness.

"To have the Sydney Opera House as my international debut and share a stage with artists who are Muslim, Hindu, Christian and Jewish is special," Ms Gilboa said.

" I'm so happy to come back to my family, friends … it's a privilege. "

World.title: Military vehicle model involved in fatal rollover had previously flipped
World.content:
The six-wheel model of Supacat transporter that rolled killing an Australian soldier had previously been involved in a tip over incident in training, the ABC has confirmed.

A four-wheeled variant used by British forces had been involved in more than 30 rolls including one that caused the death of a Scottish reservist, the ABC also confirmed.

The British rollover led to calls in 2021 from the UK Defence Safety Authority to upgrade roll protection measures in the UK Supacats and modified training operations.

Corporal Brendan Hannam died, and five soldiers were injured when their open-top Supacat High Mobility Transporter rolled at the Mount Bundey training area about 115 kilometres south-east of Darwin on October 5.

Corporal Brendan Hannam died when a Supacat high-mobility vehicle rolled at the Mount Bundey training area on October 5. (Supplied: ADF)

Defence has confirmed Corporal Hannam was not the driver of the vehicle.

Following the incident Chief of Army Susan Coyle said Supacat operations had been paused, and it would be "premature" to make any other comment about how the incident occurred.

She said there had "not been" any other incidents involving those kind of vehicles.

Defence has since confirmed one of the Supacat vehicles had tipped in a previous training exercise, after the ABC later revealed it had photographic evidence of an incident showing a vehicle tipped over on its side.

Defence says not a rollover

A spokesperson said the image obtained by the ABC was likely of a 2020 accident on a driver training course which did not cause any injuries or damage to the vehicle.

The spokesperson said the vehicle in the image was not considered to have "rolled over" but to have "layed over".

A Supacat on operations at Mount Bundey. (Supplied: Australian Defence Force)

The incident was classed as a "lay over" because the vehicle had not undertaken "significant rotational movement onto its roof after one or more complete rotations", according to the spokesperson.

Asked if Lieutenant General Coyle was aware of the 2020 "lay over" incident and what investigation had resulted, the spokesperson said it was inappropriate to comment due to the ongoing investigation into the Mount Bundey incident.

Do you know more about this story? Email Callinan.Rory@abc.net.au

Questions over UK incidents

Defence has also declined to comment on whether any safety upgrades or changes to training were made in relation to Australia's Supacat fleet following the death of a UK soldier in 2019 in a four-wheeler British variant of the Supacat high mobility vehicle called a Jackal.

The Jackal, developed from the same platform that was used as the base for Australia's six-wheel Supacat Extenda models, is the company's flagship model.

Supacat provides military vehicles for countries including Australia, the UK, and the United States. (Supplied: Supacat)

It boasts a similar "open architecture" design with a series of roll bars to protect crew and has been in service with the UK forces from 2007.

In 2019 one of the Jackals, a model 2, rolled during a training exercise in the UK, killing the driver, Staff Sergeant John McKelvie, and throwing the instructor from the vehicle at a training ground.

An official UK military inquiry was held into the incident in 2021 and an inquest in 2024.

A UK inquiry made more than 50 recommendations to improve safety in Supacat's Jackal model. (Supplied: Supacat)

The inquest heard there had been more than 30 rollover incidents involving the UK Jackals that had led to some soldiers suffering head and neck injuries.

The military inquiry findings, released in 2021, raised concerns about the Jackal's inadequate rollover protection and officially recommended roll safety upgrades to all high mobility Supacats and changes to training operations.

Veterans say training safety a delicate balance Members of Darwin's defence community mourning the loss of Corporal Brendan Hannam say the defence force must balance training safety with readiness for active duty.

Concerns were raised about the individual roll bars not being designed to support the full weight of the vehicle and occupants being at risk from objects intruding into the open cabin area during a roll.

It also raised questions how a Jackal had failed a tilt trial but there had been no evidence that the results of this trial had been used to determine a safe operating envelope of the vehicle.

"Additionally the panel found that vehicle crews had no means by which to measure the tilt of the vehicle while driving or surveying the ground on foot,'' the inquiry report stated.

This was considered a "contributory factor", it stated.

The inquiry made more than 50 recommendations to improve safety with many related to rollover protection including that crews should be informed of vehicle tilt limitations and there be a mechanism to determine vehicle angle to stay within safe operational limits.

Some of the recommendations called for changes in the UK to "all High Mobility Truck variant vehicles" such as a demand to improve protection of crew members taking into account "rollover events, neck protection, helmet design and vehicle design to ensure adequate protection is provided to vehicle occupants".

Changes to the wire cutter bar design to reduce the risk of crew injury in a rollover, were also recommended.

Efforts to obtain comment from Supacat have been unsuccessful.

In 2023 Supacat's UK company released a promotional video on Youtube that said: "to meet the new roll over protection requirements Supacat have designed a new system that will be integrated into the current fleets whilst already built into the new integrated armoured cab."

Four deaths in five years

Corporal Hannam's funeral was held on October 19.

The highly experienced soldier who had done two tours of Afghanistan left a wife and two children. The five soldiers who were injured in the crash have since been discharged from hospital, Defence says.

Corporal Hannam is the fourth soldier to die in the past five years in rollover incidents involving military vehicles.

Brendan Hannam leaves behind his partner and two young children. (Supplied: ADF)

In October 2025, Australian soldier Lance Corporal Tulsa Rumney was killed when an armoured personal carrier rolled at a training area west of Townsville.

In August 2021, Craftsman Brendon Payne and Warrant Officer Ryan Leslie died when the heavy recovery vehicle they were driving rolled near the Townsville Field Training area in North Queensland.

Following the Mount Bundey accident Defence Minister Richard Marles said he had asked Chief of Defence Admiral Mark Hammond "to look at what might be the best vehicle to examine issues such as risk settings, management of fatigue, appropriate training across Army and the defence force".

Funeral held for Australian soldier Corporal Brendan Hannam has been remembered as a "man of character" and "a loving partner" at his funeral today.

Australia's Supacats have largely been used by the special forces, the commandos and the Special Air Service Regiment.

In the 2000s, Australia purchased a four-wheel version of the Supacat that is similar to the Jackal and was named the Nary after Special Air Service Regiment Warrant Officer David Nary who died in a pre-deployment training exercise in Kuwait in 2005.

In the mid 2010s, Australia purchased 89 of Supacat's high mobility transporter Extenda vehicles at a cost of about $130 million according to official statements from the then-Defence Minister David Johnson.

The Extendas were filmed on operations at Mount Bundey as recently as earlier this year.

World.title: Working mum who lived in car left wondering how she would survive
World.content:
Adelaide mother Amira lived in her car for 10 months following a relationship breakdown.

She and her ex-partner wanted their children to have stability, so they took turns staying home with the kids on alternate weeks.

On weeks Amira did not stay with the children, she had to move out.

Offers of accommodation from generous friends arrived, but she eventually felt like a burden and opted for winter nights in car parks around Adelaide.

Amira recalls a group of five men banging on her window one night while she was sleeping in her car. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"It happened over one weekend, and I went from being stable and accomplished to: 'how do I survive until the next day?'" Amira said.

The 39-year-old said the change was difficult to process, describing herself as a working-class mum who hosted parties and had just been promoted.

"I had everything together and now I really don't. I was quite hard on myself and really struggling to see a way out," she said.

Amira lived in her car for 10 months following a relationship breakdown. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Amira, who did not want her last name published for privacy reasons and because her children did not know the full extent of her living situation at the time, said she often would go without.

" I made sure all of my money was spent on [my children] and if I had to miss out, I had to miss out. "

Seeking safety in well-lit car parks

Amira said she still remembered the trauma of a group of five men banging on her car window one night.

"One was even trying to unlock the door and trying to get in," she said.

"[It was] terrifying, absolutely terrifying," she said.

Amira says she would pick well-lit places close to public bathrooms to stay overnight. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Recent data from local homelessness service, Hutt St Centre, showed a 77 per cent rise in female clients over four years.

Amira described taking extra precautions as a woman sleeping rough, such as picking well-lit car parks with toilet blocks and a close escape route.

"I had to purchase a couple of cricket bats so that I could feel that sense of security or safety," she said.

Turning a corner

Her children's school stepped in to help and Amira was able to get back on her feet.

"I started picking up other jobs, I started accessing my psychologist more often, I started accessing other services, things started to change slowly," she said.

She now works to help people in similar situations access transitional housing and mental health supports.

"I thought, 'Wow if that was around when I was sleeping rough, that would have been the perfect place to reset'," Amira said.

"I can relate and tell people there is hope, there's no stigma."

Amira said more short and long-term housing were needed for people experiencing homelessness and mental health challenges.

Long-term housing help

Olav Nielssen, a member of The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists, has been working to provide long-term housing for people with chronic mental illness.

The charity has created 20 self-contained purpose-built homes for people in Sydney.

Dr Olav Nielssen is working to provide permanent housing for people with chronic mental illness. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

"It's a really cost saving and efficient form of care," Dr Nielssen said.

He believed state governments should fund more long-term housing models to help alleviate homelessness.

"It's just embarrassing to see people sleeping in the open in such a rich society.

"It's very much in our self-interest too because it costs more to neglect the mentally ill than what it does to house and treat them."

An SA government spokesperson said it was spending $78.6 million for homelessness services in 2026–27.

"Our specialist homelessness services provide access to 261 crisis beds, alongside 459 transitional housing properties across the four regional Homelessness Alliances," the spokesperson said.

An integrated social housing network for people with mental health challenges opened this month in Clearview in Adelaide's northern suburbs.

"Haven Clearview is a Mind Australia supported housing service for people experiencing mental health challenges, with NDIS-funded supports," the spokesperson said.

The facility received $5.8 million in state government funding and was said to be the first of its kind in the state.

World.title: Live: Helen Haines still critical, more than two days after car attack
World.content:
Cathy McGowan held the seat of Indi from 2013 until her retirement from politics in 2019.

Helen Haines has held the seat since Ms McGowan's retirement.

Ms McGowan attended a vigil for Ms Haines in the north-east Victorian city of Wodonga last night and says she's glad Ms Haines is still alive, despite her horrific ordeal.

"Her heart and her brain are there, she's alive. So, grasp the mercies that we've got, be grateful for what we've got, and continue to support her family as it does its next bit of work," she says. "Her brain, her wisdom and her personality are still going to be with us."

Cathy McGowan spoke to the ABC on Wednesday. (ABC News)

Ms McGowan joined the chorus of MPs pleading for the political temperature to be turned down as Victoria heads into the state election next month.

World.title: Helen Haines attack live updates: Indi MP loses both legs, husband confirms as vigil held in Wodonga; more details emerge about alleged attacker Brendan Nugent’s past
World.content:
Police are not ruling out laying further serious charges against Brendan Nugent, the man accused of attacking Haines, as detectives continue to examine possible motives and his potential connections to the sovereign citizen conspiracy movement.

A trail of deleted social media posts from Nugent reveals years of serious psychological struggle as police warn of a dangerous link between extreme ideology and “mental health vulnerabilities”.

Nugent appeared in Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court yesterday, staring vacantly from the dock as he was remanded behind bars without applying for bail.

A sketch of Brendan Nugent in Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday. Anita Lester

Magistrate Allison Vaughan ordered that Nugent be seen by a mental health professional as he began his first stint behind bars.

Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said yesterday detectives were still working to understand the “deliberate” attack and whether Nugent had any personal contact with Haines or had been waiting for her outside her Wangaratta office.

Nugent is to appear before court again in February.

World.title: Opening date locked in for final stage of Sydney’s M1 metro line
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWSydney Metro Opening date locked in for final stage of Sydney’s M1 metro line Matt O'Sullivan October 22, 2026 — 6:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The final section of Sydney’s $30 billion M1 metro rail line will open to passengers on Friday, October 30, ending more than two years of major disruptions for commuters who have been forced to catch replacement buses in the south-west. The NSW government confirmed the date for the opening of the 13-kilometre stretch of the metro rail line between Sydenham and Bankstown in a posting to one of Premier Chris Minns’ social media accounts. The premier will hold a press conference on Thursday to announce the opening. Dulwich Hill station, pictured, is one of 10 on the M1 line’s south-west section. Sitthixay Ditthavong The long-awaited opening has hinged on approval for passenger services by the national rail regulator, which was last week handed the final safety case and supporting evidence by the M1 line’s private operator, Metro Trains Sydney. It is later than a target date of “mid-October”, which was detailed in confidential Sydney Metro documents earlier this year.



The ribbon cutting for the metro line on October 30 will come just over two weeks before a new rail timetable for the Sydney Trains network is introduced. This will have the greatest impact to services on the T4 Eastern Suburbs and Illawarra line. As part of the timetable changes on November 15, all T4 trains will stop at Sydenham station to enable passengers to switch to driverless trains on the M1 metro line. Bankstown metro station is finally set to welcome commuters. Sitthixay Ditthavong To assure safety regulators, the government will keep a tiny fraction of the 360 platform screen doors closed when the south-west section opens. Three screen doors will remain closed at Dulwich Hill station, and one each at Canterbury, Campsie and Marrickville to reduce the risk of “even minor safety issue”. Curved platforms have required 170 mechanical gap fillers to be installed at eight stations. The small hydraulic platforms extend to the metro carriages before screen doors open, ensuring that commuters can safely step on and off.



The opening of the M1 line’s south-west section will finally put an end to pink-coloured replacement buses, which have significantly lengthened commuters’ trips along the corridor and cost taxpayers about $200 million. Related Article Sydney Metro Why Sydney’s metro line won’t be getting longer trains Tens of thousands of commuters have had to catch the replacement buses each day between Sydenham and Bankstown since September 2024, when the T3 heavy rail line was shut to complete the final 13-kilometre section of the M1 line. In mid-2018, the former Coalition government told commuters that the line would need to be closed for three to six months. Even before it closed in September 2024, the Minns government said the shutdown might last longer than its earlier estimates of 12 months. The total cost of the city and south-west sections of the 66-kilometre M1 line is forecast to cost as much as $23 billion, up from $21.6 billion previously.



The government has not broken out the cost of each section. However, the increase of almost $1.5 billion in the forecast last December is mostly due to the final stage between Sydenham and Bankstown given the city section opened in August 2024. World.title: Victoria’s long-awaited public school deal comes with a catch
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaSchool funding Victoria’s long-awaited public school deal comes with a catch Kieran Rooney and Angus Delaney October 22, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Victorian government will fully fund public schools by 2031, and could get there as early as 2029, after signing a long-called-for agreement with the Commonwealth to meet the state’s Gonski requirements. Premier Ben Carroll will on Thursday also announce a major funding boost for Victorian integrity and anti-corruption agencies. Premier Ben Carroll and Victorian Education Minister Gabrielle Williams have signed an agreement with the Commonwealth for schools funding. Eddie Jim Carroll revealed on Wednesday he had delivered on his promise to sign an agreement with the federal government before the November 28 state election to meet the School Resource Standard (SRS), the minimum requirement established under the landmark 2012 Gonski review of school funding. The Age revealed last year that the state government had secretly delayed its promise to fulfil the reforms by providing 75 per cent of the SRS matched by 25 per cent from the Commonwealth, from 2028 until 2031.



The delay denied public schools access to $2.4 billion in funding from the earlier start date and left the state and federal governments operating on transitional, yearly funding agreements. Related Article Education ‘Humans were built to learn from other humans’: The schools capping screen time Victorian Education Minister Gabrielle Williams on Wednesday confirmed a long-term deal had been signed that would include the state meeting full funding for public schools by 2031 and run until 2034. Though public schools will still have to wait longer than promised, Williams said the agreement had a unique provision saying the state government will seek to bring that funding forward, if possible, to as soon as 2029. This would rely on Victoria being able to reach its end of the bargain – 75 per cent of the SRS, earlier.



“We are and will continue to aggressively seek the sorts of budget efficiencies which will enable us to continue to prioritise frontline services,” Williams said. Over the life of the agreement in its current form, Victoria will spend $13.6 billion while the Commonwealth will spend $2.5 billion. Details of the agreement published online show most of the additional funding will flow from 2029, with the deal heavily back-ended. Commonwealth funding will reach 25 per cent in 2034, similar to their agreement with New South Wales. Justin Mullaly, president of the Victorian branch of the Australian Education Union, said the agreement would deliver billions in extra funding, but criticised the delay.



“We welcome the certainty and increases that the deal provides, but the arrangements confirmed today means Victorian public schools will not receive some of the additional funding as soon as other states and territories,” he said. “The delay in signing and the decision to back-end the deal, will shortchange Victorian public schools by hundreds of millions of dollars over the next few years. “Funding delays have real consequences, and this needs to be addressed.” In another major funding commitment, Labor on Thursday will announce $139.5 million in additional funding to the Independent Broad-based Anti-Corruption Commission (IBAC), Victorian Ombudsman and Integrity Oversight Victoria. The boost follows long-awaited reforms to IBAC passed last month, which included granting the watchdog broader jurisdiction to investigate corruption, hold public hearings more often and have “follow-the-money” powers to investigate businesses that receive public money.



Provided over four years, the extra money is locked in and not an election commitment. Related Article Analysis

IBAC Victoria’s anti-corruption watchdog finally has teeth. These are its new powers “We’ve strengthened IBAC’s powers, now we’re providing an immediate uplift in their resources to stamp out corruption,” Special Minister of State Ingrid Stitt said. “Victorians rightly expect public money to be spent properly; we’re making sure this happens.” The reforms come after Labor was dogged by allegations of corruption on taxpayer-funded construction sites and allegations of misconduct.



Carroll promised to strengthen IBAC in his first press conference as premier in July when he committed to calling a royal commission into the construction sector. Both IBAC and the Ombudsman earlier this year warned they may have to shelve investigations and cut staff after being under-resourced by the state budget. Integrity advocates, the Greens and former IBAC commissioner Robert Redlich have previously called for IBAC’s budget to be set by parliament, rather than the government. World.title: The 14 most anticipated TV shows still to come this year
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

These days, television never stops. In the earlier broadcast network era, new releases would disappear as the end of the year approached and the all-important ratings period came to a close. But with the growth of streaming, nearly every week on the calendar has a new release of some kind. The close of 2026 may be in sight, but there are still numerous shows – from blockbuster adaptations to crucial documentaries – lined up to debut. Here are 14 to watch out for. Jaalen Best (right) as Muhammad Ali in The Greatest. The Greatest Few sporting lives have been as immense as that of Muhammad Ali’s. The iconic American boxer was charismatic, gifted and often confronted by controversy. For the creator of this biographical series, Ben Watkins (Cross), there’s no shortage of material to embrace, and no shortage of biopic cliches to avoid. The estate of the former heavyweight champion of the world helped produce the show, with relative newcomer Jaalen Best (All American: Homecoming) given the demanding lead role. Amazon Prime Video, November 4. Ned Jampijinpa-Hargraves in 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback. 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback Already acquired by Netflix for international release, this true-crime docuseries examines the fateful moment in 2019 when 19-year-old Warlpiri-Luritja man Kumanjayi Walker was fatally shot in his grandmother’s home by 28-year-old Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe. Directed by Darren Dale (Total Control), the four episodes chart the pair’s differing lives as well as the private and public aftermath of their intersection – Rolfe was charged with murder but was acquitted by a jury in March 2022. NITV/SBS, November 10.



Kristina Bogic as Anya in The Body. The Body Quinn Shephard, who made the crushing true-crime drama Under the Bridge, sticks with teenage protagonists for this new series, but they’re having a lot more wicked fun in this horror thriller. The setting is a Catholic girls’ school where the illicit initiation party for the dance team gets out of hand – did they make a pact with the devil in exchange for competitive success? The absurd and the supernatural get heated up in a narrative that looks keen to push some enjoyably insightful buttons. Netflix, November 11. Nazeem Hussain and Urzila Carlson in Separated at Birth. Separated at Birth Coping with unexpected chaos is the comic engine of this six-part series from comedian and actor Nazeem Hussain (Orange is the New Brown). Set in Melbourne, the comedy stars Hussain as paramedic Sameer, whose wife asks for a divorce while they’re still in the birthing suite with their newborn. As Sameer struggles with co-parenting and family expectations, his unlikely ally – and new tenant – is his straight-talking friend and co-worker Donna (Urzila Carlson). ABC, November 11. Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan in 12 12 12.



12 12 12 Set against Europe’s cobblestoned streets and imposing mountains, this twisty heist thriller about the daring robbery of a Swiss bank unfolds across three timelines: the 12 months planning the robbery, the 12 minutes executing it, and the 12 days required to get away safely. The plot centres on two obsessive foes, with Jamie Dornan (The Fall) as criminal mastermind Paul Galvin and Anthony Mackie (Twisted Metal) as pursuing FBI agent Jack Strickland. Done right, this should be catnip for Hijack and Lupin fans. Apple TV, November 13. Rose Byrne as Samantha and Meghann Fahy as Charlotte in The Good Daughter. The Good Daughter The troubled history that lingers between estranged sisters underpins this crime drama, which stars Rose Byrne (Platonic) and Meghann Fahy (The Perfect Couple) as siblings Samantha and Charlotte Quinn, who are forced to reunite when they have to care for their ailing criminal lawyer father and defend his new client, a young woman charged with a double murder. Are their traumatic family secrets waiting to surface? Absolutely. Is this a formidable pair of leads? Absolutely. Stan*, November 13. Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison in The Altruists. The Altruists



They were an idealistic young couple committed to changing the world. They ended up being responsible for the $12 billion collapse of a global cryptocurrency exchange, blaming each other in court, and receiving prison sentences. The headline-making financial saga of FTX is dramatised through the relationship of its founders, Sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle, Say Nothing) and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner, Ozark). There is some jaw-dropping reporting for this limited series to draw on. Netflix, November 18. Justine Clarke, Kate Box and Mandy McElhinney in Shakedown. Shakedown The robodebt scandal, where welfare recipients were unlawfully issued incorrect debt notices by the Australian government, remains a shameful national scandal. Television’s first reply was the essential SBS documentary series, The People vs Robodebt, with the second being this four-part drama about those who empowered the scheme and those who suffered from their actions. Justine Clarke (RFDS), Kate Box (Deadloch), and Mandy McElhinney (Wakefield) lead the ensemble cast. ABC, November 22. Michelle Yeoh as Olwen and Hunter Schafer as Cora in Blade Runner 2099. Blade Runner 2099 Blade Runner is an intoxicating franchise, and the seeds planted by Ridley Scott’s ground-breaking 1982 science fiction movie continue to inspire new iterations. The latest is a sequel series, set further forward in a future Los Angeles where the Replicant cyborgs are now the ruling class above humanity’s second-class citizens. The trailer looks amazing, but the story – with Michelle Yeoh (Everything Everywhere All at Once) as a Replicant police officer and Hunter Schafer (Euphoria) as her desperate human partner – has to deliver. Amazon Prime Video, November 25.



From left: Emma Corrin, Freya Mavor, Olivia Colman, Hopey Parish, Rhea Norwood and Hollie Avery in Pride and Prejudice. Pride and Prejudice How do you adapt a beloved novel that’s already been on the screen numerous times? “Boldly” appears to be the answer of English author, podcaster and screenwriter Dolly Alderton, whose take on Jane Austen’s 1813 novel of romantic manners is reportedly “progressive”. Alderton certainly has a terrific cast, with Emma Corrin (The Crown) and Jack Lowden (Slow Horses) as respectively the unwed Elizabeth Bennet and her less than conventional suitor Mr Darcy, plus Olivia Colman (Fleabag) as Elizabeth’s mother. Netflix, December 3. Clive Owen as John Bennett Ramsey and Melissa McCarthy as Patsy Ramsey in The Murder of JonBenet Ramsey. The Murder of JonBenet Ramsey Aside from OJ Simpson’s murder trial, no criminal case has exerted more of a distorting hold on America than the 1996 murder of six-year-old JonBenet Ramsey in her Colorado family home. With Melissa McCarthy (Nine Perfect Strangers) and Clive Owen (Impeachment: American Crime Story) as JonBenet’s parents (and suspects) Patsy and John, this true crime drama faces numerous crucial choices in how it unfolds the tragic events. Netflix, December 10. Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter in the Harry Potter TV series.

World.title: ASX set for flat start, Wall Street climbs; Meta ordered to pay $36 billion in privacy case; Tesla results ahead
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set for flat start, Wall Street climbs; Meta ordered to pay $36 billion in privacy case; Tesla results ahead Stan Choe October 22, 2026 — 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The US stock market is ticking higher as strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies offset updates from Netflix and AT&T that investors found disappointing. The S&P 500 rose 0.6 per cent and was on track for a third straight modest gain. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 205 points, or 0.4 per cent, in early afternoon trade and the Nasdaq composite was 1.2 per cent higher. Wall Street is digesting a raft of results from high-profile companies. AP Futures are pointing to a flat start for the Australian sharemarket. The ASX added 0.2 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US70.32¢ at 5.25am AEDT. SpaceX helped lead the market and climbed 10.1 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company.



Tesla, which will report its latest quarterly results after the closing bell, rose 3.6 per cent and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. Related Article Opinion

Investment banking Could a 164-year-old Swiss giant quit Switzerland? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Meanwhile, a judge has ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $US25 billion ($36 billion) after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy and content moderation policies on Facebook. Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount. The state had sought $US35 billion to $US40 billion. Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws when a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, harvested Facebook user data to generate targeted political ads for the 2016 election. Meta will release its results after the closing bell. Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 3.7 per cent, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 9 per cent.



Expectations are high for profit growth during the summer, and companies will need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made toward records despite worries about high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street. Winnebago was able to report a more resilient profit than analysts expected even as high fuel prices and frustration among US shoppers restrain interest in recreational vehicles, for example. CEO Michael Happe said its more expensive towable RVs are a tougher sell, but customers are interested in its “more accessible” offerings. On the losing side of Wall Street was Netflix, which fell 5.2 per cent even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. The company’s forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts’ expectations. AT&T fell 6.5 per cent even though it likewise delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts’ expectations. Among AI stocks, which have been at the centre of the market’s action in recent weeks, the movements remained unsettled.



After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centres may slow because of how much more expensive it’s become to borrow money. Related Article Opinion

Gadgets I love Apple’s iPhone Duo. But here’s why you shouldn’t buy one David Swan Technology editor CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly volatile. It bounced between an early gain of nearly 4 per cent and a drop of 4.5 per cent Wednesday morning before moderating to a dip of 1.1 per cent. A day earlier, it had careened between similarly wide gains and losses. Other AI-linked stocks were more resilient. Nvidia’s rise of 1.8 per cent was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500. Besides SpaceX’s profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of “increased demand for AI platforms,” and its stock rallied 9.3 per cent.



Another potential boost for the AI industry came from an easing of Treasury yields, which help dictate how expensive loans are for the US government, companies and regular Americans. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.10 per cent from 5.12 per cent late Tuesday, though it remains far above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation higher. Oil prices remained unsteady on Wednesday following big recent swings on uncertainty about when the energy industry can return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude added 0.1 per cent to $US108.95 after flipping up and down through the morning. It’s been yo-yoing between $US97 and $US112 in October. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength. World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘On repeat’: Labuschagne’s maddening exit puts Test career in peril Daniel Brettig October 22, 2026 — 5:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Gqeberha: Marnus Labuschagne’s Test career is again hanging by the slimmest of threads after he was out twice in a single humiliating day for Australia, as coach Andrew McDonald admitted speaking “on repeat” about the number three’s failure to make big scores. In perhaps the most maddening of all the 13 wickets to fall on day four at St George’s Park, Labuschagne had got to 39 when he tried to loft spinner Simon Harmer against a strong wind, only to watch the ball hold up nicely for Marco Jansen to claim the catch. South Africa’s Anrich Nortje, right, celebrates the wicket of Australia’s Marnus Labuschagne, left on day four. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe It’s now well over three years since Labuschagne’s last Test hundred, and his ninth score between 13 and 48 in the past 14 innings. In parallel, Cameron Green (abdominal strain) and Josh Inglis (broken finger) will both be fit to play in the third Test in Cape Town, while Cooper Connolly and Sam Harper are also available. “There’s probably some shots that players need to take back,” McDonald said. “He did a lot of hard work once again, and I think it feels like I’m on repeat around the amount of 30s that he has got, and you would say that’s been a danger period for him.



“What they had there, they had a good partnership going and starting to claw our way back into the game, albeit a long way behind the game from obviously the first innings’ disappointment. Yeah, so for me, when you do that hard work, you’ve got to cash in, and unfortunately, that wasn’t to be the case for Marn. “So he’d be disappointed. We’re disappointed, and we find ourselves in this situation. What I will say is, we’ve still got six wickets in hand, so there is a long way to go in the game. So we’ve got to conjure up some belief for tomorrow.” Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket This was Australia’s worst day under Cummins. Thirteen wickets made all kinds of bad history Australia are also facing a troubling scenario for Steve Smith, who was clearly affected by a neck injury in the first innings, and did not bat in his usual spot in the second. “He’s got a neck issue at the moment, it’s giving him some grief, and I think that was probably something that everyone sort of witnessed in that first innings, and he had to sort of adjust the way that he plays,” McDonald said. “Sometimes he changes his technique when he’s sort of fully fit.



“But he, yeah, he was limited in what he could do, and then yeah, we felt it was best to hopefully get the batting unit through to tomorrow, and then hopefully he’s better placed for that tomorrow. “You would have seen the physio working on him, so he’ll bat tomorrow. It’s not something that will rule him out of the innings, but it was just that it took a little bit more time than we expected on the back of the first innings.” South Africa’s Simon Harmer and Temba Bavuma celebrate the wicket of Marnus Labuschagne. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe McDonald refused to talk about selection for the next Test of the series in Cape Town mid-match, but highlighted both shot selection and the team’s inability to recognise and build partnerships as an issue of significant concern. “I think any time when anything’s done at that speed, it takes a couple of players to connect and communicate and navigate through that, and we weren’t able to get any partnerships,” he said. “And yeah, we’ve had some of these moments across the journey, so we’re not a perfect batting unit. I’ve never said that we are.



“And yeah, the speed in which that happened, and the momentum that you know South Africa were able to gain through that, and yeah, we didn’t envisage coming here and yeah, looking at a follow-on. “You do have to give a little bit of credit to the South African attack as well. The way they exposed some of that, some of our deficiencies in that, I don’t take anything away from that. But there was some batter error there. I think we are better than that. But as it sits right now, I can’t defend that.” Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket ‘Testosterone to burn’: Rabada rejoins battle with Smith after 2018 flashpoint Pressed on questions over the likes of Labuschagne, Nic Maddinson and Beau Webster, McDonald said: “I never sit in a press conference in the middle of the game and start to talk about selection for the next Test match. I think it’s too early to navigate through that, it’s something that we do post-match. We’ll work through that process as we lead into Cape Town. So as we sit here right now, there’ll be no selection chat.” Given their grim position in this game, McDonald conceded that they may have to deal with the unexpected situation of going to Newlands in Cape Town for the first time since the infamous 2018 sandpapergate match with the score at 1-1.



“Those players that sit in that room are still the same players that performed exceptionally well last week,” he said. “I have great belief and trust that the skill sets in that room, in particular tomorrow, can go out there and potentially turn this one around. “If that doesn’t unfold, then we move into Cape Town and we reload and we go again. A great strength of this group is on significant setbacks, and I’d say this is a significant setback in terms of the way that we played. We’ve been able to respond, and that’s been one of the strengths. So, looking forward to that opportunity tomorrow and further down the track in Cape Town.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Arson squad boss warns firebombers off Brad Battin’s ‘innocent’ neighbours
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Arson squad boss warns firebombers off Brad Battin’s ‘innocent’ neighbours Fiona Byrne Updated October 22, 2026 — 5:01am ,first published 12:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
