Shadow police minister Brad Battin has, for the second week running, had Melbourne’s plague of arson attacks fall on his doorstep. Last week, CBD brought news of an attempted firebombing at the cafe next to Battin’s Berwick electorate office on October 12. A cafe next to Brad Battin’s office in Berwick has twice been targeted in attempted firebombings. Simon Schluter Now it’s been revealed that in the very early hours of Sunday, the offenders returned for a second attempt at incinerating the joint with police discovering “tens of litres of accelerant” left inside the cafe when the crooks were disturbed. Fortunately, no one was injured. In a highly disturbing twist, Victoria Police has confirmed that the offenders have been targeting the wrong address.



Arson and explosives squad Detective Inspector Chris Murray didn’t mince words, describing the two attacks as incredibly reckless and dangerous acts that have caused fear, disruption and significant distress. Murray said there was the “potential for catastrophic consequences not only for the business owners but also for surrounding properties and members of the public” from the latest attack. “This level of violence and disregard for community safety is completely unacceptable,” Murray said. “In this case, the business and its owners appear to have been wrongly targeted, while the person believed to be the intended victim has no association whatsoever with the cafe. “Innocent people are being placed at risk because criminals are treating serious violence as a contract.”



We reached out to Battin on Wednesday for his view on crime across our city and the repeated firebombing attempts next door to his office. “Innocent small business owners are being put in danger because violent criminals are running amok under Labor,” Battin told us. “This is the frightening reality of crime after 12 years of Labor.” De Blasio, Moreno kick on in Melbourne In Melbourne, it is a given that any visiting international guest will have a brush with a football.



So it was just a matter of time before former mayor of New York City Bill de Blasio would eventually get his hands on a Sherrin – the only surprise was that it took four days. Loading De Blasio and urbanist Carlos Moreno, both in town as guests of the Melbourne Assembly, were gifted footballs at a Committee For Melbourne networking evening on Wednesday. De Blasio showed some sporting form, immediately having a short kick to kick with the Committee For Melbourne’s Agostino Giramondo at the gathering. “Who here has insurance,” de Blasio asked before putting boot to ball.



We are pleased to report nothing got broken. Earlier in the week, de Blasio and Moreno were presented with AFL club jumpers – Carlton for Moreno and a Melbourne for de Blasio. Just what they will do with them is anyone’s guess, but footy as the city’s diplomatic currency continues unabated. ‘Not how I wanted it to end’: Carrie Bickmore, Tommy Little end radio show After almost a decade as a radio team, Gold Logie winner Carrie Bickmore and comedian Tommy Little have called time on their Carrie & Tommy national drive show and will exit the Hit Network at the end of the year.



Bickmore fought back tears while making the announcement on air on Wednesday, while her co-host Little said it was “certainly not how I wanted it to end”. Carrie Bickmore and Tommy Little have been the Hit Network’s national drive radio team for almost 10 years. The future of the show had been a talking point in industry circles for some months. “It’s not every day you get to come and have a laugh and call it your job with your best mate and the funniest guy in the country,” an emotional Bickmore said. “I think we’ve been able to do something on this show that often people are too scared to do, to talk about stuff that sometimes is uncomfortable. We hope that we’ve had some small impact on your life in some small way … [and been] company for you on shitty days and [made] you laugh.”



Little said he was sad that this chapter of his radio career was coming to an end. “I loved this job and I would have kept doing it for a long time, but I don’t always get my way,” Little said. “I feel very grateful. I feel very lucky to have had the opportunity. We’re going to be on air until the end of the year, and we’re going to try and make the best radio we can.” Bickmore is rumoured to have been courted by ARN over recent months to move to rival KIIS FM to helm that station’s drive show in 2027. Whether Little was part of that discussion is unclear. The KIIS drive shift is up for grabs with the Will & Woody drive show, hosted by Will McMahon and Woody Whitelaw, finishing up at the end of the year.



Matthew O’Reilly, the head of broadcast content for Southern Cross Austereo, owner of the Hit Network, informed staff via an internal memo of the end of the Carrie & Tommy show. “Over the next few weeks, we look forward to celebrating everything Carrie and Tommy have given to their listeners over the last 10 years,” O’Reilly said in the note. “Thank you to Carrie, Tommy and everyone who worked on the show, pouring their energy, creativity, and passion into making it what it is today. We wish them the very best for what’s next.” No announcement has been made yet as to who will replace the pair in the drive shift next year. Pencil case to blame for premier’s petrol station blunder



It is not quite the dog-ate-my-homework excuse, but Premier Ben Carroll has blamed a pencil case, forgetfulness and human error for an embarrassing moment at the bowser. Carroll, who has toughened up the state government’s crackdown on crime since assuming the role of premier in July, found himself on the wrong side of the law on Monday night after he filled up his car at a petrol station in Airport West and drove off without paying. Loading “Late Monday night, I was running some errands and filled up the car with petrol. Found out yesterday I forgot to pay,” he fessed up on Wednesday morning. A call from Victoria Police to the Department of Parliamentary Services alerted the premier to the bungle, and Carroll returned to the service station to settle his bill on Tuesday night.



Related Article Melbourne Assembly Melbourne Assembly day three as it happened: Major events at risk if city ‘rests on its laurels’ “It shows that politicians are human beings and even premiers make mistakes,” Carroll said of the forgetful moment on Wednesday morning. Speaking at Melbourne Assembly, he said he was on dad duty and running errands when the accidental drive-off occurred. “Monday was a tough day for a lot of reasons, and I got home and I had a busy night on the phone, and my wife and I had a discussion,” Carroll said, referencing the attack on federal MP Helen Haines. “She [Carroll’s wife, Fiona] was going to return [daughter] Maddie’s friend’s pencil case. I said, ‘I’ll do it and I’ll get petrol’. And then I found out the following day I didn’t pay,” he said.



“That has since been rectified.” As it happens, Carroll is not alone in being a politician with problems at the petrol pump. Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush Penny Stephens “I have been contacted by the former deputy premier John Thwaites, who told me, ‘Don’t worry, Ben. I didn’t pay for the petrol, and I also drove off with the nozzle in the car, with the petrol hose together’,” Carroll said. “And that made me feel a lot better.” Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush also weighed in on the petrol palaver on Wednesday, saying not every drive-off was a criminal matter.



“Our point of view is that a petrol drive-off is a civil matter until it’s proven otherwise,” Bush said. “If it turns out that it’s a criminal matter, there was intent, etc, etc, charges will follow subsequently. But everyone’s got the opportunity to address an error.” The commissioner said he was aware that the premier had paid his outstanding debt. “We’re very careful not to criminalise every petrol drive-off. We do understand, and I’m very empathetic and sympathetic to petrol station owners who do suffer, but it’s not always criminal.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The secret (cringe-free) weapon for solo travellers looking to connect
World.content:
Reviews & adviceSavvy traveller The secret (cringe-free) weapon for solo travellers looking to connect Nina Karnikowski October 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If the thought of marching into a hotel happy hour and introducing yourself to strangers makes you want to run to your room and hide, you’re not alone. As someone who occasionally runs group trips, I can confirm that even the most competent adults revert to high school disco mode when faced with a room full of strangers: everyone wants to connect, but nobody wants to be the first person on the dance floor. Fortunately, making friends while travelling solo doesn’t require hostel pub crawls or even an outgoing personality, just a few simple tricks and a willingness to occasionally put your book down. The beauty of activities is that you don’t have to invent reasons to talk to people. iStock First, choose stays that offer natural opportunities to connect. That might mean a hostel if you’re on a budget, or a design hotel with a great lobby bar or co-working space.



If your room feels like a luxury cocoon, though, don’t be surprised if you rarely emerge from it. Better to choose somewhere that nudges you out into the world. 



Because solo dining can be the Big Bad Wolf of solo travel, use counter seating as your secret weapon, where you’re usually shoulder-to-shoulder with other diners. And resist the urge to retreat behind your phone; people are much more willing to approach you when your eyes aren’t glued to a glowing rectangle. Related Article Opinion

Tours After six months of travelling solo, I needed a holiday from myself Georgia Dunkley Travel writer When conversations do happen, remember there’s an art to making good chat without sounding like you’re conducting a job interview. Ask questions you’d genuinely like the answer to. “What’s been the highlight of your trip so far?” tends to lead somewhere much more interesting than, “so what do you do?” These questions can be supremely practical, too. Need someone to take your photo? Trying to work out whether you’ve boarded the right ferry, or how the train ticket machine works? Ask the person next to you. People are usually warmer when they’re responding to a request than a random introduction. It also helps to remember that most people aren’t scrutinising you nearly as much as you think they are. They’re worrying about whether they’re being weird, too. And hey, if none of this works and you still find yourself solo, there are worse fates than a great meal, a good book and nobody to answer to. One of the joys of travelling alone is discovering that your own company can be pretty excellent, too.

Police are not ruling out laying further serious charges against Brendan Nugent, the man accused of attacking Haines, as detectives continue to examine possible motives and his potential connections to the sovereign citizen conspiracy movement.

A trail of deleted social media posts from Nugent reveals years of serious psychological struggle as police warn of a dangerous link between extreme ideology and “mental health vulnerabilities”.

Nugent appeared in Wangaratta Magistrates’ Court yesterday, staring vacantly from the dock as he was remanded behind bars without applying for bail.

World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWSydney Metro Opening date locked in for final stage of Sydney’s M1 metro line Matt O'Sullivan October 22, 2026 — 6:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The final section of Sydney’s $30 billion M1 metro rail line will open to passengers on Friday, October 30, ending more than two years of major disruptions for commuters who have been forced to catch replacement buses in the south-west. The NSW government confirmed the date for the opening of the 13-kilometre stretch of the metro rail line between Sydenham and Bankstown in a posting to one of Premier Chris Minns’ social media accounts. The premier will hold a press conference on Thursday to announce the opening. Dulwich Hill station, pictured, is one of 10 on the M1 line’s south-west section. Sitthixay Ditthavong The long-awaited opening has hinged on approval for passenger services by the national rail regulator, which was last week handed the final safety case and supporting evidence by the M1 line’s private operator, Metro Trains Sydney. It is later than a target date of “mid-October”, which was detailed in confidential Sydney Metro documents earlier this year.



The ribbon cutting for the metro line on October 30 will come just over two weeks before a new rail timetable for the Sydney Trains network is introduced. This will have the greatest impact to services on the T4 Eastern Suburbs and Illawarra line. As part of the timetable changes on November 15, all T4 trains will stop at Sydenham station to enable passengers to switch to driverless trains on the M1 metro line. Bankstown metro station is finally set to welcome commuters. Sitthixay Ditthavong To assure safety regulators, the government will keep a tiny fraction of the 360 platform screen doors closed when the south-west section opens. Three screen doors will remain closed at Dulwich Hill station, and one each at Canterbury, Campsie and Marrickville to reduce the risk of “even minor safety issue”. Curved platforms have required 170 mechanical gap fillers to be installed at eight stations. The small hydraulic platforms extend to the metro carriages before screen doors open, ensuring that commuters can safely step on and off.



The opening of the M1 line’s south-west section will finally put an end to pink-coloured replacement buses, which have significantly lengthened commuters’ trips along the corridor and cost taxpayers about $200 million. Related Article Sydney Metro Why Sydney’s metro line won’t be getting longer trains Tens of thousands of commuters have had to catch the replacement buses each day between Sydenham and Bankstown since September 2024, when the T3 heavy rail line was shut to complete the final 13-kilometre section of the M1 line. In mid-2018, the former Coalition government told commuters that the line would need to be closed for three to six months. Even before it closed in September 2024, the Minns government said the shutdown might last longer than its earlier estimates of 12 months. The total cost of the city and south-west sections of the 66-kilometre M1 line is forecast to cost as much as $23 billion, up from $21.6 billion previously.



The government has not broken out the cost of each section. However, the increase of almost $1.5 billion in the forecast last December is mostly due to the final stage between Sydenham and Bankstown given the city section opened in August 2024. World.title: Victoria’s long-awaited public school deal comes with a catch
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaSchool funding Victoria’s long-awaited public school deal comes with a catch Kieran Rooney and Angus Delaney October 22, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Victorian government will fully fund public schools by 2031, and could get there as early as 2029, after signing a long-called-for agreement with the Commonwealth to meet the state’s Gonski requirements. Premier Ben Carroll will on Thursday also announce a major funding boost for Victorian integrity and anti-corruption agencies. Premier Ben Carroll and Victorian Education Minister Gabrielle Williams have signed an agreement with the Commonwealth for schools funding. Eddie Jim Carroll revealed on Wednesday he had delivered on his promise to sign an agreement with the federal government before the November 28 state election to meet the School Resource Standard (SRS), the minimum requirement established under the landmark 2012 Gonski review of school funding. The Age revealed last year that the state government had secretly delayed its promise to fulfil the reforms by providing 75 per cent of the SRS matched by 25 per cent from the Commonwealth, from 2028 until 2031.



The delay denied public schools access to $2.4 billion in funding from the earlier start date and left the state and federal governments operating on transitional, yearly funding agreements. Related Article Education ‘Humans were built to learn from other humans’: The schools capping screen time Victorian Education Minister Gabrielle Williams on Wednesday confirmed a long-term deal had been signed that would include the state meeting full funding for public schools by 2031 and run until 2034. Though public schools will still have to wait longer than promised, Williams said the agreement had a unique provision saying the state government will seek to bring that funding forward, if possible, to as soon as 2029. This would rely on Victoria being able to reach its end of the bargain – 75 per cent of the SRS, earlier.



“We are and will continue to aggressively seek the sorts of budget efficiencies which will enable us to continue to prioritise frontline services,” Williams said. Over the life of the agreement in its current form, Victoria will spend $13.6 billion while the Commonwealth will spend $2.5 billion. Details of the agreement published online show most of the additional funding will flow from 2029, with the deal heavily back-ended. Commonwealth funding will reach 25 per cent in 2034, similar to their agreement with New South Wales. Justin Mullaly, president of the Victorian branch of the Australian Education Union, said the agreement would deliver billions in extra funding, but criticised the delay.



“We welcome the certainty and increases that the deal provides, but the arrangements confirmed today means Victorian public schools will not receive some of the additional funding as soon as other states and territories,” he said. “The delay in signing and the decision to back-end the deal, will shortchange Victorian public schools by hundreds of millions of dollars over the next few years. “Funding delays have real consequences, and this needs to be addressed.” In another major funding commitment, Labor on Thursday will announce $139.5 million in additional funding to the Independent Broad-based Anti-Corruption Commission (IBAC), Victorian Ombudsman and Integrity Oversight Victoria. The boost follows long-awaited reforms to IBAC passed last month, which included granting the watchdog broader jurisdiction to investigate corruption, hold public hearings more often and have “follow-the-money” powers to investigate businesses that receive public money.



Provided over four years, the extra money is locked in and not an election commitment. Related Article Analysis

IBAC Victoria’s anti-corruption watchdog finally has teeth. These are its new powers “We’ve strengthened IBAC’s powers, now we’re providing an immediate uplift in their resources to stamp out corruption,” Special Minister of State Ingrid Stitt said. “Victorians rightly expect public money to be spent properly; we’re making sure this happens.” The reforms come after Labor was dogged by allegations of corruption on taxpayer-funded construction sites and allegations of misconduct.



Carroll promised to strengthen IBAC in his first press conference as premier in July when he committed to calling a royal commission into the construction sector. Both IBAC and the Ombudsman earlier this year warned they may have to shelve investigations and cut staff after being under-resourced by the state budget. Integrity advocates, the Greens and former IBAC commissioner Robert Redlich have previously called for IBAC’s budget to be set by parliament, rather than the government. World.title: The 14 most anticipated TV shows still to come this year
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

These days, television never stops. In the earlier broadcast network era, new releases would disappear as the end of the year approached and the all-important ratings period came to a close. But with the growth of streaming, nearly every week on the calendar has a new release of some kind. The close of 2026 may be in sight, but there are still numerous shows – from blockbuster adaptations to crucial documentaries – lined up to debut. Here are 14 to watch out for. Jaalen Best (right) as Muhammad Ali in The Greatest. The Greatest Few sporting lives have been as immense as that of Muhammad Ali’s. The iconic American boxer was charismatic, gifted and often confronted by controversy. For the creator of this biographical series, Ben Watkins (Cross), there’s no shortage of material to embrace, and no shortage of biopic cliches to avoid. The estate of the former heavyweight champion of the world helped produce the show, with relative newcomer Jaalen Best (All American: Homecoming) given the demanding lead role. Amazon Prime Video, November 4. Ned Jampijinpa-Hargraves in 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback. 2.6 Seconds: Death in the Outback Already acquired by Netflix for international release, this true-crime docuseries examines the fateful moment in 2019 when 19-year-old Warlpiri-Luritja man Kumanjayi Walker was fatally shot in his grandmother’s home by 28-year-old Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe. Directed by Darren Dale (Total Control), the four episodes chart the pair’s differing lives as well as the private and public aftermath of their intersection – Rolfe was charged with murder but was acquitted by a jury in March 2022. NITV/SBS, November 10.



Kristina Bogic as Anya in The Body. The Body Quinn Shephard, who made the crushing true-crime drama Under the Bridge, sticks with teenage protagonists for this new series, but they’re having a lot more wicked fun in this horror thriller. The setting is a Catholic girls’ school where the illicit initiation party for the dance team gets out of hand – did they make a pact with the devil in exchange for competitive success? The absurd and the supernatural get heated up in a narrative that looks keen to push some enjoyably insightful buttons. Netflix, November 11. Nazeem Hussain and Urzila Carlson in Separated at Birth. Separated at Birth Coping with unexpected chaos is the comic engine of this six-part series from comedian and actor Nazeem Hussain (Orange is the New Brown). Set in Melbourne, the comedy stars Hussain as paramedic Sameer, whose wife asks for a divorce while they’re still in the birthing suite with their newborn. As Sameer struggles with co-parenting and family expectations, his unlikely ally – and new tenant – is his straight-talking friend and co-worker Donna (Urzila Carlson). ABC, November 11. Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan in 12 12 12.



12 12 12 Set against Europe’s cobblestoned streets and imposing mountains, this twisty heist thriller about the daring robbery of a Swiss bank unfolds across three timelines: the 12 months planning the robbery, the 12 minutes executing it, and the 12 days required to get away safely. The plot centres on two obsessive foes, with Jamie Dornan (The Fall) as criminal mastermind Paul Galvin and Anthony Mackie (Twisted Metal) as pursuing FBI agent Jack Strickland. Done right, this should be catnip for Hijack and Lupin fans. Apple TV, November 13. Rose Byrne as Samantha and Meghann Fahy as Charlotte in The Good Daughter. The Good Daughter The troubled history that lingers between estranged sisters underpins this crime drama, which stars Rose Byrne (Platonic) and Meghann Fahy (The Perfect Couple) as siblings Samantha and Charlotte Quinn, who are forced to reunite when they have to care for their ailing criminal lawyer father and defend his new client, a young woman charged with a double murder. Are their traumatic family secrets waiting to surface? Absolutely. Is this a formidable pair of leads? Absolutely. Stan*, November 13. Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison in The Altruists. The Altruists



They were an idealistic young couple committed to changing the world. They ended up being responsible for the $12 billion collapse of a global cryptocurrency exchange, blaming each other in court, and receiving prison sentences. The headline-making financial saga of FTX is dramatised through the relationship of its founders, Sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle, Say Nothing) and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner, Ozark). There is some jaw-dropping reporting for this limited series to draw on. Netflix, November 18. Justine Clarke, Kate Box and Mandy McElhinney in Shakedown. Shakedown The robodebt scandal, where welfare recipients were unlawfully issued incorrect debt notices by the Australian government, remains a shameful national scandal. Television’s first reply was the essential SBS documentary series, The People vs Robodebt, with the second being this four-part drama about those who empowered the scheme and those who suffered from their actions. Justine Clarke (RFDS), Kate Box (Deadloch), and Mandy McElhinney (Wakefield) lead the ensemble cast. ABC, November 22. Michelle Yeoh as Olwen and Hunter Schafer as Cora in Blade Runner 2099. Blade Runner 2099 Blade Runner is an intoxicating franchise, and the seeds planted by Ridley Scott’s ground-breaking 1982 science fiction movie continue to inspire new iterations. The latest is a sequel series, set further forward in a future Los Angeles where the Replicant cyborgs are now the ruling class above humanity’s second-class citizens. The trailer looks amazing, but the story – with Michelle Yeoh (Everything Everywhere All at Once) as a Replicant police officer and Hunter Schafer (Euphoria) as her desperate human partner – has to deliver. Amazon Prime Video, November 25.



From left: Emma Corrin, Freya Mavor, Olivia Colman, Hopey Parish, Rhea Norwood and Hollie Avery in Pride and Prejudice. Pride and Prejudice How do you adapt a beloved novel that’s already been on the screen numerous times? “Boldly” appears to be the answer of English author, podcaster and screenwriter Dolly Alderton, whose take on Jane Austen’s 1813 novel of romantic manners is reportedly “progressive”. Alderton certainly has a terrific cast, with Emma Corrin (The Crown) and Jack Lowden (Slow Horses) as respectively the unwed Elizabeth Bennet and her less than conventional suitor Mr Darcy, plus Olivia Colman (Fleabag) as Elizabeth’s mother. Netflix, December 3. Clive Owen as John Bennett Ramsey and Melissa McCarthy as Patsy Ramsey in The Murder of JonBenet Ramsey. The Murder of JonBenet Ramsey Aside from OJ Simpson’s murder trial, no criminal case has exerted more of a distorting hold on America than the 1996 murder of six-year-old JonBenet Ramsey in her Colorado family home. With Melissa McCarthy (Nine Perfect Strangers) and Clive Owen (Impeachment: American Crime Story) as JonBenet’s parents (and suspects) Patsy and John, this true crime drama faces numerous crucial choices in how it unfolds the tragic events. Netflix, December 10. Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter in the Harry Potter TV series.

The US stock market is ticking higher as strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies offset updates from Netflix and AT&T that investors found disappointing. The S&P 500 rose 0.6 per cent and was on track for a third straight modest gain. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 205 points, or 0.4 per cent, in early afternoon trade and the Nasdaq composite was 1.2 per cent higher. Wall Street is digesting a raft of results from high-profile companies. AP Futures are pointing to a flat start for the Australian sharemarket. The ASX added 0.2 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US70.32¢ at 5.25am AEDT. SpaceX helped lead the market and climbed 10.1 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company.



Tesla, which will report its latest quarterly results after the closing bell, rose 3.6 per cent and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. Related Article Opinion

Investment banking Could a 164-year-old Swiss giant quit Switzerland? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Meanwhile, a judge has ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $US25 billion ($36 billion) after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy and content moderation policies on Facebook. Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount. The state had sought $US35 billion to $US40 billion. Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws when a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, harvested Facebook user data to generate targeted political ads for the 2016 election. Meta will release its results after the closing bell. Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 3.7 per cent, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 9 per cent.



Expectations are high for profit growth during the summer, and companies will need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made toward records despite worries about high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street. Winnebago was able to report a more resilient profit than analysts expected even as high fuel prices and frustration among US shoppers restrain interest in recreational vehicles, for example. CEO Michael Happe said its more expensive towable RVs are a tougher sell, but customers are interested in its “more accessible” offerings. On the losing side of Wall Street was Netflix, which fell 5.2 per cent even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. The company’s forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts’ expectations. AT&T fell 6.5 per cent even though it likewise delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts’ expectations. Among AI stocks, which have been at the centre of the market’s action in recent weeks, the movements remained unsettled.



After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centres may slow because of how much more expensive it’s become to borrow money. Related Article Opinion

Gadgets I love Apple’s iPhone Duo. But here’s why you shouldn’t buy one David Swan Technology editor CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly volatile. It bounced between an early gain of nearly 4 per cent and a drop of 4.5 per cent Wednesday morning before moderating to a dip of 1.1 per cent. A day earlier, it had careened between similarly wide gains and losses. Other AI-linked stocks were more resilient. Nvidia’s rise of 1.8 per cent was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500. Besides SpaceX’s profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of “increased demand for AI platforms,” and its stock rallied 9.3 per cent.



Another potential boost for the AI industry came from an easing of Treasury yields, which help dictate how expensive loans are for the US government, companies and regular Americans. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.10 per cent from 5.12 per cent late Tuesday, though it remains far above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation higher. Oil prices remained unsteady on Wednesday following big recent swings on uncertainty about when the energy industry can return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude added 0.1 per cent to $US108.95 after flipping up and down through the morning. It’s been yo-yoing between $US97 and $US112 in October. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength. World.title: ‘On repeat’: Labuschagne’s maddening exit puts Test career in peril
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘On repeat’: Labuschagne’s maddening exit puts Test career in peril Daniel Brettig October 22, 2026 — 5:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Gqeberha: Marnus Labuschagne’s Test career is again hanging by the slimmest of threads after he was out twice in a single humiliating day for Australia, as coach Andrew McDonald admitted speaking “on repeat” about the number three’s failure to make big scores. In perhaps the most maddening of all the 13 wickets to fall on day four at St George’s Park, Labuschagne had got to 39 when he tried to loft spinner Simon Harmer against a strong wind, only to watch the ball hold up nicely for Marco Jansen to claim the catch. South Africa’s Anrich Nortje, right, celebrates the wicket of Australia’s Marnus Labuschagne, left on day four. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe It’s now well over three years since Labuschagne’s last Test hundred, and his ninth score between 13 and 48 in the past 14 innings. In parallel, Cameron Green (abdominal strain) and Josh Inglis (broken finger) will both be fit to play in the third Test in Cape Town, while Cooper Connolly and Sam Harper are also available. “There’s probably some shots that players need to take back,” McDonald said. “He did a lot of hard work once again, and I think it feels like I’m on repeat around the amount of 30s that he has got, and you would say that’s been a danger period for him.



“What they had there, they had a good partnership going and starting to claw our way back into the game, albeit a long way behind the game from obviously the first innings’ disappointment. Yeah, so for me, when you do that hard work, you’ve got to cash in, and unfortunately, that wasn’t to be the case for Marn. “So he’d be disappointed. We’re disappointed, and we find ourselves in this situation. What I will say is, we’ve still got six wickets in hand, so there is a long way to go in the game. So we’ve got to conjure up some belief for tomorrow.” Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket This was Australia’s worst day under Cummins. Thirteen wickets made all kinds of bad history Australia are also facing a troubling scenario for Steve Smith, who was clearly affected by a neck injury in the first innings, and did not bat in his usual spot in the second. “He’s got a neck issue at the moment, it’s giving him some grief, and I think that was probably something that everyone sort of witnessed in that first innings, and he had to sort of adjust the way that he plays,” McDonald said. “Sometimes he changes his technique when he’s sort of fully fit.



“But he, yeah, he was limited in what he could do, and then yeah, we felt it was best to hopefully get the batting unit through to tomorrow, and then hopefully he’s better placed for that tomorrow. “You would have seen the physio working on him, so he’ll bat tomorrow. It’s not something that will rule him out of the innings, but it was just that it took a little bit more time than we expected on the back of the first innings.” South Africa’s Simon Harmer and Temba Bavuma celebrate the wicket of Marnus Labuschagne. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe McDonald refused to talk about selection for the next Test of the series in Cape Town mid-match, but highlighted both shot selection and the team’s inability to recognise and build partnerships as an issue of significant concern. “I think any time when anything’s done at that speed, it takes a couple of players to connect and communicate and navigate through that, and we weren’t able to get any partnerships,” he said. “And yeah, we’ve had some of these moments across the journey, so we’re not a perfect batting unit. I’ve never said that we are.



“And yeah, the speed in which that happened, and the momentum that you know South Africa were able to gain through that, and yeah, we didn’t envisage coming here and yeah, looking at a follow-on. “You do have to give a little bit of credit to the South African attack as well. The way they exposed some of that, some of our deficiencies in that, I don’t take anything away from that. But there was some batter error there. I think we are better than that. But as it sits right now, I can’t defend that.” Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket ‘Testosterone to burn’: Rabada rejoins battle with Smith after 2018 flashpoint Pressed on questions over the likes of Labuschagne, Nic Maddinson and Beau Webster, McDonald said: “I never sit in a press conference in the middle of the game and start to talk about selection for the next Test match. I think it’s too early to navigate through that, it’s something that we do post-match. We’ll work through that process as we lead into Cape Town. So as we sit here right now, there’ll be no selection chat.” Given their grim position in this game, McDonald conceded that they may have to deal with the unexpected situation of going to Newlands in Cape Town for the first time since the infamous 2018 sandpapergate match with the score at 1-1.



“Those players that sit in that room are still the same players that performed exceptionally well last week,” he said. “I have great belief and trust that the skill sets in that room, in particular tomorrow, can go out there and potentially turn this one around. “If that doesn’t unfold, then we move into Cape Town and we reload and we go again. A great strength of this group is on significant setbacks, and I’d say this is a significant setback in terms of the way that we played. We’ve been able to respond, and that’s been one of the strengths. So, looking forward to that opportunity tomorrow and further down the track in Cape Town.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Arson squad boss warns firebombers off Brad Battin’s ‘innocent’ neighbours
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Arson squad boss warns firebombers off Brad Battin’s ‘innocent’ neighbours Fiona Byrne Updated October 22, 2026 — 5:01am ,first published 12:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Shadow police minister Brad Battin has, for the second week running, had Melbourne’s plague of arson attacks fall on his doorstep. Last week, CBD brought news of an attempted firebombing at the cafe next to Battin’s Berwick electorate office on October 12. A cafe next to Brad Battin’s office in Berwick has twice been targeted in attempted firebombings. Simon Schluter Now it’s been revealed that in the very early hours of Sunday, the offenders returned for a second attempt at incinerating the joint with police discovering “tens of litres of accelerant” left inside the cafe when the crooks were disturbed. Fortunately, no one was injured. In a highly disturbing twist, Victoria Police has confirmed that the offenders have been targeting the wrong address.



Arson and explosives squad Detective Inspector Chris Murray didn’t mince words, describing the two attacks as incredibly reckless and dangerous acts that have caused fear, disruption and significant distress. Murray said there was the “potential for catastrophic consequences not only for the business owners but also for surrounding properties and members of the public” from the latest attack. “This level of violence and disregard for community safety is completely unacceptable,” Murray said. “In this case, the business and its owners appear to have been wrongly targeted, while the person believed to be the intended victim has no association whatsoever with the cafe. “Innocent people are being placed at risk because criminals are treating serious violence as a contract.”



We reached out to Battin on Wednesday for his view on crime across our city and the repeated firebombing attempts next door to his office. “Innocent small business owners are being put in danger because violent criminals are running amok under Labor,” Battin told us. “This is the frightening reality of crime after 12 years of Labor.” De Blasio, Moreno kick on in Melbourne In Melbourne, it is a given that any visiting international guest will have a brush with a football.



So it was just a matter of time before former mayor of New York City Bill de Blasio would eventually get his hands on a Sherrin – the only surprise was that it took four days. Loading De Blasio and urbanist Carlos Moreno, both in town as guests of the Melbourne Assembly, were gifted footballs at a Committee For Melbourne networking evening on Wednesday. De Blasio showed some sporting form, immediately having a short kick to kick with the Committee For Melbourne’s Agostino Giramondo at the gathering. “Who here has insurance,” de Blasio asked before putting boot to ball.



We are pleased to report nothing got broken. Earlier in the week, de Blasio and Moreno were presented with AFL club jumpers – Carlton for Moreno and a Melbourne for de Blasio. Just what they will do with them is anyone’s guess, but footy as the city’s diplomatic currency continues unabated. ‘Not how I wanted it to end’: Carrie Bickmore, Tommy Little end radio show After almost a decade as a radio team, Gold Logie winner Carrie Bickmore and comedian Tommy Little have called time on their Carrie & Tommy national drive show and will exit the Hit Network at the end of the year.



Bickmore fought back tears while making the announcement on air on Wednesday, while her co-host Little said it was “certainly not how I wanted it to end”. Carrie Bickmore and Tommy Little have been the Hit Network’s national drive radio team for almost 10 years. The future of the show had been a talking point in industry circles for some months. “It’s not every day you get to come and have a laugh and call it your job with your best mate and the funniest guy in the country,” an emotional Bickmore said. “I think we’ve been able to do something on this show that often people are too scared to do, to talk about stuff that sometimes is uncomfortable. We hope that we’ve had some small impact on your life in some small way … [and been] company for you on shitty days and [made] you laugh.”



Little said he was sad that this chapter of his radio career was coming to an end. “I loved this job and I would have kept doing it for a long time, but I don’t always get my way,” Little said. “I feel very grateful. I feel very lucky to have had the opportunity. We’re going to be on air until the end of the year, and we’re going to try and make the best radio we can.” Bickmore is rumoured to have been courted by ARN over recent months to move to rival KIIS FM to helm that station’s drive show in 2027. Whether Little was part of that discussion is unclear. The KIIS drive shift is up for grabs with the Will & Woody drive show, hosted by Will McMahon and Woody Whitelaw, finishing up at the end of the year.



Matthew O’Reilly, the head of broadcast content for Southern Cross Austereo, owner of the Hit Network, informed staff via an internal memo of the end of the Carrie & Tommy show. “Over the next few weeks, we look forward to celebrating everything Carrie and Tommy have given to their listeners over the last 10 years,” O’Reilly said in the note. “Thank you to Carrie, Tommy and everyone who worked on the show, pouring their energy, creativity, and passion into making it what it is today. We wish them the very best for what’s next.” No announcement has been made yet as to who will replace the pair in the drive shift next year. Pencil case to blame for premier’s petrol station blunder



It is not quite the dog-ate-my-homework excuse, but Premier Ben Carroll has blamed a pencil case, forgetfulness and human error for an embarrassing moment at the bowser. Carroll, who has toughened up the state government’s crackdown on crime since assuming the role of premier in July, found himself on the wrong side of the law on Monday night after he filled up his car at a petrol station in Airport West and drove off without paying. Loading “Late Monday night, I was running some errands and filled up the car with petrol. Found out yesterday I forgot to pay,” he fessed up on Wednesday morning. A call from Victoria Police to the Department of Parliamentary Services alerted the premier to the bungle, and Carroll returned to the service station to settle his bill on Tuesday night.



Related Article Melbourne Assembly Melbourne Assembly day three as it happened: Major events at risk if city ‘rests on its laurels’ “It shows that politicians are human beings and even premiers make mistakes,” Carroll said of the forgetful moment on Wednesday morning. Speaking at Melbourne Assembly, he said he was on dad duty and running errands when the accidental drive-off occurred. “Monday was a tough day for a lot of reasons, and I got home and I had a busy night on the phone, and my wife and I had a discussion,” Carroll said, referencing the attack on federal MP Helen Haines. “She [Carroll’s wife, Fiona] was going to return [daughter] Maddie’s friend’s pencil case. I said, ‘I’ll do it and I’ll get petrol’. And then I found out the following day I didn’t pay,” he said.



“That has since been rectified.” As it happens, Carroll is not alone in being a politician with problems at the petrol pump. Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush Penny Stephens “I have been contacted by the former deputy premier John Thwaites, who told me, ‘Don’t worry, Ben. I didn’t pay for the petrol, and I also drove off with the nozzle in the car, with the petrol hose together’,” Carroll said. “And that made me feel a lot better.” Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush also weighed in on the petrol palaver on Wednesday, saying not every drive-off was a criminal matter.



“Our point of view is that a petrol drive-off is a civil matter until it’s proven otherwise,” Bush said. “If it turns out that it’s a criminal matter, there was intent, etc, etc, charges will follow subsequently. But everyone’s got the opportunity to address an error.” The commissioner said he was aware that the premier had paid his outstanding debt. “We’re very careful not to criminalise every petrol drive-off. We do understand, and I’m very empathetic and sympathetic to petrol station owners who do suffer, but it’s not always criminal.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The secret (cringe-free) weapon for solo travellers looking to connect
World.content:
Reviews & adviceSavvy traveller The secret (cringe-free) weapon for solo travellers looking to connect Nina Karnikowski October 22, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If the thought of marching into a hotel happy hour and introducing yourself to strangers makes you want to run to your room and hide, you’re not alone. As someone who occasionally runs group trips, I can confirm that even the most competent adults revert to high school disco mode when faced with a room full of strangers: everyone wants to connect, but nobody wants to be the first person on the dance floor. Fortunately, making friends while travelling solo doesn’t require hostel pub crawls or even an outgoing personality, just a few simple tricks and a willingness to occasionally put your book down. The beauty of activities is that you don’t have to invent reasons to talk to people. iStock First, choose stays that offer natural opportunities to connect. That might mean a hostel if you’re on a budget, or a design hotel with a great lobby bar or co-working space.



If your room feels like a luxury cocoon, though, don’t be surprised if you rarely emerge from it. Better to choose somewhere that nudges you out into the world. 



Because solo dining can be the Big Bad Wolf of solo travel, use counter seating as your secret weapon, where you’re usually shoulder-to-shoulder with other diners. And resist the urge to retreat behind your phone; people are much more willing to approach you when your eyes aren’t glued to a glowing rectangle. Related Article Opinion

Tours After six months of travelling solo, I needed a holiday from myself Georgia Dunkley Travel writer When conversations do happen, remember there’s an art to making good chat without sounding like you’re conducting a job interview. Ask questions you’d genuinely like the answer to. “What’s been the highlight of your trip so far?” tends to lead somewhere much more interesting than, “so what do you do?” These questions can be supremely practical, too. Need someone to take your photo? Trying to work out whether you’ve boarded the right ferry, or how the train ticket machine works? Ask the person next to you. People are usually warmer when they’re responding to a request than a random introduction. It also helps to remember that most people aren’t scrutinising you nearly as much as you think they are. They’re worrying about whether they’re being weird, too. And hey, if none of this works and you still find yourself solo, there are worse fates than a great meal, a good book and nobody to answer to. One of the joys of travelling alone is discovering that your own company can be pretty excellent, too.

World.title: Can National reclaim Tāmaki electorate after 2023 upset?
World.content:
The Auckland electorate of Tāmaki - one of the three richest electorates in the country alongside Epsom and the newly created Wellington North - is an intriguing seat to watch in the November election for multiple reasons.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406812331112

What's so interesting about it?

For the first time in New Zealand's electoral history, a major party has nominated a candidate of Indian descent to reclaim a traditionally loyal seat.

Historically, Kiwi Indian candidates were typically assigned hard-to-win electorates in which their party lacked a competitive track record.

Audio player for " Redrawn boundaries add new dimension to Tāmaki contest " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/indonz_featured/2072244%2Fcan-national-reclaim-tamaki-electorate-after-2023-upset

Redrawn boundaries add new dimension to Tāmaki contest Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The National Party was guilty of this in 2023, with all five National candidates of Indian origin losing their respective electoral seats.

Low list rankings and unexpected electoral wins for National ensured none of those five candidates made into the Parliament.

As a result, National hasn't had a lawmaker of Indian heritage for two terms now.

"Wider representation, particularly for New Zealanders of Indian origin, has been an issue with [the] National Party for the last few years," said Veer Khar, president of the New Zealand Indian Central Association.

Mahesh Muralidhar is the National Party candidate for Tāmaki electorate. RNZ / Blessen Tom

In February, National announced venture capitalist Mahesh Muralidhar as its Tāmaki candidate for the general election.

Muralidhar also managed to secure a list ranking of 24 this time - a decent improvement on his 2023 ranking of 43.

"This election, a possible chance has been given to Mahesh Muralidhar … and we are hopeful that he will make it to the Parliament," Khar said.

"While NZICA does not want the ticket allocation to be based on ethnic basis, it definitely is aware of the poor mindset some parties have," he said.

"Just a name on the list does not show the intent."

A similar sentiment was expressed by Bhav Dhillon, former honorary consul of India in Auckland and managing director of construction company Cemix, who called Muralidhar's candidacy from Tāmaki - a traditional National Party stronghold - "significant with lots of meaning" for New Zealand's Indian community.

"A mainstream constituency has been given to a person of Indian origin," said Dhillon, who has lived in Tāmaki for over 15 years. "It is a clear signal and messaging that [the] Indian community across New Zealand has well and truly arrived."

A closer look at past elections explains why Tāmaki is as blue as it comes.

Bhav Dhillon is a Tamaki resident and managing director of Cemix. RNZ / Blessen Tom

What has happened in previous elections?

Created in 1946, the constituency has voted Labour only twice.

Former Prime Minister Robert Muldoon secured the seat for National in 1960, representing the electorate until he left Parliament in 1991.

National's Clem Simich and Allan Peachey followed before Simon O'Connor held it from 2011 to 2023.

While Labour narrowly won the party vote (39 percent to National's 37 percent) in its 2020 election landslide victory, O'Connor has consistently garnered more than 50 percent of candidate votes.

That was until former ACT deputy leader Brooke van Velden campaigned hard for the seat in 2023.

She interrupted O'Connor's four-term reign, beating him by a majority of 4158 votes in what was considered a major upset for National.

But even then, National won the party vote in the electorate three years ago, with the party winning 52 percent to Labour's 17 percent. ACT secured just 12 percent.

Former ACT deputy leader Brooke van Velden won the electorate seat in 2023. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

An RNZ analysis suggested van Velden was able to capitalise on voter unease with O'Connor's conservative stance on abortion and other conscience issues.

O'Connor's defeat was touted as a failure of Christian conservatism in mainstream politics in the country, RNZ reported.

A not-so-subtle personal endorsement of the ACT candidate by Paula Bennett, former deputy leader of the National Party, created a "permission structure for Nat voters" to break rank and vote for van Velden, it quoted National Party member Liam Hehir saying.

Sudesh Jhunjhnuwala, chief executive of Sudima Hotels and Hind Management, said van Velden was "very visible" in the electorate and worked hard to win people's support.

Jhunjhnuwala, has lived in Kohimarama for 25 years, which along with Mission Bay, St Heliers and Ōrākei forms part of the affluent eastern bays with high-income households.

"I used to say we are an 'orphan seat'. National knew it is always going to win, and Labour knew it will never win," Jhunjhnuwala said.

"So, nobody tried hard until the last election," he said, adding that the energy on the ground is different this time with National, ACT and Labour all campaigning hard to entice voters.

"The last thing you want is your electorate to be taken for granted."

James Christmas is the ACT Party candidate for Tāmaki electorate. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Who is standing?

With van Velden's retirement from politics and Muralidhar replacing O'Connor, the above factors seem no longer relevant - giving Tāmaki a fresh suite of candidates to choose from.

ACT has put up 2023 National list-only candidate and lawyer James Christmas, placing him seventh on its party list.

On current polling, Christmas is most likely to be a lawmaker next term even if he loses Tāmaki.

Labour's candidate is Max Harris, who is also a lawyer and author of a 2017 book titled The New Zealand Project, which he says was a call for a "return to value-based politics" in New Zealand.

Harris is ranked 29 on Labour's party list and, on current polling, might just sneak in even if he is unable to turn the electorate left.

The Auckland electorate of Tāmaki is one of the three richest electorates in the country alongside Epsom and the newly created Wellington North RNZ / Blessen Tom

Muralidhar's case is straightforward.

National typically performs strongly in electorate races and with current polling showing support below 30 percent, his chances of becoming a first-term lawmaker via the party list look slim given his ranking.

As a result, it looks like Muralidhar must win Tāmaki to avoid the same disappointment he faced in Auckland Central in 2023 when he lost to Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick by 3896 votes.

Green candidate Donald Mackenzie Mayo (list ranking 43) has already asked voters in the electorate to cast a vote for Harris.

Opportunity Party has put up Sacha Haskell (list ranking 31) as its candidate, while Ryan Pausina and Finlay Smith are standing as independents.

Realistically, though, it's a fight between Christmas and Muralidhar for the electorate seat, with Harris set to benefit if the right vote splits and he is able to consolidate left-leaning votes in Glen Innes, St Heliers, St Johns and the newly added suburb of Point England.

Harris' other challenge, as one Labour volunteer in Point England said, was to ensure party's traditional voters enrol no later than 25 October.

Unlike past elections, voters must enrol well before Election Day this year to have a say at the ballot box.

Max Harris is the Labour Party candidate for Tāmaki electorate. RNZ / Blessen Tom

What do the candidates say?

Harris, who is a Rhodes Scholar and a former Supreme Court researcher, is confident of his chances.

"I believe we can win this time … as Labour has done well in pockets of this electorate in the past," he said.

"We even won the party vote here in 2020."

Cost of living woes due to rising food and fuel prices combined with a need for more public transport, longer waiting times in emergency departments and delayed access to GPs have emerged as national issues, but they appear to be just as relevant to voters in some sections of the Tāmaki electorate.

"That's why the next Labour government will offer a return to universalism in public services … getting us further along a free universal public healthcare," Harris said.

"Another step forward would be a more hands-on approach to the economy … an example of which is the targeted capital gains tax to redirect investment into the productive economy."

Point England is one of the communities within the newly drawn Tāmaki electorate. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Harris wants the next Labour government to invest in services for people with substance abuse problems and mental health issues.

"I have heard this in Glen Innes and Point England repeatedly that the best thing we can do for young people at the risk of offending is to keep them out of the system," he said.

Christmas wants to focus on noisy vehicles.

"We have a huge problem in this area of noise from cars, especially in Mission Bay," he said.

"So, I have announced an ACT policy based on the feedback I have received from residents to crack down on noisy vehicles and increase penalties for drivers being a nuisance to neighbourhoods."

ACT's proposal would establish a fleet of relocatable noise cameras, introduce an objective and enforceable noise standard, and increase penalties for excessive vehicle noise.

"People should be able to sleep and enjoy their homes without having their street turned into someone else's racetrack," he said.

One local issue where there seems to be consensus across parties is housing intensification in the Tāmaki electorate that is out of sync with infrastructure.

"I must have door-knocked over 13,000 houses this year, and this has been the major issue in every conversation," Muralidhar said.

"We have challenges with our pipes, and parking availability. ... [Hence] I have already started conversations with senior ministers on what is the right policy for new builds in regard to parking.

"Crime was [also] an issue. … [That's why] I raised $15,000 for a brand-new community patrol vehicle in Glen Innes during this campaign."

Acknowledging there was a cost-of-living crisis in the country, Muralidhar said his "background [would] ... address that".

He is chief executive of Phase One Ventures, a venture capitalist firm that invests in New Zealand start-ups, and has worked at online graphic design tool unicorn Canva between 2015 and 2017.

The Kiwi Indian candidate credited Prime Minister Christopher Luxon for delivering on his election promise of getting a free trade agreement with India across the line this term.

Dhillon and Jhunjhnuwala, both of whom have good connections in the country's business sector, agree.

"The signing of the trade deal with India is an amazing outcome for both sides, and [the business community] is very positive about it," Dhillon said.

What do the locals say?

Auckland City Councillor from Maungakiekie-Tāmaki Ward Josephine Bartley, who was the Labour electoral candidate in 2008 and has lived in Tāmaki for two decades, highlighted the electorate's diverse nature.

"We have richest of the rich and we have areas of high deprivation," said Bartley, the first Pacific woman elected to Auckland Council.

"We hope the new MP is a champion of Tāmaki Regeneration - a social experiment which started years ago and would deliver 10,500 better homes into the community. It should not be left in the lurch."

She said water quality and sewage overflows in areas around Mission Bay, in addition to public safety in all areas of the electorate, were also issues being discussed this election cycle.

Joel Carpenter is vicar of St Mary's Church in Glenn Innes. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Reverend Joel Carpenter of St Mary's Church in Glen Innes who has lived in the area for six years wants the next Tāmaki MP "to represent the full flavour of the electorate".

"It has been a challenging time in this parish, especially the last year," Carpenter said.

"The demand for petrol vouchers, food, clothing, bedding and other essentials, including counselling support, have all increased hugely."

The needs of richer parts such as Mission Bay and Ōrākei were very different from the needs of the working class in Glen Innes and Point England, he said.

World.title: No traces of rats found in part of Raukūmara Forest where population of kiwi live
World.content:
Audio player for " First rat-free result offers hope for Raukumara kiwi " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/environment/2070708%2Fno-traces-of-rats-found-in-part-of-raukumara-forest-where-population-of-kiwi-live

First rat-free result offers hope for Raukumara kiwi Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A big conservation project on the East Cape is thrilled to discover no traces of rats in a large block of the Raukūmara Range where a small population of kiwi live.

150,000 hectares of the forest has been poisoned with 1080 as part of a project to save the forest, and the creatures living in it, from pests.

The national park stretches across 250,000ha of the rugged East Cape and is the largest continuous native forest remaining in the North Island.

But the Raukūmara Pae Maunga Restoration Project said after generations of neglect, the health of the forest is suffering with trees dying, canopy collapsing and birdsong scarce.

In 2020, Raukūmara Pae Maunga Restoration Project - a partnership between Ngāti Porou, Te-Whānau-ā-Apanui and the Department of Conservation Te Papa Atawhai - received $34.4 million in government funding as part of the Jobs for Nature scheme.

Trustee Ora Barlow told RNZ they've built the only integrated large scale operation of its kind in the country, with 110,000ha of deer and goat culling, and 150,000ha of aerial 1080.

"Our people have a deep relationship with the whenua, and the awa, and the ngahere... so when you're talking about putting a toxin into that environment of course people are going to have concerns and questions," she said.

To overcome that, they took locals into the forest to see the damage for themselves.

"The loss of young forest growth, the silence of the forest, the 1000-year-old trees that had fallen down and been eaten from inside out. This is the reality of what we are dealing with in an enormous area of rugged country that you simply can't walk into," Barlow said.

The understory of the Raukūmara forest has been destroyed by pests such as deer, pigs and goats. Supplied

Once people saw the state of the forest, they realised the scale of the issue.

"Everyone agreed we had a problem, and they could see that. At the end of the day 1080 is a great tool - I used to be anti-1080 but now I realise that wasn't based on good information.

"You really have to understand the concerns and take people on a journey about the forest," Barlow said.

In August this year, 1080 was dropped over nearly 50,000ha. The team used tracking tunnels with ink pads to find rats, and to see what was left. It revealed in one area that rat numbers fell from 80 percent before the poison drop, to zero percent afterwards.

Then a trail camera captured a kiwi strutting through the forest.

"It's super exciting... a big booty kiwi! The first time we saw it on the trail cam the screams of joy coming from our team was just fantastic.

"These kiwi have been holding in there. They've been present pre and post 1080, so no - 1080 doesn't kill everything," she said.

This kiwi was captured on camera shortly after the August 1080 drop. Supplied

Wiremu Wharepapa from Te Kaha has been hunting in the Raukūmara range since he was a boy, living off the land and calling the forest his "garden".

"We got a big problem - I mean the possums were here, they'd move in and the numbers grew. Then the deer moved in - it was like rabbits moving into a lettuce garden," he said.

Wiremu Wharepapa grew up hunting in the Raukūmara range. Supplied

He became worried about destructive pests in the forest, and felt the forest had been neglected for too long.

"It's most probably one of the last of the Mohican - it's the forgotten ngahere in Aotearoa," he said.

He's proud of the mahi going into restoring the forest, and is grateful to be re-connecting with the Raukumara's.

World.title: 'We've been really generous': Opportunity's Qiulae Wong on bottom lines
World.content:
Audio player for " Jo Moir's analysis of the minor parties' debate " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2067964%2Fwe-ve-been-really-generous-opportunity-s-qiulae-wong-on-bottom-lines

Jo Moir's analysis of the minor parties' debate Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong says she would walk away from government rather than support a policy through to first reading that her party doesn't believe in.

Even if the deal was simply to appease another coalition partner, and required no support beyond first reading, Wong told RNZ she would choose being in opposition over compromising on values.

The newest political leader on the block was front and centre in the third debate of the so-called minor party leaders on Wednesday night - the New Zealand Herald Powerbrokers' Debate moderated by Ryan Bridge.

Wong has been questioned heavily in these debates on her party's bottom lines and no-go areas as Opportunity continues to poll over the five percent threshold and hold the position of kingmaker if the results were replicated on 7 November.

From left: Debate host Ryan Bridge, Marama Davidson (Greens), David Seymour (ACT), Qiulae Wong (TOP) and Winston Peters (NZ First). NZ Herald / Dean Purcell

On Morning Report on Wednesday Wong said she would not have propped up the current coalition of National, New Zealand First, and Act or signed up to its agreements.

"I want to be clear: we are not here to prop up the current coalition government. If that coalition agreement was put in front of us, we would have walked away," she told Morning Report.

"We're not supporting things like a Treaty Principles Bill in this next term of government. But if there are other things that we can work with parties on, whether that's tackling competition or investing in innovation, then we will work with them on that."

Audio player for " Lauren Crimp breaks down the Powerbrokers debate " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2067964%2Fwe-ve-been-really-generous-opportunity-s-qiulae-wong-on-bottom-lines

Lauren Crimp breaks down the Powerbrokers debate Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Asked by RNZ following the Powerbrokers' Debate what the threshold was for walking away and being in opposition over government, Wong said "the way that we approach those things is we genuinely have to believe that it's a good idea".

She said New Zealand First's proposal to buy back the BNZ bank was an example of a policy the party wouldn't support, not even through to first reading, adding "but I don't think anyone really believes that's going to happen".

Other policies the party wouldn't give even initial support to include ACT's freezing the minimum wage, National's drug testing beneficiaries and both ACT and New Zealand First's pledge to abolish the Waitangi Tribunal.

Wong told RNZ Opportunity had been "really generous putting out our bottom lines" when other parties did not, and that had made it really clear what the party's vision for the future of the country was.

'I learnt the hard way' - Peters on being smacked as a child

Winston Peters during The New Zealand Herald Powerbrokers' Debate. NZ Herald / Dean Purcell

The other eye-opener of the debate in Auckland was New Zealand First leader Winston Peters saying he was smacked as a child and that he "thoroughly deserved them".

Peters was one of 11 children in his family growing up in Whananaki and following the debate he expanded on what trouble he had got into, which had caused him to be punished.

He said he was one of the more naughty of his siblings - "I can't deny that but then heavens I was shown the error of my way, so to speak."

Asked to recall an example of this behaviour, Peters told RNZ he and his brother had got into trouble for racing horses on the beach.

"The previous night we had a fantastic time having the horse race but this night it was so quiet my father heard it, so in the middle of the race he comes rushing out of the trees, and all of a sudden we're walking home having rather sore legs, and then we had to walk to school for the next month.

"That was the punishment, yeah, I learnt the hard way," he said.

Peters and Wong took part in the debate alongside Greens' co-leader Marama Davidson and ACT leader David Seymour.

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson during The New Zealand Herald Powerbrokers' Debate. NZ Herald / Dean Purcell

Te Pāti Māori was also due to be there but pulled out after news of the death of co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer's mother, who had been ill throughout the campaign.

Davidson was asked for her response to Peters speaking positively about being hit as a child - it was the Green Party's Sue Bradford that got the anti-smacking law passed in 2007 after introducing it as a member's bill.

She told RNZ she fully understood as a parent how stressful it could be raising young children.

"It's really ordinary for people to feel wigged out many times as a parent of young children, but I think that where we have to be putting our emphasis is in all of us supporting each other to just end violence of all forms towards any child."

'The political market is changing'

Seymour spoke during the Powerbrokers' Debate of being proud of the work he had done cross-party to get the assisted dying legislation passed through Parliament.

Asked following the debate what advice he had for Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins about how to reach bipartisanship on the tough issues, Seymour told RNZ "there's no limit to what you can achieve if you don't care who takes the credit".

ACT leader David Seymour during The New Zealand Herald Powerbrokers' Debate. NZ Herald / Dean Purcell

"I, still, as recently as a couple of weeks ago, credited Chloe Swarbrick for her role in helping get the End of Life Choice Act passed. Now, as you know, Chloe and I don't always see eye to eye, but on that issue, I'm happy to do so.

"Secondly, you've got to be prepared to not make the perfect the enemy of the good. The bill that we finally passed is not the one that I introduced. So, if you're prepared to make the odd compromise where necessary, if you're prepared to share the credit, there's no limit to what you can achieve," he said.

Seymour was of the belief the "political market is changing" and voters wanted to see better collaboration between political parties on things like transport and infrastructure.

"It takes 10 years to build a decent road - that's three electoral cycles.

World.title: Rugby League World Cup: Pacific teams brace for crucial round two clashes
World.content:
Round two of the 2026 Rugby League World Cup (RLWC) will determine which Pacific Island teams will stay in the race for a top-two finishes in both the men's and women's competitions.

In the women's competition, the clash between the Papua New Guinea Orchids and Fiji Bulikula in Port Moresby on Saturday will determine which team keeps its hopes alive in Pool B.

The PNG Orchids had a big 58-4 win over France in round one at home, while the Fiji Bulikula lost 12-18 to the Kiwi Ferns.

If the Orchids win, then they should be in the running for a top-two finish, but if the Bulikula gets the victory then that throws the pool wide open.

New Zealand will beat France in Christchurch and are set to finish as the number one team from the pool.

Pool A has Australia leading but they meet England in what is also expected to be a fiery contest. Both sides claimed wins in the opening round.

Fetu Samoa meets Wales, with a chance to get a win if they can repeat their performance against the Jillaroos but get points on the board.

In the men's competition, a lot of interest will be on Toa Samoa and PNG Kumuls match on Saturday afternoon.

Both teams recorded wins in the first round.

The Kumuls are playing at home and will have a lot of home support, while Samoa has NRL stars packed across their team. Whichever team wins has a good chance of finishing in the top two in the poll, where focus will also be on how Tonga and England fare this weekend.

Tonga, who beat England for the first time last weekend, take on Lebanon, while England meets France.
