If you’ve been curious about Star Wars Zero Company, the XCOM-like strategy game set in the Star Wars universe, Amazon has both the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X physical editions on sale for $47.99 and $49.99, respectively. The game usually sells for $59.99. While I’m not usually enthused by turn-based strategy games, I’ve been impressed enough with the story and characters to keep playing, and any fan who’s familiar with the world surrounding the battles should make the experience more immersive.

Related EA is shutting down BioWare

There’s a surprising depth here, as well, with branching story missions that have consequences, and higher difficulty modes that punish you more severely for mistakes. The character creator is impressive, too, with a huge number of unlockable outfits and accessories, as well as classic alien races from the movies and cartoons. Plus, isn’t it every Star Wars fan’s dream to lead a crew of rag-tag heroes into battle against Droidekas and outlaws?

Tech.title: Will TP-Link really make routers in the US? Here’s what it told us
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

But TP-Link is willing to do something those companies weren’t — to invest nearly $1 billion to make routers in the United States, creating “hundreds of high-paying research and development, manufacturing, and construction jobs for American workers over the next four years,” according to a letter TP-Link sent to the FCC.

This week, it announced a letter of intent with US contract manufacturer Key Tronic to begin “domestic assembly” of its Wi-Fi 8 routers in Corinth, Mississippi. It could begin producing routers “as early as next year.”

Intriguingly, this might not just be slapping boards into a plastic box.

“If you look at what we do with the products in Vietnam, you’ve got raw components coming in and you’ve got completed, tested, shrink-wrapped products coming out,” TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky tells The Verge. “You’ve got surface-mount technology, many layers of testing quality control, we’re doing plastic injection molding, and as far as I know that is what we intend to do in Mississippi.”

But how likely is that “letter of intent” to turn into a true manufacturing plant? After talking to Kovsky, it sounds like the stars might need to align.

What is TP-Link waiting for?

A deal with the Federal Communications Commission. Kovksy confirms the offer hinges on the FCC granting that router ban waiver — formally known as “conditional approval” — before it can proceed.

Kovsky wouldn’t tell me how long ago TP-Link applied for that waiver, but it sounds like the FCC hasn’t yet given the company any idea whether it’ll be approved. TP-Link had to provide lots of info about the company’s structure, ownership, and supply chain, but Kovksy confirms the FCC hasn’t asked any follow-up questions about other topics, and he says the FCC doesn’t exactly tell companies when it denies conditional approval.

“We’re looking at offering total transparency to these agencies, and we’re open to negotiations,” he says. “Nothing is written in stone.”

Why does TP-Link need an import waiver if it’ll be building routers in the US?

“I have asked that question myself,” Kovsky tells The Verge. The short answer is components. Even though TP-Link buys its chipsets from US companies like Qualcomm and Broadcom, those companies don’t actually produce those chips in the US. “Do they count as US product?” Kovsky rhetorically asks.

“It’s not a lock, and we would rather have [the waiver],” he says.

Why might the FCC hesitate?

Five states have now sued over TP-Link’s alleged ties to China, and many more are directly asking the FCC not to grant a waiver, claiming the company dominates the consumer router market, that it’s a Chinese company posing as a US one, that the routers have brought serious security vulnerabilities into US homes, and more.

Kovksy suggests it’s all based on misinformation, even the company’s market share: “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three. It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.” TP-Link’s website clarifies that it has 10 percent market share when you count all the routers that internet providers put into people’s homes.

“We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever. We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category to my knowledge,” Kovsky says.

If it gets the waiver, does TP-Link intend to produce all US-bound routers in the US?

TP-Link is not willing to commit to that yet. “I don’t think that’s entirely determined,” Kovksy says. “Some of that is going to be: What are the FCC and the administration really trying to achieve?”

The administration already has a stated goal, though: It wants Made-in-USA products where at least 65 percent of their components are also made here. Kovsky says that TP-Link would be “happy to comply with that, to the extent that it can continue to produce products that meet its criteria for quality and affordability.”

“That is going to be challenging, certainly in the short term, [because] those components for the most part just are not produced in the US,” Kovsky says.

He says TP-Link believes components will become more available and affordable if the US pushes other manufacturers to invest, but the waiver isn’t the only factor in its decision.

If it gets the waiver, will TP-Link invest, or will it need to find an inexpensive source of components or other things before it can go ahead?

“I think those are probably going to be business decisions that the CEO will ultimately have to make,” Kovksy begins. “Well, I hope he doesn’t have to make those decisions, frankly, that everything falls in line. He is very committed to making this investment,” he says.

Notably, TP-Link would not confirm Kovsky’s suggestion that it might completely manufacture routers in the US and only source the raw components. I told the company that if I could say TP-Link was committed to anything other than “final assembly,” it’d be well worth sharing with readers.

“At this stage, TP-Link is not sharing specific job numbers or detailed technical details of the assembly process beyond what’s in today’s press release,” third-party spokesperson Ricca Silverio told me.

I don’t think this is Foxconn in Wisconsin all over again because TP-Link probably won’t get its conditional approval, let alone invest in empty buildings. Foreign gadget bans from President Trump and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr seem explicitly designed to target companies China hawks claim to be worried about, like DJI or Unitree, while letting favored companies through. But the hawks, including a coalition of congresspeople led by Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR), seem to hate TP-Link, too.

Tech.title: GM promises smarter cars, faster updates, and autonomous dry-cleaning runs
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

General Motors is still very much in the business of selling gas-guzzling trucks and massive SUVs. But if you listen to its leadership, the Detroit giant is rapidly transforming into a nimble, software-defined tech player with a tightened grip on AI.

That was the pitch today, when GM hosted its tech-focused Onward event to unveil a wide-ranging slate of EV, autonomous vehicle, and AI initiatives — all aimed at fending off the rising threat of tech-heavy Chinese automakers.

The promises are big: GM claims it will use AI to cut vehicle development times in half, introduce compute units up to 40 times more powerful than its current hardware, model next-gen battery chemistries in record time, and bring eyes-off autonomous driving to its top-selling trucks and SUVs.

In short, GM wants to transition from a legacy automaker into an AI-driven tech enterprise, leveraging its massive scale across both electric and gas-powered fleets. It’s a bold strategy, even if we’ve heard variations of it before.

Faster R&D and digital factory twins

For decades, GM has wrestled with sluggish four- to five-year vehicle development cycles that lag behind the light-speed pace of consumer tech. The company tried to bridge that divide with aggressive EV targets and software like Super Cruise. But as software-defined architecture evolved from an industry buzzword into a table-stakes requirement, maintaining fragmented vehicle platforms and dozens of disparate control units began to severely drag down engineering efforts.

Now, GM says it’s aiming to slice that development cycle down to just two years using “digital thread virtualization.” Instead of operating in silos or relying on slow, step-by-step handoffs, the company says it will unify design, engineering, and manufacturing digitally from day one. (We’ve already reported on GM’s efforts to inject AI directly into its vehicle design process.)

GM points to its new battery development program as proof of concept. The automaker tested over 300,000 virtual battery designs before building a single physical prototype, eventually settling on a lithium manganese rich (LMR) chemistry. That virtual process let GM’s battery team go from initial concept to formal approval in just one month.

These new LMR cells will power GM’s fourth-generation EV platform. The company claims the cells offer 33 percent higher energy density than traditional lithium iron phosphate cells at a comparable cost alongside a 20 percent boost in efficiency per kilowatt-hour, yielding longer-range EVs without forcing drivers to haul around a heavier pack. The batteries will be produced by Ultium Cells, GM’s joint venture with LG Energy Solution, at its factory in Spring Hill, Tennessee.

Beyond the battery, GM engineered the entire powertrain as a single integrated system. The new drive units feature 40 percent fewer internal parts than current hardware. Because the drivetrain is lighter and takes up significantly less space, future cabins theoretically should offer more room for passengers and cargo.

A single, liquid-cooled brain

To fix its messy electronic setup, GM is replacing dozens of small, scattered electronic control units and heavy wiring harnesses with a single central computer. GM claims this unified unit — which is liquid-cooled and connected by high-speed lines — delivers 40 times the computing power while stripping out 30 percent of the physical wiring.

That extra horsepower should translate into snappier screens, smarter voice controls, and seamless over-the-air (OTA) updates for automated driving features and battery management.

Granted, GM has been promising smarter cars and faster software updates for years. The automaker launched a “digital nerve system” in the 2020 Cadillac CT5 and later rolled out its Ultifi software platform with big promises about OTA capabilities. While drivers generally give GM high marks for hardware dependability, the company’s software rollout has faced its fair share of stumbles and consumer frustration over unnecessary complexity. (Remember the disastrous Chevy Blazer rollout?)

GM is extending this digital integration to the factory floor with a project dubbed — and capitalized rather oddly — “PlantBrAIn.” By pairing real-time factory floor data with digital-twin simulations across stamping, casting, welding, painting, and assembly, GM hopes workers can catch physical errors and equipment bottlenecks in a virtual model before they disrupt actual production.

Personal autonomy — and an autonomous dry-cleaning pickup?

GM’s newly upgraded compute platform will make its production debut in 2028 on the Cadillac Escalade IQ — the same vehicle GM announced last year would be the first to receive its hands-free, eyes-off highway driving system. (Given that GM teased this centralized compute platform last year, today’s hardware announcement is a bit of a retread.)

However, GM isn’t keeping its eyes-off tech locked behind the price tag of a $120,000 luxury SUV. The automaker confirmed plans to roll out hands-free, eyes-off highway driving across its broader lineup, spanning both EVs and gas-powered models.

As GM puts it:

Our vision is to build vehicles that can drive themselves or their occupants anywhere they need to be. This includes a future where your vehicle can handle mundane tasks for you, like heading out into bumper-to-bumper traffic to pick up groceries or dry cleaning, giving you valuable time back.

An uncrewed pickup truck executing a dry-cleaning run through morning traffic is certainly a vision, though one we’ll need to see to believe.

GM also teased a futuristic vision for autonomous cabins called “Concept Horizon,” which reimagines the interior as an open space purely dedicated to relaxing, working, or unwinding.

Overhauling OnStar for its 30th birthday

Finally, GM is celebrating OnStar’s 30th anniversary by giving the iconic service a massive AI overhaul. Rather than acting strictly as a backup button for roadside emergencies, OnStar is being rebranded as an active, AI-driven intelligence platform.

Drivers can trigger the new OnStar AI Assistant by saying, “Hey OnStar” to tweak cabin temperatures, open the glove box, pop the EV charge port, or check tire pressure and battery diagnostics. The assistant will debut on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq through an OTA update before expanding to other models.

While GM previously rolled out Google’s Gemini-powered voice assistant to 2022 and newer models, this new OnStar assistant operates at a deeper system level. Unlike Gemini, it can execute physical vehicle functions and run hardware-level diagnostics, such as managing specific HVAC zones, interpreting dashboard warning lights, or running battery health checks on the fly.

GM’s vision of a central, AI-driven vehicle architecture is undeniably ambitious, and if it works, it could genuinely streamline how cars are built and updated. But for an automaker that has spent years pitching software transformations while occasionally stumbling, execution remains everything. Until an uncrewed Silverado actually pulls into a suburban driveway with a load of fresh dry cleaning, drivers will likely treat these grand AI promises like any other product roadmap: best taken with a healthy dose of patience.

Tech.title: Xbox Cloud Gaming’s pay-as-you-go option starts at $3.99 for 10 hours
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft announced last month that it will let anyone access Xbox Cloud Gaming in November, without the need to subscribe to Xbox Game Pass. The new pay-as-you-go model will require players to purchase bundles of cloud hours, and now Microsoft is revealing today that bundles will start at $3.99 for 10 hours of cloud playtime.

Xbox Insiders who don’t have a Game Pass subscription will be able to start purchasing cloud playtime today, ahead of a broader rollout next month. Insiders can access “introductory” launch pricing bundles:

10 hours for $3.99

25 hours for $7.99

50 hours for $11.99

All of these cloud hours will include ad-free cloud gaming, shorter wait times, and higher-quality streaming. These aren’t monthly bundles of hours either, so once you purchased a pack it remains available until the hours are used.

The pay-as-you-go Xbox Cloud Gaming option arrives just in time for Grand Theft Auto VI. I reported earlier this month that Microsoft has secured Grand Theft Auto VI streaming rights, but it’s not yet clear if this will be limited to just Xbox consoles. Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball revealed on X that Microsoft won’t be streaming Grand Theft Auto VI to PCs, suggesting that the web browsers and apps that can usually access Xbox Cloud Gaming will not be able to stream Grand Theft Auto VI.

Microsoft also continues to test free, ad-supported cloud gaming for Xbox Insiders, offering up another way to stream games without Game Pass. The free streaming sessions are limited to games you already own, and sessions are capped at one hour.

Tech.title: Samsung’s latest 55-inch Frame TV is down to its lowest price yet
Tech.content:
If you want a TV but prefer something that won’t clash with your room’s decor, Samsung’s The Frame is a standout option that’s designed to look like a piece of framed art instead of a black, monolithic rectangle mounted to your wall. You can buy the latest version of the 55-inch Samsung Frame TV on sale for around $897.99 ($402 off) at Amazon, which marks a new low price. Larger sizes are on sale, too, including the new 98-inch model, which is down to $3,749.99 ($1,252 off).

The 2026 model is largely the same as its predecessor; The biggest hardware change is that this size of the TV features built-in ports instead of using Samsung’s One Connect Box. Like previous models, it has a matte, canvas-like display that more closely resembles an actual painting better than a glossy TV screen. Its built-in motion sensor detects when someone enters the room and can automatically display artwork, even adjusting its brightness and colors based on ambient lighting. It supports Samsung’s Art Store, which offers access to more than 5,000 works ranging from world-famous galleries to lesser known, independent artists. A full subscription costs $49.99 annually, though you can also enjoy 30 new free, rotating artworks every month. Samsung includes a wall mount and a black bezel in the box, with additional magnetic frame styles available separately to better match your space or taste.

In terms of performance, the Frame prioritizes style over image quality, so it’s not necessarily the best choice for cinephiles who may be willing to pay more for a brighter picture, deeper blacks, and more lifelike colors. Still it offers a refresh rate of up to 144Hz with variable refresh rate support for smoother gaming, along with HDR10 Plus and Dolby Atmos support for a more immersive audio/visual experience.

Tech.title: The internet is having a very bad cybersecurity day
Tech.content:
The internet is having a bad day, from a cybersecurity perspective. Government websites around the world went offline, Reuters reported, after AI discovered critical security vulnerabilities that impacted the programming language PHP. The issues were severe enough that the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) advised organizations using PHP on their systems to either immediately update or take their systems offline until they could.

But the PHP update wasn’t the only headache cybersecurity folks were facing on Wednesday. Node.js, the open-source JavaScript runtime environment, also dropped a security surprise of its own when it shared that four high-severity vulnerabilities were just patched in its latest release. One allowed remote code execution, and two others would have permitted a TLS validation bypass, potentially allowing attackers to bypass checks intended to verify a server’s identity.

In addition, LiteLLM, a popular open source proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, was compromised by an attacker who injected malicious code, the company shared in a post on X on Wednesday afternoon. The malicious artifacts were published to PyPI (Python Package Index), Docker Hub, and GHCR (GitHub Container Registry), the post noted.

The malicious code was said to include an information stealer that targeted cloud credentials, passwords, and AI service credentials, in addition to a remote access trojan that could allow hackers to execute commands on compromised systems.

LiteLLM said it has now removed the malicious releases and images and advised anyone who installed them to follow the remediation guidance it provided.

And wait, there’s more! An Indian certificate authority, eMudhra, had its private keys compromised, potentially allowing attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. Security pros have called this a massive cleanup job and one that’s “bigger than Heartbleed.” (The latter is a reference to the critical security vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptographic software library).

These issues come on the heels of other security breaches and hacks, including the breach of the cloud-native database-as-a-service, TiDB Cloud, which the company announced on Monday. Other hackers have been exploiting four patched Plex Media Server flaws, collectively called Plex2Shell. And last week, cybersecurity company BeyondTrust warned customers to patch a critical zero-day in its Remote Support product, which had been exploited since August.

Though the issues were unrelated to each other, their back-to-back arrival highlights the challenges cybersecurity teams now face. This is particularly important as AI could make it easier for attackers to exploit vulnerabilities once discovered.

Tech.title: Legal AI startup Legora raises $550M Series E at $8.8B valuation
Tech.content:
In Brief

Legal AI startup Legora announced Wednesday that it raised a $550 million Series E round, valuing it at $8.8 billion.

The company helps automate and assist with workflow tasks for legal professionals, as the industry moves beyond AI assistants to AI services that help them get work done.

The news comes just a month after Harvey, Legora’s biggest competitor, announced a $550 million raise at a $15.5 billion valuation; back in March, Harvey also said its annual recurring revenue (ARR) was more than $ 200 million.

Legora’s Series E follows the company’s April announcement of a $50 million extension of a $550 million Series D round, which valued the company at $5.6 billion. At the time, the company said its ARR had reached $100 million. That number now stands at over $200 million, the company shared on Wednesday.

Investors in the latest financing include Atreides Management, which led the round, as well as Baron Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, Menlo, and other top names. The company plans to use the fresh capital to further expand across North America.

Tech.title: GM is giving OnStar an AI makeover
Tech.content:
General Motors is adding a personal AI assistant to OnStar as part of a broader makeover of the subscription-based connected car service that the U.S. automaker launched 30 years ago.

The OnStar AI Assistant will debut in the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV in the coming months, with more GM vehicles to follow, the company said Wednesday at its GM Forward event in New York, where it made a series of other technology announcements covering software, automated driving, EVs, and its electrical architecture. The company said it will launch a new OnStar mobile app in 2027 that will complement and sync up with its in-car software.

The new OnStar mobile app will replace the current OnStar Guardian app that launched in 2020 as well as vehicle brand apps for Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC.

This tech-centric reboot is unlike other attempts to modernize OnStar and it notably puts agentic AI at the center. The company has updated the safety and roadside assistance service numerous times in its history, especially in the past five years as it tried to stay apace of emerging and tech-forward competitors like Tesla.

In 2021, the company expanded its OnStar Guardian app, which offered crash detection, emergency assistance and location sharing, to anyone with a compatible phone, even if they didn’t own a GM vehicle. A year later, GM started using Google Cloud’s conversational AI Dialogflow to recognize specific spoken requests and expanded in 2023 to give drivers responses to common queries like routing and navigation assistance — all part of GM’s plan to build a $25 billion subscription business by 2030.

GM continued to focus on generative AI, but relied on Google to provide the experience. The company said last year that Google Gemini would roll out in vehicles in 2026.

Image Credits:GM /

The OnStar AI Assistant is an in-house effort and one aimed at giving the driver and passengers an interactive and custom experience — and become even more embedded in their daily lives.

“OnStar is now transitioning to be a connected intelligence platform, not just the call center that it’s historically been known as, but a mechanism for interpreting, understanding, and providing predictive, proactive support to its owners,” GM’s VP of global product and chief product officer Sterling Anderson told TechCrunch in an interview ahead of the GM Forward event.

For instance, cameras on the vehicle will be connected to the software to offer live views as well as crash and safety recordings. Users can set up the connected cameras to turn on automatically if the vehicle senses an impending event — for instance an aggressive horn honk — then capture the event and upload it to the OnStar app. Users will be able to use voice to control certain functions on the vehicle, including climate, and ask questions about any specific vehicle feature.

The launch coincides with efforts throughout the auto industry to stay apace of Chinese automakers with technology that is central to the vehicle — and no longer a slapped on gimmick or feature. But that has required GM to change its approach to software development, adopt AI tools, and even design a new electrical and centralized compute vehicle architecture.

The announcement also comes after GM has been criticized and even fined for sharing data with third parties. Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission finalized an order that bans General Motors and its OnStar telematics service from sharing certain consumer data with consumer reporting agencies. The finalized order also requires the automaker to be more transparent with its consumers and obtain their explicit consent on certain data collection.

GM said Wednesday that customers will have the ability to decide what data is shared, and that the recordings have time limits and are encrypted. GM said it and OnStar cannot access Connected Camera recordings.

A GM spokesperson later shared that third-party sharing a “feature-specific and consent-based, with information shared only as needed to provide requested functionality.” Customers can manage permissions and withdraw consent, however those who choose not to share certain data may have limited access to related features, while other OnStar services would continue, according to GM.

This article was updated to include comments from a GM spokesperson.

Tech.title: PHP armageddon: OpenAI, Google’s Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet
Tech.content:
The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation.

PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites. It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress.

The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app.

Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12.

So how did two such ubiquitous, decades-old flaws that affect nearly every website on the internet suddenly come to light? AI, naturally, particularly via OpenAI and Google’s Wiz.

Security testing company Calif was engaged in OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative to find flaws in open-source source software. Using GPT‑5.6 Sol, it found one of the flaws, OpenAI disclosed in a blog post. Separately, the Wiz team also used AI, namely its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to find multiple vulnerabilities in PHP.

Both OpenAI and Wiz followed responsible security research practices and worked with PHP on patches before publicly disclosing the flaws. Then they all worked together to flesh out what they found, and test the patches, drawing in a host of others to help.

Wiz thanked Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. (While WordPress sites use PHP, WordPress has issued a statement saying that the flaw isn’t WordPress specific, and sites running its CMS must patch their servers and work with their web-hosting companies to ensure their sites are protected.)

OpenAI says that these flaws were found by researchers before hackers discovered them. So there were no reports of exploits in the wild. This is also in part because, before AI, these flaws were too hard for hackers to exploit. “With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts,” Wiz warned in its blog about the flaws.

In other words, this is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented because of AI, but is also a high risk only because of AI.

Now that the issue has been disclosed, hackers are fully in the know. The race is on for the internet to patch tens millions of websites before hackers can attack the unpatched ones. Hence the NSA’s guidance that if you can’t patch your PHP website right away, you’re better off pulling it offline until you can.

Tech.title: Blacksmith hits unicorn valuation after Sequoia leads Series C
Tech.content:
In Brief

Blacksmith, a platform that helps companies more efficiently build and test software, including code written by AI, announced Wednesday a $66 million Series C funding round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.

In announcing the round, Blacksmith co-founder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said the company was founded to make continuous integration (CI) — the process of building, testing, merging, and validating code changes — “less painful.” In a blog post, he said that “most companies are struggling to keep up with the volume of CI they need to run,” especially in an era where so much code is written by AI.

“As agents write more of the world’s software, the question that matters is whether it can be trusted,” he added.

The company also announced that its annual recurring revenue has grown 17x and that it has run over 90 million CI jobs, or individual automated code checks. Customers include Mercury and Granola.

The Series C comes just two months after its $45 million Series B, which valued the company at $550 million. A year ago, Blacksmith was valued at $60 million after raising a $10 million Series A. It has raised $125 million to date.

Tech.title: Waymo starts offering rides at the Las Vegas airport
Tech.content:
In Brief

Waymo is now shuttling customers to and from the Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, with pickups and dropoffs happening at dedicated “autonomous vehicle zones” at Terminal 1 and Terminal 3, the company announced Wednesday.

This is the sixth major airport that Waymo is serving. The company already offers rides at Phoenix Sky Harbor, Nashville International, San Antonio International, San Francisco International, and San José International airports.

Waymo only just started offering rides to the public in Las Vegas in September, but is already serving a 24-square-mile area in the city. The company said the rides to and from the Las Vegas airport will be limited at first to just a few riders, before opening up to all customers.

Amazon-owned Zoox already offers rides at the Vegas airport, and more robotaxis are coming to Sin City. In August, state regulators approved permits that will allow Tesla and Uber to put thousands of them on the city’s streets in the next year.

Tech.title: Foursquare co-founder says equity holders saw no returns from the company’s acquisition
Tech.content:
Last month, advertising company Infillion acquired location-data platform Foursquare, a once popular social network, at an undisclosed value. Now, in a new blog post, Foursquare co-founder and former CEO Dennis Crowley said that investors didn’t see any returns from the sale.

Crowley referenced a post by an angel investor, inferred that neither preferred nor common stockholders got any value out of the deal, and said he was disappointed by the outcome.

“I was heartbroken by this ending. So many people put so much time and energy and passion and love into building Foursquare — the company, the products, the brand, the culture. If you were part of it (or even close to it), you know exactly what I’m talking about. To our ~1600 former employees over 17 years, I am sorry the Foursquare story ended in such a way that makes it seem like our collective efforts were worth … nothing?” he said in the post.

Crowley said that the company did well after it started focusing on enterprise business and had consecutive years with over $100 million in revenue. In 2019, the company raised capital from a private equity firm and in 2021 brought in the banker who led the raise as CEO. Crowley blamed the final outcome on that transition, saying that the management of the company wasn’t able to preserve or create new value.

Foursquare, which had raised over $411 million in funding according to PitchBook data, eventually shut down its app in 2024.

Several people reacted to Crowley’s post and said that Foursquare was very useful to them in discovering new places in their cities and also gave ideas for new apps. After Foursquare, startups like Zenly and Jagat, along with Instagram and Snapchat, have explored social maps.

Tech.title: AI promises productivity, but for managers, it’s mostly a headache for now
Tech.content:
Companies are giving employees AI tools to make them more productive, but the tools appear to be creating new problems for their managers.

More than half of senior leaders say they find it harder to evaluate employees’ work after adopting AI, according to a Nielsen survey of 1,700 directors and senior managers across seven countries, commissioned by work-management company Monday.com. The reason is that much of employees’ output now arrives polished in the manager’s inbox, making it hard to tell how much came from the employee and how much from AI. As a result, nearly half of managers say they spend more time reviewing and guiding their teams’ output than they used to.

That’s not to say managers are unhappy about AI. Quite the opposite, in fact: 94% of the managers polled said they were excited to improve work using AI, and many are confident they know where to use it to get the most value. Michal Miller Levi, head of market research and customer insights at Monday.com, compared the enthusiasm to the early days of the internet in the 2000s, saying people see a similar kind of “magic” to AI.

But the problem, she told TechCrunch, is simply that AI is developing faster than companies can adapt. “AI works very well for [managers] individually, but they also have a different role as managers. They need to drive the organization as well … Their struggle is [due to] the fact that AI is just moving faster than the organizational processes,” Levi said.

Managers are also reconsidering how they judge their teams: 78% of respondents said they have changed how they evaluate employees after adopting AI, placing greater weight on how well staff can create prompts, decide which tasks to delegate to AI, and experiment with new ways of working.

But how fairly can employees be judged when managers can’t easily tell how much of their work was produced by AI? And what if the managers themselves are increasingly relying on AI to make those judgments? The survey found that 46% of managers use AI to help inform their decisions, and 39% of leaders are using AI to draft performance reviews.

That practice runs the risk of introducing even more bias than usual into the review process, given that LLMs are, at their core, prediction machines and tend to repeat human patterns found in their training data. Research from the Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research earlier this year found that “in the absence of clear objective standards and when individuals are rated independently,” LLMs tend to rate performance similarly to humans. And a research paper in early 2025 found that AI models can be biased against black male candidates, and “demonstrate significant biases, varying in terms of the directions and magnitudes across different social groups.”

When I asked Levi whether using AI to weigh in on people’s performance could introduce outside bias into the process, she said companies have yet to work out how to handle such issues.

AI is also changing what a manager’s day looks like. Someone has to decide which tasks to hand over to AI agents, check what they produce, and step in when something goes wrong. The report suggests that this supervision could amount to a new layer of “invisible labor.”

The software itself is becoming harder to manage. Fifty-seven percent of managers say their organizations now have more tools in circulation than before, and about 51% said their tools had grown more interdependent and clustered since adopting AI. Only 29% described their AI infrastructure as fully optimized and centralized.

Levi said businesses had expected AI to help shrink their software stacks. Instead, they’re dealing with more apps, integrations, and shadow AI usage as employees adopt tools outside their companies’ approved systems.

“Managers completed 2025 with the feeling that they will consolidate tools, actually, that they’ll reduce the number of software. But what happened is that the number of tools that they’re using increased,” Levi said. “More than 50% are saying that they’re using more tools now than they did last year, and it’s not stopping.”

This need for control seems to be growing urgent as companies deploy AI agents that can act on their own. The survey found that 58% of managers expect to oversee more AI agents than human employees within the next year, and 46% worry about losing control over those agents’ actions.

There’s also quite a bit of fear over being held responsible for decisions made by AI (35% of respondents said so), as LLMs are still largely unpredictable. “They don’t want their agents to be fully autonomous,” Levi said, explaining that managers want people to be involved and consulted by AI when it comes to crucial tasks and decisions.

At heart, the report’s findings show that AI adoption is increasingly becoming as much a governance problem as it is an opportunity to raise productivity. Without proper processes and infrastructure to deal with it, managers seem to be scrambling to keep things chugging.

Tech.title: Eufy Security Wall Light Cam S4 Deal: Save $80 on This Versatile Gadget
Tech.content:
While security cameras are ostensibly for, well, security, they can also be super handy for making sure your kids came home at the right time, checking up on your pets when you’re away, and investigating that weird sound in the middle of the night without having to get out of your toasty bed.

I’ve tested so very, very many security cameras, and there are a few reasons I think you should snap up this particular Eufy Security Wall Light Cam S4 deal at $80 off. I’m also going to highlight a couple of other Eufy options currently on sale.

The Eufy Wall Light Cam S4 looks and acts as a modern, motion-activated wall light, perfect for illuminating a driveway, porch, or back gate, which is where I have mine (no more stubbed toes when I take out the trash at night). Eufy has also packed in a 4K camera that you can swivel to get the right angle, offering a wide, crisp view of your chosen spot. It records locally, with 32 GB of storage built-in, and it's subscription free, including the on-device AI detection, which can accurately distinguish between people, vehicles, and pets. Installation is quick and easy, and it connects directly to your Wi-Fi. You’ll just need a decent signal at your chosen spot.

To sweeten the deal, there’s a solar panel to keep the battery topped off. It sits neatly on top, but you can detach it for better placement to catch the sun’s rays. Despite being in a busy spot, mine has stayed charged for the last couple of months, though I suspect that may change as we head into winter.

What I like best about this security camera is the wall light functionality. You can set the brightness and color temperature (I like a warm light). You can also schedule it to only trigger between specific hours or set it to be activated from sunset to sunrise based on your location. I also love that it doesn’t scream outdoor security camera; you only notice it if you look closely.

Some downsides: the frame rate is just 15 fps, so fast-moving subjects can appear blurry, particularly in the dark (though the light helps with that). Some folks will also need to top off the battery off on occasion, so you’ll want to keep it somewhere within reach. I also feel it’s overpriced at the original $250, but at $170 ($80 off), that's less of an issue.

If you need an indoor camera, the Eufy S350 is also on sale right now at $100 ($40 off), and it’s a wonderfully versatile, feature-packed, dual-lens camera. It even has automatic tracking, making it ideal for checking in on your cat or dog throughout the day. It regularly dips down to this price, so you might want to wait for Black Friday, when I predict it will drop another $20.

The EufyCam C35 2-Cam Kit at $130 ($70 off) is also worth considering right now. These cameras work inside or out with an easy magnetic mount and come with a handy HomeBase Mini for local recording and onboard AI that includes facial recognition. This is a common discount, but it's still a great deal for a two-camera kit with hub.

Tech.title: Ruggable’s Washable Rugs Are Worth It and Now on Sale (2026)
Tech.content:
It’s a great time to buy a rug. The floors are getting cold, and you need to be prepared for your winter hibernation. Fall is also hosting season, which means making your place more presentable for the holidays. Maybe you’ve moved, like many do this season, and are still furnishing your new space. Fortunately, home goods sales are plentiful this time of year.

Ruggable’s October Hosting Sale is one of my favorite excuses to redecorate, with up to 30 percent off select styles. It runs through October 25, so your window is closing as I type. Keep reading for more reasons I love Ruggable, plus a few of my favorites currently on sale.

For People Who Make Messes

I adore Ruggable. The entire WIRED Reviews team adores Ruggable. I have the Pamir Moroccan Flatwoven runner under my kitchen sink, and it's gorgeous, but I don’t panic when spills and stains happen. In fact, I welcome them. The beauty of a washable rug is that you can actually live on it, which feels almost radical when so much home decor seems designed for childless, pet-free people who never eat or drink.

WIRED editor Harry Rabinowitz has a toddler and a cat, both of whom have peed on his hallway rug. Both times, he was grateful he could toss it in the washing machine and dryer and move on. Commerce executive director Cooper Fleishman was debating between the Wendel Ochre Rug by Anthropologie, the bohemian Yara Navy & Bronze Rug, and the Berber-inspired Enya Multicolor Rug for his office. Reviewer Simon Hill has the Santiago Persian Tufted Rug in his home in Scotland (yes, they ship to the UK and Europe) and recommends the Mandalore Tufted Rug for any Star Wars fans out there.

Ruggable has thousands of designs to choose from—2,122 to date. It’s a blessing and a curse. The brand also regularly offers alternatives to discontinued styles, so all is not lost if you were eyeing a piece you can no longer find. Note that the sale does exclude the new Easy Care Wool collection, along with gift cards, spot cleaner, and rug pads. Read the terms and conditions before you buy, and don’t delay; the sale ends October 25.

Is Ruggable Worth It? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron While we stan Ruggable, it’s not without its shortcomings. WIRED editor Kat Merck has the Jonathan Adler Venom Flatwoven Rug in her kitchen; the edges curl up, and it drives her nuts. I will say my Ruggable’s nonslip pad has betrayed me more than once. It shifts around the kitchen and is the occasional tripping hazard. Aligning a rug onto the pad is also two-person job, but it’s not impossible if you live alone. Customers online have also reported issues with prints fading over time, but that’s practically a given with high-traffic, machine-washable rugs. We also like Revival, which has an assortment of hand-knotted and woven imported wool rugs at reasonable prices. Plus, the company is having its own 20-percent-off sitewide sale that ends on Sunday.

Tech.title: GM Wants Your Car to Do Your Chores
Tech.content:
Americans spent about 95 billion hours behind the wheel last year, traveling something like 2.76 trillion miles. On Wednesday, General Motors executives are outlining the future of automotive at the company’s annual GM Forward event in New York City, and they say their goal isn’t to reduce that number. After all, it’s a car company.

But GM does want to make car time better. Or, as Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson put it in an interview with WIRED, “make it more productive, make it more relaxing, make it more engaging. We’d like to make your vehicle a more central, more useful part of your life than it has been historically.” Your future car is sort of a personal assistant, and sort of a spouse, and sort of a tool, and sort of a best friend.

It’s a tall order. But in a raft of announcements this week, GM hopes to demonstrate that, armed with AI-enabled capabilities, the automaker is inching closer to that future.

GM says it will roll out a new in-car AI assistant, called OnStar AI, starting with 2027 Cadillac Lyriqs. (The name borrows from the 30-year-old roadside assistance and security service, which has 12 million subscribers.) Paired with a new app, the system will start by letting drivers, for example, turn on their air conditioning with a voice command without navigating through a menu. Eventually, though, it might coordinate kid pickups and drop-offs depending on which spouse’s car is closer, Anderson says.

Tech.title: The Best Art TV Deals: Samsung Frame, Hisense Canvas, and More (2026)
Tech.content:
We're big fans of art TVs here at WIRED. They're perfect for people who don't want a TV to be the constant center of attention in their living room. No art TV maker is better than the pioneer: Samsung. Specifically, Samsung's The Frame Pro series of TVs. The 2026 models (LS03HW) add tons of new features, including more intuitive software, a higher refresh rate for gaming, and even better picture quality.

The Best Art TV

The problem with The Frame Pro has always been the price. The smallest 55-inch model dropped to $1,098 during Prime Day earlier this month, and I've been happy to see that the price has stayed around. (In fact, earlier this week, it dropped by an additional $100 to its lowest price ever.) Seeing it discounted to under $1,000 was fantastic, but even at $1,098, it's a really solid deal. It was selling for $200 more in September and for the full retail price of $1,498 in August. Beyond the smallest 55-inch model, you also have size options for The Frame Pro of a 65-inch, 75-inch, or 85-inch TV.

A Great Runner-Up at Its Lowest Price Ever

Courtesy of Amazon Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Samsung The Frame (2026) $898 Amazon $1,000 Best Buy

Samsung also has an entry-level version of The Frame, which has an even deeper discount right now. It's just $898, which is $100 off its Prime Day price—the cheapest it's even been! It's actually the same price as the older 2025 model.

We haven't tested this model yet ourselves, but the main difference between The Frame and The Frame Pro is the brightness and image quality. They both use a matte finish, but The Frame Pro has nearly double the max brightness, while the standard Frame only goes up to around 650 nits. The Frame Pro also comes with a wireless connect box for a cleaner and simpler setup. It's definitely the one to get if you can swing the extra $200.

Other Art TVs on Sale

As we have documented, there's been an explosion of interest in art TVs in 2026, with competitors like Amazon, Hisense, and TCL joining the game. We've tested many of these new options—many of which try to undercut The Frame in price. The one on sale right now that I'd point to is the Hisense S7 CanvasTV (55S7SG). It's not even as bright as the standard Frame, but at $750 (for the 55-inch size), it's the cheapest art TV you can buy right now.

With Black Friday coming up next month, it's certainly possible that prices on these art TVs will drop even more. The 2025 Samsung Frame and Frame Pro both dropped to their lowest prices during Black Friday last year. It's a gamble—you could wait for Black Friday or get a sure thing right now.

Tech.title: This Startup Is All In on Recursive Self-Improvement. Its Latest Model Is Scary Good
Tech.content:
For the past few days I’ve been testing an impressive open-weight AI coding model called Flint. It suggests that fully recursive self-improvement, or RSI—an exciting and controversial approach that uses AI to build AI—is getting closer.

Flint is the first offering from Recursive, a company that aims to use RSI to advance both AI itself and other areas of science using AI. “Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI,” Recursive CEO and cofounder Richard Socher told me.

Socher says his company used its recursive AI system, dubbed the Eureka Machine, to automate most elements of the model’s development. This enabled a company with a handful of researchers to build a world-class model in just a few months, he says.

Socher told me that the Eureka Machine devised a number of innovations, including a new way of training the base model, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon chips. Recursive shared benchmark scores that suggest Flint outperforms other models of similar size and architecture on coding tasks.

AI is already widely used to help build, test, and improve AI thanks to its amazing coding skills. This can speed up the process of refining a model and testing new ideas without the need for as much input from humans.

Tech.title: Jensen Huang’s Vision for Europe Runs on Plug-In Data Centers
Tech.content:
Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics, AI agents, and modular data centers, with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all.

“To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.”

The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face—doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch.

Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said.

The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out.

Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs.

Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said.

On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data.

He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher.

In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair.

Tech.title: 7 Best Phones You Can’t Buy in the US (2026)
Tech.content:
Other Good International Phones

Haven’t seen anything you like? The following phones are also worth considering:

Photograph: Simon Hill

TCL P80 Ultra for £480: I love that the 6.8-inch AMOLED screen transforms into an e-ink screen at the flick of a switch; it’s also wonderfully matte, even in AMOLED mode, which makes it more comfortable to read for hours than most phone screens. TCL has also packed in a versatile camera, including a decent telephoto lens, and solid battery life. But the plain design and occasional sluggishness make it a tough sell at this price. If reading is your main priority, the compromises may be worth it.

Xiaomi Poco F9 Ultra for £999 and F9 Pro for £799: This year's unfortunate price jump, combined with Xiaomi's weird pricing (low early-bird prices and frequent discounts, but very high MSRPs), makes these phones tough to recommend. Both are actually very good, with lovely displays, good battery life and performance, great stereo speakers, and versatile triple-lens cameras. Naturally, the Ultra is slightly bigger and better. Sadly, they signal a major departure from Poco’s budget roots, but if you see them discounted (I’ve seen the Ultra for £669 and the Pro for £579), they are worth considering.

Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 Pro Max for £499: With a huge battery that easily lasts two days, a big screen, great build quality, and impressive durability, the Redmi Note 17 Pro Max makes a strong first impression. Performance is mediocre, the camera is limited, and it’s packed with bloatware. Unless battery life is your top priority, I’d pick something else.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Honor Magic 8 Pro for £894: This phone boasts excellent camera performance and AI assistance across the board, with a raft of refinements over Honor’s Magic 7 Pro. Its slimmed-down design with subtle curves makes it a pleasure to handle, and Honor has managed to pack in a much larger silicon-carbon battery. The versatile camera also zooms farther (3.7X optical zoom) and handles low light and shaky hands with aplomb (night photography is especially strong). That said, the image processing can be heavy-handed at times. The 6.71-inch screen is gorgeous, razor-sharp, and gets very bright. Honor’s Magic OS 10 is seriously slick on top of Android 16, and Honor AI genuinely adds value, from photo editing to contextual task handling; you can bring it to life with the dedicated AI button. There’s also support for Google Gemini, if you prefer. This is definitely not a phone for AI skeptics. Throw in secure face unlock, incredibly fast wired (100 watts) and wireless charging (80 watts) with the right gear, plus seven years of Android and security patch updates, and you get a supremely sophisticated smartphone with very few discernible weaknesses. But with its successor due to land shortly, you should only snag this right now if you can get a decent discount.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Xiaomi Poco X8 Pro for $390 (£479) and Poco X8 Pro Max for $510 (£599): If anything, a slight step down from the now-discontinued F7, the X8 sports a smaller 6.59-inch AMOLED screen, a MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Ultra chipset, and 8 GB of RAM in the basic model. Performance is solid (though it’s worth noting I used a 12-GB RAM review unit). And the slightly smaller body is a touch easier to handle. You get a big 6,500-mAh battery with plenty of stamina, plus 100-watt charging that gets you back to full in under an hour. The main camera is a solid 50-MP shooter, though the 8-MP ultrawide and 20-MP front-facing cameras aren’t great. I like the mint green model, but it also comes in black or white. There’s still too much bloatware to deal with, and Xiaomi’s software is not my favorite, but you get decent support, including four Android versions and six years of security updates. There’s no wireless charging, but that’s par for the course in this bracket. Overall, the Poco X8 Pro is the best phone for its price. If battery life is a priority, consider the X8 Pro Max, which jumps up to 8,500 mAh. It also has a bigger screen, a better processor, and Wi-Fi 7 support.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Xiaomi 17T for £649 and 17T Pro for $780: Without Honor’s aggressively low pricing, one of these phones (probably the 17T) would have claimed the best mid-range spot above. Compared with the Honor 600, the 17T offers slightly better performance with more RAM and a more reliable camera that has superior zoom capability. Unfortunately, it also comes with a lot of bloatware, and the software needs some tinkering to get the best it offers. The 17T Pro adds wireless charging, a bigger battery, much better performance with a faster chipset, and a larger screen—but it’s even more expensive, pushing the top end of what I’d consider midrange.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Oppo Find N6 for $1,899: Touting an 8.12-inch display, the Find N6 is a beautifully engineered folding phone that’s impossibly slim and light. Despite its creaseless promise, the fold is still discernible. You’ll hardly notice it with the screen on, but you’ll feel it if you use the optional stylus. Performance is impressively slick, with enough stamina to see you through a busy day, and the camera system is excellent. It’s a big step up from last year’s N5, with a 200-MP main shooter, 50-MP telephoto, and 50-MP ultrawide, though it can’t quite compete with the Xiaomi 17 Ultra above. The global model supports familiar Google apps, but you’ll have to import them, since the phone won’t officially launch in the West, which is why it can't edge out Honor’s foldable above.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Xiaomi 17 Pro Max for $1,129: The Xiaomi 17 Pro Max differs from the 17 Pro mainly with a refreshing design that adds a second, smaller screen on the back to house the camera lenses. Xiaomi offers several creative ways to use this auxiliary display, including a selfie preview for better main-camera selfies, music controls, customizable themes, and virtual pets. There’s even a retro gaming case that lets you play Angry Birds, though it feels a bit silly when there’s a 6.7-inch screen on the other side. Aside from the second screen, the 17 Pro Max is a typical Xiaomi specs beast, and the 17 Pro isn’t far behind, but neither has been officially released outside China yet.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Oppo Find X9 Pro for £1,099: Photography fans simply must check out the Oppo Find X9 Pro. The 200-megapixel telephoto lens supports 3X optical zoom and can take excellent shots at 6X zoom by cropping images down to 50 megapixels. To maximize camera capabilities, though, you’ll need the detachable Hasselblad Teleconverter Kit ($400). This enormous lens slots into place on the case and adds another 3.28X zoom, though it’s tricky to use without a tripod. An additional trio of 50-MP lenses, with all supporting 4K video recording at 60 fps with HDR, makes this a great pick for creatives. Impressive specs include a 6.78-inch flat display, IP66/68/69 ratings, and a 7,500-mAh silicon-carbon battery that’ll last for two days.

Xiaomi Poco F8 Ultra for £649 and F8 Pro for £406: Xiaomi’s cheaper, youthful brand Poco provides room for experimentation, but the company’s own 15T Pro is a better buy in this price bracket. What the F8 Ultra offers that you won’t find elsewhere is a fun (or awful, depending on your tastes) denim finish on the back. There are also Bose-tuned speakers, an excellent 6.9-inch display, and an enormous 6,500-mAh battery. It also has a flagship-level Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and generous RAM and storage. There’s even a trio of 50-MP lenses in the camera. The F8 Pro is slightly smaller but has similar specs, making it the better bargain.

Honor Magic 7 Pro for $985: Honor’s Magic 7 Pro features a solid triple-lens camera, a gorgeous 6.8-inch screen, speedy performance, good battery life, and dual IP68 and IP69 dust- and water-resistance ratings. Honor’s Magic OS boasts polished AI features, and Honor announced an increased commitment to seven years of Android version and security patch updates with this phone. The Magic 7 Pro’s downsides include its large camera cutout on the front, camera processing that’s sometimes heavy-handed, and an ultrawide camera that struggles to match the other two lenses.

Doro Aurora A20 for £250: Doro is a Swedish company focused on providing devices that are accessible for older folks. It primarily offers phones but also sells a decent video doorbell. The Aurora A20 is an odd spin on the flip phone that may help some people transition to a touchscreen device. It’s like an old candy bar HTC Android phone with a flip-out keypad attached to the bottom. There are lots of thoughtful features, including an alarm button, a spacious keypad, and simplified software. It’s also fairly cheap, but I found the performance sluggish, the camera poor, and the design a bit chunky and heavy.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Realme 14 Pro+ for €369: The color-changing finish may be gimmicky, but it's fun, and this phone looks and feels far more expensive than it is. There are more highs than lows on the spec sheet: You get a triple-lens camera, an IP68/69 water-resistance rating, a 6,000-mAh battery, and a 6.83-inch OLED display with a 120-Hz refresh rate. But the Snapdragon 7s Gen 3 chipset is limited, there's no wireless charging support, and you don’t get a charger in the box. Even so, it’s still quite a bargain.

Xiaomi 15 for $690: Folks seeking a compact phone could do a lot worse than the Xiaomi 15. It feels lovely and has a 6.36-inch screen, a decent triple-lens camera, and top-notch internals. But it’s a conservative design, and it has software and bloatware issues.

Honor Magic 7 RSR for £1,550: Designed with Porsche, this souped-up version of the 7 Pro above has a fancier design with a hexagonal camera module, a slightly improved telephoto lens, 24 GB of RAM, 1 TB of storage, and a bigger battery (5,850 mAh). It’s lovely, but it doesn’t justify the extra cost.

Avoid These Phones

These aren’t necessarily bad phones, but I think you’d be better served by an option above.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Nothing Phone (3a) Lite: Nothing’s translucent hardware and pixelated software give it a retro-cool vibe, and it is currently the cheapest phone it offers in the UK (it wasn’t released in the US). The screen, battery life, and software are decent, but the camera and bloatware were disappointing. I don’t think the Nothing Phone (3a) Lite is the worst, but you can do better.

Nubia Z80 Ultra: Like my gaming pick above, the Nubia Redmagic 11S Pro, the Nubia Z80 Ultra trades a better camera for slightly lower performance and screen quality. It’s also a real brick, with an enormous camera module on the back that makes it awkward to handle, though I do like the dedicated camera button. Despite a very impressive spec sheet for the money, it manages to feel like less than the sum of its parts. Nubia’s software is subpar, and for this phone, it commits to only three years of security updates and a single Android version upgrade.

Oppo Reno 13 Pro 5G: This slim, lightweight midrange phone boasts a 6.8-inch screen (brightness is limited), a triple-lens camera (solid 50-MP main and telephoto lenses with a disappointing 8-MP ultrawide), and an impressive IP69 water-resistance rating. Battery life is good, and wired charging is fast, but there’s no wireless charging. It’s packed with bloatware, but it also adds AI features and tools for transcription, summarization, image editing, and more that may add value for some folks. After some time with the 13 Pro, I feel you can do better for the money.

Xiaomi Mix Fold 4: Officially released only in China, the Xiaomi Mix Fold 4 is a stylish folding phone with a 6.56-inch outer screen that folds open to reveal a 7.98-inch inner screen. It also offers solid performance and battery life, but despite having a large quad-lens camera module, the camera is underwhelming. The crease is also pronounced, and using a Chinese model is a bit of a pain, as various items are not translated and getting the apps you want takes work.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Realme GT7 Pro: This potential flagship killer has a 6.78-inch OLED screen, a Snapdragon 8 Elite chip, and an enormous 6,500-mAh battery. You also get a triple-lens camera, but the 50-megapixel main and telephoto lenses are let down by the 8-megapixel ultrawide. It also lacks wireless charging, and it only seems to be for sale in Germany.

Xiaomi Redmi Note 14 Pro+: Here, you get an attractive, durable design (IP68), a 200-megapixel Samsung camera sensor, and decent battery life with superfast charging (120 watts). But those wins come at the price of middling performance, poor ultrawide (8 MP) and macro (2 MP) lenses, and a ton of bloatware. Ultimately, there’s little improvement over last year’s Redmi Note 13 Pro+. Not only are there better phones for the same money, but there are also better Xiaomi phones.

Should You Import One of These Phones? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron While some phones are not officially sold in the US (or certain other countries), you can still get your hands on them if you’d like. They're often easy to buy online, and you may even find some on Amazon, often via third-party sellers. But before you buy, you’ll want to consider a few factors. Phone Model and Supported Bands The technologies and specific bands upon which cellular networks rely differ from country to country. While models described as “global” and even specifically UK or European models are likely to work in the US, they may not support all the bands your carrier uses. Missing LTE or 5G bands can mean patchy service or even relegate you to 3G. Chinese and other country-specific models will almost certainly lack some common US bands and may not work on some carrier networks. You will often find this information in the listing or aggregated on websites like Kimovil, but I recommend checking directly with the manufacturer and your carrier. Customs Charges Depending on where you buy, importing a phone can lead to customs charges and add a significant expense to the overall cost. Do your research and factor in any extra fees before you buy. Android and Google Services It is common for phones released only in China to ship without any Google services, including the Google Play Store. Many Chinese manufacturers have their own app stores or preinstall third-party app stores for the Chinese market. Sometimes it's a simple case of checking a box to unlock and download Google services, but it’s not always so easy. Even where Google services are supported, some Chinese phones won’t work properly with certain apps, such as Android Auto. Lack of support can leave you stuck with specific Chinese default apps and services, and many banking apps won’t work as they would on a US or global model. With regard to Huawei phones in particular, the company developed an independent ecosystem of apps and services following its US ban. The latest models run HarmonyOS. Although it was originally forked from the Android Open Source Project, it is now completely separate, and Huawei phones can no longer run Android apps. How I Test Smartphones AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron I try to use every smartphone I test as my main phone for at least a week, sometimes longer. I stress-test performance by playing the most demanding mobile games and recording videos at the highest resolution. I make calls to test the smartphone's microphone and speaker quality. I often test the camera side by side with a competing phone and analyze the photos on a larger, more color-accurate screen. I've been reviewing all kinds of smartphones, from budget devices to flagships, for more than a decade.

Tech.title: ‘This Is Not a Drill’: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Are Setting the Internet on Fire
Tech.content:
Internet security and web administration teams around the world are scrambling to prevent widespread disaster. On Wednesday, the developers behind the much-used PHP programming language released emergency security updates designed to fix critical flaws that could be exploited to allow attackers to gain dangerous remote control of victim systems.

The PHP Foundation detailed the two critical vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—which impact “all PHP installations serving web requests” going back to PHP version 5, released in July 2004. However, only PHP 8.2 and newer are still supported and will receive patches, according to the alert. The PHP Foundation noted, though, that some PHP distributions and third-party vendors still produce legacy fixes. The caveat is significant because ubiquitous and foundational web layers like PHP can persist forgotten and un-updated in historic internet infrastructure.

“There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice,” the PHP Foundation wrote in its advisories. Security experts warn of the potential dire consequences of overlooking unpatched systems.

“This is not a drill,” says Lukasz Olejnik, an independent security consultant and visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London. Since its development in the 1990s, PHP has evolved into an essential scripting language for web development and is used across vast swaths of the internet in websites and software. Everything from publishing systems like WordPress and Drupal to e-commerce platforms like Adobe’s Magento are built on PHP.

Olejnik likens the widespread use of the programming language to critical infrastructure.

“The impact is enormous,” he says of PHP’s security flaws, adding that millions of systems could be impacted. “Especially if attackers would turn to exploiting these vulnerabilities fast. Worst case is wormable malware affecting big chunks of the internet.”

The overriding fear for security teams and developers is that malicious hackers could quickly jump upon the vulnerabilities and begin exploiting deployments before they are fixed. Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare reported it was “seeing early attacks emerging” before the PHP Foundation had detailed the vulnerabilities and released fixes. “We expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release,” security firm Sansec wrote ahead of the fixes, which were released just before 10 am ET on Wednesday.

“Most of the web runs on PHP and this bug is in a file upload interface that’s like a front door with no lock,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “An attacker does not need to know which site they are hitting or even the actual software it runs. They send one crafted upload to any server they can find, and that is the entire attack.”
